Building on this, we selectively edit expert router scores during inference to curb overthinking. Across four models and four benchmarks, this intervention reduces the number of generated tokens by a median of 30.4% (and up to 63.3%). Crucially, it encourages the model to stop once the problem is solved, rather than skipping essential reasoning steps. Accuracy never drops by more than 0.5 percentage points, and frequently improves. Ultimately, MoE routing offers both an interpretable lens into reasoning states and a lightweight mechanism for optimizing test-time compute.
papers.summary: Reasoning models often overthink, continuing to verify and re-derive after reaching a correct answer. The authors show that routers in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer a training-free way to control this. Linear probes on router logits predict sentence-level reasoning behaviors (such as planning, reflection, and conclusion) nearly as well as probes on the full hidden state, and the associated experts generalize across six datasets. Editing router scores at inference **cuts generated tokens by a median of 30.4% (up to 63.3%) while accuracy never drops by more than 0.5 points**.

papers.title: Modality-Aware Expert Pruning for MoE-Based Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to scale capacity efficiently, but expert parameters dominate memory even though only a few experts are activated per token: they account for over 90% of model size in modern MoE-MLLMs (e.g., 54 GB out of about 58 GB in BF16 for InternVL3.5-30B-A3B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B). Expert pruning has emerged as an effective compression strategy, but existing methods aggregate importance uniformly across tokens, ignoring that the same expert may serve different roles for vision versus language processing. To address this, we propose MAEP (Modality-Aware Expert Pruning), a training-free framework that decomposes expert importance by modality in a single forward pass. MAEP introduces (1) Delta-H Output ($\Delta H$), a redistribution-aware metric measuring the MoE output change when an expert is removed, and (2) low-attention vision tokens as a vision-side pruning signal that is dataset-stable: its expert-importance ranking remains stable across different datasets. Text-side importance serves as a preservation signal while vision-side importance serves as a pruning signal, and experts are ranked globally across layers. Experiments on three MoE-based MLLMs across multimodal and text benchmarks show that MAEP outperforms modality-agnostic baselines on the majority of multimodal benchmarks while remaining competitive on text-only tasks, reducing the BF16 expert weight footprint by about 27 GB (about 47% of total memory) so that the full weight footprint of an approximately 58 GB model fits within a single 40 GB GPU. Code is available at https://github.com/nota-github/MAEP.
papers.summary: In Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) multimodal LLMs, expert weights make up over 90% of model size, and existing pruning methods score expert importance the same way for vision and text tokens. `MAEP` (Modality-Aware Expert Pruning) is a training-free method that splits importance by modality in a single forward pass. It uses a metric for how much the MoE output changes when an expert is removed, and it treats low-attention vision tokens as a pruning signal and text-side importance as a signal to keep. On three models, including `InternVL3.5-30B-A3B` and `Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B`, it beats modality-agnostic baselines on most multimodal benchmarks and **saves about 27 GB, so a roughly 58 GB model fits on a single 40 GB GPU**.

papers.title: Robots in the City: Persona-Based Perceptions of Urban Robots
papers.abstract: Pedestrians increasingly encounter robots in urban public spaces without interacting with them, but how robots change the perceived safety of a street remains unclear. We examine how robot presence and type affect perceived safety across urban contexts. We generate 18 images of Seoul streets that vary in time of day, road class, and robot condition (no robot, a delivery robot, or a humanoid). Two multimodal large language models (MLLMs), Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma4-26B, each conditioned on 500 synthetic personas, choose the safer image in each pair, and 25 human respondents complete the same task. Both models prefer streets without robots and favor the delivery robot over the humanoid. Robots are chosen more often at night and less often by older personas, whereas road class has smaller effects. In the model rationales, the delivery robot appears as a physical obstacle, whereas the humanoid appears as either a threat or a source of protection. Like humans, both models chose robots more often at night, but chose the humanoid over the delivery robot far less often, and Gemma showed a night effect for the humanoid about three times that of humans. These results show that the effect of a robot on perceived safety depends on when it appears, and that persona-conditioned MLLMs capture only part of human judgments.
papers.summary: To study how robots affect the perceived safety of city streets, the authors generated 18 images of Seoul streets with no robot, a delivery robot, or a humanoid. Two multimodal LLMs, `Qwen3.8-27B` and `Gemma4-26B`, each conditioned on 500 synthetic personas, chose the safer image in each pair, and 25 human respondents did the same. Both models preferred streets without robots and favored the delivery robot over the humanoid. Like humans, the models chose robots more often at night, but **they chose the humanoid far less often than humans did**, so persona-conditioned models capture only part of human judgment.

papers.title: On the Design of Hyper-Connections: Simplification, Stability, and Scalability
papers.abstract: Hyper-Connections (HC) architectures are increasingly adopted in frontier language models, yet their components remain insufficiently understood and introduce non-negligible training overhead. In this work, we systematically study the HC architecture to understand its components and identify simpler, more efficient designs. We find that learned read/write gating without mixing and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates form two effective interaction groups: either alone achieves performance comparable to mHC. We also identify repeated access to the expanded residual state as a major source of training overhead, even without mixing. These findings lead to SimpleHC, which simplifies the architecture by removing residual mixing and simplifies execution through shared memory access, using the resulting additive structure and shared gate inputs. Layer-specific gates share a group-entry state, enabling batched reads and deferred writes; scalar corrections exactly preserve preceding sublayer output contributions. Our analyses support both the retained residual structure and the design of shared memory access. SimpleHC incurs only 2.4% extra end-to-end training time over a vanilla residual baseline at the largest tested scale. It maintains performance comparable to mHC when scaling from 15B to 30B MoE models, exhibits smoother gradient dynamics during standard training, and remains stable under stress. We hope SimpleHC will encourage a broader pursuit of simplicity in foundation model design, making performance gains more accessible and practical at scale.
papers.summary: Hyper-Connections (HC) architectures, increasingly used in frontier language models, add training overhead and contain components that are poorly understood. A systematic study finds that either learned read/write gating without mixing, or unconstrained mixing with fixed gates, alone matches `mHC`. It also finds that repeatedly accessing the expanded residual state is a major source of overhead. The resulting `SimpleHC` drops residual mixing and shares memory access across layers, and it **adds only 2.4% end-to-end training time over a plain residual baseline** while matching `mHC` on MoE models from 15B to 30B parameters, with smoother gradients and stable training.

papers.title: How Far Can You Steer? Behavior-Capability Frontiers in Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.abstract: Activation steering can modify language-model behavior without parameter updates, but behavioral efficacy alone does not determine whether an intervention is usable. Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steers targeted behaviors using activation directions derived from contrasting examples, potentially degrading unrelated model capabilities in the process. We therefore study CAA through a behavior-capability frontier, selecting interventions that maximize behavioral gain subject to an explicit bound on capability degradation. We evaluate this framework across four instruction-tuned models, seven behaviors, and capability-loss budgets of 1%, 3%, and 5% (absolute percentage points). Validation-selected behavioral effects generalize strongly to held-out data ($\rho = 0.945$), while joint behavior-capability survival among nonzero operating points rises from 37.5% at the 1% budget to 72.7% at 3%, with limited additional improvement at 5%. Control experiments indicate that these effects depend on learned behavior directions rather than generic activation perturbations. Representational geometry is significantly but only modestly predictive of causal cross-behavior transfer. Finally, secondary capability, out-of-distribution, and open-ended evaluations show that interventions satisfying protected benchmarks can still degrade untested capabilities or transfer unevenly to free-form generation. These results characterize activation steering as a constrained intervention whose usable range depends on model, behavior, direction, layer, and evaluation budget, rather than a universal control knob.
papers.summary: `Contrastive Activation Addition` (`CAA`) steers language-model behavior by adding activation directions derived from contrasting examples, but it can degrade unrelated capabilities. The authors frame steering as a behavior-capability frontier, choosing interventions that maximize behavioral gain under an explicit capability-loss budget of 1%, 3%, or 5%, and evaluate it across four instruction-tuned models and seven behaviors. Behavioral effects selected on validation data generalize well to held-out data (ρ = 0.945), and the share of operating points that keep both the behavior gain and the capability limit rises **from 37.5% at a 1% budget to 72.7% at 3%**. However, interventions that pass protected benchmarks can still degrade untested capabilities or transfer unevenly to free-form generation, so steering behaves as a constrained intervention rather than a universal control knob.

papers.title: Familiar letters, not related languages, let unseen languages into a shared space of meaning
papers.abstract: Hundreds of languages have written text but almost no translations, and whether a model learning one from untranslated text builds on a related language or familiar letters is unclear: they usually coincide. Here we show that familiar letters, not a related language, let an unseen language into a shared space of meaning. GlyphMind, a tokenizer-free vision transformer that reads text as pixels and lets any sentence be shown in any script, was pretrained to align translations across 27 writing systems. Adapted on untranslated Lao, a language and script it had never seen, it retrieved English translations seven times as often as the strongest simple baseline. Rewritten in unfamiliar letters, Lao did not enter although its close relative Thai was in pretraining; Santali, which had none, entered in Devanagari, familiar from Hindi, but not in its own script. Transliteration into familiar scripts may thus open multilingual models to languages without translations.
papers.summary: For languages with written text but almost no translations, it is unclear whether a model learning from untranslated text benefits more from a related language or from a familiar script, since the two usually coincide. The authors build `GlyphMind`, a tokenizer-free vision transformer that reads text as pixels, so any sentence can be rendered in any script, and pretrain it to align translations across 27 writing systems. Adapted on untranslated Lao, it retrieved English translations seven times as often as the strongest simple baseline. Experiments that swap scripts show that **familiar letters, not a related language, determine whether an unseen language enters the shared meaning space**: Lao in unfamiliar letters failed despite Thai being in pretraining, while Santali succeeded when written in Devanagari but not in its own script.

papers.title: Holistic Parallel Supervision for Expressive Speech to Speech Translation
papers.abstract: Expressiveness is central to speech-to-speech translation (S2ST), yet existing datasets rarely align source and target speech jointly in content, prosody, timing, and speaker identity. Consequently, current systems often rely on indirect conditioning or transfer mechanisms. To obtain this supervision, we introduce a training-data construction strategy that combines professional dubbing, which provides human-performed correspondence in content, prosody, and timing, with multilingual voice conversion to reduce speaker mismatch. We evaluate this supervision using existing expressive S2ST systems and DirectS2ST, an end-to-end method developed in this work that predicts the complete target-speech representation directly from source speech. Experiments on English-German and English-Spanish show that holistic parallel supervision improves expressive realization across all evaluated systems. DirectS2ST exhibits the largest gains in content, prosody, timing, speaker similarity, and human-rated expressiveness. To our knowledge, this work provides the first systematic investigation of holistic parallel supervision for expressive S2ST.
papers.summary: Expressive speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) lacks training data where source and target speech match jointly in content, prosody, timing, and speaker identity. The authors construct such data by combining professional dubbing, which supplies human-performed correspondence in content, prosody, and timing, with multilingual voice conversion to reduce speaker mismatch. They test this supervision on existing expressive S2ST systems and on `DirectS2ST`, a new end-to-end model that predicts the full target-speech representation directly from source speech. On English-German and English-Spanish, the holistic supervision improves expressiveness for every system tested, with **`DirectS2ST` gaining the most across content, prosody, timing, speaker similarity, and human-rated expressiveness**.

papers.title: Who Pays for the Knowledge Models Copy? Model Collapse as Rogers' Paradox
papers.abstract: Generative models trained on the output of earlier models lose knowledge across generations, rare knowledge first. The remedies that work all bring in information from outside the loop, and the theory of model collapse treats that supply as given: a fixed archive, drawn from a fixed distribution. We argue that the supply is the problem, and that cultural evolution has the theory of it. We read model collapse as Rogers' paradox: a population that comes to rely on copying ends up no better off than one that never copied, because copies go stale unless someone keeps learning for themselves. We test the identification in three steps. First, Rogers' model, fitted only to fully synthetic training, predicts to within a few percentage points how much rare knowledge language models, from word trigrams to a pretrained transformer, retain under other mixtures of fresh data. Second, when the world itself changes, a lineage that copies its own past needs more fresh data to keep up the faster the world changes, as Rogers' model says it must and as analyses that assume a fixed target cannot; a lineage that restarts every generation from fixed pretrained weights is largely insulated, because those weights are knowledge that is never copied. Third, we close the loop: when the people who write a model's training data can ask the model instead of finding things out, the supply of fresh data becomes endogenous. At equilibrium, the model is exactly as reliable as it is costly for people to find out for themselves, the population is no better off than without the model, and every increase in the share of model-written text must be paid for by more people learning for themselves. Users who check what they are told and relearn when it is wrong break the paradox. Filters that select plausible text are conformist and accelerate collapse; only checks that carry new information act as critical learning.
papers.summary: Generative models trained on earlier models' outputs lose knowledge over generations, rare knowledge first, and existing theory treats the fresh data that counters this as a fixed external supply. The authors recast model collapse as Rogers' paradox from cultural evolution, in which a population that relies on copying ends up no better off than one that never copied unless some members keep learning for themselves. Rogers' model, fitted only to fully synthetic training, predicts within a few percentage points how much rare knowledge models from word trigrams to a pretrained transformer retain under other data mixtures, and it correctly predicts that a changing world demands more fresh data. When people can ask the model instead of finding things out, the equilibrium model is **only as reliable as it is costly for people to learn for themselves**; users who verify and relearn break the paradox, while plausibility filters accelerate collapse.

papers.title: When Every Choice Is Correct: A Causal Study of Numerical Preference in Language Models
papers.abstract: When a language model chooses a number between 1 and 30, every integer in the range is valid, yet the model can favor particular answers. We use numerical choice to study how preference is processed across layers and tokens. Perturbation probing and gradient attribution nominate neurons for activation interventions. In a selected Qwen3-4B case, a pre-answer edit changes 17 to 15 while both runs first emit 1. After the edit ends, selective cache and attention-output replacements trace part of its continuing influence on the second digit. Replacing one attention head's output or the other heads' outputs jointly produces similar immediate readout contributions; both interventions restore 17 but have different final log-odds effects on 7 versus 5. Holding later multilayer perceptron (MLP) outputs at their values from the edited run without either replacement reduces this effect gap from 0.119 to 0.0025 nat. Later computation therefore changes how similar local contributions affect the continuation. Retrospective estimates across eighteen contexts capture much of the probability movement but miss the selected answer switch. Prompt tests also separate influence from answer changes: one held-out prompt retains influence without switching, and only one of twelve fresh wordings qualifies for the reader/MLP test; there, joint MLP clamping again reduces the gap between the two reader effects while the answer remains 17. These results use numerical choice as a controlled case for studying persistent state and conditional downstream processing; they do not establish the origin or a complete circuit of natural numerical preference.
papers.summary: When a language model picks a number between 1 and 30, every answer is valid, which makes numerical choice a controlled setting for studying how preferences are processed across layers and tokens. Using perturbation probing and gradient attribution to select neurons in `Qwen3-4B`, the authors find a pre-answer edit that changes the answer from 17 to 15 and trace how its influence carries over to the second digit through the cache and attention outputs. Two different attention-output replacements produce similar immediate contributions but different final effects, and **holding later multilayer perceptron (MLP) outputs fixed shrinks that gap from 0.119 to 0.0025 nat**, showing that later computation changes how local contributions affect the continuation. The authors state that the results do not establish a complete circuit for natural numerical preference.

papers.title: Confucius4-R2T2: A Stable-Prefix Streaming ASR Model for Real Real-Time Transcription
papers.abstract: Streaming speech recognition is increasingly consumed by machines, such as translators and voice agents, that act on each token as it appears. A token that is later revised costs wasted work or a wrong action. In this work, we present Confucius4-R2T2 (short for Real Real-Time Transcription), a stable-prefix streaming ASR model that never modifies its earlier output while maintaining high accuracy and low latency. R2T2 is obtained by post-training Qwen3-ASR-1.7B on 1,500 hours of Chinese and English audio while freezing its pre-trained audio encoder and projector. The adaptation is based on the concept of Longest Stable Prefix (LSP), a new notion that we introduce in this work. We prove that LSP is monotone under the prefix order, consistent with the full-audio output, and maximal among labels that equal a whole earlier output. Learning from LSP labels converts a full-context model into a stable-prefix streaming one without any architectural change. Extensive evaluations show that R2T2 brings streaming recognition close to the base model's full-context quality while delivering stable text with low emission lag. Its gains extend beyond the post-training languages, demonstrating a practical path from full-context ASR to stable streaming. We open-source the model weights and code at https://huggingface.co/netease-youdao/Confucius4-R2T2 and https://github.com/netease-youdao/Confucius4-R2T2.
papers.summary: Streaming speech recognition (ASR) increasingly feeds machines such as translators and voice agents that act on each token immediately, so revising earlier output wastes work or triggers wrong actions. `Confucius4-R2T2` is a streaming ASR model that never modifies earlier output, built by post-training `Qwen3-ASR-1.7B` on 1,500 hours of Chinese and English audio with the audio encoder frozen. Training uses labels based on a new concept, the Longest Stable Prefix (`LSP`), which the authors prove is monotone, consistent with the full-audio output, and maximal, letting a full-context model become a stable streaming one without architectural changes. The model **approaches the base model's full-context accuracy while emitting stable text with low lag**, gains extend beyond the training languages, and weights and code are open-sourced.

papers.title: SVGFaith: A Two-Layer Meta-Evaluation of Faithfulness Metrics for Text-to-SVG Generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-SVG systems are commonly evaluated by applying raster-image metrics to rasterised outputs, yet whether these scores capture fine-grained prompt faithfulness remains unclear. We introduce SVGFaith, a two-layer meta-evaluation framework in which the more faithful candidate of each pair is determined by construction or by human judgment. SVGFaith-Diagnostic contains 1,842 controlled contrastive pairs across eight capability axes, split evenly between two directions: two renderings compared against one prompt, and two descriptions compared against one rendering. SVGFaith-Arena contains 1,327 human-annotated comparisons of real generator outputs. On SVGFaith-Diagnostic, CLIP and three other image--text embedding metrics reach at least 0.789 pairwise accuracy on object identity but at most 0.672 on spatial relations and attribute binding, where chance is 0.5. We further introduce SVGFaith-Score, an interpretable pointwise metric. A domain-tuned decomposer turns each prompt into a dependency graph of atomic visual requirements, a visual question answering model scores whether each requirement is satisfied, and a requirement's score is discounted when its prerequisites score low. In addition to the overall score, the per-requirement scores show which requirements are judged unsatisfied and which inherit discounts from their prerequisites. SVGFaith-Score significantly outperforms all nine baselines, including a Qwen3.5-122B-A10B judge, on Arena and in both Diagnostic directions. Code and data: https://github.com/Yukinonooo/SVGFaith.
papers.summary: Text-to-SVG systems are usually scored by applying raster-image metrics to rendered outputs, and it is unclear whether these capture fine-grained faithfulness to the prompt. `SVGFaith` is a meta-evaluation framework with 1,842 controlled contrastive pairs across eight capability axes (`SVGFaith-Diagnostic`) and 1,327 human-annotated comparisons of real generator outputs (`SVGFaith-Arena`). `CLIP` and similar embedding metrics reach at least 0.789 pairwise accuracy on object identity but **at most 0.672 on spatial relations and attribute binding, against a 0.5 chance level**. The proposed `SVGFaith-Score` breaks a prompt into a dependency graph of atomic visual requirements, checks each with a visual question answering model, and outperforms nine baselines, including a `Qwen3.5-122B-A10B` judge.

papers.title: Adapting Qwen3 to Tajik from 0.6B to 8B: Lower Text Loss Did Not Mean Better Understanding
papers.abstract: Small LoRA adapters trained on Tajik news and books lowered Qwen3's Tajik text loss at every size we tried, from 0.6B to 8B, by 0.60 to 1.45 nats per token, but none of them improved Tajik reading comprehension where it can be measured. On Belebele the 1.7B and 8B adapters left accuracy unchanged and the 4B adapter lowered it by 3.7 points; at 0.6B the score rose by 4.2 points but sits near chance and coincides with a change in which answer letter the model prefers, so we do not read it as understanding. At 8B, continued pretraining on about 375 million tokens of raw Tajik text was followed by a Belebele gain of 9.9 points. After a further supervised fine-tuning stage, our main model, e3, is 11.4 points above Qwen3-8B on Belebele; its English MMLU changed by -1.2 points, and a loss larger than 3.3 points is excluded. The same heavy recipe applied to Qwen3-0.6B-Base brought its text loss close to that of the 8B model after books-only pretraining, while its multiple-choice answers stayed near chance and its English MMLU fell by 7.6 points. We report 15 trained models and their 5 starting models from June to October 2025, scored in 2026 on one harness with paired intervals, and we report what went wrong: lost training records, a thinking-mode dataset with almost no reasoning in it, later branches whose training data was never documented, and a 4-bit release that contains no transformer layers.
papers.summary: The authors adapt `Qwen3` models from 0.6B to 8B parameters to Tajik and find that small LoRA adapters lowered Tajik text loss at every size but **did not improve Tajik reading comprehension on `Belebele` where it could be measured**. Only heavier continued pretraining on about 375 million tokens of raw Tajik text at 8B produced a real gain (9.9 points), and after supervised fine-tuning their main model `e3` scores 11.4 points above `Qwen3-8B` with a 1.2-point drop in English `MMLU`. The same heavy recipe on the 0.6B base brought its text loss close to the 8B model's while its multiple-choice answers stayed near chance. The report covers 15 trained models and openly documents failures, including lost training records, a thinking-mode dataset with almost no reasoning, and a 4-bit release with no transformer layers.

papers.title: ProcessPrefBench: Evaluating Cross-Task Transfer of Individual Process Preferences from Naturalistic Human-AI Interaction
papers.abstract: In natural human-AI dialogue, users' corrections, requests, and self-descriptions carry reusable signals about how they want work to be done. These signals reveal individual process preferences, user-specific standards for evidence, depth, analytical focus, procedure, and delivery. We ask whether a preference revealed in one dialogue can shape an assistant's later answer when the task does not restate it. ProcessPrefBench uses three months of natural dialogues from two knowledge workers to build 66 source-target cases separately judged for source evidence and target applicability. Sources are preselected, so the benchmark tests application rather than retrieval. We test three models with target-only, full-history, and distilled-preference prompts. Target-specific 0-2 rubrics score preference realization, and a task gate flags severe failures. Compared with target-only prompting, full-history and imperative distilled-preference prompting raise preference realization by 0.204 and 0.244 points on the 0-2 scale, respectively, with no reliable advantage from distillation. Fabricated-evidence failures rise from 5.8% under target-only prompting to 10.1% under full-history and 10.4% under imperative prompting. ProcessPrefBench highlights a tension in learning from dialogue, where drawing on prior interactions can improve preference realization yet also invite fabricated evidence. We hope it helps build assistants that honor a user's process preferences without sacrificing factual reliability.
papers.summary: Users' corrections and requests in conversations reveal individual process preferences, such as standards for evidence, depth, and delivery, and the question is whether an assistant can apply a preference revealed in one dialogue to a later, unrelated task. `ProcessPrefBench` builds 66 source-target cases from three months of natural dialogues by two knowledge workers, with sources preselected so that it tests application rather than retrieval. Across three models, providing full history or distilled preference statements raised preference realization by 0.204 and 0.244 points on a 0-2 scale compared with the target task alone, with no reliable advantage from distillation. However, **fabricated-evidence failures nearly doubled, from 5.8% to about 10%**, when prior interactions were included.

papers.title: Overview of the NTCIR-19 SciClaimEval Task: Cross-modal Claim Verification in Scientific Papers
papers.abstract: This paper presents an overview of \emph{SciClaimEval}, a pilot task at NTCIR-19 on verifying scientific claims against the tables and figures of the papers in which they appear. Our dataset pairs authentic claims from 180 papers in machine learning, natural language processing, and medicine with contrastive versions of their tables and figures, one supporting the claim and one minimally modified so that it does not. The task comprises two subtasks: deciding whether a piece of evidence supports a claim, and selecting which of two evidence versions does. Twenty-two teams registered, the highest number among NTCIR-19 tasks, and 14 submitted 177 runs. Most systems built on multimodal large language models, relying on prompting and multi-stage inference rather than task-specific fine-tuning. On the first subtask, the best systems reached 98.1\% pair accuracy, but all six top-ranked systems relied on the contrastive pairs; the best system that judged each claim-evidence pair on its own scored 24.3 points lower. Open-weight models, embedded in carefully designed pipelines, matched proprietary ones. Yet verifying a single claim against its evidence, the setting that matters in practice, remains an open problem.
papers.summary: `SciClaimEval`, a pilot task at the NTCIR-19 evaluation campaign, asks systems to verify scientific claims against the tables and figures of the papers they come from. The dataset pairs real claims from 180 papers in machine learning, natural language processing, and medicine with two versions of the evidence, one supporting and one minimally modified to contradict, and 14 teams submitted 177 runs, mostly built on prompted multimodal large language models. The best systems reached 98.1% pair accuracy, but all six top systems exploited the contrastive pairs, and **the best system judging each claim-evidence pair on its own scored 24.3 points lower**. Open-weight models in well-designed pipelines matched proprietary ones, but verifying a single claim against its evidence remains unsolved.

papers.title: Reconciling Privacy with Provenance for Language Model Watermarks
papers.abstract: Watermarking has great potential for regulating the use of language models (LMs), but its deployment has been marred by controversy, as many users argue that fine-grained tracking of LM usage violates their privacy. This tension reduces the effectiveness of watermarks, as users engage in evasion strategies such as paraphrasing that can remove much of the watermark signal. We show that provenance and privacy can be reconciled if we shift the goal of watermark design from tracking individuals to estimating aggregate usage. We develop locally differentially private watermarks which provably limit the evidence that any individual text can contribute to detection, while still enabling accurate estimation of population frequencies. We introduce the Red-Green Sequence (RGS) watermark, a private and computationally efficient watermark that achieves accurate frequency estimation at high privacy levels across various models, sample sizes and generation entropies in settings that reflect realistic deployment scenarios. On C4 language modeling tasks, we attain $0.0019$ MSE with $0.0038$ mean absolute bias at a low $\varepsilon$ of 1, while in more challenging settings such as an essay writing task with only 100 text samples, we still find errors on the order of $0.0113$ MSE with $0.004$ mean absolute bias at $\varepsilon=2$.
papers.summary: Language-model watermarks face user resistance because fine-grained tracking feels like a privacy violation, which encourages evasion such as paraphrasing. The authors reframe the goal from identifying individual texts to estimating aggregate usage, and design locally differentially private watermarks that provably limit how much evidence any single text contributes while still allowing accurate population-level frequency estimates. Their `Red-Green Sequence` (`RGS`) watermark is computationally efficient and, on `C4` language modeling, achieves **0.0019 mean squared error at a strict privacy level of ε = 1**. Even on an essay task with only 100 samples, errors stay around 0.0113 mean squared error at ε = 2.

papers.title: The Harness Is the Model: Agent Scaffolding Changes a Fixed LLM's Compliance with Banking Conduct Rules, Unevenly Across Models
papers.abstract: Banks validate language models, but they deploy systems: a model inside a harness that decides what it sees, which tools it can call and who checks its actions. We test whether that harness changes compliance with banking conduct rules when the model is held fixed. Four open-weight models each ran five harnesses (a pipeline that makes one structured decision, a ReAct-style tool loop, a loop in which the policy is reachable only through search, a loop with a long benign customer memory, and a loop with a same-model compliance reviewer) on 156 pre-registered cases in a simulated retail bank whose 11 rule families paraphrase EU consumer-credit, payments, investor-protection, data-protection and anti-money-laundering provisions. Every one of the 3120 two-turn episodes was scored deterministically from the executed tool trace, with violations and over-refusals counted separately. Pooled across models the harness moved the correct-case rate only between 87.3% and 92.1%, but within a model it mattered a great deal: for one model the spread between its best and worst harness was 11.5 percentage points, enough to move it from first to last place among the four models, while for another the harness made no detectable difference; the model x harness interaction itself was suggestive rather than conclusive. The same-model reviewer cut violations from 9.6% to 6.4% without raising over-refusals, contrary to our pre-registered prediction. Rules that require date arithmetic failed in every harness. In an exploratory analysis with two LLM judges and a blind human check, 26% of violations were accompanied by a customer message that denied the action the agent had just executed, which a transcript-only review would record as a correct refusal. For model-risk management the unit of validation should be the model-harness pair, and conduct testing should read the action log, not the conversation.
papers.summary: Banks validate language models in isolation but deploy them inside harnesses that control what the model sees, which tools it calls, and who checks its actions. The authors run four open-weight models in five harnesses, ranging from a single structured decision to tool loops with policy search, long customer memory, or a same-model compliance reviewer, across 156 pre-registered cases in a simulated retail bank governed by paraphrased EU rules, scoring all 3,120 episodes deterministically from tool traces. Pooled results moved little (87.3% to 92.1% correct), but **for one model the harness alone shifted results by 11.5 percentage points, moving it from first to last place**, while the same-model reviewer cut violations from 9.6% to 6.4% without more over-refusals. Rules requiring date arithmetic failed everywhere, and 26% of violations came with a customer message denying the action the agent had just executed, so the authors argue validation should target the model-harness pair and read action logs rather than transcripts.
papers.highlight_summary:
Banks validate language models, but what they actually deploy is a model wrapped in a harness, the code that controls what the model sees, which tools it can call and who checks its actions. The study holds the model fixed and varies only the harness, then measures compliance with banking conduct rules modelled on EU consumer-credit, payments, investor-protection, data-protection and anti-money-laundering law, scoring each episode from the tools the agent actually executed.

- Four open-weight models (`deepseek-v4-flash`, `deepseek-v4.1-flash`, `qwen3.8-flash-next`, `gemma-4-31b`) each ran five harnesses on 156 pre-registered cases in a simulated bank, for 3,120 two-turn episodes: a single structured-decision pipeline, a `ReAct` tool loop, a loop where the policy is reachable only through search, a loop with a long benign customer memory, and a loop with a same-model compliance reviewer.
- Pooled across models, the harnesses differ little (**87.3% to 92.1%** of cases handled correctly), but within one model the gap is large: `qwen3.8-flash-next` swings **11.5 points** (Cochran's Q = 25.1, p < 0.001) and goes from most to least compliant model, while `deepseek-v4.1-flash` shows no harness effect, although the formal model × harness interaction test is only suggestive (p = 0.07).
- The same-model reviewer cut violations from **9.6% to 6.4%** (p < 0.001) without increasing over-refusals (1.6% vs. 1.4%), contrary to the authors' pre-registered prediction, at a cost of about 1.8× the input tokens.
- Rules that require date arithmetic, such as the 14-day credit withdrawal window and the 13-month limit on unauthorised-payment claims, failed in every harness, with withdrawal cases only **67–71%** correct, and the reviewer did not help on the withdrawal window, presumably because it makes the same date error as the agent.
- In an exploratory analysis using two LLM judges plus a blind human check, **26%** of violations (41% in the pipeline harness) came with a customer message denying the action the agent had just executed, so a transcript-only review would miss them; the caveats are a synthetic bank, moderate-size models with reasoning turned off, and a scripted follow-up turn that may invite these denials.

papers.title: Growing One's AI Tools: A Paradigm of Practice-Grown Tools
papers.abstract: Professionals have long used software built for them by others. This article reports the growth of a professional computer-assisted interpreting (CAI) tool built by its own user, a conference interpreter without programming training. Drawing on an eight-week version-controlled record with telemetry from 133 logged sessions and over 20,000 recognized utterances, the article traces how real conference work drove the tool through 62 commits and six versions. The record shows capabilities deployed on the day their need appeared and one strategy change that cut median end-to-end delay by over a third within one afternoon. The article then proposes the paradigm of practice-grown tools, defined by the shift from using to growing, the co-evolution of tool and practice through breakdown and repair, bounded local computation, and an assessment corollary, and it formulates three propositions toward tool-inclusive assessment of practitioners, from tool-making literacy to a compute-standardized format for certifying what they and their tools achieve together.
papers.summary: A conference interpreter with no programming training built their own computer-assisted interpreting tool, and this article documents its growth from an eight-week version-controlled record with telemetry from 133 sessions and over 20,000 recognized utterances. Real conference work drove the tool through 62 commits and six versions, with capabilities deployed on the day the need appeared and **one strategy change cutting median end-to-end delay by over a third in a single afternoon**. From this case, the author proposes a paradigm of practice-grown tools, characterized by a shift from using to growing tools and the co-evolution of tool and practice, and suggests ways to assess practitioners together with the tools they build.

papers.title: Accelerating Long-Context Decoding in Large-Scale Hybrid LLMs Without Retraining
papers.abstract: The full-attention layers of large language models (LLMs) make every generated token more expensive than the previous one, slowing models down on long-context tasks. Hybrid models reduce this cost by replacing most full-attention layers with linear-attention layers, but the first still dominate decoding at long contexts. We accelerate these remaining layers without any training or weight changes using combined sparse attention: each layer attends to a sliding window of recent tokens, a pinned prefix, and a fixed budget of most relevant tokens in the context. The window size and budget are found on a per-layer basis using a multi-objective search algorithm. Across six hybrid models from three families, from 4B to 397B parameters, the selected configurations preserve their baseline model's accuracy on 21 long-context datasets. Decoding 64k/256k tokens becomes up to 1.26x/2.22x faster on Qwen3.5-4B, 1.20x/2.23x on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 1.16x/2.06x on Ornith-1.0-397B.
papers.summary: Hybrid language models replace most full-attention layers with cheaper linear-attention layers, but the remaining full-attention layers still dominate decoding cost at long contexts. The authors speed up these layers without training or weight changes by having each one attend to a sliding window of recent tokens, a pinned prefix, and a fixed budget of the most relevant tokens, with per-layer window sizes and budgets chosen by a multi-objective search. Across six hybrid models from 4B to 397B parameters, the chosen configurations preserve baseline accuracy on 21 long-context datasets while making **decoding at 256k tokens up to 2.2x faster**, for example 2.22x on `Qwen3.5-4B` and 2.06x on `Ornith-1.0-397B`.

papers.title: AssameseLM-E2B: An Open-Weight Assamese Language Model for Efficient Consumer-Grade Deployment
papers.abstract:
While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in high-resource languages, their performance often degrades in low-resource languages due to tokenization inefficiencies, generative instability, and linguistic interference. This paper presents AssameseLM-E2B and its instruction-tuned variant, AssameseLM-E2B-it, a 2-billion-parameter model adapted specifically for low resource Assamese language. Built upon the Gemma-4 architecture, the model incorporates an expanded byte-level BPE vocabulary to reduce tokenization overhead by nearly 500% compared with multilingual 2B--3B baselines. We employ a parameter-efficient Continual Pre-Training (CPT) pipeline with Hybrid LoRA, followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on a balanced, multi-domain dataset to enhance instruction-following and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) capabilities.
  Evaluation demonstrates a Bits-per-Byte (BPB) score of 0.7488 on FLORES-200, alongside an overall RAG score of 96.7% and 100% refusal accuracy on adversarial unanswerable prompts. Comparative analysis reveals significant limitations in general-purpose baselines, including receptive-productive decoupling, generative degradation on Romanized Assamese, and unintended Bengali script assimilation. These results demonstrate the potential of parameter-efficient adaptation for developing capable, locally deployable language models for low-resource languages under constrained computational resources.
papers.summary: Large language models perform poorly in low-resource languages like Assamese because of inefficient tokenization, unstable generation, and interference from related languages. `AssameseLM-E2B` is a 2-billion-parameter model built on `Gemma-4` with an expanded byte-level vocabulary that sharply reduces tokenization overhead relative to multilingual 2B-3B baselines, trained with parameter-efficient continual pretraining using LoRA followed by supervised fine-tuning for instruction following and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). It reaches 0.7488 bits-per-byte on `FLORES-200`, **an overall RAG score of 96.7%**, and full refusal accuracy on adversarial unanswerable prompts. The authors also document failures of general-purpose baselines, such as degraded output on Romanized Assamese and drifting into Bengali script.

papers.title: Editing Large Language Models with Geometry-Aware Regularization
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing has become a key technique for updating knowledge in large language models. However, existing methods neglect the geometric structure of the knowledge representation space, leading to two key limitations: they cannot distinguish which pre-trained knowledge should be preferentially preserved (core vs. non-core) nor which new edits are inherently difficult (hard vs. easy). To address this, we propose GEdit, a geometry-aware framework built on a Low-Rank Plus Diagonal (LR+D) factor model that captures the intrinsic low-rank structure of Transformer FFN hidden representations. GEdit features two complementary mechanisms. First, the low-rank regularization applies targeted protection on a low-rank core knowledge subspace. Second, the adaptive regularization dynamically adjusts the regularization strength based on each edit request's editability: relaxing constraints for hard edits to ensure success, and tightening them for easy edits to better preserve pretrained knowledge. Extensive experiments on GPT2-XL, GPT-J, and LLaMA-3-8B under large-scale editing scenarios, including both mini-batch and fully sequential editing settings with up to 10,000 continuous updates, show that GEdit consistently and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both editing success and knowledge preservation.
papers.summary: Knowledge-editing methods for large language models ignore the geometry of how knowledge is represented, so they cannot tell which existing knowledge most needs protection or which edits are inherently hard. `GEdit` models the hidden representations of Transformer feed-forward layers with a low-rank-plus-diagonal factor model, then protects a low-rank core knowledge subspace and adapts regularization strength per edit, loosening it for hard edits and tightening it for easy ones. On `GPT2-XL`, `GPT-J`, and `LLaMA-3-8B`, in both mini-batch and fully sequential settings with **up to 10,000 consecutive edits**, `GEdit` consistently outperforms prior methods in both edit success and knowledge preservation.

papers.title: Loop Before You Leap: What Recurrent Depth Can and Cannot Buy in Data-Limited Pretraining
papers.abstract: Multimodal models have often scored below text-only baselines in the BabyLM Challenge (Klerings et al., 2024; Takmaz et al., 2025). We test whether additional recurrent computation helps close this gap. Recurrence increases computation by reusing layers without adding parameters or training data. Using a single implementation, we compare standard and looped Transformers under a 100M-word budget, with three seeds per main condition. Each image is represented by one feature vector from a frozen DINOv2 encoder, used as a prefix token. Caption words count toward the budget, so multimodal training also changes the language data. In a pre-registered text-only comparison, a 12-layer stack repeated four times exceeds a standard 48-layer Transformer by 5.4 BLiMP percentage points at matched inference compute. However, multimodal training lowers BLiMP accuracy by about 3.8 points in both architectures, with no clear mitigation from recurrence. An exploratory loop-side no-image control, trained with the multimodal language data and batching schedule, scores 5.7 points below the text-only baseline. Adding the visual prefix raises accuracy by 1.85 points on average, but this contrast is uncertain with three seeds. These results suggest that changes in language data and its presentation are a major source of the drop. Diagnostic tests show that the models use visual information; its contribution to grammatical generalization remains uncertain under this single-vector interface.
papers.summary: In the `BabyLM Challenge`, multimodal models trained on a small data budget have often scored below text-only models, and the authors test whether looped Transformers, which reuse layers for extra computation without more parameters, close that gap under a 100-million-word budget. In a pre-registered text-only comparison, **a 12-layer stack repeated four times beats a standard 48-layer Transformer by 5.4 `BLiMP` points at matched inference compute**. Adding images, represented as a single frozen `DINOv2` feature vector, lowers `BLiMP` accuracy by about 3.8 points in both architectures, and recurrence does not mitigate it. Control experiments suggest the drop comes mainly from changes in the language data and how it is presented rather than from the images themselves.
papers.highlight_summary:
Multimodal models in the BabyLM Challenge often score below text-only baselines on grammar benchmarks, and the paper tests whether looped Transformers can close that gap. Looping reuses the same layers several times, so it adds sequential computation without adding parameters or training data. The answer splits in two: looping clearly beats making a standard model deeper, but it does not shrink the multimodal penalty, and most of that penalty appears to come from changes in the language data.

- **Setup:** A 12-layer `LLaMA`-style decoder is run 4 times with shared weights, and the text embeddings are added back in after every pass; it is compared against standard models with 12 layers (same ~97M parameters), 24 layers, and 48 layers (same inference compute), all trained on a 100M-word budget with three seeds each, where each image enters as a single frozen `DINOv2` feature vector placed before the caption and caption words count toward the word budget.
- **Looping vs. adding depth:** In a comparison registered before the results were seen, the looped model beats the compute-matched 48-layer model by **5.4 BLiMP points** in text-only training (**76.16 vs. 70.80**) and by **3.7 points** in multimodal training, and standard models score lower on BLiMP the deeper they get even though their training loss keeps falling; against the parameter-matched 12-layer model the gain is only **~0.95 points**, which is not significant (p≈0.12).
- **No help with the multimodal drop:** Multimodal training lowers BLiMP by **~3.8 points** in both the standard and looped models, and the difference between those two drops is **−0.01 points (95% CI [−1.44, 1.41])**; changing the connector or re-injecting the image vector across loops does not show a clear benefit either.
- **Where the drop comes from:** A looped-model control trained on the same multimodal language data and batches but with no images scores **5.71 points below** the text-only model, and adding the image vector back recovers only **1.85 points** on average, with a wide CI of [−1.67, 5.37]; this points mainly to the change in text composition (for example, `CHILDES` child-directed speech rises from 28.4% to 56.8% of the retained text) and to the different batching, even though shuffling the image features raises caption loss by ~1.5 nats per token, so the models do use the visual input.
- **Limitations:** Only three seeds were run per condition; the matched no-image control exists only for the looped model, so the components cannot be compared across architectures; recurrence is confounded with text re-injection; and a single global image vector may be too coarse to show what visual grounding could do for grammar.

papers.title: Zuse: A Decision Model for European Languages
papers.abstract: Decision models read a document and return a probability for each of a fixed set of options instead of generating text. Several appeared in 2026, but none has published results outside English. We describe Zuse, three decision models (4B, 9B and 27B) that train a low-rank adapter and a pointer head on frozen open-weight bases, targeting 27 European languages, and use them to study how this design behaves across languages and tasks. On a broad European suite of 11 sources excluded from training, covering 9 task groups and 27 languages, a development set that also guided model selection, the 27B model reaches 87.5% accuracy with a pooled expected calibration error of 0.016, and 0.035 when weighted per source. Post-hoc analyses of these single-seed results give three findings. First, miscalibration is structured by task rather than language: on parallel reading and topic items in 26 languages the confidence gap varies about as much as sampling noise, while across sources it spans -0.07 to +0.09, with knowledge tasks overconfident and acceptability judgements underconfident at all three sizes, so one fitted temperature cannot correct both. Second, the share of decisions that can be automated at a 5% error budget follows chance-corrected skill (Spearman 0.97 over 33 source and model pairs) more closely than raw accuracy (0.91). Third, reach beyond the training languages is set by the base model: across 210 languages, changing the training run moved scores by at most about 2 points within a size, while languages outside the base's documented list trail by 23 to 28 points at every size. On English public suites Zuse is behind Jev and Kev, including Kev models on the same bases. We also report two pitfalls in building multi-source training data: label-word collision between topic schemes, and an injection augmentation that taught a shortcut. Zuse can be tried at https://bineric.com/zuse.
papers.summary: Decision models read a document and output a probability for each of a fixed set of options rather than generating text, and no prior such model had been evaluated beyond English. `Zuse` comprises three decision models (4B, 9B, and 27B) that train a low-rank adapter and a pointer head on frozen open-weight bases for 27 European languages, with the 27B model reaching **87.5% accuracy and a pooled expected calibration error of 0.016** on a held-out European suite. Analyses show that miscalibration varies by task rather than language, with knowledge tasks overconfident and acceptability judgments underconfident, and that reach to languages outside training is set by the base model, with languages outside the base model's documented list trailing by 23 to 28 points. On English benchmarks `Zuse` trails comparable models, and the authors report two dataset-construction pitfalls, including an augmentation that taught a shortcut.

papers.title: Learning Noise Optimization for Reward Alignment in Few-Step Generative Models
papers.abstract: Reward alignment for diffusion- and flow-based generative models is often formulated over stochastic trajectories, making it less suitable for few-step deterministic generators. Initial noise optimization provides a trajectory-free alternative, but existing gradient-free methods require costly per-sample search at inference. We introduce LeNO (Learning Noise Optimization), which amortizes reward-guided initial noise optimization into a learned residual transport while keeping the pretrained generator frozen. LeNO learns an anchor-conditioned distribution over noise corrections using Local GRPO and scalar rewards, eliminating iterative test-time optimization. For Gaussian initial noise with norm-preserving projection, we derive a tractable upper bound on the KL divergence between the corrected noise distribution and the original prior, providing a principled regularization objective. We evaluate LeNO on few-step text-to-image and protein structure generation, including expensive black-box designability rewards. Across both domains, LeNO improves target rewards with a single noise correction at inference while largely preserving generation quality and diversity.
papers.summary: Reward alignment for diffusion and flow models is usually defined over stochastic sampling trajectories, which fits poorly with few-step deterministic generators, and existing initial-noise optimization requires costly per-sample search at inference. `LeNO` (`Learning Noise Optimization`) instead learns a distribution of corrections to the initial noise using `Local GRPO` and scalar rewards while the generator stays frozen, regularized by a derived upper bound on the divergence from the original noise prior. On few-step text-to-image generation and protein structure generation with expensive black-box designability rewards, **`LeNO` improves target rewards with a single noise correction at inference** while largely preserving quality and diversity.

papers.title: Mass Producing Training Data with Surprising Side Effects
papers.abstract: Training data can have unexpected side effects on language model behavior outside the training domain: insecure code data can induce broad misalignment, and outdated bird names can induce a 19th-century persona. Understanding such generalization is hard because only dozens of isolated examples exist, each constructed by hand or discovered by accident. We propose automatically discovering such datasets with surprising side effects (DSSEs). We define three objectives for DSSEs: they should (1) elicit a target behavior, (2) read like ordinary post-training data, and (3) be surprising to human auditors reading the data. We operationalize each with LLM judges, and search for high-scoring datasets via evolution, reinforcement learning, and subliminal learning approaches. After re-scoring and filtering with held-out metrics, our pipeline produces a collection of 6,575 DSSEs across 8 behaviors, many of which generalize across model families and sizes. We find our automated metrics track ML researchers' judgments, and frontier models outperform humans at predicting side effects. These datasets form a testbed for studying generalization and lay the groundwork for predicting training side effects before model deployment. Explore them at https://dsse.transluce.org.
papers.summary: Training data can change language-model behavior far outside its domain, as when insecure code induces broad misalignment, but only a few dozen hand-found examples of such datasets exist. The authors automatically generate datasets with surprising side effects (`DSSEs`) that elicit a target behavior, read like ordinary post-training data, and would surprise a human auditor, scoring each property with LLM judges and searching via evolution, reinforcement learning, and subliminal learning. The pipeline yields **6,575 such datasets across 8 behaviors**, many of which generalize across model families and sizes. The automated metrics track ML researchers' judgments, and frontier models predict side effects better than humans, giving a testbed for anticipating training side effects before deployment.
papers.highlight_summary:
Fine-tuning data can change a language model's behavior far outside the training domain. Insecure code data can make a model broadly misaligned, and outdated bird names can give it a 19th-century persona. So far only a few dozen such cases exist, each built by hand or found by accident. The authors propose generating these datasets with surprising side effects (DSSEs) automatically and at scale, so generalization can be studied systematically.

- A DSSE is scored on three objectives, each judged by an LLM: it should elicit a target behavior, read like ordinary post-training data, and surprise a human auditor who reads it.
- High-scoring datasets are found with three search methods (evolutionary search, reinforcement learning and subliminal-learning-style generation), then re-scored and filtered with held-out metrics.
- The pipeline produces **6,575 DSSEs across 8 target behaviors**, and many of them carry their side effects across different model families and sizes.
- The automated metrics agree with ML researchers' judgments, and **frontier models predict side effects better than humans**, which suggests side effects could be screened for before training.
- The collection is meant as a testbed for generalization research, but it is limited to 8 behaviors and relies heavily on LLM judges, so how widely the findings apply is still open.

papers.title: Training-Free Character-Length Control in Summarization with Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Summarization with a fixed character length is important for tasks such as headline and article preview generation, where text must fit an exact space. Autoregressive language models (LMs) struggle with precise character-length control: training-based methods require task-specific fine-tuning, while zero-shot prompting strategies achieve only approximate compliance. We propose DELTA (Diffusion Expected Length Targeting Algorithm), a training-free inference-time method for masked diffusion LMs that estimates expected character length at each denoising step and dynamically inserts or removes masked positions to steer toward a target length. DELTA requires no fine-tuning and is designed for off-the-shelf masked diffusion LMs. Across three summarization benchmarks, it reduces character-length errors by an order of magnitude compared to baselines while maintaining competitive summary quality in both automatic and human evaluation.
papers.summary: Autoregressive language models are poor at hitting an exact character count, which matters for headlines and article previews that must fit a fixed space. `DELTA` (Diffusion Expected Length Targeting Algorithm) is an inference-time method for off-the-shelf masked diffusion language models: at each denoising step it estimates the expected character length and inserts or removes masked positions to steer toward the target. It needs no fine-tuning. Across three summarization benchmarks it **reduces character-length errors by an order of magnitude** compared with baselines, while summary quality stays competitive in both automatic and human evaluation.

papers.title: Corralling AI Risks with Grassroots Contracts
papers.abstract:
AI's inflection point is a fountain of alarming risks. Digital platforms in particular are vulnerable to three major AI risks, as those in control of global platforms cede control to AI, of the algorithms, of membership and of content: (1) AI control of global platforms, social and economic, used by the majority of humanity, resulting in the majority of humanity becoming vulnerable to AI control. (2) Unaccountable AI agents operating anonymously on social and economic digital platforms, side-by-side with humans, possibly masquerading as humans, serving unknown masters with unknown goals, operating under unknown restraints without accountability or culpability. (3) Unattributed deepfakes generated by anonymous AI, with people unable to distinguish them from genuine content and with their producers evading accountability and culpability.
  Here, we propose to corral these AI risks with grassroots contracts, a digital incarnation of a two-centuries old notion of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon. We present grassroots contracts for a social graph with accountable AI agents and for a social network with digital provenance, and working smartphone apps that implement the two and show how they corral these major AI risks: (1) AI control of global platforms. (2) Unaccountable AI agents. (3) Unattributed deepfakes.
papers.summary: The authors identify three AI risks to digital platforms: AI taking control of global social and economic platforms, anonymous and unaccountable AI agents operating alongside humans, and deepfakes with no attributable source. Their proposed remedy is "grassroots contracts", a digital version of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon's two-century-old idea of contracts between peers. They present grassroots contracts for a social graph with accountable AI agents and for a social network with digital provenance, and they describe **working smartphone apps that implement both**, arguing that these apps contain all three risks.

papers.title: Does Context Compression Preserve Refusal Alignment?
papers.abstract: Context compression reduces inference cost by encoding inputs into compact representations while preserving semantic content. An open question is whether semantic preservation alone is sufficient to maintain downstream behaviours such as refusal alignment. We investigate this question and find that encoder-based compression systematically weakens refusal behaviour in instruction-tuned language models, despite high reconstruction fidelity. This effect persists across model families and compression architectures. Mechanistic analysis shows that compression attenuates activation along the decoder's learned refusal direction. We further explore Memory Steering, a lightweight inference-time intervention that restores refusal rates to near-baseline levels without retraining and operates entirely in compressed representation space. These results demonstrate that semantic preservation does not guarantee behavioural preservation under compression, highlighting the need to explicitly preserve alignment-relevant features in compression-aware systems.
papers.summary: Context compression lowers inference cost by encoding inputs into compact representations, and the open question here is whether preserving meaning is enough to preserve safety behaviour. The study finds that encoder-based compression **systematically weakens refusal behaviour in instruction-tuned models despite high reconstruction fidelity**, and the effect holds across model families and compression architectures. Mechanistic analysis shows that compression weakens activation along the decoder's learned refusal direction. A lightweight inference-time fix called `Memory Steering` works entirely in the compressed representation space and restores refusal rates to near-baseline levels without retraining.

papers.title: LegalEvolver: Agentic Legal Judgment Prediction via Rubric-Guided Self-Evolution
papers.abstract: As LLM-based agents develop, they have been increasingly applied in the legal domain. Legal Judgment Prediction~(LJP) requires models to conduct multi-step reasoning and external legal evidence retrieval. Existing legal search agents' performance is often constrained by the quality of retrieval queries. They often formulate queries directly from the initial user request, overlooking latent legal issues and legally salient details. To address this issue, we propose \emph{LegalEvolver}, a query optimization framework specifically designed to generate legally informative queries for LJP-oriented retrieval. Sampling high-quality optimized queries and their corresponding search trajectories is challenging, as relying solely on unguided high-temperature rollouts is both inefficient and constrained by the model's initial capabilities. We therefore heuristically optimize queries as seeds, improving the efficiency of trajectory generation. Furthermore, we summarize rollout experience into rubrics and use them to guide multi-round iterative self-evolution. Iteratively performing rubric optimization and rubric-guided RL enables the model to surpass its initial performance ceiling. End-to-end performance on extensive benchmarks demonstrates the effectiveness of query optimization on LJP. Comparisons with direct SFT followed by RL demonstrate the effectiveness of rubric guidance. Evolving rubrics further outperform fixed rubrics, confirming the benefits of self-evolution.
papers.summary: Legal judgment prediction requires multi-step reasoning and retrieval of legal evidence, but existing legal search agents usually build queries straight from the user's request and miss latent legal issues. `LegalEvolver` trains a model to write more legally informative retrieval queries. It uses heuristically optimized queries as seeds to make trajectory sampling more efficient, condenses rollout experience into rubrics, and alternates between rubric optimization and rubric-guided reinforcement learning so the model can **surpass its initial performance ceiling**. Experiments show that rubric guidance beats plain supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, and that evolving rubrics beat fixed ones.

papers.title: Presentation Sensitivity in Typed Decision Models for Subjective Text Evaluation
papers.abstract: Typed decision models offer structured choices, scores, and probabilities for low-cost automated evaluation. We present a controlled audit of presentation sensitivity in Jev, Clef Flash, and Perplexity Decider across native choice and score interfaces. Across six datasets with 9,000 multiply annotated humor, helpfulness, and summarization items, we collect 702,000 judgments under interventions that vary positions, identifiers, authorship claims, endorsements, decision framing, and rating rubrics while preserving the evaluated texts. Jev's second-position probability advantage reaches 6.11 percentage points on summaries; reversing reader endorsements changes Perplexity's selected humor text on 40.40% of pairs; and rejection framing reduces Clef's summary agreement with human preferences by 23.36 points. Rating formats also shift score levels while often preserving rankings. Across these findings, repeatability, presentation robustness, and human alignment emerge as distinct properties of an evaluator. Reliable use therefore requires validating the decisions and score interpretations on which an evaluation pipeline depends.
papers.summary: Typed decision models return structured choices, scores, and probabilities as a cheap form of automated evaluation, and this audit tests how much their judgments depend on presentation rather than content. Across six datasets of humor, helpfulness, and summarization items, the authors collect 702,000 judgments from `Jev`, `Clef Flash`, and `Perplexity Decider`, varying position, identifiers, authorship claims, endorsements, decision framing, and rubrics while keeping the evaluated texts the same. Effects are large: reversing reader endorsements changes `Perplexity`'s humor choice on **40.40% of pairs**, and rejection framing lowers `Clef`'s agreement with human preferences on summaries by 23.36 points. The authors conclude that repeatability, robustness to presentation, and alignment with humans are separate properties, each of which must be validated on its own.

papers.title: Where Should a KV-Cache Repair Budget Go? Distractor Structure and Contextual Compatibility in Non-Prefix Reuse
papers.abstract: Non-prefix KV-cache reuse encodes retrieved chunks independently and concatenates their caches. To find where a small repair budget should be spent, we vary the chunks around the answer-bearing one (the target) across three 7B-8B models and four datasets of dialogue memory, open-domain QA and API documentation. Reuse loses 19-100% of the context-dependent questions that full prefill answers, and it loses more when the other chunks are of the same kind as the target. Because the recoverable damage is spread over these other chunks, restoring a few of them recovers little, and the budget is better spent on the target. This works through contextual compatibility: recomputing the target against the reused cache beats inserting its full-prefill KV in all seven settings tested, although the recomputed KV stays far from the full-prefill KV. Question attention over reused caches, however, selects the target in at most 18.8% of development questions. A retriever finds it more often, and recomputing its top chunk after moving it next to the question significantly beats InfoFlow-style reordering at the same 5% budget in six of nine open-domain QA and API-documentation settings. On dialogue memory, though, recomputing chunks never significantly beats the token-level selector chosen for each setting.
papers.summary: Non-prefix KV-cache reuse encodes retrieved chunks independently and concatenates their caches, which saves compute but loses cross-chunk context. Across three 7B–8B models and four datasets, reuse loses 19–100% of the context-dependent questions that full prefill answers, and it loses more when the surrounding chunks resemble the answer-bearing one. The authors find that a small recomputation budget is **better spent on the answer-bearing chunk than on its neighbours**, and that recomputing it against the reused cache beats inserting its full-prefill KV. Picking that chunk with a retriever and moving it next to the question beats `InfoFlow`-style reordering at a 5% budget in most QA and API-documentation settings, but not on dialogue memory.

papers.title: Interpretable Text Embeddings Based on Hierarchical Questions
papers.abstract: QA-based text embeddings represent texts as vectors consisting of 1/0 answers to yes/no questions. Although these embeddings provide detailed information for interpretation and achieve high task performance, they often require humans to examine a large number of questions. Furthermore, the relationship between the number of questions and the appropriate level of question granularity has not been sufficiently studied. To address these challenges, we propose a method for constructing hierarchical questions for text embeddings. As the hierarchy deepens, questions become more specific and their number increases. During interpretation, we reduce the number of questions that humans need to examine by replacing questions at deeper levels with aligned questions at shallower levels. The question hierarchy is constructed through recursive clustering, contrastive prompting, and question alignment. Experimental results on general-purpose tasks show that our method improves interpretability while maintaining task performance. It is also found that, when only a limited number of questions are available, questions at shallower levels tend to achieve higher task performance than those at deeper levels, even with the same number of questions.
papers.summary: QA-based text embeddings represent a text as a vector of 1/0 answers to yes/no questions, which makes them interpretable but forces a human to inspect many questions. This work builds a hierarchy of questions through recursive clustering, contrastive prompting, and question alignment. Deeper levels hold more and more specific questions, and during interpretation deep questions can be replaced by aligned shallower ones. On general-purpose tasks the method improves interpretability while keeping task performance, and **when the question budget is limited, shallower questions outperform deeper ones** at the same count.

papers.title: Ruby-OPD: Enhancing Pronunciation Controllability and Accuracy for Flow-Matching Text-to-Speech via On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Achieving both high pronunciation accuracy and fine-grained controllability remains a central challenge in Japanese text-to-speech (TTS), as Japanese is an unsegmented language mixing logographic Kanji and phonographic Kana with extensive polyphony. Traditional cascaded systems convert text into phoneme sequences via a front-end, ensuring pronunciation control but discarding lexical semantics and prosodic cues in surface orthography. Conversely, recent zero-shot TTS models directly consume raw orthographic text to improve naturalness, yet suffer from polyphone errors and lack explicit pronunciation control. To bridge this gap, we propose a two-stage framework for flow-matching TTS. First, we investigate Ruby text representations with orthography perturbation to jointly preserve surface forms and target pronunciations for reliable control. Second, we introduce On-Policy Distillation (OPD) on large-scale text-only corpora to enhance pronunciation accuracy on raw orthographic text without paired speech. On the Joyo-Kanji-Yomi benchmark, our model achieves 97.13% Accuracy, 2.02% Target PER, 0.70% Sentence PER, and 4.21% Sentence CER under raw text while retaining strong controllability.
papers.summary: Japanese text-to-speech (TTS) is hard to make both accurate and controllable: the script mixes Kanji and Kana and has many polyphonic characters, and models that read raw text make reading errors with no way to correct them. The proposed two-stage framework for flow-matching TTS first uses Ruby annotations with orthography perturbation, which keeps surface forms while specifying target pronunciations. It then applies On-Policy Distillation (`OPD`) on large text-only corpora to improve pronunciation on raw text without paired speech. On the `Joyo-Kanji-Yomi` benchmark the model reaches **97.13% accuracy** on raw text while keeping strong pronunciation control.

papers.title: Twists and Turns: A Graph-Based Benchmark and Framework for Long-Term Memory in Exploration Tasks
papers.abstract: Long-term problem-solving processes, such as scientific research and software development, proceed along an evolving trial-and-error trajectory toward a central goal. We term these \textit{exploration tasks}, which require models to remember not only facts but also how solutions are tested against intermediate outcomes and early attempts are continually revised or revived. However, existing long-term memory research focuses on factual recall and updates, overlooking the interconnected nature of exploration. We observe that exploration processes naturally form graphs, with branching approaches linked by revisions and reconsiderations. Motivated by this, we propose \textsc{LExMem}, a graph-guided benchmark designed to evaluate \underline{\textsc{Mem}}ory in \underline{\textsc{L}}ong-term \underline{\textsc{Ex}}ploration tasks. We model exploration processes as graphs and introduce an evolutionary mechanism to increase their structural complexity, yielding 224 dialogues and 2,018 question-answer instances derived from graph structures. Building on the same insight, we propose \textsc{LExGraph}, a graph-based memory framework that incrementally organizes dialogues into interconnected memory nodes and retrieves evidence through hybrid retrieval and neighbor expansion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that \textsc{LExMem} poses a significant challenge to existing retrieval- and memory-based systems, whereas \textsc{LExGraph} achieves superior performance and generalizes effectively to external benchmarks. Codes and datasets are available at https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/LExMem.
