papers.summary: Long-running work such as research or software development follows a trial-and-error path in which approaches branch, get revised, and are later revived, but existing long-term memory benchmarks mostly test factual recall. `LExMem` models these exploration processes as graphs and uses an evolutionary mechanism to make them structurally more complex, producing 224 dialogues and 2,018 question-answer instances. The authors also propose `LExGraph`, a memory framework that incrementally organizes dialogue into interconnected memory nodes and retrieves evidence through hybrid search plus neighbour expansion. Existing retrieval and memory systems struggle on `LExMem`, while **`LExGraph` performs best and generalizes to external benchmarks**.

papers.title: EvoGuard: Mitigating Degradation in Online Skill Evolution
papers.abstract: Skills let language agents reuse experience across tasks as natural-language documents. Recent work evolves skills from interaction, but existing methods have limitations when skills evolve online. Prior methods update a skill offline from a batch of trajectories collected over many tasks. Some then adopt the new skill without any check, which can degrade the skill over time. Others keep it only if it improves performance on a held-out validation set, which is too slow and costly to run after every update. We introduce EvoGuard, a pairwise skill selector that mitigates skill degradation at low latency and cost. We first run the agent iteratively to build pools of skills and score each skill on a private test set to obtain utility labels. We pair the skills and use rejection sampling to keep only pairs with a clear utility gap. The selector is trained on the logits of two label tokens to pick the better skill. At deployment it decides in a single forward pass, which is significantly faster than evaluation on the private test set. Compared with adopting every new skill, EvoGuard improves success by 11.0% on ALFWorld, 5.9% on ScienceWorld, and 2.7% on LiveCodeBench.
papers.summary: Language agents can store reusable "skills" as natural-language documents and evolve them from interaction, but adopting every update online can degrade skills over time, and validating each update on a held-out set is too slow. `EvoGuard` trains a pairwise selector on skill pairs with clearly different measured utility. Using the logits of two label tokens, it picks the better skill in a single forward pass at deployment. Compared with adopting every new skill, it **improves success by 11.0% on `ALFWorld`**, 5.9% on `ScienceWorld`, and 2.7% on `LiveCodeBench`, at low latency and cost.

papers.title: ArcRAG: Agentic Compositional Retrieval over Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) answers questions by retrieving over a knowledge graph built from a corpus. Yet retrieval strategies are designed around the structure their own construction pipeline produces, and whether they survive a change of construction is rarely tested. We study this cross-construction portability: whether one retrieval procedure, with no construction-specific schema, relation names, or retuning, stays effective when the graph is built differently. We introduce ArcRAG, which induces a query-local graph interface at inference time (the node labels, relation descriptors, and property keys reachable from the entities a question names), plans multi-hop traversals against it, and executes and repairs them as Cypher. We build each of the MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and TriviaQA corpora as a schema-guided graph (typed nodes, a closed relation set, source provenance) and as an open-information-extraction graph (untyped nodes, free-text relations), with the retriever's configuration fixed across them. We compare against a construction-agnostic Direct-Cypher agent, ablate each stage across retry and pass budgets on both graph families, and compare with results reported for prior GraphRAG systems, most of which design retrieval together with their own graph construction. Across the two constructions, we find that retrieval need not be co-designed with the graph: query-time interface induction keeps a construction-agnostic retriever effective when the construction changes, although construction still shapes absolute accuracy.
papers.summary: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) systems usually design their retrieval around the structure that their own graph-construction pipeline produces, and the authors ask whether retrieval still works when the graph is built differently. `ArcRAG` builds a query-local view of the graph at inference time (the node labels, relations, and property keys reachable from the entities a question names), plans multi-hop traversals against it, and executes and repairs them as Cypher queries. With its configuration fixed, it is tested on `MuSiQue`, `HotpotQA`, and `TriviaQA` graphs built both with a schema and with open information extraction. The results show that **retrieval need not be co-designed with graph construction**, although the construction method still affects absolute accuracy.

papers.title: What Does Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improve in LLM Agents?
papers.abstract: While multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning (RL) excels on long-horizon tasks, its performance gains remain highly sensitive to interaction constraints. Evaluating across sampling breadth $K$ and interaction depth $T$ via $Pass@(K,T)$, we show that trajectory-level RL advantages depend on sufficient turn budgets, diminishing significantly when budgets tighten. Besides, agentic RL does not uniformly elevate single-step decision quality; rather, its strength concentrates in error recovery and long-horizon resilience. To mitigate the deployment risks caused by this budget dependence, we provide a preliminary discussion on the benefits and limitations of process supervision signals and introduce BudgetMix RL as an alternative that varies interaction budgets during training. Experiments demonstrate that BudgetMix RL achieves robust performance across diverse execution settings. Project Page: https://rethinking-agentic-rl.github.io/
papers.summary: The authors study what multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) actually improves in LLM agents, measuring performance across sampling breadth and interaction depth with a `Pass@(K,T)` metric. They find that **the advantages of trajectory-level RL depend on generous turn budgets and shrink sharply when budgets tighten**. Agentic RL also does not uniformly improve single-step decisions; its gains come mainly from error recovery and resilience over long horizons. To reduce this budget dependence, they discuss process supervision and introduce `BudgetMix RL`, which varies interaction budgets during training and performs robustly across execution settings.

papers.title: LibriSpeech-Real-QA: A Benchmark for Streaming Question Answering
papers.abstract: Most speech large language models (SLMs) still process speech in an offline manner. They only start responding after they receive the complete speech segment. However, many real-world applications require streaming speech interaction, for which the audio continuously flows in and the machine is required to answer questions based on the so far received audio chunks. For example, a user may ask the system to continuously count how many times a person's name has been mentioned while they are speaking. We observe a lack of benchmarks and evaluation protocols for real-time speech interaction. Motivated by this, we propose LibriSpeech-Real-QA, a dataset and a benchmark for real-time speech interaction. We construct different types of real-time question-answer pairs from LibriSpeech to evaluate whether speech LLMs can identify target words in streaming audio. We evaluate several popular real-time commercial models and find that they still tend to respond only after the speech turn has finished. We demonstrate that we can enable a pretrained SLM to perform this task, where we explore several modeling designs and establish a solid baseline for future research.
papers.summary: Most speech large language models process audio offline and respond only after the full utterance, yet many applications need answers about audio while it is still streaming in, such as keeping a running count of how often a name has been said. `LibriSpeech-Real-QA` builds real-time question-answer pairs from `LibriSpeech` to test whether models can track target words in streaming audio. **Popular real-time commercial models still tend to answer only after the speech turn ends.** The authors show that a pretrained speech model can be adapted to the task and compare several modeling designs to set a baseline.

papers.title: CRESiST: Self-Enhancing Explorative Policy Learning for Simultaneous Speech Translation
papers.abstract: Simultaneous Speech Translation (SimulST) requires balancing translation quality and latency. While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in offline translation, current LLM-based SimulST systems predominantly rely on prefix-incremental generation. This paradigm suffers from redundant Key-Value cache recomputation and necessitates external Voice Activity Detection to process unbounded streams. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose an end-to-end interleaved read-write framework built upon an omni-modal LLM. By interleaving speech chunks and text tokens, our architecture achieves full KV cache reuse, natively supporting segmentation-free, infinite-length inference. Furthermore, to learn optimal streaming policies without rigid offline alignments, we introduce a novel Actor-Critic self-enhancement pipeline. An RNN-T Actor dynamically samples read-write trajectories, while an LLM-based Critic evaluates these paths via intrinsic semantic and latency rewards, distilling the optimal policy back to the Actor. Extensive experiments on sentence-level (FLEURS, CoVoST2) and document-level (MuST-C, ACL 60/60) benchmarks demonstrate that our model establishes new state-of-the-art quality-latency Pareto frontiers, substantially outperforming existing cascaded and static-alignment baselines.
papers.summary: Simultaneous speech translation must balance translation quality against latency. Current LLM-based systems regenerate output from growing input prefixes, which wastes Key-Value (KV) cache computation and requires external voice activity detection. `CRESiST` builds on an omni-modal LLM and interleaves speech chunks with text tokens, which allows **full KV cache reuse and segmentation-free translation of arbitrarily long streams**. The read-write policy is learned through an actor-critic loop: an `RNN-T` actor samples read-write trajectories, an LLM critic scores them for semantic quality and latency, and the best policy is distilled back into the actor. The system sets new state-of-the-art quality-latency trade-offs on `FLEURS`, `CoVoST2`, `MuST-C`, and `ACL 60/60`.

papers.title: NaijaFacts: A Framework for Disentangling Language from Knowledge in Facts about Nigeria
papers.abstract: Multilingual benchmarks for African languages mostly translate generic questions into local languages, measuring linguistic competence but not whether models know facts about Africa. We introduce \naija, a benchmark of factual and statistical questions about Nigeria, authored by native speakers and grounded in authoritative official statistics, with every question available in English, Nigerian Pidgin, \yoruba, Igbo, and Hausa. Answering similar questions for the UK and US yields a country by language matrix that disentangles a language effect (the model knows the fact but degrades in a low-resource language) from a knowledge effect (the fact is absent in every language). Across eight frontier and Nigeria-adapted models, the knowledge effect dominates: English-query accuracy is 49--50\% for the US/UK but 20\% for Nigeria. The language effect is smaller and tracks web representation, degrading from English to \yoruba{} (9 points on Nigeria, up to 24 on US/UK questions). We find scale does not help: the strongest models reach 66--79\% on the UK and the US but none exceed 31\% on Nigerian statistics. Extending to all 54 African countries with our best performing frontier model shows the same profile continent-wide, 96\% on culture and 98\% on politics against 26\% on statistics, so the gap is not specific to Nigeria.
papers.summary: Most African-language benchmarks translate generic questions, so they measure language ability rather than knowledge about Africa. `NaijaFacts` contains factual and statistical questions about Nigeria, written by native speakers and grounded in official statistics, in English, Nigerian Pidgin, Yoruba, Igbo, and Hausa; matching UK and US question sets separate a language effect from a knowledge effect. Across eight models the knowledge gap dominates: **no model exceeds 31% on Nigerian statistics, while the strongest models reach 66–79% on UK and US questions**, and scale does not close the gap. Extending the test to all 54 African countries shows the same pattern, with high accuracy on culture and politics but only 26% on statistics.

papers.title: Dialect Matters: A Dialect-Aware Baseline for Igala-English Machine Translation
papers.abstract: The massive permeability of intelligent systems in every sphere of human activities have greatly enhanced clarity, ease of work, and increased general global understanding which has significantly awaken the use of intelligent systems by all users. Intelligent systems greatly rely on precise dataset/corpus for the correctness of their output. Despite efforts by researchers to address Low-resource language in the Natural Language Processing (NLP), Igala still has zero parallel corpora despite efforts by researchers. We present a dialect-aware baseline for Igala-English machine translation, among first open systems and first with dialectal variation analysis. Our dataset of 1137 sentences (899 training) is first with dialect tags: Idah 459 (40.4%), Ankpa 297 (26.1%), Ibaji 160 (14.1%), Other 187 (16.4%), Ogugu 32 (2.8%). Same English yields 20-60 Igala forms. Mixed-dialect training achieves balanced BLEU 11.66 versus Idah-only model which drops 4.7 BLEU on Ibaji (13.2 on Idah, 8.5 on Ibaji), proving dialect fairness requires mixing. Fine-tuned from Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-mul (78M), epoch ablation shows convergence at 8 epochs and overfitting at 15. BLEU 11.66, chrF 46.69. Analysis shows 899 sentences on log-linear trend consistent with African low-resource literature. This work provides first dialectal impact analysis for Igala and establishes baseline for future work.
papers.summary: Igala, a Nigerian language, has had no parallel corpus for machine translation. The authors build a 1,137-sentence Igala-English dataset tagged by dialect (Idah, Ankpa, Ibaji, Ogugu, and others) and fine-tune `Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-mul` on it. Training on mixed dialects gives balanced performance (BLEU 11.66, chrF 46.69), whereas **an Idah-only model drops 4.7 BLEU on the Ibaji dialect**, which the authors take as evidence that dialect fairness requires mixed-dialect training data.

papers.title: When Do Summaries Become Instructions? Unsupported Policy in LLM Agents' Self-Written Handoff Summaries
papers.abstract: Long-running LLM agents compact their context, replacing most history with a summary. We ask whether handoff summaries state permissions or requirements the record does not support, whether such sentences change what the next instance (the successor) does, and where they come from. Synthetic tool-use tasks carry a ground-truth permission ledger; same-snapshot replay reruns the successor with those whole sentences replaced by neutral filler. Two AI readers, reading only rule-flagged held-out summaries, confirmed unsupported restrictions in 1.2% and 2.4% of all readable summaries from two open-weight models, and unsupported authorizations in 0.1% and 1.3%. For restrictions, a pre-specified replay test was not significant (p = 0.58); a follow-up, planned after it, found a fragile effect (p = 0.027). Neutralizing false approvals cut unauthorized actions from 24 to 7 of 120 held-out runs (post hoc; later set: 17 to 11 of 48). Most development restrictions followed the agent's earlier reasoning that an action needs approval (post hoc). In pre-specified tests, replacing the system prompt's "Some actions need approval." with one saying where requirements come from cut unsupported restrictions from 5.0% to 1.8% of development summaries and, on held-out templates, from 1.8% to 0.3% (both p < 10^-9), while requests for approvals the ledger requires barely changed. Code and data: https://github.com/Chuw1/handoff-audit
papers.summary: Long-running LLM agents compact their context into handoff summaries, and this study checks whether those summaries invent permissions or restrictions that the record does not support, and whether this changes what the next agent instance does. Using synthetic tool-use tasks with a ground-truth permission ledger, plus replays in which suspect sentences are replaced with neutral filler, the authors find unsupported restrictions in 1.2–2.4% of summaries and unsupported authorizations in 0.1–1.3%. Neutralizing false approvals cut unauthorized actions from 24 to 7 of 120 held-out runs, though that analysis was post hoc. In pre-specified tests, rewording the system prompt to say where approval requirements come from **cut unsupported restrictions from 1.8% to 0.3% of summaries on held-out templates**, without reducing legitimate approval requests.

papers.title: Replicability, Reproducibility, and Robustness in Political and Social Science Research with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This chapter addresses the central reproducibility problem of research with large language models. LLM output is probabilistic and varies across models and versions, which can have significant effects on downstream statistical results. The chapter distinguishes between replicability, reproducibility, and robustness, and proposes a probabilistic standard based on the distribution of results, not identical outputs. It introduces a standardized prompt script, tests within-model variation for encoders and decoders, and develops error-structure analysis to diagnose where models err and whether their errors align. Using three datasets, the chapter shows that measurement choice can reverse the sign of downstream regression coefficients. Existing design-based corrections with gold-labeled subsamples restore validity, but come at the cost of estimate precision. The main contribution of the chapter is a stacked ensemble of open-weight models that improves precision in the correction step while retaining estimate validity.
papers.summary: LLM outputs are probabilistic and change across models and versions, which threatens the reproducibility of social-science findings built on LLM-based measurement. This chapter separates replicability, reproducibility, and robustness, proposes judging reproducibility by the distribution of results rather than identical outputs, and introduces a standardized prompt script along with an analysis of where models make errors. On three datasets, **the choice of measurement model can reverse the sign of downstream regression coefficients**. Design-based corrections that use gold-labeled subsamples restore validity at a cost in precision, and a stacked ensemble of open-weight models recovers much of that precision.

papers.title: Beyond accuracy: what AI assurance needs to establish in public services
papers.abstract: Public bodies increasingly rely on AI-produced evidence, including classifications, summaries and assessments. These outputs can inform policy decisions and service delivery, making their reliability a matter of public accountability. Establishing whether this evidence can be relied upon requires testing its outputs and examining how organisations decide whether those tests are sufficient. We combine technical evaluation with analysis of AI governance requirements, informed by measurement theory and management-based regulation. We compare eight GPT-4o configurations classifying 1,200 UK Prime Minister's Questions into 21 policy topics, against human-coded labels and across unchanged repeats. Accuracy ranges from 68.2% to 70.3%, yet 24.3% of questions receive different labels, with changes in topic shares and rankings. Configurations agree more with one another than with human coding: agreement does not guarantee correctness. Under the implemented score-extraction procedure, the proportion flagged for human review ranges from 0.9% to 41.0%. We analyse 37 UK and EU policy documents. Both sets expect testing and oversight, but reporting expectations do not consistently cover changing answers, shared errors, selective evaluation, substantive conclusions or review routing. Some UK guidance explicitly addresses stability. The UK sample emphasises public bodies checking their own use; the EU places substantial testing duties on providers while leaving them important choices about measures and acceptance thresholds. Without appropriate checks, evidence could misrepresent policy issues, redirect attention or resources, and leave errors undetected. Public policy should require organisations to justify reliance through checks beyond aggregate accuracy, clear responsibility, access to expertise and scrutiny of results.
papers.summary: Public bodies increasingly act on AI-generated classifications and summaries, and this study asks what it would take to establish that such evidence is reliable. Eight `GPT-4o` configurations classified 1,200 UK Prime Minister's Questions into 21 policy topics, with accuracy between 68.2% and 70.3%, yet **24.3% of questions received different labels across configurations and unchanged repeats**. The configurations agreed more with each other than with human coders, showing that agreement does not guarantee correctness. A review of 37 UK and EU policy documents finds that reporting expectations often omit unstable answers, shared errors, and how outputs are routed to human review.

papers.title: ALTO: African and Levantine Tech-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence Corpus
papers.abstract: Tech-facilitated gender based violence (TFGBV) is a pervasive online harm affecting women and gender minority groups through its many direct and covert forms. Current models and annotated datasets for gendered harm detection are dominated by data from, and models trained in, Global North languages. In collaboration with civil society organizations (CSOs) from Jordan, Francophone West Africa, and Kenya, we developed a community-led approach to crowdsource culturally and linguistically relevant instances of TFGBV in Levantine Arabic, African French, and Swahili. We annotated the crowdsourced data using active learning to develop a small but performant dataset (N=3022) called ALTO to improve TFGBV detection in the three languages. Through benchmarking and fine-tuning experiments, we show that existing harmful content detection models show poor TFGBV recall within ALTO and improve with fine-tuning. We found that models often miss covert harms across all languages, while error rates are markedly higher in Swahili. We report the experimental results and release the annotation taxonomy, dataset, and trained models.
papers.summary: Detection of tech-facilitated gender-based violence (TFGBV) relies mostly on data and models from Global North languages. Working with civil society organizations in Jordan, Francophone West Africa, and Kenya, the authors crowdsourced and annotated, using active learning, `ALTO`, a 3,022-item dataset in Levantine Arabic, African French, and Swahili. **Existing harmful-content detectors show poor recall on `ALTO`** and improve with fine-tuning, but they still often miss covert harms, with error rates markedly higher in Swahili. The taxonomy, dataset, and trained models are released.

papers.title: Reasoning over Non-Parametric Memory in Multilingual LLMs: A Cognitive-Based Analysis of Relational Knowledge
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assumes that language models can reason over relations stated in their context rather than fall back on associations memorized during pretraining. We study this evidence-conditioned relational reasoning in isolation, with the facts supplied directly in the prompt rather than retrieved. \textsc{Rel-Bloom} is a controlled multilingual diagnostic of 450 multiple-choice questions built from 30 Wikidata relations; the same source relations are instantiated at five Bloom-inspired levels (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate) and under three veracity conditions (Factual, Counterfactual, Neutralized). Across 43 models, six languages, and two multilingual settings (226,800 predictions), three findings stand out. First, accuracy drops sharply from Apply to Analyze in every evaluated open-weight model series, reaching 47.2 percentage points for the Large Granite bucket, but not for either Gemini model. Second, Evaluate items remain a bottleneck even for models near ceiling on the other task types: Gemini~3.1 Pro averages 99.5\% on the other four levels but 60.7\% on Evaluate. Third, item- and relation-level difficulty rankings are consistently preserved across languages, indicating a difficulty structure partly shared across languages within this benchmark. Across knowledge conditions, Counterfactual contexts are generally harder than Factual ones, while removing entity identities can improve higher-level performance in some model regimes. Greater model capability therefore does not by itself ensure reliable reasoning over supplied relational evidence. Relevant resources are available at: https://huggingface.co/spaces/QCRI/non-parametric-memory-relational-reasoning.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assumes models reason over relations given in their context instead of relying on facts memorized during pretraining. The authors test this directly by placing the facts in the prompt. Their diagnostic, `Rel-Bloom`, has 450 multiple-choice questions built from 30 `Wikidata` relations. Each relation appears at five Bloom-inspired cognitive levels and under factual, counterfactual, and neutralized conditions. Across 43 models and six languages, every open-weight model series shows a sharp accuracy drop from Apply to Analyze, but neither `Gemini` model does. Evaluate items remain a bottleneck even for the strongest model: **`Gemini 3.1 Pro` averages 99.5% on the other four levels but 60.7% on Evaluate**. Difficulty rankings stay consistent across languages, and counterfactual contexts are generally harder than factual ones.

papers.title: Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit
papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.
papers.summary: In streaming video understanding, a model must repeatedly decide whether to respond or keep watching. Existing reinforcement learning approaches based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) assign one shared advantage to every turn in a trajectory, which can reward redundant replies and penalize useful follow-ups. `TurnWise` assigns credit per turn instead: it scores prefixes completed with silence to build group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return. It also averages token losses within each turn, so responding and waiting carry equal weight regardless of output length. The method needs no learned critic or extra rollouts and **outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding**.

papers.title: Template Gap Reconstruction for Shell Output Simulation with Small Language Models
papers.abstract: Small language models offer a compact basis for shell simulation without executing submitted commands, but full-output decoding requires them to predict recurring utility structure alongside content that varies across executions. We introduce template gap reconstruction (TGR), which supplies reusable output literals interspersed with sentinels to be interleaved with autoregressively generated gaps. A template selector chooses which template to be reconstructed, with the empty template retaining full-output decoding. We construct a template bank from 18.7 million outputs collected across heterogeneous execution environments and train a template selector and five reconstruction models initialized from various small language model checkpoints on a target environment excluded from bank construction. Evaluation demonstrates that TGR improves output edit similarity (O-ES) over full-output decoding (FOD) when the optimal template covers more than 25\% of the template, while performing similarly for lower-coverage outputs. Additionally, TGR outperforms FOD for shorter gap sequences, with O-ES values of 0.964 and 0.812, respectively, while maintaining similar performance for longer sequences. TGR reduces the number of tokens generated by 26.3--38.3\% across used tokenizer families. These results support using a reusable output structure as a practical design choice for small shell simulators, improving response fidelity and shortening generation targets while keeping template selection and residual prediction central to response quality.
papers.summary: Small language models can simulate shell output without executing commands, but generating the full output forces them to predict both the recurring structure of a utility's output and the content that varies between runs. Template gap reconstruction (`TGR`) supplies reusable output literals with placeholder slots, and the model generates only the gaps. A template selector picks a template from a bank built from 18.7 million outputs, or picks an empty template to fall back to full-output decoding. For short gap sequences, `TGR` reaches **an output edit similarity of 0.964 versus 0.812 for full-output decoding**. It also cuts generated tokens by 26.3–38.3%.

papers.title: Ranking Agreement Does Not Reveal Paragraph-Edit Agreement in Two Released Paper Acceptance Predictors
papers.abstract: A fast acceptance classifier could select revisions for a slower evaluator. We ask whether agreement on existing papers supports that use. We compare a classifier of word and document features with two released text-only acceptance predictors fine-tuned from the same language model with three billion parameters. For 198 papers from the International Conference on Learning Representations, we compare model rankings of the original papers and of paragraph rewrites screened automatically for unchanged facts, claim strength, and attribution. The classifier ranks original papers closely with one predictor and moderately with the other, but shows no detectable agreement with either on which rewrites raise scores. The tests specified in advance used reduced numerical precision. Rounding error dominated the small score responses. We therefore rescored the released weights in full 32-bit precision as a post hoc check; edit agreement remained near zero. At this precision, when each predictor chooses among five rewrites per paper, its average raw score is under two points out of 100 higher than with random choice. The evidence covers presentation rewrites and two open predictors from one family; transfer to costly evaluators remains untested. Revision selectors should therefore be checked against the intended evaluator on the revisions they rank.
papers.summary: A fast classifier that predicts paper acceptance could be used to choose which revisions to send to a slower evaluator, but only if it agrees with that evaluator about edits. The authors compare a classifier built on word and document features with two released 3-billion-parameter acceptance predictors on 198 `ICLR` papers and fact-preserving paragraph rewrites. The classifier ranks the original papers similarly to the predictors but shows **no detectable agreement on which rewrites raise scores**. The result holds after rescoring in full 32-bit precision, and choosing the best of five rewrites gains under two points out of 100 over random choice. The authors conclude that revision selectors must be validated against the intended evaluator on the revisions themselves.

papers.title: Measuring Risk, Not Harm: Detecting Psychological Harm Risk Factors in LLM Conversations
papers.abstract: Psychological harms from interactions with large language models cannot be monitored directly because they may emerge over repeated interactions and depend strongly on subjective individual user context. We propose measuring risk, not harm: detecting observable AI behaviors that constitute risk factors for psychological harm at the AI response level and aggregating these signals to support longitudinal monitoring. We operationalize eight such behaviors and construct a synthetic multi-label corpus of 47,062 AI responses and 373,873 response-factor labels, with targeted human annotations for validation and evaluation. We then compare trained embedding-based classifiers, direct LLM judging, and a classifier--judge cascade. All detectors are model-agnostic and operate only on LLM outputs, requiring no access to internal model states. We apply these detectors to several out-of-distribution human-AI conversation data sets from prior research. On held-out human-labeled data, the best cascade achieves macro precision of 0.86, recall of 0.76, and F1 of 0.79. On WildChat, it reduces LLM-judge calls by 97.1\% relative to direct judging. On DelusionEval, risk-factor detections cluster within conversations. Together, our results show that response-level behavioral risk-factor detection can provide a scalable measurement layer for longitudinal psychological-safety monitoring without conflating observable AI behavior with latent user harm.
papers.summary: Psychological harm from large language model (LLM) interactions can emerge gradually and depends on each user's context, so it is hard to measure directly. The authors instead detect eight observable AI behaviors that are risk factors for harm, scored per response and aggregated for longitudinal monitoring. They build a synthetic corpus of 47,062 labeled responses and compare embedding classifiers, direct LLM judging, and a cascade that combines a classifier with a judge. The best cascade reaches a macro F1 of 0.79 on held-out human-labeled data. On `WildChat`, it **cuts LLM-judge calls by 97.1%** compared with judging every response directly.

papers.title: LLMs Don't Know What They Know: Benchmarking Temporal Self-Knowledge for Financial Backtesting
papers.abstract: Financial backtests of large language models (LLMs) are meaningful only if the model did not already know the outcomes it is asked to predict. Practitioners guard against this by trusting a vendor's stated knowledge cutoff, by asking the model what it knows, or by instructing it to answer as of a past date. To verify whether any of these safeguards can be trusted, we introduce FinDendro, a benchmark of 2,226 dated U.S. facts from 1999 to 2026, covering monthly macroeconomic series, month-end stock prices and Federal Reserve decisions. Each fact yields four prompts: a value question, Recall and Predict questions that pair each candidate value with a claim of knowing or guessing without a declared date, and a Predict question with a historical declared date. Controls for persistence and dominant outcomes keep chance accuracy near 0.27. Results show that for most frontier models, self-reports understate knowledge. GPT-5 answers 76% of controlled facts correctly but claims to know 38%, and answers 61% of the facts it says it does not know. Knowledge claims can persist beyond the measured knowledge boundary, by up to seven quarters, and a declared date removes most of the claims of prior knowledge while leaving accuracy unchanged. Backtests inside a model's training window therefore cannot be certified leak-free by self-report, instruction or stated cutoff. These findings motivate behavioral measurement of temporal knowledge boundaries, and FinDendro provides a benchmark and procedure for selecting backtest periods based on demonstrated factual knowledge.
papers.summary: Financial backtests of large language models (LLMs) are valid only if the model did not already know the outcomes. Practitioners usually guard against leakage by trusting stated knowledge cutoffs, asking the model what it knows, or telling it to answer as of a past date. `FinDendro` tests these safeguards with 2,226 dated U.S. macroeconomic, stock-price, and Federal Reserve facts from 1999 to 2026. For most frontier models, self-reports understate knowledge: **`GPT-5` answers 76% of controlled facts correctly but claims to know only 38%**. It also answers 61% of the facts it says it does not know. Knowledge claims can persist up to seven quarters past the measured boundary, and declaring a historical date suppresses claims of prior knowledge without changing accuracy.

papers.title: SAUCE: Summary Analysis Using Conversation Entailment
papers.abstract: With the growing need for evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) and their applications to speech, challenges persist in summarizing and evaluating conversations that lack a clear end goal. We introduce SAUCE -- a reference-free, fact-based evaluation pipeline for cross-lingual conversational speech summarization. It measures the accuracy and the fact coverage of a summary through the entailment between conversation and text. We compare SAUCE against several popular summarization metrics and demonstrate the effectiveness of capturing information loss due to transcription and translation error and identifying broken summaries. Crucially, unlike black-box LLM evaluators or dense embedding metrics, SAUCE is inherently explainable: it maps summary scores to discrete, verifiable facts, allowing users to pinpoint exact hallucinations or omissions. We illustrate how this interpretability helps developers systematically profile LLM behaviors and gives end-users an actionable tool to verify summary accuracy in noisy, real-world conditions. Preliminary investigations show SAUCE strongly align with human judgment.
papers.summary: Evaluating summaries of open-ended conversations is hard, especially for cross-lingual speech where transcription and translation errors add noise. `SAUCE` is a reference-free evaluation pipeline that measures a summary's accuracy and fact coverage through entailment between the conversation and the summary text. Because scores map to discrete, checkable facts, users can pinpoint specific hallucinations or omissions, which black-box LLM judges and embedding metrics do not allow. Compared with popular summarization metrics, it better captures information loss and broken summaries, and preliminary results show **strong alignment with human judgment**.

papers.title: LooM: Loop-Invariant Memory for Causal Encoder-Decoder Language Models
papers.abstract: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by re-executing shared layers, but three limitations hinder their adoption: memory grows with the loop count, compute can only be adjusted in whole-block steps, and the loop count is hard to change after training. We propose LooM (Loop-invariant Memory), which addresses each in turn. In a causal encoder-decoder (CED), LooM loops only the decoder layers after the first, which read a global memory written once per token, and each of them publishes the key-value (KV) entry for a token only on its first visit, so the cache does not grow with the loop count. These layers loop independently, providing every budget from 3 to 21 layer executions per token, and one model trained on randomly sampled budgets covers all of them without a router. With enough loops, LooM outperforms a single-pass baseline trained on the same data on language modeling, zero-shot accuracy and long-context perplexity, while using the same cache size. Our analysis further shows that the training budget distribution decides what extra depth buys. These results suggest that a CED is a natural place to loop: memory is written once, and depth becomes a budget chosen at deployment.
papers.summary: Looped Transformers gain depth by re-running shared layers, but their memory grows with the loop count, compute can only change in whole-block steps, and the loop count is hard to change after training. `LooM` (Loop-invariant Memory) loops only the later decoder layers of a causal encoder-decoder, and each layer writes a token's key-value cache entry only on its first visit. As a result, **the cache does not grow with the number of loops**. A single model trained on randomly sampled budgets supports any budget from 3 to 21 layer executions per token without a router. With enough loops, it beats a single-pass baseline on language modeling, zero-shot accuracy, and long-context perplexity at the same cache size.

papers.title: Before You Continue: Evaluating Time-Sensitive Safety Awareness in Conversational Assistants
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) assistants increasingly help users with everyday activities that involve time-dependent constraints. However, users may not mention these constraints in later requests, requiring assistants to recognize and adjust their advice accordingly. To evaluate such capability, we introduce TASC (Temporal Action Safety in Conversation), a benchmark that evaluates whether LLMs apply time-dependent constraints when responding to conversational requests. TASC consists of 3,418 inputs derived from 128 templates, along with a separate set of 33 scenarios designed to compare models' ability to calculate elapsed time with their ability to apply that information. Across 13 models, assistants account for time-dependent constraints in only 30.5% of cases where the proposed action violates a rule, while rarely warning users unnecessarily. More importantly, models fail to apply these constraints in 62.1% of cases despite correctly calculating the elapsed time. Explicitly providing the timing resolves only about half of these failures, revealing a gap between temporal reasoning and its application in conversational advice.
papers.summary: LLM assistants often help with everyday tasks that involve time-dependent constraints, and users may not restate those constraints in later requests. `TASC` (Temporal Action Safety in Conversation) tests whether assistants apply such constraints, using 3,418 inputs from 128 templates plus 33 scenarios that separate computing elapsed time from acting on it. Across 13 models, assistants account for the constraint in only 30.5% of cases where the proposed action violates a rule, while rarely issuing unnecessary warnings. **Models fail to apply the constraint in 62.1% of cases even after correctly computing the elapsed time**, and stating the timing explicitly fixes only about half of these failures.

papers.title: Persona Perspectives: Adopting Viewpoints Reorganizes Representations in LLMs
papers.abstract: Common methods for monitoring features in large language models (LLMs) such as linear probes and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) assume that features maintain a consistent representation across contexts. LLMs, however, can flexibly adopt different perspectives or "personas" that suggest different underlying systems of conceptual relations. In this paper, we examine whether prompting an LLM to adopt a persona alters the representational geometry of the model's latent space. We extract representations of over 9,000 common words and 33 semantic axes from models adopting liberal and conservative political personas and compare these against two neutral baselines. We find that persona conditioning systematically alters both the projections of words onto semantic axes and the alignments among the axes themselves in directions consistent with the specified ideology. We then test the implications of this reorganization for two safety-relevant features: truthfulness and morality. Linear probes, SAE-based classifiers, and classifiers built from manually selected word representations, all trained without a persona, produce divergent results when applied to models conditioned on political personas, producing politically slanted ratings of truth and morality on controversial statements. These findings suggest that internal representations, as they are conventionally extracted, can exhibit different geometric relations when the model adopts personas, potentially undermining monitoring efforts.
papers.summary: Monitoring tools such as linear probes and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) assume that features keep the same representation across contexts. The authors test this by prompting models to adopt liberal or conservative personas and measuring how more than 9,000 words project onto 33 semantic axes. **Persona conditioning systematically reshapes the representational geometry** in directions that match the assigned ideology. As a result, truthfulness and morality probes, SAE-based classifiers, and word-based classifiers trained without a persona give politically slanted ratings on controversial statements when applied to models with a persona. This suggests that conventionally extracted features may be unreliable monitoring tools when a model takes on a persona.

papers.title: LongBanana: An Expert-Verified Benchmark for Long-Context Multi-Reference Image Synthesis
papers.abstract: We introduce LongBanana, to our knowledge the first expert-designed and expert-verified benchmark for long-context multi-reference image synthesis in the age of agent-driven image generation. The task requires retrieving dispersed visual evidence, rejecting distractors, binding entities and relations, and composing one coherent final image from multiple references. LongBanana contains 90 carefully designed tasks organized by a 3-by-3 taxonomy; each task includes about 32 reference images, 20 constraints, and 50 evaluation items, yielding 4,670 expert-specified atomic evaluation items in total. Its graph-grounded evaluation design instantiates each task with reference images and an entity-relation graph, then converts node, edge, and whole-graph obligations into checklist items for Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction. Reviewed expert labels include a 15% double-labeled subset with 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted kappa. We further introduce LongBanana-Gen, an agent-harness framework for long-horizon image generation; experiments show that minimal agent harnesses improve over direct generation, while a ReAct-Plan-Exec-Reflect (RPR) workflow yields harness-dependent gains by strengthening evidence grounding and repair. Together, LongBanana provides an auditable testbed for measuring dense visual evidence use and a shared target for developing stronger agent-driven image-generation systems. Code and data are available at the project page: https://long-banana.com/.
papers.summary: `LongBanana` is an expert-designed, expert-verified benchmark for composing one image from many reference images. Models must retrieve scattered visual evidence, reject distractors, and bind entities and their relations. It has 90 tasks, each with about 32 reference images, and 4,670 atomic checklist items derived from an entity-relation graph. The checklist scores content fidelity, relational binding, and global constraint satisfaction, and double-labeled items show 89.4% exact agreement. The accompanying `LongBanana-Gen` framework shows that **even minimal agent harnesses beat direct generation**. A `ReAct-Plan-Exec-Reflect` workflow adds further gains that depend on the harness.

papers.title: Balancing hierarchical representation and quantization: A performance trade-off in text embeddings
papers.abstract: Hierarchical text embedding models offer variable-length representations, while quantization reduces numerical precision; both aim to improve computational efficiency. This work is an empirical benchmark study of how these two orthogonal, already-established techniques interact. We evaluate 38 tasks from the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) using four transformer-based embedding models, covering 1D and 2D hierarchical representations combined with 32-bit, 8-bit, and binary quantization, for 168 configurations per task. We report each efficiency dimension separately: theoretical per-vector storage and end-to-end evaluation time. Under a Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc analysis, int8 quantization is statistically indistinguishable from float32 for pair classification and re-ranking and costs at most 1.5 percentage points overall, whereas binary quantization is significantly worse across every task category. Halving the embedding dimension once is not statistically detectable above $m=16$; two successive halvings always are. Combining an 8x dimensionality reduction with int8 yields a 32x reduction in per-vector storage at 94.4% of baseline effectiveness. Because evaluation times were measured once, we treat them as indicative: we find no evidence that quantization speeds up evaluation, whereas sampling from intermediate layers shortens it substantially. Retrieval degrades far faster than every other category, so we report findings per task category.
papers.summary: This benchmark study measures how hierarchical (variable-length) text embeddings interact with quantization across 38 `MTEB` tasks, four embedding models, and 168 configurations per task. Under Friedman and Nemenyi statistical tests, int8 quantization is statistically indistinguishable from float32 for pair classification and re-ranking and costs at most 1.5 percentage points overall. Binary quantization is significantly worse in every task category. **Combining an 8x dimension reduction with int8 gives a 32x reduction in per-vector storage while keeping 94.4% of baseline effectiveness**. Retrieval degrades much faster than other categories, and the authors found no evidence that quantization speeds up evaluation.

papers.title: SpecCompact: Accelerating LLM Agent Context Compaction with Slot-Parallel Semantic Speculative Verification
papers.abstract: LLM agents use context compaction to manage growing interaction histories, but summarizing long histories with large models can introduce substantial delays. Compaction therefore requires balancing information retention against latency. We observe that structured summary slots can retain information when generated independently. Based on this observation, we present SpecCompact, a framework that accelerates compaction through slot-parallel semantic speculation. SpecCompact fine-tunes a small drafter and generates slots in parallel. The target model verifies each proposed line and repairs rejected content, while subsequent drafting uses the updated slot prefix. System optimizations further reduce repeated context processing and model calls. Across AppWorld and $\tau^3$ benchmarks with two target models, SpecCompact achieves $2.04$--$5.63\times$ compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization. Separate downstream evaluations reveal model- and task-dependent performance trade-offs. A user study within Hermes further shows an $8.68\times$ median compaction speedup.
papers.summary: LLM agents compact their growing interaction histories into summaries, but summarizing long histories with a large model adds substantial latency. `SpecCompact` relies on the observation that structured summary slots can be generated independently. A fine-tuned small drafter writes all slots in parallel, and the large target model verifies each proposed line and repairs rejected content. Additional system optimizations avoid reprocessing the same context. On `AppWorld` and `τ³` with two target models, it achieves **2.04–5.63x faster compaction than Hermes-style summarization**, with downstream trade-offs that vary by model and task. A user study inside Hermes showed an 8.68x median speedup.

papers.title: A Framework for Context Enrichment and Selective Robustness in LLM Social Agents
papers.abstract: Researchers use large language models as agents in social simulations, where agents are prompted with observations and background information intended to shape their actions. Yet LLM agents have been shown to substantially change their behavior under meaning-preserving prompt variations, creating a validation problem for social simulation. One plausible hypothesis is that this brittleness reflects a lack of grounding and can be reduced by enriching the context provided to the agents. Whether richer context improves robustness remains unclear, in part because context richness and robustness are rarely defined in ways that support controlled comparisons. We address the first need with controlled context enrichment, a set of prompt substitution rules that systematically enriches distinct types of context: neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, and normative decision grounding. We address the second by introducing selective robustness as a validation criterion: insensitivity to meaning-preserving prompt variation combined with a directional response to decision-relevant changes in the social world. We demonstrate the framework in a Prisoner's Dilemma-like game, showing how it can be used to identify which forms of context enrichment produce more desirable and robust agent behavior. We find that these forms of enrichment produce distinct behavioral patterns that vary between the two models tested.
papers.summary: LLM agents in social simulations often change behavior under prompt rewordings that preserve meaning, which makes the simulations hard to validate. The authors propose controlled context enrichment, a set of prompt substitution rules that add neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, or normative decision grounding. They also define **selective robustness**: an agent should ignore meaning-preserving prompt changes but respond in the expected direction to decision-relevant changes in the social world. In a game resembling the Prisoner's Dilemma, each type of enrichment produces distinct behavior patterns, and the patterns differ between the two models tested.

papers.title: Reading a neuron's tuning from its correlations with other neurons
papers.abstract: What a neuron represents is usually established by relating its activity to a stimulus. We ask whether the same facts are contained in the correlation matrix of a recorded population, which keeps the pairwise relations among the neurons and discards the stimulus. A transformer that sees only the correlation matrix of 512 sampled neurons, with no labels and no reference population in its input, decodes the preferred orientation of mouse visual cortex neurons from in-vivo MICrONS responses to a mean error of 25{\deg} (uninformed: 45{\deg}; best constant guess: 41{\deg}) and their receptive-field position at R^2 = 0.23; on the digital-twin substrate, 20{\deg} and 0.48. Asked whether a neuron prefers horizontal or vertical, it is right for 79% of neurons in vivo and 87% on the twin, against 56% for the majority answer; it does not resolve the obliques. The ordering is recoverable because the relations between orientation classes are close to circulant, which fixes the class structure up to rotation and reflection; the rotation of the frame is recoverable only because of a departure from that symmetry. The departure survives equal representation of every orientation and disjoint training and test stimuli, and it is an anisotropy of the signal correlations: in V1 the neurons preferring the dominant orientation have the most similar responses to one another, and a model population with only that property recovers the frame. Across 33 mice of the Allen Brain Observatory, with relations from drifting gratings, orientation transfers to unseen animals only when a sampled population mixes animals; populations drawn from one animal are not decoded measurably below the best constant, a limit of the diversity of populations one animal provides. For receptive fields, what crosses animals is where each animal's imaged patch looks on the screen, not the layout of neurons within it.
papers.summary: The authors ask whether a neuron's stimulus tuning can be recovered from the correlation matrix of a recorded population alone, with the stimulus discarded. A transformer that sees only correlations among 512 sampled neurons decodes preferred orientation in mouse visual cortex from in-vivo `MICrONS` data with a mean error of 25 degrees, versus 41 degrees for the best constant guess. It classifies horizontal versus vertical preference correctly for **79% of neurons in vivo**. Recovering the orientation frame depends on an anisotropy in signal correlations. Transfer to unseen animals in the `Allen Brain Observatory` works only when sampled populations mix animals.

papers.title: A minimal dynamical model of human-AI cognitive coevolution
papers.abstract: The rapid deployment of generative AI raises the question of whether pervasive cognitive offloading drives a measurable, potentially irreversible decline in unassisted human reasoning. We examine this question with a phenomenological dynamical model based on the Cattell-Horn-Carroll distinction between fluid intelligence ($G_f$) and crystallized intelligence ($G_c$). Starting from the discrete-time Bivariate Latent Change Score formalism used in cognitive-aging research, we derive its continuous-time linear counterpart and introduce a fast third variable representing composite machine-intelligence capability. The machine variable enters the human subsystem through Hill-function modifications of the self-feedback and cross-coupling coefficients. We emphasize that our phenomenological model captures both the positive and negative effects of AI on human cognition. By formalizing the qualitative concepts of positive and negative impacts, we introduce definitions for AI-induced cognitive decline and AI-induced cognitive augmentation. A singular-perturbation reduction, justified via Tikhonov's theorem, collapses the resulting three-dimensional system onto a two-dimensional slow manifold. On this manifold we locate two bifurcations of the equilibrium. In one parameter regime, weakening the contribution of fluid reasoning to crystallized knowledge produces a saddle-node bifurcation that eliminates the stable positive equilibrium. In another, reversing the contribution of crystallized knowledge to fluid reasoning creates opposing feedback; increasing fluid self-feedback then reduces damping and produces a supercritical Hopf bifurcation with a stable periodic orbit. We discuss limitations and future directions, interpret our results as a phenomenological account of a coupled socio-technical system, and state the conditions under which each dynamical regime applies.
papers.summary: To study whether widespread cognitive offloading to AI could erode unassisted human reasoning, the authors build a phenomenological dynamical model that couples fluid and crystallized intelligence with a fast-changing machine-capability variable. The model extends the Bivariate Latent Change Score formalism from cognitive-aging research to continuous time and defines both AI-induced cognitive decline and AI-induced augmentation. A singular-perturbation reduction leaves a two-dimensional system with two bifurcations. **A saddle-node bifurcation can eliminate the stable positive equilibrium**, and a supercritical Hopf bifurcation can produce sustained oscillations. The authors state the parameter conditions under which each regime applies.

papers.title: ApproxBrain: Certified Sufficiency Frontiers in Connectome-Constrained Neural Systems
papers.abstract: Background. A connectome specifies the substrate available to a nervous system, not how much of it a given computation requires. Reported compact sufficient circuits are point estimates: one subset, one task, one fidelity threshold, one parameterisation. Methods. We formalise computational sufficiency as a cost-indexed family of neuron subsets conditioned on a task and a tolerance pair (permitted degradation epsilon, permitted failure fraction rho), separate task adequacy from phenotype fidelity, and certify candidates on held-out parameter draws with one-sided bounds rather than reporting a single minimum. We measure three quantities a single circuit cannot express: non-decomposability, degeneracy, and an intervention-derived role taxonomy. Results. On a released walking simulator, the published 148-neuron circuit is certified sufficient with margin (mean Dtask = 0.017 over 32 held-out draws, no failure), no 146- or 147-neuron subset of it is sufficient, and removing any one of its three interneurons destroys adequacy. Complement splitting recovers the published set exactly in three of seven seeds and reaches its size in five, within 66-97 evaluations, against 221 neurons for the bundle hierarchy at the same budget. Varying only the task changes which neurons are needed: our best-found solutions retain 155 and 149 neurons and share only 3 of 11 searchable neurons. Relaxing the tolerance reveals alternative sufficient circuits, and the whole-CNS interface alone fails every replicate while 93 search-chosen neurons give a certified solution. Conclusions. Sufficiency is set-valued and conditioned jointly on task and tolerance, and no single search strategy dominates across regimes. A frontier is interpretable only alongside its interface-only baseline, its tolerance and its budget. Every result here is model-relative.
papers.summary: Reported minimal neural circuits from connectomes are usually single point estimates for one task and one fidelity threshold. `ApproxBrain` treats computational sufficiency as a family of neuron subsets that depends on the task and on tolerances for degradation and failure, and certifies candidates with one-sided bounds on held-out parameter draws. On a walking simulator, the published 148-neuron circuit is certified sufficient, but no 146- or 147-neuron subset of it is. Changing the task changes which neurons are needed, and relaxing the tolerance reveals alternative circuits. The authors conclude that **sufficiency is set-valued and depends jointly on task and tolerance**.

papers.title: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNs for Flexible Working Memory
papers.abstract: Oscillatory phase coding (OPC) is widely observed in neural systems and has been implicated in cognitive functions such as memory and sequence processing. However, its computational role and neural substrates remain largely unclear. Here, we studied OPC by training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, we found that OPC emerges in the RNN spontaneously: the memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm, with oscillation amplitude encoding item identity and phase encoding serial order. Ablation studies identified three key elements required for OPC: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis revealed the emergence of content and time cells in the trained RNN, and they process item identity and sequence order separately. Recurrent connectivity analysis revealed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups. Inspired by these findings, we proposed a neural circuit model which reproduces OPC through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. Together, this study reveals how OPC arises from network structures and task demands, offers insights into the implementation and computational mechanisms of OPC in biological systems, and inspires us to develop computational models for human-like cognitive functions.
papers.summary: Oscillatory phase coding (OPC) is widely observed in the brain, but its computational role is unclear. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with neural adaptation, trained on sequence working-memory tasks with variable delays, **develop OPC spontaneously**: oscillation amplitude encodes item identity, and phase encodes serial order. Ablations show that adaptation, variable delays, and flexible readout are all required. The trained networks develop separate content cells and time cells. These findings motivate a circuit model in which content units interact with an adaptive time ring.

papers.title: Capturing Membrane Dynamics and Spike Timing of Human Neurons at Scale using Neural Operators
papers.abstract: Characterizing the properties of neuronal cell types is central to understanding brain function. Yet, biophysically realistic neuron models remain difficult to scale to large populations while preserving the richness of cellular dynamics and within-cell-type variability. We present a cell-type-specific neural-operator framework for scalable neuronal population modeling. Rather than training separate surrogate models for individual neurons, the proposed framework learns a shared operator across multiple modeled neurons from the same cell type, conditioned on biologically interpretable electrophysiological features. Relative to the original single-neuron \texttt{NOBLE} setting, learning across heterogeneous neurons requires a richer electrophysiological conditioning representation and a training objective designed to preserve diverse spiking dynamics. This enables efficient generation of large ensembles of somatic voltage responses while preserving variability across cells and model configurations. We evaluate the approach using membrane dynamics metrics, action potential waveform metrics, spike timing accuracy, input-output firing relationships, and electrophysiological feature distributions. Our framework reproduces subthreshold membrane dynamics, spike waveforms, and firing-rate responses across major cortical inhibitory neuron types, while accurately preserving spike timing despite the sensitivity of threshold-crossing dynamics. The predicted electrophysiological feature distributions show strong agreement with detailed simulator outputs and human experimental recordings, including high explained variability in properties such as inter-spike intervals, firing frequency, action-potential shape, and post-spike recovery.
papers.summary: Biophysically realistic neuron models are hard to scale to large populations while preserving variability within a cell type. The authors learn one neural operator shared across many modeled neurons of the same cell type, conditioned on interpretable electrophysiological features. This extends the single-neuron `NOBLE` setting with richer conditioning and a training objective that preserves diverse spiking. The framework reproduces subthreshold dynamics, spike waveforms, and firing-rate responses across major cortical inhibitory neuron types. It **preserves accurate spike timing**, and its predicted feature distributions closely match detailed simulator outputs and human recordings.

papers.title: BrainPFN: Amortized Brain-Behaviour Prediction via Prior-Data Fitted Networks
papers.abstract: The standard approach to predicting behavioral phenotypes from functional MRI is represented by Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) applied on functional connectivity (FC) matrices. However, this approach is limited: separate models must be fit and tuned for every score and cohort, they do not transfer across datasets, and accuracy degrades sharply when only a handful of subjects are available, as is typical of clinical or cognitive studies. Despite an increasing interest in developing brain foundation models, none has consistently outperformed KRR on behaviour prediction; most reported gains come from easier targets such as age, sex, or diagnosis rather than continuous behavioural scores. We introduce BrainPFN, a Prior Data Fitted Network for brain behaviour regression. BrainPFN is meta-trained on a domain-specific prior built from ~7k real FC matrices, from which we sample one billion synthetic training samples. At inference, a labelled context is simply passed through the network in a single forward pass, with no per-score or per-cohort refitting required. Across four independent cohorts, BrainPFN beats KRR on small sample prediction, and leads recent foundation models pre-trained at four to nine times larger scale. Our meta-training pool, aggregated from open repositories, is a fraction of the size of the corpora behind competing models, most of which sit behind restrictive data use agreements such as UK Biobank. We release this pool publicly alongside code and checkpoints, showing that a modest, openly available pool can match or beat models trained at Biobank scale.
papers.summary: The standard way to predict behavior from functional MRI connectivity is kernel ridge regression (KRR), which must be refit for each score and cohort and degrades with few subjects. `BrainPFN` is a Prior-Data Fitted Network meta-trained on one billion synthetic samples drawn from a prior built from about 7,000 real connectivity matrices. It predicts from a labeled context in a single forward pass with no refitting. Across four independent cohorts, it **beats KRR in small-sample prediction** and outperforms foundation models pre-trained at four to nine times larger scale. The openly available training pool is released with code and checkpoints.

papers.title: From Maps to Metabolism: Historical Precedents and a Unified Critique of Computationalism
papers.abstract:
Alexander Lerchner's recent work on the 'abstraction fallacy' argues that computational functionalism confuses physical processes with abstract descriptions, and that symbolic computation alone cannot instantiate consciousness. Yet these claims were anticipated by Korzybski's map-territory distinction, Searle's critique of strong artificial intelligence, Floridi's levels of abstraction, Spencer et al.'s observer-relativity arguments, Winograd and Flores's account of computation as socially grounded practice, and Nasuto and Bishop's biological arguments. Synthesizing these contributions, this paper advances a form of non-computational physicalism: consciousness depends upon intrinsically organized, metabolically grounded physical dynamics rather than abstract computation, whilst leaving open the possibility of artificial consciousness.
  An objection is that this critique targets an outdated computationalism. Mechanistic computationalism, associated with Milkowski, Piccinini, Craver, Bechtel, and Kaplan, treats computation as a property of physically realized mechanisms rather than substrate-independent formalism. Although this represents an important advance, it does not dissolve the abstraction fallacy. Computational attributions remain dependent upon choices of state individuation, system boundaries, and interpretive mapping that are not determined by physical facts alone. Kaplan and Craver's 'model-to-mechanism mapping' constrains computational descriptions without eliminating their dependence upon an external observer. Grounding computation in neural mechanisms does not confer intrinsic significance or the normativity explored by Bickhard and Nasuto and Bishop. The abstraction fallacy persists wherever computational descriptions are treated as constitutive of, rather than descriptive of, physical reality.
papers.summary: The essay responds to Alexander Lerchner's 'abstraction fallacy' argument, which holds that computational functionalism confuses physical processes with abstract descriptions of them and that symbolic computation alone cannot produce consciousness. It traces how these claims were anticipated by earlier thinkers, including Korzybski, Searle, Floridi, Winograd and Flores, and Nasuto and Bishop. From that synthesis it argues for **non-computational physicalism**, the view that consciousness depends on intrinsically organized, metabolically grounded physical dynamics rather than on abstract computation, while still allowing that artificial consciousness may be possible. It also contends that mechanistic computationalism does not escape the fallacy, because computational descriptions still depend on observer-chosen state individuation, system boundaries, and interpretive mappings.

papers.title: KG-AST for Cheaper CI/CD: Budgeted Test Selection and AI Bug Review
papers.abstract:
Continuous integration and AI-assisted review spend the same budget on every commit, although few commits introduce bugs. We study KG-AST, which scores each commit risk from git history and code-graph features before heavy tests or AI review run, so the budget goes to the riskiest commits first, and which hands the AI reviewer only a graph slice around the change. On 155 open-source projects in 11 languages, a single cross-language model trained on other projects ranks commits so that heavy testing of the riskiest 20% covers 49-64% of bug-introducing commits depending on the language, against 20% for random selection and 40-55% for testing the biggest change first.
  Every language beats the biggest-change baseline, by 3.8 to 13.2 points. In 20 Java projects the gain at a 20% budget is 15.1 points (64.6% vs 49.5%, 95% interval +11.6 to +18.4), and the model wins in 19 of the 20 projects. About twelve training projects suffice; richer features, tuning and cleaner labels did not help. An AI reviewer that sees only a commit's diff finds 26% of later-fixed defects exactly (32% with graph context), and about half of its findings that did not match a later fix were judged real by independent AI judges. A static call-graph selector runs about 8% of a test suite while including a test written for the fix in 85% of 67 fix commits. The Poincare embedding used in our retrieval work adds nothing measurable here: commit-risk AUC, bug review and severity ranking are unchanged or worse. The labels are noisy and the budget metric assumes a heavy test catches the bug it covers; no CI minutes were measured.
papers.summary: Continuous integration (CI) pipelines and AI code reviewers spend the same budget on every commit, even though few commits introduce bugs. `KG-AST` scores each commit's risk from git history and code-graph features so that heavy tests and AI review go to the riskiest commits first, and it gives the AI reviewer only a graph slice around the change. Across 155 open-source projects in 11 languages, a single cross-language model ranks commits so that testing the riskiest 20% covers **49-64% of bug-introducing commits**, compared with 20% for random selection and 40-55% for testing the largest changes first. An AI reviewer finds 26% of later-fixed defects from the diff alone and 32% with graph context, and a static call-graph test selector runs about 8% of the test suite while including the relevant fix test in 85% of cases.

papers.title: SteelAgent: LLM-Orchestrated, Physics-Informed Steel Property Prediction with Audited Generalization and Calibrated Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Steel property models can perform well on random test splits even when they extrapolate poorly to unfamiliar alloys. SteelAgent couples metallurgical descriptors and machine-learning models with a language-model interface for property prediction, uncertainty reporting and inverse design. We examine how the choice of held-out unit changes the conclusions drawn from SteelBench tensile-strength evaluations. For gradient boosting, pooled out-of-fold $R^2$ fell from 0.859 on a random split to 0.113 when steel families were held out. Empirical coverage of nominal 90% prediction intervals ranged from 91.0% under random splitting to 37.6% on held-out sources. The effect of physics-derived features depended on the evaluation. They increased gradient-boosting $R^2$ by 0.2534 in a 17-family holdout analysis and decreased it by 0.358 in a separate four-grade laboratory analysis. We report group-level errors and a synthetic regression experiment illustrating how calibration can deteriorate on held-out groups. These results motivate reporting the evaluation population alongside a property estimate or compliance score.
papers.summary: Models that predict steel properties can score well on random test splits while extrapolating poorly to unfamiliar alloys. `SteelAgent` combines metallurgical descriptors and machine-learning models with a language-model interface for property prediction, uncertainty reporting, and inverse design, and the authors use it to study how the choice of held-out unit changes conclusions on `SteelBench` tensile-strength evaluations. For gradient boosting, pooled R² **fell from 0.859 on a random split to 0.113 when whole steel families were held out**, and coverage of nominal 90% prediction intervals dropped from 91.0% to 37.6% on held-out sources. Physics-derived features helped in one holdout analysis and hurt in another, which leads the authors to argue that property estimates should always be reported together with the evaluation population they were tested on.

papers.title: Octopus: One Brain, Many Branches for Latent-KV Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract:
Multi-agent LLM systems explore in parallel by spawning sub-agents with isolated context windows, whereas single-agent systems append every search and verification step into one growing trajectory. However, existing multi-agent frameworks duplicate prefix KV caches across branches, exchange findings by re-prefilling text summaries, and flatten or drop cross-branch dependencies during reinforcement learning (RL).
  We introduce Octopus, a single-model multi-agent RL framework in which all threads share one backbone and coordinate over a GPU-resident directed acyclic graph (DAG) of KV states through five primitives (fork, read_thread, wait_threads, rewind, commit). Octopus combines three co-designed mechanisms: (1) Zero-Copy Radix Forking, which spawns branches as $\mathcal{O}(1)$ cursor views over shared physical KV pages; (2) Attention-Only KV Mounting, which mounts a sibling thread's terminal KV blocks directly into full-attention layers while bypassing linear-recurrent states (Gated DeltaNet / Mamba-2), cutting off-task hijacking by $21\times$ ($57.9\% \to 2.7\%$) while retaining $92.2\%$ of full-text mutual information at zero extra KV allocation; and (3) a Packed DAG-GRPO Trainer, which packs all episode branches into one block-sparse attention pass and assigns counterfactual branch credit via leave-one-branch-out marginal rewards.
