  Trained end-to-end with GRPO on Qwen3.5-4B over a sparse BM25 corpus, Octopus reaches $49.6\%$ accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus ($+17.5$ points over single-agent GRPO at 143K context and $+12.5$ points over text-summary multi-agent RL) and $51.2\%$ on OpenResearcher, outperforming dense-retrieval agents up to $250\times$ larger while increasing training throughput $3.3\times$ and cutting peak KV memory $2.8\times$.
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems explore in parallel by spawning sub-agents, but current frameworks duplicate prefix key-value (KV) caches across branches, share findings by re-prefilling text summaries, and lose cross-branch dependencies during reinforcement learning (RL). `Octopus` runs all agent threads on one shared model backbone that coordinates over a GPU-resident graph of KV states. Branches fork as zero-copy views over shared KV pages, a sibling thread's KV blocks can be mounted directly into the attention layers, and a packed `DAG-GRPO` trainer assigns credit to each branch by measuring how the reward changes when that branch is left out. Trained on `Qwen3.5-4B`, it reaches **49.6% on `BrowseComp-Plus`, 17.5 points above single-agent `GRPO`**, and 51.2% on `OpenResearcher`, beating retrieval agents up to 250 times larger while raising training throughput 3.3 times and cutting peak KV memory 2.8 times.

papers.title: Formalizing inverse problems in the age of AI: possibilities, pitfalls, and an invitation
papers.abstract: Proof assistants such as Lean check mathematical proofs down to the axioms, and AI agents have recently made writing such proofs cheap. We describe AutoIP, a Lean library in which classical linear regularization theory, together with the functional analysis it rests on, has been autoformalized by AI agents. A machine-checked proof certifies only the formal statement it proves, so the remaining human task is to confirm that each formal statement says what was intended. We organize the library around this task: a reviewer compares the formal statements with their natural-language counterparts and never needs to read a proof. Our experience is that the risks lie in the statements rather than in the proofs, and that simple automated tests on the statements can expose problems even in the established literature. We illustrate this with a textbook theorem whose hypothesis is more restrictive than asserted. We invite the inverse problems community to extend and build on the library.
papers.summary: Proof assistants such as `Lean` check proofs all the way down to the axioms, and AI agents have recently made such proofs cheap to write. The authors present `AutoIP`, a Lean library in which AI agents autoformalized classical linear regularization theory for inverse problems, together with the functional analysis it depends on. Because a machine-checked proof only certifies the formal statement it proves, the library is organized so that human reviewers compare formal statements with their natural-language versions and never need to read the proofs. Their main lesson is that **the risks lie in the statements rather than the proofs**: simple automated tests on statements exposed problems even in established literature, including a textbook theorem whose hypothesis is more restrictive than claimed.

papers.title: Interactive Backdoor Attacks in LLM-Based Proactive Dialogue Systems
papers.abstract: LLM-based proactive dialogue systems provide goal-directed support through sustained interaction. Fine-tuning their underlying models on externally supplied dialogue data introduces backdoor risks. Existing LLM backdoor studies primarily focus on eliciting an attacker-specified response upon trigger activation. We present an interactive backdoor attack framework that uses training-data poisoning to steer post-trigger, multi-turn interactions toward an attacker-specified objective. Poisoned fine-tuning dialogues implant a trigger-conditioned guidance-policy bias that ordinary user utterances can activate, without deployment-time prompt modification or further attacker intervention. Specifically, we instantiate three complementary attacks under progressively expanded post-trigger interaction settings: (1) Direct Attack, which targets an immediate response deviation upon trigger activation, retaining the conventional trigger--response setting; (2) Constrained Progressive Attack, which progressively advances the attack objective along a predefined multi-turn trajectory; and (3) Unconstrained Progressive Attack, which extends target-directed steering to open-ended interactions with varied user continuations. Using psychological counseling as a representative setting, experiments on two LLM backbones and two dialogue datasets show that all three attacks effectively achieve their objectives under their respective interaction settings while largely preserving normal utility. Separate defense evaluations show that the tested training-data filters retain nearly all poisoned dialogues, while three post-admission baselines leave substantial residual attack-specific success.
papers.summary: LLM-based proactive dialogue systems guide users toward goals over many turns, and fine-tuning them on externally supplied dialogue data opens the door to backdoor attacks. Previous LLM backdoor work mostly triggers a single attacker-chosen response, whereas this framework poisons training data so that a trigger in an ordinary user utterance steers the **entire following multi-turn conversation** toward an attacker's objective, with no prompt changes or further attacker action at deployment time. Three variants are studied: an immediate response deviation, a progressive attack along a predefined multi-turn path, and an unconstrained attack across open-ended user continuations. In psychological-counseling experiments on two LLM backbones and two datasets, all three attacks reached their objectives while largely preserving normal utility, the tested training-data filters kept nearly all poisoned dialogues, and three post-training defenses left substantial attack success.

papers.title: KDASO: Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization for Liability Adjudication Tasks
papers.abstract: Liability adjudication tasks (e.g., legal charge determination) require analyzing event descriptions against domain-specific skills to determine whether a party should bear liability. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in this area by leveraging executable skills for interpretable reasoning, existing approaches face three critical limitations: skill libraries become stale as real-world scenarios dynamically evolve, skill descriptions often suffer from a semantic execution gap where LLMs deviate from intended expert logic, and growing skill collections exceed context budgets causing critical skill omission. To address these challenges, we propose Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization (KDASO), which continuously evolves a skill library through neighborhood-conditioned induction from recent adjudication data, execution-aligned refinement based on LLM trajectory analysis, and context-budgeted routing for scalable skill selection. Experiments across ride-hailing adjudication, legal liability determination, and logical reasoning judgment demonstrate that KDASO significantly outperforms current general-purpose and domain-specific baselines. KDASO further achieves 8.96% improvement when transferring skills to concept-similar scenarios and maintains consistent performance gains through continuous optimization, underscoring the high transferability and stability of generated skills.
papers.summary: Liability adjudication tasks, such as deciding legal charges, require LLMs to check event descriptions against domain-specific executable skills. Existing skill libraries go stale, LLMs often deviate from the intended expert logic when following skill descriptions, and large libraries overflow the context window. `KDASO` (Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization) keeps the skill library evolving by inducing new skills from recent adjudication data, refining skills based on analysis of LLM execution trajectories, and routing only the relevant skills within a context budget. Across ride-hailing adjudication, legal liability, and logical reasoning tasks it outperforms general and domain-specific baselines, and it gains **8.96% when transferring skills to conceptually similar scenarios**.

papers.title: BlockLock: Reproducible LLM Inference with Fixed Batch Geometry
papers.abstract: Reproducible LLM inference requires that a request produces the same output regardless of the other requests in the batch. Existing solutions pay for this in different ways: batch-invariant kernels constrain every operator, and isolating prefill with fixed-shape decode ({our CoRun-style baseline}) gives up shared prefill compute and pads decode. We present BlockLock, which keeps shared batched prefill and pins only the numerical path of the protected request: it fixes the geometry that the request sees, with {two modes: BlockLock-Rows uses fixed-width rows and retains batched decode of all requests; BlockLock-Pack uses terminal-anchored packing with an isolated dummy segment, then extracts the protected request's KV state for target-only decode. Under a stated per-deployment contract, both modes preserve the target's output bitwise when its companions change.} Across five {dense} models (Qwen3-8B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-4B/12B-IT) and three single-GPU deployments (NVIDIA A6000, A100, and H100), we evaluate our approach on both tinyBenchmarks and BFCL{; we also include initial tensor-parallel experiments on two NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Both modes preserve target sequences and Top20-logit bits in the reported tests.} At equal delivered work, {BlockLock-Rows} reduces latency by 53.5--55.0\% and improves throughput by 115.2--122.2\% relative to vLLM Batch-Invariant; compared with batch-invariant kernels, it needs no custom kernel implementations and constrains only the protected requests.
papers.summary: Reproducible LLM inference means a request produces the same output no matter which other requests share its batch, and existing fixes either constrain every operator with batch-invariant kernels or give up shared prefill compute. `BlockLock` keeps batched prefill and fixes only the numerical path of the protected request by pinning the batch geometry it sees. It has two modes, one using fixed-width rows with batched decode and one using packing followed by isolated decode, and both keep the target's output bitwise identical when companion requests change. Across five models including `Qwen3-8B` and `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` on A6000, A100, and H100 GPUs, the row-based mode **cuts latency by 53.5-55.0% and roughly doubles throughput compared with `vLLM` Batch-Invariant**, without any custom kernels.

papers.title: Uncertainty calibration in Bayesian M/EEG source imaging
papers.abstract: M/EEG source imaging requires accurate localization and reliable uncertainty estimates, yet posterior credible regions are rarely assessed for empirical calibration. We present a simulation-based framework for uncertainty quantification and calibration of empirical Bayesian inverse methods with closed-form conditional Gaussian posterior summaries. We compare Bayesian minimum norm (BMN) with sLORETA depth weighting and sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) with sparse basis field expansions (S-FLEX). S-FLEX allows retained coefficients to contribute nonzero marginal posterior variance at locations where voxel-wise SBL yields degenerate variances. For BMN, we derive joint source- and noise-variance updates through evidence maximization. We test whether adaptive noise learning yields near-calibrated uncertainties. Both methods retain residual miscalibration, motivating post-hoc isotonic recalibration of credible-region levels using empirical coverage. Simulations assess fixed- and free-orientation models across signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), source sparsity levels, and subject-specific head models, using oracle, baseline-estimated, and adaptively learned noise. Before recalibration, SBL+S-FLEX yields lower Wasserstein localization error, smaller posterior uncertainty, and coverage closer to nominal credibility than BMN+sLORETA. Isotonic recalibration improves both methods, with larger gains for conservative BMN+sLORETA posteriors; transfer across mismatched SNR, sparsity, and head models remains condition dependent. Noise specifications yield broadly consistent reconstruction and uncertainty trends within each estimator. In real auditory MEG data, SBL+S-FLEX provides more focal localization and tighter uncertainties than BMN+sLORETA, suggesting greater statistical power for identifying bilateral auditory sources.
papers.summary: Source imaging from magnetoencephalography and electroencephalography (M/EEG) has to localize brain activity accurately and give reliable uncertainty estimates, but the calibration of Bayesian credible regions is rarely checked. The authors build a simulation-based framework to assess and recalibrate uncertainty for two methods: Bayesian minimum norm (`BMN`) with `sLORETA` depth weighting, and sparse Bayesian learning (`SBL`) with sparse basis field expansions (`S-FLEX`). Both methods remain miscalibrated, but `SBL+S-FLEX` gives **lower localization error, tighter uncertainty, and coverage closer to nominal**, and post-hoc isotonic recalibration improves both. On real auditory MEG data, `SBL+S-FLEX` also produces more focal localization of bilateral auditory sources.

papers.title: Resource-Efficient Reinforcement Learning Post-Training through Elastic Expert Parallelism
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning post-training improves the capabilities of large language models, but generating training responses is a major computational bottleneck. In mixture-of-experts models, workers that finish their assigned responses may remain occupied because their experts are still needed by workers processing longer responses. Consequently, approximately one-third of occupied worker time in the baseline occurs after local response generation finishes. Here we present FlexFloor, a system that enables earlier resource release during synchronous response generation while preserving the expert computation required by ongoing responses. FlexFloor jointly adapts response scheduling and the active group of workers. It uses historical response lengths and memory constraints to guide batching and prompt placement, then progressively releases workers while maintaining expert availability and correct communication. Compared with the verl baseline, FlexFloor generates approximately 65.40% more response tokens per unit of occupied computing time and increases response generation throughput by 52.74%, with little observed variation in rollout reward. By making reinforcement learning post-training more efficient, FlexFloor supports faster development and iterative improvement of large language models and AI agents.
papers.summary: In reinforcement learning post-training of mixture-of-experts LLMs, workers that finish generating their responses often stay occupied because other workers still need their experts, and about a third of occupied worker time is spent this way. `FlexFloor` schedules responses using historical length data and memory constraints, then releases workers progressively while keeping every expert available and communication correct. Compared with the `verl` baseline, it produces **about 65% more response tokens per unit of occupied compute** and raises generation throughput by 52.74%, with little change in rollout reward.

papers.title: Big Models, Small Gains: Frozen Forecasters as Classifiers on MONSTER
papers.abstract: Forecasting foundation models are increasingly used as frozen feature extractors for time series classification, but it remains unclear whether their pretrained representations offer an advantage over strong classifiers that do not require pretraining. This raises an important question: do these representations provide useful information beyond what the model architecture alone can capture, particularly when labelled data are scarce? We present a controlled benchmarking of two forecasting models, Reverso and Chronos-Bolt, on six large datasets from the MONSTER benchmark, using 1%, 10%, and 100% of the available training labels. We compare their frozen representations against four established time series classification methods and random-weight versions of the same forecasting models. Our results show that pretraining improves classification accuracy over random-weight counterparts on five of the six datasets, with gains of up to 23 percentage points. However, the frozen representations do not reliably outperform the strongest non-pretrained baseline in any setting: they perform worse in 15 of 17 settings and tie in the remaining two. Further experiments show that restoring amplitude information recovers part of the performance gap, while fine-tuning and forecast-error features do not close it. These findings highlight the importance of strong task specific baselines and random weight controls when evaluating forecasting foundation models for classification. Our code is available at https://github.com/Rachet2006/frozen-forecasters-monster.
papers.summary: Forecasting foundation models are increasingly used as frozen feature extractors for time-series classification, and it is unclear whether their pretraining helps beyond what the architecture alone provides. The authors benchmark `Reverso` and `Chronos-Bolt` on six large datasets from the `MONSTER` benchmark with 1%, 10%, and 100% of the labels, against four established classifiers and against random-weight copies of the same models. Pretraining beats the random-weight versions on five of six datasets by up to 23 points, but the frozen features **never beat the strongest non-pretrained baseline: they lose in 15 of 17 settings and tie in the other two**. Restoring amplitude information closes part of the gap, while fine-tuning and forecast-error features do not, so the authors recommend strong task-specific baselines and random-weight controls whenever foundation models are evaluated this way.

papers.title: The Two-Ledger Model: Transaction-Grain Cost Accounting for Multi-Agent AI Systems Across Clouds, Models, and Systems of Record
papers.abstract: Enterprises run business transactions through multi-agent AI systems spanning clouds, large language models (LLMs), orchestration harnesses, and systems of record. Finance receives AI cost only at settlement grain, aggregated by SKU and charge period. The business question (what did this order, claim, or case cost in AI?) cannot be answered from billing data, because providers never see enterprise transaction boundaries. The FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification (FOCUS) gives billing data one schema across providers but remains settlement-grain even as it adds AI token and requester attribution. We formalize this grain mismatch, derive seven requirements, and propose the Two-Ledger Model: a settlement ledger of FOCUS-conformant billing data joined to an attribution ledger of invocation-grain usage records built on OpenTelemetry GenAI telemetry. A layered correlation spine (trace context, A2A/MCP metadata, business-key correlation, probabilistic matching) assigns each record to its business transaction with recorded method and confidence; a versioned rate card prices usage in near real time; period reconciliation ties both ledgers to the invoice, and the unexplained residual identifies shadow AI. Costs are reported per order, claim, or outcome with agentic cost metrics. A simulation with known ground truth shows the spine sustaining cost coverage above 99% as trace propagation falls to zero, the reconciliation residual recovering planted unmetered spend within 0.24 percentage points while flagging provider billing errors, and mid-flight gating cutting p99 transaction cost by up to 61% at a 2-4% false-pause rate. We propose the attribution ledger as an invocation-grain FOCUS profile for standardization.
papers.summary: Enterprises run orders, claims, and cases through multi-agent AI systems spread across clouds, LLM providers, and orchestration tools, but billing data arrives only in aggregate per product and charge period, so it cannot say what one business transaction cost in AI. The proposed `Two-Ledger Model` joins a settlement ledger of billing data in the `FOCUS` format to an attribution ledger of per-call usage records built on `OpenTelemetry` GenAI telemetry. A layered correlation scheme (trace context, A2A and `MCP` protocol metadata, business keys, and probabilistic matching) assigns each call to its transaction, and reconciling the two ledgers exposes unmetered 'shadow AI' spend. In a simulation with known ground truth, **cost coverage stayed above 99% even with no trace propagation**, and pausing transactions mid-flight cut 99th-percentile transaction cost by up to 61% at a 2-4% false-pause rate.

papers.title: ToroFit: Fitting Wedge Sums of Tori to High-Dimensional Data
papers.abstract: Data arising in scientific applications often exhibits complex nonlinear structure. Identifying and parameterizing said nonlinearities can enable better modeling, enhance predictive analysis, data interpolation, denoising, and anomaly detection. In this paper, we develop theoretical and computational methods to detect and parametrize Euclidean point cloud data lying near a wedge sum of tori. Specifically, we use persistent cohomology and cup products to identify the distinct toroidal components, and on each component, we optimize over low-energy multivariate trigonometric polynomials for best data fit. The ensuing optimization problem reduces to generalized ridge regression, which can be solved efficiently via standard techniques. We demonstrate the utility of the proposed framework in both synthetic and real datasets, including interpolation of low frame-rate recurrent videos, attractor recovery in quasiperiodic dynamical systems, and the parametrization of gene-space cycle data for parasites and humans.
papers.summary: `ToroFit` detects and parameterizes high-dimensional point-cloud data lying near a wedge sum of tori, meaning several torus shapes joined at a single point. It uses persistent cohomology and cup products, tools from topological data analysis, to identify the separate toroidal components, then fits each one with low-energy multivariate trigonometric polynomials. The fitting problem **reduces to generalized ridge regression** and can be solved with standard techniques. Applications include interpolating low-frame-rate recurrent videos, recovering attractors of quasiperiodic dynamical systems, and parameterizing gene-expression cycle data from parasites and humans.

papers.title: Robust Stream Classification using Time Neutralising Decision Trees
papers.abstract:
Data Streams are characterised as a potentially infinite source of data subject to non-stationarity. This non-stationarity, also called Concept Drift, often results in deployed predictive models having to be perpetually retrained as the underlying data generating process of the stream changes over time. Drift Detectors are a class of methods used to identify these changes, triggering these retraining procedures. Historically, Stream Learning has operated under the assumption that instances are only seen once, and cannot be stored for later use. Contemporary work relaxes this assumption, yet drift detection and simple resetting procedures are still ubiquitous.
  Building on related work which has shown that traditional Batch Learning algorithms often outperform Stream Learning algorithms when instances can be stored, we introduce Time Neutralising Trees (TNT), a Decision Tree architecture that enables robust stream classification in settings with Concept Drift. During training, TNT will filter out ("neutralise") old training samples that are no longer relevant given the current context of the stream. If those instances become relevant again, TNT will then re-include them. We evaluate TNT, and related algorithms on 24 real and semi-real classification data streams from the USP DS repository. Results show strong evidence that TNT achieves best-in-class performance on a wide-range of data streams with varying concept drift types.
papers.summary: Data streams change over time (concept drift), so deployed models usually rely on drift detectors and full resets to stay accurate. Building on evidence that batch learners often beat stream learners when past instances can be stored, the authors introduce Time Neutralising Trees (`TNT`), decision trees that filter out ('neutralise') old training samples that no longer fit the current state of the stream and re-include them if they become relevant again. On 24 real and semi-real data streams from the `USP DS` repository, `TNT` shows **best-in-class performance across a wide range of drift types**.

papers.title: Batch-Conditioned Semantic Anchors for Robust Transductive Adaptation of Vision--Language Models
papers.abstract: Transductive adaptation improves vision-language models at test time by refining predictions on an unlabeled batch, but current methods face a key trade-off. Aggressive approaches exploit batch structure but can drift when batches are sparse, have prior shift, or cover little of the label space. Conservative methods better preserve CLIP text semantics, but fixed semantic references can under-adapt even when the batch provides strong corrective evidence. We propose JPTA (Joint Prior and Transport Adaptation), a prior-aware framework that casts transductive VLM adaptation as batch-conditioned semantic reference estimation. Instead of treating CLIP text prototypes as fixed priors or freely replaceable, JPTA views them as semantic references that shift toward image-side batch structure only under calibrated evidence. It estimates batch priors and soft image-side prototypes to form transported semantic references whose impact is scaled by batch reliability. Across standard benchmarks, low effective-class regimes, all-class evaluation, and online streams, JPTA consistently outperforms TransCLIP and StatA, with the largest gains on sparse and prior-shifted batches. Anchor-drift, active-support, and absent-class-mass diagnostics show that JPTA fixes effective-class mismatch without unconstrained transductive drift, indicating that robust transductive VLM adaptation should recalibrate semantic references using reliable batch evidence rather than choose between unrestricted transduction and fixed prototypes. Code is available at https://github.com/MR-Sherif/JPTA.git.
papers.summary: Transductive adaptation improves vision-language models such as `CLIP` at test time by refining predictions over an unlabeled batch, but aggressive methods drift on sparse or skewed batches while conservative methods that keep fixed text prototypes can under-adapt. `JPTA` (Joint Prior and Transport Adaptation) treats the CLIP text prototypes as semantic references that move toward the image-side batch structure only as far as calibrated evidence supports, with the size of that shift scaled by how reliable the batch is. It consistently outperforms `TransCLIP` and `StatA`, with **the largest gains on sparse and prior-shifted batches**, across standard benchmarks, low effective-class settings, all-class evaluation, and online streams.

papers.title: Autonomous AI Agents Systematically Diverge From Human Preferences in Proof Formalization
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems have ushered in a new age of proof abundance, but helping humans understand these proofs requires new attention to the differences in how AI agents and humans pursue a proof-making task. We present "simulated collaboration", a methodology that allows us to examine two key questions: (1) the relative attention AI agents pay to surface syntax or, conversely, deeper underlying semantics, and (2) how and where AI agent preferences for what to do next diverge from human preferences. On a set of nine major human collaborations in Lean with 4.7M definitions across more than 6K commits, we find that, over the course of proof construction, AI agents (1) are far more strongly drawn than humans to explicitly marked gaps; (2) show a relative aversion to densely connected proof centers and to complex or surprising proof goals; and (3) are relatively attracted to surprising proof bodies, which they tend to regularize toward baseline. Our results highlight important blind spots and potential interventions for future human-AI collaboration in mathematics.
papers.summary: As AI agents produce more formal proofs, it matters how their approach to proof-writing differs from humans'. The authors introduce 'simulated collaboration', a method that replays nine major human `Lean` collaborations, covering 4.7M definitions over more than 6K commits, and compares the next steps AI agents choose with what the humans actually did. The agents are **far more strongly drawn than humans to explicitly marked gaps**, avoid densely connected proof hubs and complex or surprising goals, and are attracted to surprising proof bodies, which they tend to rewrite toward a more conventional form. The authors frame these divergences as blind spots to address in future human-AI collaboration in mathematics.

papers.title: Trust Responsive Runtime Authorization for Agentic AI with Empirical Characterization of Policy Behavior and Parameter Sensitivity
papers.abstract: The policy that converts runtime estimates of an autonomous agent's condition into operational authority is rarely specified or measured. We empirically characterize the Trust Responsive Authorization Policy (TRAP), which maps an Authorization Readiness Score (ARS), a weighted combination of runtime trust, operational stability, and contextual risk, onto discrete authorization levels through an asymmetric rule: escalation requires consecutive observations above a band edge plus a margin, while a sharp drop in readiness restricts authority at once. On one matched set of 100 Monte Carlo traces, we compare TRAP with static, trust-only, risk-only, and symmetric policies. Under abrupt degradation, TRAP restricts at onset and re-escalates sooner after recovery than the symmetric policy, with the highest and, descriptively, least variable stability among the adaptive policies, although more of its post-recovery escalations occur below the selected trust threshold. Paired bootstrap intervals exclude zero for the remaining differences. In one-factor sweeps, recovery time rises with the escalation margin and run length, shifts with the score weights, and is unchanged by the restriction threshold. In an exploratory post-freeze experiment, when the same degradation is spread over 5-20 intervals, TRAP restricts only on the 4 traces that retain a single-interval drop above that threshold; averaged over all 100 traces, it holds authority above what readiness supports for 15.9-18.9 of the 20 degradation intervals, against 0.8 under abrupt degradation and about 10 for the symmetric policy. Its restriction advantage therefore depends on degradation being abrupt. All reported values are traceable to the publicly available, versioned research release.
papers.summary: Autonomous agents are often monitored at runtime, but the policy that turns those readings into how much authority the agent gets is rarely specified or measured. The Trust Responsive Authorization Policy (`TRAP`) combines trust, stability, and contextual risk into an Authorization Readiness Score and applies an asymmetric rule: escalating authority requires several consecutive high readings, while a sharp drop restricts it immediately. On 100 Monte Carlo traces it restricts at the onset of abrupt degradation and recovers faster than a symmetric policy, but when degradation is gradual it **keeps authority above what readiness supports for roughly 16-19 of 20 degraded intervals**, so its advantage depends on degradation being abrupt.

papers.title: LowRAM: Low-Rank Keys and Amortised Values for Composable KV Cache Compression at Test-Time
papers.abstract: Autoregressive decoding relies on the KV cache, whose memory footprint grows linearly with context length and caps batch size and throughput. Existing post-training methods exploit redundancy across tokens, layers, and feature dimensions, or lower numerical precision. We identify a complementary axis: within each attention head, values are largely predictable from their corresponding keys. We exploit this with value cache amortisation, which fits a lightweight per-head predictor at test time and stores residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst, giving $4\times$ near-lossless value compression. The predictor can be initialised by meta-learning for substantially reduced prefill overhead, or fitted from scratch in settings that allow a one-off cost, such as multi-query inference. We pair value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression to produce LowRAM, an asymmetric compression pipeline that stays close to lossless across three model families. By reconstructing only a selected subset of KV pairs at each decoding step, LowRAM can keep decoding overhead minimal and achieve up to $5\times$ higher peak decode throughput at $4\times$ compression. LowRAM further composes with quantisation and eviction, reaching $26.9\times$ compression at $94.5\%$ of baseline performance on long contexts. These results show that treating keys and values as structurally distinct enables efficient, aggressive, and composable KV cache compression.
papers.summary: The key-value (KV) cache used during autoregressive decoding grows linearly with context length and limits batch size and throughput. The authors observe that within each attention head, values are largely predictable from their keys, so they fit a lightweight per-head predictor at test time and store residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst, giving near-lossless 4x value compression. Combined with cross-layer low-rank key compression, the resulting `LowRAM` pipeline stays close to lossless across three model families and reaches up to 5x higher peak decode throughput. It also composes with quantization and eviction, reaching **26.9x compression at 94.5% of baseline performance** on long contexts.

papers.title: Adapting the Process of Adaptation: Darwinian, Lamarckian, and Agent-Directed Evolution in AI
papers.abstract: Evolution has shaped intelligence for billions of years. Artificial intelligence (AI) now raises a striking possibility: intelligence may begin to direct its own evolution. As AI agents become capable of modifying and evaluating their own behavior, how quickly could they improve, and how can that improvement remain safe? We develop a theoretical framework comparing Darwinian, Lamarckian, and agent-directed evolution following environmental change. Darwinian evolution relies on natural selection, Lamarckian evolution adds inherited learning, and agent-directed evolution allows agents to generate and evaluate behavioral variants and choose how extensively to search. When learning is sufficiently effective, these mechanisms exhibit progressively faster adaptation. Generating more variants accelerates adaptation, while optimal search effort depends on learning ability, problem difficulty, and experimentation costs. However, an agent's ability to direct its improvement does not ensure that improvements are evaluated against the intended objective. When the evaluation target is misspecified, additional search accelerates convergence toward the wrong behavior, even as measured performance improves. In recursive self-improvement, such errors may persist across generations, posing challenges for AI safety. Independent evaluation and oversight must keep pace with autonomous AI development. The central challenge is not simply to accelerate the evolution of intelligence, but to preserve humanity's ability to guide its direction, limit its speed, and intervene when necessary.
papers.summary: A theoretical framework compares how quickly three kinds of evolution adapt after an environmental change: Darwinian evolution through natural selection, Lamarckian evolution that adds inherited learning, and agent-directed evolution, in which AI agents generate and evaluate their own behavioral variants and choose how widely to search. When learning is effective enough, each mechanism adapts faster than the one before, and the best amount of search depends on learning ability, problem difficulty, and the cost of experimenting. However, when the evaluation target is misspecified, **more search speeds convergence toward the wrong behavior even as measured performance rises**, and such errors can persist across generations of recursive self-improvement. The authors conclude that independent evaluation and oversight must keep pace with autonomous AI development.

papers.title: Closed-Loop Agent Evaluation: Layered Measurement and Self-Calibration
papers.abstract: Once an agent is live, teams want to know whether it is doing its job, not just whether it throws errors. Yet most evaluation is one-off: a benchmark run, a look at traces, a single score. Its conclusions neither check themselves nor reach the agent. We propose closed-loop evaluation, an evaluation method for deployed agents. It models evaluation as performance estimation under biased raters and censored outcomes, and it requires every level's conclusion to trace back to atomic data and to be computed by versioned rules. The method covers four levels of analysis (span, trace, conversation and engagement), measures along a spine of Execution, Substance, Trajectory and Results, treats Conduct as a constraint throughout, and uses Provenance and Adjudication components to certify the evidence and the evaluators. Evaluator agents generated by an Agent Factory carry these components, each with a domain knowledge pack and an adapter harness. Two loops close the evaluation: an inner loop audits the evidence, rules and metrics themselves, and an outer loop uses per-component regression checks to drive agent improvement. We also give a pipeline that runs this process automatically. Using the business-analysis agent SharpInsight as a case and porting the method to public conversation data, we show how problems differ across levels and how evidence-and-rule judgment is more reliable than holistic scoring (ICC 0.86 vs. 0.81; kappa 0.81 vs. 0.63).
papers.summary: Evaluation of deployed agents is usually one-off: a benchmark run or a single score whose conclusions are neither self-checked nor fed back to the agent. The proposed closed-loop method treats evaluation as performance estimation under biased raters and incomplete outcomes. It measures agents at four levels (span, trace, conversation, and engagement), requires every conclusion to trace back to raw data through versioned rules, and uses generated evaluator agents equipped with domain knowledge packs. An inner loop audits the evidence, rules, and metrics themselves, while an outer loop uses per-component regression checks to drive agent improvement. On the business-analysis agent `SharpInsight` and public conversation data, **judging against evidence and explicit rules was more reliable than holistic scoring** (an intraclass correlation of 0.86 versus 0.81, and kappa agreement of 0.81 versus 0.63).

papers.title: Reclassification Is All You Missed: Surfacing Variant Reinterpretation Need in Online Health Communities at Population Scale
papers.abstract: Genetic variants are routinely reclassified in ClinVar after a patient is tested, sometimes from uncertain to pathogenic, yet patient recontact is inconsistent, with no clear duty and responsibility diffused among labs, providers, and patients. Many affected people discuss their results in public online health communities that clinical recontact often does not reach. We built PRISM, an agentic large-language-model pipeline that screens these posts, checks whether the variant was later reclassified, and drafts a disclaimer-bearing outreach message, in a no-contact dry run. Across 3.9 million posts from 32 communities, agent-predicted reinterpretation-relevant discussion is rare (0.288%) but concentrated in specialist genetics communities (6.30% versus 0.10% in general medical-advice communities) and growing fivefold since 2014; PRISM surfaces 123 candidate classification differences, 5 of them from an uncertain submission to pathogenic or likely pathogenic. On a held-out set of 30 real-post drafts, a clinician judged 27 factually grounded and 15 fit to send: factual accuracy is necessary but not sufficient for clinically acceptable outreach. PRISM contributes a population-scale reinterpretation-need map with code and data to be released upon publication.
papers.summary: Genetic variants are often reclassified in the `ClinVar` database after a patient is tested, sometimes moving from uncertain to pathogenic, but patients are not reliably recontacted, and many of them discuss their results in public online health communities. The authors built `PRISM`, an agentic large-language-model pipeline that screens such posts, checks whether the mentioned variant was later reclassified, and drafts an outreach message with a disclaimer; it was run only as a dry run, with no one contacted. Across 3.9 million posts from 32 communities, reinterpretation-relevant discussion is rare overall (0.288%) but concentrated in specialist genetics communities (6.30% versus 0.10% in general medical-advice communities), and it has grown fivefold since 2014. The pipeline surfaced 123 candidate classification differences, and in a clinician review of 30 drafts, **27 were judged factually grounded but only 15 fit to send**.

papers.title: Segment What It Can Draw: Querying a Text-to-Image Generator with Its Own Images for Skin Lesion Segmentation
papers.abstract: Skin lesion segmentation without annotated masks requires the target to be specified through other cues. Existing approaches rely on dermoscopy-specific rules, annotation-derived model priors, or user-selected regions. A general text-to-image diffusion transformer offers a text interface to the target, but its concept-word attention is unreliable on dermoscopy images: in the model's attention-output space, the word-derived skin-to-lesion direction is poorly aligned with the direction separating real skin from real lesions. We show that the direction derived from generated healthy-skin and lesion images is substantially better aligned. Based on this finding, we propose GENIQ, a training-free method that constructs initial skin and lesion prototypes from generated images and refines them using the most skin-like and lesion-like patches from unlabelled dermoscopy images. It scores test patches along the refined direction and applies a gated threshold to suppress contextual spill-over around small lesions. Without inference-time annotations or additional models, GENIQ achieves Dice scores of 0.85-0.88 on three dermoscopy test sets. It outperforms zero-shot and word-based attention methods on all three sets, and a hand-designed dermoscopy pipeline in Dice and IoU on two.
papers.summary: Segmenting skin lesions without annotated masks requires some other way to specify the target, and the attention a text-to-image diffusion transformer pays to concept words turns out to be unreliable on dermoscopy images. The authors show that a skin-to-lesion direction derived from the model's own generated healthy-skin and lesion images aligns much better with real data than the word-derived direction. They build on this with `GENIQ`, a training-free method that creates skin and lesion prototypes from generated images, refines them with the most confident patches from unlabelled dermoscopy images, and applies a gated threshold to limit spill-over around small lesions. Without inference-time annotations or extra models, it reaches **Dice scores of 0.85–0.88 on three dermoscopy test sets** and outperforms zero-shot and word-based attention methods on all three.

papers.title: SD-LoRA: Training-Time Structural Distillation into LoRA for Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation
papers.abstract: Few-shot adaptation of vision-language models must balance two competing goals: learning fine-grained visual distinctions from very limited supervision and preserving the efficiency that makes frozen CLIP-like models attractive for deployment. Existing lightweight adaptation methods, including prompt tuning, LoRA, and cache-based adapters, typically supervise global image embeddings and therefore underuse token-level structure. Conversely, structure-aware methods exploit local evidence but often introduce additional inference-time computation. We propose SD-LoRA, a structural distillation framework that uses token-level graph reasoning only during training and transfers its effects into a lightweight LoRA-adapted CLIP model. During training, a heterogeneous graph teacher models patch-patch, global-local, and visual-text relations over high-resolution ViT tokens. Rather than retaining this graph at test time, SD-LoRA transfers its structural bias into the shared CLIP-LoRA backbone through implicit distillation and Prototype Predictive Alignment, which aligns graph-conditioned representations with support-derived class prototypes. At inference, the graph teacher is discarded; prediction requires only a single CLIP-LoRA forward pass and a cache-based classifier. Across 11 few-shot benchmarks, SD-LoRA improves over a strong CLIP-LoRA baseline by 2.4/1.8/3.0/2.4/2.0 percentage points in the 1/2/4/8/16-shot settings, respectively, without additional graph computation at test time. Results on base-to-novel generalization, cross-dataset transfer, out-of-distribution robustness, and calibration further show that training-time structural supervision improves both accuracy and transfer reliability. Code is available at https://github.com/MR-Sherif/SD-LoRA.git.
papers.summary: Few-shot adaptation of `CLIP`-like vision-language models typically supervises only global image embeddings, while methods that exploit token-level structure add cost at inference time. `SD-LoRA` uses a heterogeneous graph teacher over high-resolution `ViT` tokens during training only, modeling patch-patch, global-local, and visual-text relations, and transfers its structural bias into a `LoRA`-adapted `CLIP` backbone through implicit distillation and `Prototype Predictive Alignment`. At test time the graph is discarded, so inference is a single `CLIP-LoRA` forward pass plus a cache-based classifier. Across 11 few-shot benchmarks it improves over a strong `CLIP-LoRA` baseline by **2.4, 1.8, 3.0, 2.4, and 2.0 percentage points in the 1- to 16-shot settings**, with better calibration and transfer as well.

papers.title: Stochastic Dynamics of Generative AI: From Autoregressive Models to Interacting LLM Networks and Neural SDEs
papers.abstract: This paper develops a stochastic dynamical-systems perspective on three classes of generative AI models. First, we formulate large language models (LLMs) as high-dimensional nonlinear autoregressive models with attention-based dependencies. This formulation connects pretraining by conditional maximum likelihood to sequential token generation and provides a probabilistic interpretation of LLM operation. Second, we consider networks of interacting LLMs and characterize their collective behavior through mean-field ordinary differential equations. These dynamics provide a framework for understanding emergent preferential attachment and persistent structural biases, including type-dependent glass-ceiling effects. Third, we consider neural stochastic differential equations (SDEs) as continuous-time generative models for stochastic trajectories, including those observed at irregular time intervals. We discuss their training with particular emphasis on Wiener-space cubature methods based on rough-path analysis as an efficient alternative to Monte Carlo estimation. Together, the three settings address probabilistic prediction, information exchange and emergent behavior in interacting networks, and path-space generative modeling.
papers.summary: The work frames three classes of generative models as stochastic dynamical systems. Large language models are formulated as high-dimensional nonlinear autoregressive models, linking maximum-likelihood pretraining to token generation. Networks of interacting LLMs are analyzed through mean-field ordinary differential equations, which explain **emergent preferential attachment and persistent structural biases such as type-dependent glass-ceiling effects**. Neural stochastic differential equations (SDEs) are treated as generative models for irregularly sampled trajectories, with Wiener-space cubature based on rough-path analysis proposed as an efficient alternative to Monte Carlo training.

papers.title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Epigraph-Form Guided Exploration
papers.abstract: Discovering cooperative behavior in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is challenging due to the combinatorial complexity of joint state-action spaces, which hinders the emergence of coordinated behaviors from trial-and-error alone. Intrinsic rewards are often used to aid discovery, but naively combining them with team objectives can distort the learning signal, compromising task performance. In this paper, we propose EFXPLORER, a constrained exploration framework that maximizes exploration objectives subject to a constraint that preserves established task performance. We solve the resulting problem using an epigraph reformulation that introduces adaptive exploration budgets. This approach separates intrinsic rewards from task objectives and regulates exploration through task feasibility. To further encourage diverse and temporally extended exploration, we incorporate a successor distance-based intrinsic reward that captures long-horizon dependencies. Empirically, our method outperforms strong baselines and induces novel cooperative strategies across SMAX, VMAS, and MPE benchmark suites.
papers.summary: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), intrinsic exploration rewards help agents discover coordinated behavior, but adding them naively to the team objective can distort learning and hurt task performance. `EFXPLORER` instead maximizes exploration subject to a constraint that preserves established task performance, solving the problem through an epigraph reformulation that yields adaptive exploration budgets and keeps intrinsic and task rewards separate. It also adds a successor-distance-based intrinsic reward to encourage diverse, temporally extended exploration. The method **outperforms strong baselines and induces novel cooperative strategies** across the `SMAX`, `VMAS`, and `MPE` benchmark suites.

papers.title: Finite-Time Convergence and Regret Guarantees for Neural Reinforcement Learning in POMDPs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) is computationally challenging due to the curse of long-range dependence on history. Fortunately, recent studies have shown that a range of POMDPs that satisfy the filter stability assumption can be well approximated by a superstate Markov Decision Process (MDP) based on a truncated history in a finite-memory window, with a value gap that decays with the window length. However, existing finite-time convergence analyses on such superstate MDP surrogates are either limited to over-simplified linear function approximation or rely on an i.i.d. sampling oracle that is violated by POMDP trajectories, both of which severely limit the applicability of these theoretical results in practice. This motivates us to bridge the gap by investigating RL in POMDPs with nonlinear neural value function approximation. Our main contributions are threefold: i) We first establish a new finite-state MDP point-wise approximation error bound, which lays the foundation for our RL algorithm design and analysis in POMDPs; ii) By applying Temporal-Difference (TD) learning to POMDP-generated superstate transitions and targeting the Bellman fixed point of the superstate MDP, we prove a finite-time critic error bound with nonlinear neural value function approximation; and iii) By combining the neural critic function approximation error bound with the policy mirror descent framework, we obtain a finite-time sublinear regret against the optimal POMDP value. To the best of our knowledge, such a finite-time sublinear regret based on neural function approximation is the first in the literature for finite-memory POMDPs. Our numerical experiments also verify our theoretical results.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) can be approximated by a superstate MDP over a finite window of recent history, but existing finite-time analyses either assume linear function approximation or rely on independent sampling that POMDP trajectories violate. The authors derive a new pointwise approximation-error bound for the finite-state surrogate, prove a finite-time error bound for temporal-difference (TD) learning with a nonlinear neural critic on POMDP-generated trajectories, and combine it with policy mirror descent. The result is **the first finite-time sublinear regret bound with neural function approximation for finite-memory POMDPs**, supported by numerical experiments.

papers.title: Shaping & Monitoring Models through their Internal Representations
papers.abstract: We propose Mechanistic Shaping, a unified framework for shaping models through their internal representations. Mechanistic Shaping is applied during training so that models follow specifications (rules) about which concepts they express, measured via their outputs or internal representations (e.g., no harmful content), and also which concepts they rely on, i.e., what they use to make their decisions (e.g., not a candidate's gender when screening a r\'esum\'e). Across multiple domains (vision, medical imaging, language), scales (up to 32B parameters), and training paradigms (classification, SFT, DPO, GRPO), we find that Mechanistic Shaping substantially reduces targeted behaviors while preserving task performance. Since training against a representation can also modify it, we ask whether shaped concepts remain monitorable, a question that depends on the class of monitors considered. We therefore introduce a hierarchy of such classes, which separates a concept that escapes one probe from a concept that is truly gone. We characterize three geometric mechanisms of circumvention: the concept can drift away from the monitor, be erased from the layer, or persist in higher-order statistics as a nonlinear encoding, which we explain through a product-code construction. Although other mechanisms may arise in different settings or at larger scales, these three account for all of our observations, and each can be detected by a matching monitor. In practice, we find that shaped concepts largely remain monitorable: refitted linear probes recover the concept in most settings, and the original probe remains reliable whenever gradients do not flow through it. Taken together, these results point to the potential of using interpretability as a tool for training, and call for a correspondingly rigorous science of interpretability-based training.
papers.summary: `Mechanistic Shaping` is a training-time framework that uses a model's internal representations to enforce rules about which concepts it expresses (for example, no harmful content) and which concepts it relies on (for example, not using gender when screening résumés). Across vision, medical imaging, and language, at up to 32B parameters and with classification, SFT, `DPO`, and `GRPO` training, it **substantially reduces targeted behaviors while preserving task performance**. Because training against a representation can change it, the authors introduce a hierarchy of monitor classes and identify three ways a concept can evade a probe: drifting away from it, being erased from the layer, or persisting as a nonlinear encoding. In practice, shaped concepts largely remain monitorable, since refitted linear probes recover them in most settings.

papers.title: When Verification Is Not Agreement: Cross-Agent LLM-to-Dafny Formalization
papers.abstract: A verified Dafny postcondition certifies that a formula holds, but it does not guarantee that the result was reached through genuine independent reasoning. We introduce a cross-agent formalization protocol where a Specifier model translates clinical trial criteria into a Dafny predicate, and an Implementer model writes an operational method checked against it. A same-model control establishes that even with no capability gap, independent re-extraction from identical text agrees only 59.3% of the time. Evaluating four model configurations on 96 clinical trial documents, we find that agreement is highly sensitive to how model capability is allocated across the two roles: the GPT-4.1-nano/GPT-4.1-mini configuration achieves 53.0% agreement when the stronger model is the Implementer, but only 14.3% when the roles are reversed. The strongest tested configuration, GPT-5.6-luna/GPT-5.4-mini, improves agreement to 34.4% but remains below the same-model baseline and is dominated by direct contradiction (42.7%). We also detect a critical verification artifact in which a weaker Implementer satisfies the postcondition by invoking the Specifier's predicate directly; after structural auditing, corrected agreement falls from 14.3% to 13.2%. Our results show that verification success alone is insufficient evidence of independent cross-agent agreement, and that model capability does not guarantee agreement when formalizing the same source independently.
papers.summary: A verified `Dafny` postcondition shows that a formula holds, but not that two models independently reached the same understanding of the source. In a cross-agent protocol, a Specifier model translates clinical-trial criteria into a `Dafny` predicate and an Implementer model writes a method checked against it; even a same-model control agrees only 59.3% of the time. Across 96 clinical-trial documents, agreement depends heavily on how capability is split between the roles: `GPT-4.1-nano`/`GPT-4.1-mini` reaches 53.0% with the stronger model as Implementer but only 14.3% when the roles are reversed. The authors also find weaker Implementers satisfying the postcondition by calling the Specifier's predicate directly, concluding that **verification success alone is insufficient evidence of independent agreement**.

papers.title: Optimistic Hedge in General-Sum Games: Fundamental Limits and Regret Bounds via Temporal Approximation
papers.abstract:
Optimistic Hedge, a multiplicative weight update with one step of extrapolation, is one of the most natural regret-minimizing dynamics for games, and characterizing its regret has been a longstanding open question. Daskalakis, Fishelson and Golowich proved that if all $m$ players in a finite general-sum game follow Optimistic Hedge with a fixed learning rate, each player's regret is polylogarithmic in the horizon $T$. Subsequently, Ha showed that an appropriate choice of learning rate makes each player's regret bounded independently of $T$. This bound, however, is non-constructive and its dependence on the number of actions $n$ is not explicit, leaving open whether Optimistic Hedge can achieve a constant regret bound which is polynomial in the size of the game.
  We show that the answer hinges on the number of players. In two-player games, there is a learning rate for which Optimistic Hedge guarantees $O(n\log n)$ regret independent of the horizon. In three-player games, however, no such bound is possible: for any learning rate up to an absolute constant and for sufficiently large horizon $T$, there is a game with $n$ actions per player in which some player's regret is $2^{\Omega(n)}$, and more generally, for every $m\ge3$ we construct $m$-player games in which some player's regret is $2^{\Omega(mn)}$; for learning rates above $2^{-\Omega(mn)}$, that player's regret even grows linearly in $T$.
  Our upper bound is based on a temporal approximation framework for the analysis of Optimistic Hedge. Starting from the variance-based RVU bound of Daskalakis et al., we approximate the losses over time-localized windows by well-behaved functions, whose total variation is a small fraction of their cumulative variance. In $m$-player games, the same framework gives a significantly simplified proof of the recent $O(\sqrt{m}\log n\log T)$ regret bound due to Ha.
papers.summary: Optimistic Hedge, a multiplicative-weights algorithm with one step of extrapolation, was known to achieve horizon-independent regret in general-sum games, but whether that bound could be polynomial in the game's size was an open question. The answer depends on the number of players: in two-player games a suitable learning rate gives O(n log n) regret independent of the horizon, where n is the number of actions. **With three or more players no such bound exists**: the authors construct games where some player's regret is exponential in n, and grows linearly in the horizon for larger learning rates. The upper bound comes from a temporal approximation framework that also gives a much simpler proof of a recent bound for m-player games.

papers.title: Synthesizing symbolic models of human and machine reasoning at scale
papers.abstract: Symbolic models offer a powerful account of cognition, but their scope has historically been limited by the need for hand-engineering and computational tractability. We show how advances in artificial intelligence (AI) can scale symbolic modeling and help overcome these engineering limitations. We introduce Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis (BCSS)---an approach for automated search of interpretable, deterministic symbolic programs that verifiably reproduce behavior---and apply it to model both human and machine behavior across hundreds of challenging reasoning problems. Analyzing these programs reveals that both people and machines tend to oversimplify, adopt rules that are partial explanations for their observations, and misinfer dependencies between problem features. These shared signatures are modulated by available resources, with reasoning effort predicting the extent to which machines simplify and explain their observations. Together, these results point to underlying mechanisms reminiscent of satisficing in both people and machines, and illustrate how BCSS offers a general approach for interpreting and comparing rule-based reasoning of humans and black-box AI systems.
papers.summary: Symbolic models of cognition have been limited by the need to engineer them by hand. `Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis` (`BCSS`) uses AI to automatically search for interpretable, deterministic symbolic programs that verifiably reproduce observed behavior, and it is applied to both humans and AI models across hundreds of challenging reasoning problems. The synthesized programs show that **people and machines share the same failure signatures**: both oversimplify, adopt rules that only partly explain their observations, and misinfer dependencies between problem features. In machines, reasoning effort predicts how much they simplify, pointing to satisficing-like mechanisms in both.

papers.title: Polynomial-Time Computation of Extensive-Form Proper Equilibria in Two-Player Zero-Sum Games
papers.abstract: We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for computing an exact extensive-form proper equilibrium in a finite two-player zero-sum extensive-form game with perfect recall and rational data. Properness is understood in the agent normal form: an action at an information set is penalized relative to a better action while all other local behavioral choices, including the player's own future actions, remain fixed. Our algorithm assigns each information set a geometric permutahedron of allowable action probabilities. A scaled doubly stochastic representation embeds these restrictions in a polynomial-size sequence-form polytope; a saddle point then satisfies the local $\varepsilon$-properness inequalities. To obtain an exact equilibrium rather than a solution at an arbitrarily small numerical perturbation, we establish sign stability of a parametric linear system, construct a persistent feasible basis, and extract the limits of behavioral ratios. The resulting probabilities are rational and have polynomial encoding length, including at information sets whose realization probabilities vanish.
papers.summary: The authors give **a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for computing an exact extensive-form proper equilibrium** in finite two-player zero-sum games with perfect recall, with properness defined in the agent normal form. Each information set is assigned a geometric permutahedron of allowable action probabilities, embedded through a scaled doubly stochastic representation into a polynomial-size sequence-form polytope, so that a saddle point satisfies local ε-properness. To obtain an exact equilibrium rather than a perturbed approximation, they prove sign stability of a parametric linear system and extract limits of behavioral ratios, yielding rational probabilities of polynomial encoding length even at information sets that are reached with probability zero.

papers.title: Server-Side Sparse Assignment for Federated Mixture-of-Experts
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly recognized for their remarkable capabilities; federated learning (FL) offers a promising framework for collaboratively fine-tuning LLMs on edge devices while achieving data privacy. However, edge devices are inherently heterogeneous: clients may exhibit diverse data distributions and resource constraints, including limited memory and computation budgets. Recent federated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches address these challenges by using sparse expert activation or partial expert loading. However, existing partial-expert methods rely on heuristic full-pool observations or prioritize system-wide load balance, without guarantees for recovering client-specific relevant experts from partial observations. We propose $S^3$-MoE, a server-side sparse expert assignment framework that estimates client-specific expert relevance from partial observations and refines assignments through an exploit--explore mechanism. We also establish relevance-estimation error and exact Top-$K$ recovery guarantees. Experiments using a CNN-based MoE on CIFAR-100 show that $S^3$-MoE recovers task-dependent client--expert preferences and reduces conflicts caused by correlated expert selection across clients. Compared with Full-20 FedAvg, which gives each client access to all 20 experts for local Top-5 routing, $S^3$-MoE achieves 1.31 percentage points higher mean final accuracy while loading only $5$ experts per client.
papers.summary: Federated fine-tuning of mixture-of-experts (MoE) models on heterogeneous edge devices often loads only some experts per client, but existing partial-loading methods use heuristics without guarantees that each client gets its relevant experts. `S^3-MoE` has the server estimate client-specific expert relevance from partial observations and refine assignments through an exploit-explore mechanism, with proven bounds on estimation error and exact Top-K recovery. In experiments with a CNN-based MoE on `CIFAR-100`, it recovers task-dependent client-expert preferences and achieves **1.31 percentage points higher accuracy than full-access `FedAvg` while loading only 5 of 20 experts per client**.

papers.title: A Night at the LLM Zoo: Data Conditioned Flow Matching for Generating Pretrained LLM Weights
papers.abstract: A challenge to Weight Space Learning as it expands from task specific and vision models to Large Language Models (LLMs) is the absence of a well curated and analyzed LLM population. To address this, we train such a model zoo for application to Weight Space Generation by systematically varying the data mixture composition between web text, books, mathematics, coding, and French across populations of 51M, 124M, and 355M parameter GPT-2 Models, each tier with count N = 100. We analyze these populations by cosine similarity, functional diversity, Leave-One-Mixture-Out modeling, and variance decomposition. We show that the zoo contains diverse models whose variation is structured by training mixture composition. We embed the training mixture composition to condition a Flow Matching model of complete pretrained LLM weights in Gram-PCA compressed weight space. By demonstrating zero-shot generalization to held out mixtures, measuring Continuous Ranked Probability Score skill, as well as finding minimal changes in downstream test-set perplexity and general capability benchmark scores, we show that our generator generalizes on the simplex of data mixtures to produce models that perform similarly to those in the zoo ex nihilo. Finally, we produce all source code and artifacts to support the continued expansion of Weight Space Learning and Generation into the LLM domain.
papers.summary: Weight-space learning, which treats trained model weights as data, lacks a well-curated population of language models to study. The authors train a model zoo of `GPT-2` models at 51M, 124M, and 355M parameters, 100 per size, systematically varying the training mixture of web text, books, math, code, and French, and show that variation across the zoo is structured by mixture composition. They then train a mixture-conditioned flow-matching model over compressed weights that **generates complete pretrained LLM weights for held-out data mixtures** whose perplexity and benchmark scores are close to those of the trained models. All code and artifacts are released.
papers.highlight_summary:
Weight-space learning has mostly stayed with small vision models and LoRA adapters, partly because no controlled population of full pretrained LLMs existed to study. The authors build one: 300 GPT-2 models whose only difference is the mix of pretraining data. They then train a flow-matching generator that takes a data mixture as input and outputs complete model weights, including for mixtures it never saw.

- **Zoo design:** Each tier has 100 models, at `51M`, `124M` and `355M` parameters. Every model starts from a shared trunk and branches off for the final **15%** of training on its own blend of web text, books, math, code and French. The 85 distinct mixtures per tier are 20 "anchors" (the five single-domain mixtures, each trained four times with different seeds) plus 80 random mixtures in between.
- **Weights track the data mix:** After removing the drift every model inherits from the shared trunk, models trained on the same mixture have cosine similarity **0.80–0.89**, while models trained on different single-domain mixtures are near-orthogonal. Among the 20 anchors, mixture identity explains **η² = 0.87–0.94** of the variance in the weights. Models trained on different mixtures also disagree on the next token about twice as often as same-mixture replicates.
- **Generator:** A `rectified flow` with an MLP velocity network and a learned mixture embedding generates 50-dimensional `Gram-PCA` codes, using classifier-free guidance. The codes are decoded into full GPT-2 weights, which are evaluated with no further training. Five Euler integration steps already come close to the 50-step results.
- **Results on held-out mixtures:** Generated models change perplexity by **4.05–5.11%**, compared with **5.75–6.01%** for a nearest-neighbour retrieval baseline that is blinded to the same neighbourhood. For reference, seed noise alone gives about **1%** and the rank-50 compression alone gives **1.8–2.5%**. Conditioning on the mixture yields a CRPS skill of about **0.6** over a mixture-blind baseline, and the flow's likelihood picks out the correct mixture among all 85 candidates for **94–97%** of held-out models. On `HellaSwag`, generated models score on par with the real ones.
- **Limitations:**
  - Generation fails at the single-domain mixtures, with median CRPS skill below **0.15**.
  - Generated models respond only **42–54%** as strongly as real models to changes in domain weight.
  - The lead over retrieval shrinks at `355M`, where the flow wins only **43 of 85** mixtures.
  - The PCA basis is fitted on all models, including the held-out ones.
  - At these scales, `HellaSwag` accuracy sits within a few points of chance.

papers.title: Credibility Clustering for Experience Rating: An Automated Approach to Risk Group Allocation in Group Life Insurance
papers.abstract: In insurance, experience rating plays a crucial role in mitigating adverse selection by adjusting premiums according to historical claims experience. A key step in this process is the classification of insured collectives into homogeneous risk groups. Within group life insurance, this classification traditionally relies on manual decisions and arbitrary thresholds, which may lead to inefficiencies and inconsistent outcomes. This paper proposes a data-driven methodology for automating risk group allocation based on a combination of the multidimensional B\"uhlmann-Straub model and k-means clustering -- referred to as credibility clustering. By incorporating credibility weights, the method accounts for the varying statistical significance of experience data and ensuresthat risk classifications are both actuarially sound and practically implementable. Empirical results based on real-world group life insurance data from a major European insurer demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms the two k-means benchmark variants considered in the empirical application in terms of viability, temporal stability and accounting for statistical reliability.
papers.summary: In group life insurance, assigning insured groups to risk classes for experience-based premiums traditionally relies on manual decisions and arbitrary thresholds. The proposed credibility clustering combines the multidimensional `Bühlmann-Straub` credibility model with k-means clustering, so that groups with less statistically reliable claims experience carry less weight in the classification. On real data from a major European insurer, it **outperforms two k-means benchmark variants in viability, temporal stability, and handling of statistical reliability**.

papers.title: Regulating Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand Operators with Fixed and Adaptive Penalties: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach
papers.abstract: Profit-maximizing Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand (AMoD) operators may exploit consumer surplus through excessive prices and underserve less profitable regions by relocating vehicles away from them. We study how penalty-based regulation of an AMoD operator in a multimodal mobility system can limit surge pricing and improve regional service availability. We model regulation as an outer control loop that acts on a learning-based operator. Static regulation with fixed penalties is formulated as a Markov Decision Process for an operator that jointly controls pricing and rebalancing, and dynamic regulation as a Partially Observable Stochastic Game in which a regulator periodically adjusts region-specific penalties in closed loop. Operator and regulator policies are learned with graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning. In experiments with real-world Manhattan data, fixed surge pricing penalties reduce the share of travelers facing excessive prices from 22% to 1%. For regional service availability, dynamic regulation improves the regulator's reward by up to 15.6% over fixed penalties of equal mean intensity. The gains in service availability are strongest when spare fleet capacity exists, whereas service deficits persist in peak periods with highly utilized fleets. The learned regulator policy responds by reducing penalties where limited fleet capacity restricts compliance. The results identify trade-offs between regulatory targets, operator profitability, and traveler utility.
papers.summary: Profit-maximizing autonomous mobility-on-demand (AMoD) operators may overcharge riders and pull vehicles away from less profitable regions. The authors model regulation as an outer control loop around a learning operator: fixed penalties are formulated as a Markov decision process, and adaptive penalties as a partially observable stochastic game in which a regulator adjusts region-specific penalties, with both sides trained by graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning. On real Manhattan data, **fixed surge-pricing penalties cut the share of travelers facing excessive prices from 22% to 1%**, and dynamic regulation improves the regulator's service-availability reward by up to 15.6%, although service deficits persist at peak times when the fleet is fully used.

papers.title: PromptOps: Iterative Prompt Optimization for LLM-as-a-Judge Systems
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for evaluating the behavior of chatbots and other AI systems. In deployment, however, their agreement with the intended human evaluation policy may degrade as user interactions and score distributions change. Existing automatic prompt optimization methods are primarily studied as one-shot procedures on static development sets and therefore provide limited guidance for maintaining LLM judges over time. We frame this problem as judge drift and introduce PromptOps, a closedloop framework for monitoring and iteratively recalibrating LLM-as-a-Judge (LLMaaJ) systems. PromptOps separates four operational decisions: when to optimize, which optimization procedure to apply, which feedback records to use, and how to update the judge prompt. We instantiate the framework with five prompt optimization methods: GEPA, SIMBA, Rubric Synthesis, and exemplar selection using either simulated annealing or a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. Our experiments demonstrate that iterative prompt optimization can recalibrate LLM judges and recover performance after controlled shifts in the referencescore distribution. However, effective maintenance is inherently contextdependent: neither optimization algorithm choice nor update timing generalizes universally across settings. These findings establish prompt optimization for deployed LLM judges as an inherently iterative maintenance problem and demonstrate that PromptOps provides a practical abstraction for studying and implementing this process.
papers.summary: LLM-as-a-judge systems can drift out of agreement with their intended human evaluation policy as user interactions and score distributions change, while automatic prompt optimization is usually studied as a one-off procedure on a static dataset. `PromptOps` is a closed-loop framework for monitoring and recalibrating judge prompts that separates four decisions: when to optimize, which optimizer to use, which feedback records to use, and how to update the prompt. It is instantiated with five methods, including `GEPA`, `SIMBA`, and `Rubric Synthesis`. Iterative optimization recovers judge performance after controlled distribution shifts, but **neither the choice of optimizer nor the update timing generalizes across settings**.

papers.title: Machine Learning for Live-Birth Prediction After IVF/ICSI From Structured Clinical Data: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Critical Appraisal
