papers.abstract: Machine-learning models predicting live birth after in vitro fertilisation (IVF) or intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) from routine clinical data report performance from near chance to near perfect. We systematically reviewed these models under PRISMA 2020, searching OpenAlex, Scopus and Web of Science to 22 October 2026, appraised them with PROBAST+AI and TRIPOD+AI, and pooled their discrimination with random-effects meta-analysis on the logit scale. We define what fixes the meaning of a model's output (decision point, endpoint, unit of analysis, data source) and map the 48 included studies by model family, decision point and validation design. Models evaluated only internally pooled to an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.814, against 0.756 (95% prediction interval 0.546-0.889) for models evaluated on a later period or another centre, and 0.764 for studies not at high risk of bias; neither difference was significant, and heterogeneity was extreme. Models whose decision point was not stated pooled to 0.910, the only significant moderator in meta-regression. Against logistic regression fitted to the same data, the best machine-learning model gained a pooled 0.056 AUC (95% CI 0.017-0.090). Of 48 studies, 47 were at high or unclear risk of bias, only four assessed the calibration slope, and no model has evidence of clinical impact. The certainty of the pooled evidence is low to very low; the gains that survive validation came from staging predictions to decision points and local calibration, not deeper architectures. We provide a TRIPOD+AI-mapped checklist, a benchmark specification and a research agenda.
papers.summary: Machine-learning models that predict live birth after in vitro fertilisation (IVF) or intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) report performance ranging from near chance to near perfect. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 48 studies found pooled area under the curve (AUC) of 0.814 for internally validated models versus 0.756 for externally validated ones, and the best machine-learning models beat logistic regression on the same data by only 0.056 AUC. **47 of 48 studies were at high or unclear risk of bias**, only four checked calibration slope, and no model has evidence of clinical impact. The gains that survive validation came from tying predictions to specific clinical decision points and from local calibration, not from deeper architectures.

papers.title: Data-Driven Modeling of Molten Chloride Corrosion Using Static Test Data
papers.abstract: Molten chloride corrosion has been studied for decades, yet reliable prediction across different alloys, salts, and test conditions remains difficult. In this work, 291 static molten chloride corrosion experiments reported in the literature were compiled into a structured dataset and used to develop an interpretable machine-learning framework for corrosion-rate predictions. To better represent the differences in salt condition across studies, a Chloride Salt Preparation Index (CSPI) was introduced to bring the reported salt-treatment method, atmosphere control, and pre-exposure impurity condition on a common numerical scale. A blended tree-based ensemble provided the most consistent predictive performance, achieving a cross-validated \(R^2\) of 0.85 and an MAE of 0.41 mg cm\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\). The graded CSPI retained more useful information than a simple purified/unpurified classification and emerged as the dominant model descriptor. Global sensitivity and SHAP analyses further identified exposure time, temperature, and alloy chemistry as important contributors to the model predictions, with several observed trends consistent with the established molten-chloride corrosion behavior. The conformal prediction intervals were well calibrated, providing an estimate of prediction uncertainty in addition to the point prediction. Overall, the framework demonstrates that historical corrosion data can support quantitative, interpretable, and uncertainty-aware prediction when experimental context is represented explicitly, while also highlighting where more consistent reporting and targeted experiments are needed to improve future molten-salt corrosion models.
papers.summary: Predicting molten chloride corrosion across alloys, salts, and test conditions has remained difficult despite decades of experiments. The authors compiled 291 static corrosion experiments from the literature and introduced a Chloride Salt Preparation Index (`CSPI`) that puts differences in salt treatment, atmosphere, and impurities on a common numerical scale. A blended tree-based ensemble reached a **cross-validated R² of 0.85**, with `CSPI` as the dominant predictor, and `SHAP` and sensitivity analyses identified exposure time, temperature, and alloy chemistry as important factors. Conformal prediction intervals were well calibrated, giving uncertainty estimates alongside point predictions.

papers.title: Adapting LLM Judges to Observed Human Annotation Policy through Soft Prompt Tuning
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly employed as automated judges for evaluating chatbot responses. While proprietary models can achieve high agreement with human annotators, they remain costly and difficult to deploy in practical settings. Lightweight open-source LLM judges provide an attractive alternative but typically exhibit lower agreement with human ratings. In this paper, we investigate whether soft prompt tuning can align open-source LLM judges more closely with human annotation policy. We train soft prompts on the FairBotBench benchmark and evaluate the adapted judges across the dimensions of bias, toxicity, and personalization. Our findings demonstrate that hybrid soft-prompt tuning, which combines textual prompts with learned continuous prompt embeddings, consistently improves agreement with human annotations over the corresponding untuned baselines. For Qwen 3.5 9B, the adapted judges surpass both hosted reference judges across all three evaluation dimensions.
papers.summary: Proprietary LLM judges agree well with human annotators but are costly, while lightweight open-source judges agree less. The authors test whether soft prompt tuning, which learns continuous prompt embeddings, can align open-source judges with an observed human annotation policy, training on the `FairBotBench` benchmark across bias, toxicity, and personalization. Hybrid tuning, which combines a text prompt with learned embeddings, consistently improves agreement over untuned baselines, and **adapted `Qwen 3.5 9B` judges surpass both hosted reference judges on all three dimensions**.

papers.title: Scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification for Cancer Histopathology: Calibrated Uncertainty Under Distribution Shift
papers.abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification is essential for clinical deployment of cancer diagnosis models, yet neural networks and variational Gaussian process methods can produce overconfident predictions, particularly under the distribution shifts that arise when models trained at one hospital are applied at another. We present a scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification (GPC) framework that operates on frozen pathology foundation model embeddings (Phikon) and combines accelerated Randomly Pivoted Cholesky (RPCholesky) for low-rank kernel factorization, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) with non-centered parameterization for posterior sampling, and a pivots-as-inducing-points scheme for prediction. This makes HMC posterior sampling in the low-rank latent representation tractable at N approximately 300,000 training points, enabling HC-based low-rank GPC on substantially larger datasets than prior MCMC-based demonstrations. We evaluate on two histopathology benchmarks for breast cancer metastasis detection: PCam and CAMELYON17-WILDS, where the latter tests calibration under hospital-level distribution shift. Compared to stochastic variational GP and neural network baselines, our method improves calibration and predictive performance - reducing expected calibration error by up to 88% and false negative rate by up to 90% - with the largest gains appearing under distribution shift, suggesting that HMC-based posterior sampling provides more trustworthy uncertainty estimates for cross-site pathology classification.
papers.summary: Cancer histopathology classifiers need reliable uncertainty estimates, particularly when a model trained at one hospital is used at another. The authors run Bayesian Gaussian process classification on frozen `Phikon` foundation-model embeddings, combining accelerated randomly pivoted Cholesky factorization, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) posterior sampling, and pivots reused as inducing points, which makes HMC tractable on about 300,000 training points. On `PCam` and `CAMELYON17-WILDS`, it **reduces expected calibration error by up to 88% and false-negative rate by up to 90%** compared with variational Gaussian process and neural-network baselines, with the largest gains under cross-hospital distribution shift.

papers.title: Bayesian Tensor Train Kernel Machines with Automatic Model Complexity Inference
papers.abstract: Tensor Network (TN) kernel machines accelerate supervised learning by using low-rank TNs to reduce computation and memory. However, most TN-based methods are deterministic with manually tuned ranks and feature dimensions, while the existing Bayesian TN kernel machine is restricted to the CANDECOMP/PARAFAC decomposition (CPD), whose single rank is shared by all modes. We extend this framework to the tensor train (TT) and propose Bayesian Tensor Train Kernel Machines (BTT-KM), whose hierarchical ARD-type priors on the TT cores infer the TT ranks and feature dimensions from data. Since each TT core is coupled to the others only through its neighbors, its closed-form posterior update requires propagating the contributions of all other cores along the chain. Mean-field variational inference yields a Bayesian alternating least squares algorithm with the same computational complexity as its deterministic counterpart and a closed-form predictive distribution. A synthetic experiment illustrates that BTT-KM recovers the true TT ranks and feature dimensions from an over-parameterized initialization.
papers.summary: Tensor network kernel machines use low-rank tensor decompositions to cut the cost of supervised kernel learning. Most of these methods need their ranks and feature dimensions tuned by hand, and the only existing Bayesian version is limited to the CANDECOMP/PARAFAC decomposition (`CPD`), which uses a single rank for all modes. The authors extend the Bayesian approach to the tensor train (`TT`) format with `BTT-KM`. Hierarchical automatic-relevance-determination-style priors on the TT cores infer the ranks and feature dimensions from data, and mean-field variational inference produces a Bayesian alternating least squares algorithm with **the same computational complexity as its deterministic counterpart**. In a synthetic experiment, the model recovers the true TT ranks and feature dimensions starting from an over-parameterized initialization.

papers.title: Teaching Agents the "Principle", Not the "Reward"
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has achieved strong performance in many tasks by letting agents learn from nothing more than a reward signal. However, in more complex tasks, agents still struggle to learn good, generalizable policies, even with carefully designed rewards and abundant samples. We argue that this difficulty stems from the reward decoding burden: designers encode their knowledge of the desired behavior into rewards and penalties, and agents must infer this knowledge from long sequences of noisy scalars. To address this burden, we propose prescriptive policy learning (PPL), which directly teaches agents higher-level knowledge about the tasks, termed principles of behavior, such as how to maintain balance, how to accumulate energy, and how to land smoothly. Through appropriately selected key quantities and references, PPL can directly indicate at every step whether the agent follows the principles and to what extent. Our experiments show that agents can learn good, generalizable policies without any reward. Taught only simple heuristic principles, PPL agents outperform reward-based methods with far fewer samples. Their policies also transfer directly to harder settings and keep performing well, demonstrating their strong generalization ability. In summary, PPL provides a new approach in which rough knowledge of the desired behavior is enough for agents to learn good, generalizable policies, even when the system dynamics cannot be accurately modeled.
papers.summary: The authors argue that reinforcement learning agents struggle in complex tasks because they must work out the designer's intent from long sequences of noisy scalar rewards, which they call the reward decoding burden. They propose prescriptive policy learning (`PPL`), which teaches agents higher-level principles of behavior instead, such as keeping balance, accumulating energy, or landing smoothly. Selected key quantities and references tell the agent at every step whether it is following each principle and to what degree. In their experiments, **agents learn good policies without any reward**, beat reward-based methods with far fewer samples, and transfer directly to harder settings.

papers.title: A Proxy-Based Method for Measuring Racial Disparities in~Text-to-Image~Generators
papers.abstract: We present an automated method for auditing text-to-image generators for representational bias against ground-truth demographic benchmarks. Our approach adapts the racial proxy variables used in U.S. antidiscrimination law to provide a fine-grained comparative analysis of variations in racial representation in generated images. We classify each generated image by race and then compare the model's distribution to publicly available demographic benchmark data to identify patterns of over- and under-representation. We also measure skin tone using CIELAB values and calculate cosine similarity amongst groups of images in order to capture biases that don't show up in demographic comparisons such as differences in image quality across races and skin tones. We report on experiments testing three models (Imagen 4 Fast, Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large Turbo, and Flux Schnell) using three categories of proxies (geographic, occupational, and surname) and 50 variants within each category. We find notable variation across the models as well as by proxy category. For example, Imagen 4 Fast overrepresents white classified images more than the other models tested and produces images with lighter, more homogeneous skin tones. Imagen 4 Fast also had the largest representational disparity for Black demographics among surname and geographical prompts. Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large Turbo produces results that overall diverge most from census data but yield the most diverse range of skin tones. Our method yields a generalizable and legally-grounded auditing tool that surfaces detailed information about model outputs without relying on implicit normative definitions of fairness.
papers.summary: The authors present an automated way to audit text-to-image generators for racial representation bias. It adapts the racial proxy variables used in U.S. antidiscrimination law (geographic, occupational, and surname prompts) and compares the classified race of generated images with public demographic benchmark data. It also measures skin tone in CIELAB color space and computes cosine similarity within groups of images, which captures disparities such as differences in image quality. Across `Imagen 4 Fast`, `Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large Turbo`, and `Flux Schnell`, **`Imagen 4 Fast` most overrepresents images classified as white and produces lighter, more homogeneous skin tones**, while `Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large Turbo` diverges most from census data but shows the widest range of skin tones.

papers.title: Context-Aware Automated NMR Structure Elucidation
papers.abstract: Machine learning approaches are rapidly revolutionizing the ability to analyze and extract structural insights from chemical data, enabling high-throughput chemical discovery. While existing data-driven approaches have shown remarkable promise for predicting chemical structures in the de novo setting, incorporating additional chemically informed context offers the opportunity to further improve these models' performance and extend their real-world utility. Here we provide a straightforward protocol to combine artificial-intelligence-based spectroscopic elucidation pipelines with contextual chemical data, e.g., known reactants or a desired product, by using automated retrosynthetic analysis to generate large training sets of molecules and contextual data in the form of synthetic precursors. We demonstrate our approach by showing that our recently introduced NMR structure elucidation framework can be trained to effectively leverage molecular precursor context. We show that when the chemical context provides useful information on the target molecule we obtain dramatically improved accuracy over using NMR spectra alone, obtaining Top-15 accuracies of up to 95.4% for molecules up to 40 heavy atoms spanning the full elemental range of organic chemistry. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach is highly robust, such that even when the context provided is uncorrelated with the target, one still obtains accuracies commensurate with those of the original NMR structure elucidation framework. This approach provides an efficient route to improve a wide range of spectroscopic structure elucidation platforms using contextual data.
papers.summary: Machine learning models can predict a molecule's structure from its nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra, but they usually ignore chemical context that is often available, such as known reactants. The authors use automated retrosynthetic analysis to build large training sets that pair molecules with their synthetic precursors, then train their existing NMR structure elucidation framework to use this context. When the context is informative, the model reaches **Top-15 accuracies of up to 95.4% for molecules with up to 40 heavy atoms**. When the context is unrelated to the target, accuracy stays at the level of the original spectra-only model.

papers.title: More Agents, More Reliable? System-Level Reliability of Multi-Agent LLMs under Operational-Profile Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Teams increasingly build software from cooperating large language model (LLM) agents, often assuming more agents mean more reliability. Yet the usual evidence, average benchmark accuracy, ignores the input mix a deployed system meets and the rule merging the agents' answers. Building on HIP-LLM, a hierarchical imprecise-probability assessment of single LLMs, we propose a framework combining it with a Bayesian network of the system's failure logic for multi-agent systems. Agent failure-probability intervals propagate through this network, where the combining rule can itself fail, into a reliability envelope showing which evidence limits it. In a pipeline extracting regulated chemical-hazard statements, majority voting over three models protected against the weakest but did not clearly exceed the best, and a voter failing on 5\% of demands would largely erase its advantage over the middle model. More agents yield a more defensible reliability claim, not automatically a more reliable system.
papers.summary: Teams building software from cooperating large language model (LLM) agents often assume that adding agents makes the system more reliable, but average benchmark accuracy ignores both the input mix a deployed system sees and the rule that merges the agents' answers. The authors combine `HIP-LLM`, a hierarchical imprecise-probability assessment of single LLMs, with a Bayesian network of the system's failure logic. Interval estimates of each agent's failure probability propagate through the network, which also models the chance that the combining rule itself fails, and the result is a reliability envelope. In a pipeline that extracts regulated chemical-hazard statements, majority voting over three models protected against the weakest model but did not clearly beat the best one, and **a voter that fails on 5% of inputs would largely erase its advantage** over the middle model.

papers.title: FastAFD: When Does Attention-FFN Disaggregation Pay on Rack-Scale NVLink?
papers.abstract: Attention-FFN disaggregation (AFD) separates attention from the experts of a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model and has been reported to raise decode throughput over colocated serving. Whether this advantage holds on rack-scale NVLink systems such as GB200 NVL72 remains unclear: prior results were obtained on other hardware, against narrower colocated baselines, or with analytical models, whereas production engines serve large MoE models on these systems with wide expert parallelism (wide EP). We build and tune FastAFD, an AFD engine for GB200 NVL72 that overlaps the MoE of one microbatch with the attention of the other, and compare it against the best vLLM wide EP setting. Experiments show that AFD has a throughput advantage of up to 1.17x over wide EP on Qwen3 and 1.16x on Qwen3.5, and matches it on MiniMax-M2.5. We derive an analytical model that predicts AFD throughput within 3% using only profiles of colocated vLLM, telling whether switching to AFD would pay off before deploying it. The model yields a concise insight: AFD's speedup factors into a batch gain (larger batches, since attention GPUs hold no expert weights), an overlap gain (shorter steps, since the MoE runs on the expert GPUs behind attention), and a disaggregation cost (the GPUs given to experts). AFD has the advantage when the two gains outweigh the cost. This view explains which models benefit from AFD, and shows that speculative decoding helps light-expert models most, where the enlarged overlap gain outweighs the larger disaggregation cost and adds a further 8% to AFD's advantage over wide EP. Looking ahead, serving the experts on accelerators that keep their weights in on-chip SRAM, such as the Groq LPX accelerators paired with Vera Rubin NVL72, would remove most of the disaggregation cost, raising the ideal speedup to 2.48x with speculative decoding. FastAFD is open source at https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/FastAFD.
papers.summary: Attention-FFN disaggregation (AFD) runs attention and the mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers of a model on separate GPUs, and earlier work reported higher decode throughput than colocated serving. It was unclear whether that advantage holds on rack-scale NVLink systems like `GB200 NVL72`. The authors build `FastAFD`, which overlaps one microbatch's MoE computation with another's attention, and compare it against the best `vLLM` wide expert-parallel configuration. AFD comes out **up to 1.17x faster on `Qwen3`** and ties on `MiniMax-M2.5`. An analytical model predicts AFD throughput within 3% using only colocated profiles, and it breaks the speedup into a batch gain, an overlap gain, and a disaggregation cost.

papers.title: Depth or Description? When a One-Step Latent Score Replaces Lookahead in Proactive Information Acquisition
papers.abstract: A proactive agent must decide what to ask before it acts. Exact lookahead values combinations of questions but is expensive and leans on a fitted model; a one-step score is cheap but can miss them. Our main finding: the need for depth often lies in how the hidden cause is described. A one-step score on the label can be blind to an interaction among answers. A score on a suitable latent cause is not, and where that latent encodes the decision it replaces most of depth at a fraction of the search. Described differently, the same problem can defeat the score while exact values do not move, so keep the latent small and check it against exact values. Probabilities learned from one language model's answers do not carry to another unless planning allows for both; those read from tokens are worth only a few labels.
papers.summary: A proactive agent has to decide which questions to ask before acting. Exact lookahead captures how combinations of answers interact but is expensive, while cheap one-step scores can miss those interactions. The authors find that **the need for deeper lookahead often depends on how the hidden cause is described**: a one-step score computed on a suitable latent cause, rather than on the label, captures most of what lookahead provides at a fraction of the search cost. They also report that answer probabilities learned from one language model do not transfer to another unless planning accounts for both models.

papers.title: A Survey of Nonlinear Filtering Methods for Data Assimilation and Recent Advances in Generative AI-Enabled Score Filters
papers.abstract: Many real-world applications, such as numerical weather prediction or wildfire tracking, involve modeling highly nonlinear dynamical systems that are chaotic and influenced by various sources of uncertainty. To improve model prediction accuracy and reduce such uncertainties, data assimilation (DA) combines the dynamical model with partial, noisy observations to estimate the evolution of the system's state. Doing so depends on solving the optimal filtering problem: computing the conditional distribution of a hidden state given a sequence of observations. Classical approaches fail along three distinct axes: Kalman-based methods assume Gaussian posteriors and produce biased estimates under nonlinear observation operators; particle-based methods represent distributions with weighted samples and collapse in high dimensions due to the curse of dimensionality; and kernel-based methods move beyond discrete particle representations but cannot maintain their density approximation affordably as dimension grows. The Ensemble Score Filter (EnSF) avoids all three constraints by encoding the filtering density in a score function and approximating that score with a training-free Monte Carlo estimator, enabling stable filtering in high-dimensional, chaotic systems. This survey traces EnSF's mathematical foundations, establishes it as the state of the art for non-Gaussian, high-dimensional filtering, and examines fourteen extensions that expand its operational reach. Twelve of the fourteen extensions preserve this training-free Monte Carlo estimator at the core of the update, with only two departing from it to achieve planetary-scale deployment.
papers.summary: Data assimilation combines a dynamical model with noisy, partial observations, for example in weather prediction, and depends on solving a nonlinear filtering problem. Classical approaches each break down somewhere: Kalman methods assume Gaussian posteriors, particle filters collapse in high dimensions, and kernel methods become unaffordable as dimension grows. The survey traces the mathematical foundations of the `Ensemble Score Filter` (`EnSF`), which encodes the filtering density in a score function estimated by a training-free Monte Carlo estimator, and argues that it is the state of the art for non-Gaussian, high-dimensional filtering. It reviews fourteen extensions, **twelve of which keep the training-free estimator** at the core of the update.

papers.title: Structural Conditional Independence Test via Neural Quantile Resolution
papers.abstract: Conditional independence testing is difficult when dependence is weak, localized, or expressed through distributional changes rather than a global mean shift. Existing tests usually return a scalar statistic or p-value, which summarizes evidence against independence but does not describe where the conditional law changes. We propose QRCIT, a quantile-resolution conditional independence test that compares P(X|Z) and P(X|Y,Z) through a quantile deformation learned by a shared model. A lightweight residual quantile-flow model first learns the baseline conditional quantile law and then learns the additional deformation induced by Y, yielding a global predictive-gain statistic with conditional-randomization calibration and an inspectable deformation field over context and quantile level. We also introduce the Structural Dependency Benchmark (SDB), which evaluates dependence structures motivated by real applications, such as context-local, tail-only, sign-reversing, moving-ridge, and mean-neutral patterns. Across synthetic post-nonlinear (PNL) and SDB benchmarks, QRCIT improves detection of structured alternatives, with empirical Type-I behavior evaluated across settings. Higher quantile resolution improves merged-SDB power at moderate sample sizes, while diagnostics restricted to known affected regions improve detection of localized dependence. On Sachs, METABRIC breast cancer, and CCLE/PLX4720, QRCIT provides competitive real-data performance and interpretable deformation patterns. These results support quantile-resolved conditional-law deformation as a practical framework for testing and diagnosing structured conditional dependence.
papers.summary: Standard conditional independence tests return only a p-value. They also struggle when the dependence is weak, localized, or changes the shape of the distribution rather than its mean. `QRCIT` compares P(X|Z) and P(X|Y,Z) through a quantile deformation learned by a lightweight residual quantile-flow model. It produces a calibrated global test statistic along with **an inspectable deformation field showing where the conditional distribution changes**. The authors also introduce the `Structural Dependency Benchmark` (`SDB`), which covers tail-only, sign-reversing, and mean-neutral dependence patterns, and report better detection of structured alternatives along with competitive results on `Sachs`, `METABRIC`, and `CCLE` data.

papers.title: Multi-step SWE: Can Coding Agents Keep Building on Their Own Code Over Long Horizons?
papers.abstract: Developers rarely give a coding agent a single request: they ask it to build a component and then to extend, upgrade, and optimize it, each time on code the agent itself wrote. Most benchmarks, however, score one task at a time. We introduce Multi-step SWE, a long-horizon benchmark of 69 software engineering tasks, each a chain of 5-15 dependent steps on a single codebase. Every step is a complete, multi-hour engineering request that starts from the code the agent produced in the preceding steps, so early design decisions and errors carry forward. The tasks span four families of engineering work and nine languages, include both from-scratch builds and existing open-source codebases, and ground every step in an existing source of truth that defines both the instruction and its verifier. Across nine frontier models, the strongest model reaches a solve rate of only 18.5%, and 38 of the 69 tasks are not solved by any model. We release Multi-step SWE publicly at https://multistepswe.com.
papers.summary: Coding-agent benchmarks usually score one isolated task at a time, while real developers keep asking an agent to extend and optimize code the agent wrote itself. `Multi-step SWE` has 69 tasks, each a chain of 5 to 15 dependent, multi-hour engineering steps on a single codebase, so early design choices and errors carry forward. The tasks span nine programming languages and include both from-scratch builds and existing open-source projects. Each step's instruction and verifier come from an existing source of truth. Across nine frontier models, **the best solve rate is only 18.5%**, and 38 of the 69 tasks are not solved by any model.

papers.title: Meta-Frieren: Beyond Single Level Online Learning
papers.abstract: We study a two-stage online optimization problem: at each round, a meta-learner first selects an agent-environment pair, then the chosen agent interacts with the environment, and receives a reward. We introduce Meta-Frieren, a general framework for maximizing cumulative reward in this setting. Our analysis yields a simple UCB-style criterion for meta-level selection and recovers prior guarantees as special cases while extending them to broader settings. We instantiate Meta-Frieren with GP-UCB under Bayesian and frequentist assumptions. We also derive, to our knowledge, the first high-probability regret bound for Feel-Good Thompson Sampling, specialize it to finite and parametric function classes, and integrate it into Meta-Frieren. Experiments support our theoretical results and demonstrate that Meta-Frieren can be successfully applied to hyperparameter optimization across multiple model classes.
papers.summary: The authors study a two-stage online optimization setting in which, each round, a meta-learner picks an agent-environment pair and the chosen agent then interacts with that environment to earn a reward. Their framework, `Meta-Frieren`, uses a simple upper-confidence-bound-style rule for the meta-level choice, recovers earlier guarantees as special cases, and is instantiated with `GP-UCB`. They also derive what they describe as **the first high-probability regret bound for `Feel-Good Thompson Sampling`**. Experiments apply the framework to hyperparameter optimization across several model classes.

papers.title: ShapleyOG: Fast Adaptive Shapley Value Estimation with Odd Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: Shapley values are a central tool for attribution in machine learning. Since their exact computation requires evaluating the cooperative game to be explained on exponentially many player coalitions, they are typically estimated from a limited number of evaluations. Recently, ShaplEIG has shown that adaptively selecting the coalitions to evaluate substantially improves sample efficiency over classical estimators. This, however, comes at the cost of a sequential procedure that, in every iteration, refits a Gaussian process surrogate of the game and selects the coalition with the largest expected information gain about the Shapley values. The resulting computational overhead limits its applicability to costly games with low evaluation budgets. We present fast adaptive Shapley value estimation with Odd Gaussian Processes (ShapleyOG) to overcome this limitation. ShapleyOG leverages the fact that Shapley values depend only on the odd component of the game, and we show that under paired sampling a Gaussian process surrogate on this component alone yields the same Shapley value posterior and coalition selection criterion from half as many observations. Moreover, ShapleyOG refits the surrogate only on a sparse schedule and efficiently updates the selection criterion in between, and it extends quadrature-based computation schemes to the prior covariance of the Shapley values, which allows for exact or cheaper approximate computation. In extensive experiments on diverse games, ShapleyOG matches the estimation accuracy of ShaplEIG while reducing its overhead by up to three orders of magnitude. As a result, it outperforms state-of-the-art non-adaptive estimators at equal total computation time already when a single evaluation takes a tenth of a second and a budget of a few thousand evaluations suffices, thereby widening the regime in which adaptive coalition selection is applicable and pays off.
papers.summary: Exact Shapley values for model attribution require exponentially many coalition evaluations. The adaptive estimator `ShaplEIG` improves sample efficiency, but it refits a Gaussian process surrogate on every iteration, which makes it costly to run. `ShapleyOG` relies on the fact that Shapley values depend only on the odd component of the game: under paired sampling, a surrogate fit to that component alone gives the same posterior from half as many observations. It also refits on a sparse schedule and uses cheaper quadrature for the prior covariance. It matches `ShaplEIG`'s accuracy while **cutting its overhead by up to three orders of magnitude**, and it beats non-adaptive estimators once a single evaluation takes about a tenth of a second.

papers.title: Backbone-Informed Adaptation after EEG Pretraining: A Capacity-Controlled Study
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models learn representations that combine information across channels and time. This structure motivates adapters that model the same relationships during downstream learning. However, it is not clear whether such a design outperforms other candidate adapters. Moreover, in order to arrive at a fair comparison between candidate adapters, we also need to consider their trainable parameters. Here, we ask whether a backbone-informed (native) adapter makes better use of a given capacity by comparing it against a token-wise multilayer perceptron control that transforms each feature vector independently. We approximately match their trainable parameter counts and keep the pretrained encoder fixed. Across two EEG foundation models and tasks covering emotion recognition, sleep staging, and EEG event classification, the native adapter shows no consistent advantage. For one backbone, differences between the designs are small relative to variation across runs. For the other, the token-wise control performs better on emotion recognition and EEG event classification. On sleep staging, the native adapter's advantage over the token-wise control is reduced when we also train the component that processes sequences of EEG segments. The relative performance of the two adapters depends on the backbone, task, and downstream training protocol. These findings motivate evaluating backbone-informed adapters against capacity-matched alternatives.
papers.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models combine information across channels and time, which suggests that downstream adapters should model the same structure. The authors test this by comparing a backbone-informed (native) adapter against a token-wise multilayer perceptron control with roughly matched trainable parameters, keeping the pretrained encoder frozen. Across two EEG foundation models and tasks covering emotion recognition, sleep staging, and event classification, **the native adapter shows no consistent advantage**, and the token-wise control sometimes wins. Which adapter does better depends on the backbone, the task, and the training protocol.

papers.title: SeVerus: Context-Aware, Gamified Benchmarking for Rust Verification
papers.abstract: Coding agents achieve high success rates on existing benchmarks for Verus, a verifier for Rust programs. These benchmarks typically provide the auxiliary lemmas needed to complete a proof. In practice, however, such lemmas must be discovered and proved. To capture this challenge, we present SEVERUS, a context-aware technique to generate Verus benchmarks that organizes verification tasks into quests, each divided into levelsin a gamified manner. Using the original proof dependencies in verified projects, SEVERUS constructs one quest per verification target and progressively removes proof context to create individual levels. These levels range from the easiest, requiring completing only a single missing lemma, to the hardest, requiring proving the target without any supporting lemmas. An independent checker rejects changes to executable code, weakened specifications, and unsound proof constructs. A noisy binary search estimates the highest level that an agent can solve reliably. Applied to six open-source Verus projects, SEVERUS generates 819 quests comprising 10,095 levels. Experiments with Codex using GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, and with Claude Code using Sonnet 4.6, show that success decreases and cost increases as proof context is withdrawn. The strongest agent solves the final level of 52 of 60 sampled quests, yet can only reliably solve 35% of their levels, with failures concentrated in longer quests. Successful GPT-6 Sol proofs rarely reproduce the withheld lemmas, instead, using alternative proof decompositions. By systematically varying proof context, SEVERUS provides a foundation for constructing verification benchmarks that can continue to challenge increasingly capable coding agents.
papers.summary: Existing benchmarks for `Verus`, a verifier for Rust programs, usually supply the auxiliary lemmas a proof needs, while in practice those lemmas have to be discovered and proved. `SeVerus` turns verified open-source projects into gamified quests, each with levels that progressively remove proof context, from filling in a single missing lemma to proving the target with no supporting lemmas. An independent checker rejects changes to executable code, weakened specifications, and unsound proof constructs. Across 819 quests and 10,095 levels, tested with `Codex` and `Claude Code`, success drops and cost rises as context is withheld. The strongest agent solves the final level of 52 of 60 sampled quests but **reliably solves only 35% of their levels**.

papers.title: TrustMix: Graceful Degradation for Pretrained Models under Distribution Shift
papers.abstract: Predicting beyond the training domain necessarily requires assumptions about how the ground truth extrapolates, yet in most neural networks these assumptions are made only implicit through the architecture. We propose TrustMix, a lightweight post-hoc method that makes a pretrained model's extrapolative behaviour explicit and controllable. TrustMix combines the predictive distribution produced by a pretrained model with a user-specified fallback distribution $p_0(y|x)$, such that as the out-of-distribution (OOD) deviation statistic grows, we collapse towards $p_0(y|x)$. TrustMix provides graceful degradation: the predictive distribution converges toward the fallback distribution as the OOD signal grows. The fallback distribution $p_0(y|x)$ can reflect domain knowledge, if available, or rely on a domain-agnostic stationarity assumption. TrustMix does not require retraining of the base model and can be applied to both regression and classification problems. We evaluated TrustMix on several synthetic and real-world distribution shifts, including tabular, image, and natural language processing tasks. We tested TrustMix on datasets such as CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet and on numerous architectures including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Transformers. TrustMix remains competitive in-distribution while improving predictive uncertainty under distribution shift, with gains in predictive likelihood for regression and calibration for classification. Finally, we showed that TrustMix can provide useful predictive distributions for decision-making applications by utilizing it as a surrogate for Bayesian Optimisation.
papers.summary: Neural networks extrapolate outside their training domain according to assumptions that are left implicit in their architecture. `TrustMix` is a post-hoc method that blends a pretrained model's predictive distribution with a user-specified fallback distribution, shifting toward the fallback as an out-of-distribution (OOD) deviation statistic grows. It requires no retraining and works for both regression and classification. Tested on tabular, image (including `CIFAR-10/100` and `ImageNet`), and language tasks, it **stays competitive in-distribution while improving likelihood and calibration under distribution shift**. It also serves as a useful surrogate model for Bayesian optimization.

papers.title: Structured Machine Theory of Mind from Agent Trajectories
papers.abstract: Predictive models of human behavior trained on large-scale trajectory data optimize for statistical accuracy without representing the mental states that causally generate behavior. Such models support prediction but not principled intervention: they cannot answer how an agent's behavior would change if its beliefs or preferences were different. We introduce Structured Machine Theory of Mind (SMToM), a framework that attributes explicit, independently supervised belief and desire representations from observed trajectories within a Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) causal structure. The central architectural element is a goal head that consumes only the predicted mental-state channels and a current-trajectory embedding; counterfactual intervention on beliefs and desires is a direct operation. We instantiate SMToM on a controlled pedestrian navigation domain where ground-truth mental states are known by construction, enabling evaluation of attribution accuracy, local channel interventions, and trajectory-level counterfactual diagnostics. The resulting model, BDIBottleneck, improves over trajectory-only and unsupervised-context neural baselines. It is also competitive with a matched auxiliary-supervised context baseline while providing an editable mental-state interface that the unbottlenecked baseline lacks. Counterfactual experiments on desires confirm that substituting an agent's inferred preferences with a different activity type coherently shifts predicted destinations toward relevant locations. Counterfactual experiments on beliefs confirm that marking a location as unavailable in the agent's belief state reduces its predicted probability as a destination, though in a complex way. These results demonstrate, in a controlled navigation setting, that explicit BDI-structured supervision is a viable foundation for interpretable and counterfactual analysis of longitudinal trajectory data.
papers.summary: Predictive models of human behavior trained on trajectory data can forecast what people do, but they cannot say how behavior would change if a person's beliefs or preferences were different. `Structured Machine Theory of Mind` (`SMToM`) infers explicit, separately supervised belief and desire representations within a Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) causal structure. A goal head reads only these mental-state channels, so counterfactual edits become direct operations. In a controlled pedestrian navigation domain where the true mental states are known, the resulting `BDIBottleneck` model beats trajectory-only baselines, and **editing an agent's inferred desires or beliefs shifts its predicted destinations coherently**.

papers.title: Task-Calibrated Random Features via Influence-Based Error Cancellation
papers.abstract: Random features approximate kernel integrals by Monte Carlo, yet only selected frequency-sampling errors affect a downstream task. We propose Task-Calibrated Random Features (TCRF), which balance frequency moments constructed from task-specific influence using weights shared across kernel entries. Closed-form weights coincide with classical minimum-distance calibration; the contribution is a reusable, task-derived calibration space. We show that first-order variance equals the residual variance after projection onto this space. For kernel ridge regression, complete cancellation yields a non-Gaussian second-order limit. For kernel Stein discrepancy, a subset identity and disjoint-block variance decomposition eliminate the linear component of pilot noise. Positive exponential-tilting weights preserve the positive-semidefinite feature representation and support higher feasible calibration ranks. Paired experiments show improved approximation to exact kernel ridge regression at larger frequency budgets and to the exact empirical Stein discrepancy under a fixed alternative, even after accounting for a frequency-equivalent pilot budget. Gains are smaller with cross-validated ridge, landmark pilots require conservative rank selection, and near the Stein null allocating the pilot budget to additional ordinary frequencies is preferable.
papers.summary: Random features approximate kernels by Monte Carlo sampling of frequencies, but only some of the resulting sampling errors matter for a given downstream task. `Task-Calibrated Random Features` (`TCRF`) reweights frequencies to balance task-specific influence moments, using weights shared across kernel entries. The authors prove variance results for kernel ridge regression and kernel Stein discrepancy, and they show that positive exponential-tilting weights keep the feature representation positive semidefinite. Experiments show **better approximation of exact kernel ridge regression at larger frequency budgets**, with smaller gains under cross-validated ridge regularization.

papers.title: Canonical Correlation Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Relational inductive biases such as grids or graphs allow neural networks with fewer trainable parameters and improved generalization, but require a known structure beforehand. When no structure is available, the covariance matrix provides a principled substitute, and coVariance Neural Networks (VNNs) have shown that using it yields models that are theoretically grounded in Principal Component Analysis, stable to finite-sample estimation errors and parameter-efficient. This framework, however, is limited to single-view data, whereas many applications observe the same phenomenon through multiple views, each with its own in-view covariance and a cross-view covariance linking them. To incorporate these matrices as inductive biases in a principled way, we introduce CAnonical correlation NEural networks (CANEs), architectures that use in-view and cross-view covariances as distinct relational biases to solve downstream tasks. Via spectral analysis, CANEs draw analogies with Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA), a classical technique to project two-view data onto a correlated subspace. However, while CCA's objective is to compute shared view representations, CANEs are trained to solve a downstream task directly. We bound their output error under finite-sample covariance perturbations and show that it depends on controllable Lipschitz constants of the learned filters in place of the singular-value gap that governs the stability of CCA, thus guaranteeing better robustness. Experiments on seven datasets from brain imaging and motion sensing show that CANEs match or outperform single-view, two-view and CCA-based baselines, often with fewer parameters, and retain their performance when covariances are re-estimated from fewer samples.
papers.summary: coVariance Neural Networks (VNNs) use a covariance matrix as the relational structure when no graph is available, but they only handle single-view data. Canonical correlation neural networks (`CANEs`) extend the idea to two-view data by using both within-view and cross-view covariances as relational biases, and they are trained directly on a downstream task rather than to produce shared representations as Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) does. The authors prove that **the networks' stability under covariance estimation errors depends on controllable filter Lipschitz constants rather than on the singular-value gap that governs CCA**. On seven brain-imaging and motion-sensing datasets, `CANEs` match or beat single-view, two-view, and CCA-based baselines, often with fewer parameters.

papers.title: Fractional physics-informed neural networks to model social media virality
papers.abstract: Existing models of social media virality either prescribe the functional form of engagement growth or assume a fixed mechanism by which past activity influences future engagement. We present a fractional physics-informed neural network that learns both the temporal memory and nonlinear growth dynamics of social media engagement, using symbolic regression to translate the learned dynamics into interpretable equations. Synthetic experiments at the deployment resolution of 24 hourly observations demonstrate that the fractional order and reaction law can be jointly recovered from clean data. Under observation noise, however, the standard pointwise physics residual drives the fractional order toward its lower bound through a scale artifact. We address this failure using a fully whitened residual that propagates observation noise through the fractional operator. Applying the framework to 348 posts from X (formerly Twitter), we find that a single-window model estimates strongly memory-dependent dynamics but fails to accurately reconstruct held-out trajectories. Partitioning the 24-hour window into four teacher-forced segments substantially improves performance, yielding segment-specific fractional orders that increase from 0.23 to 0.99 and interpretable growth laws for each phase. The segmented model reconstructs 64% of held-out trajectories within a mean squared error of 0.01, compared with 44% for the strongest of nine classical baselines. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of fractional physics-informed equation discovery to uncover interpretable engagement dynamics while highlighting the importance of noise-aware estimation and temporal segmentation.
papers.summary: Existing models of social media virality fix either the shape of engagement growth or the way past activity influences future engagement. The authors train a fractional physics-informed neural network that learns both the memory and the nonlinear growth dynamics, then use symbolic regression to turn the learned dynamics into readable equations. Observation noise biased the learned fractional order through a scale artifact, which they fix with a fully whitened residual. On 348 posts from X, splitting the 24-hour window into four segments **reconstructs 64% of held-out trajectories within a mean squared error of 0.01, versus 44% for the best of nine classical baselines**.

papers.title: Compositional Unalignment: Auditing Safety in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are vulnerable to compositional harm: an image and a prompt that are benign in isolation become harmful through the model's cross-modal reasoning. Recent alignment methods report strong scores on compositional safety benchmarks, but an LLM judge only measures observed behavior and cannot reveal how robustly safety is integrated into the model. We argue that un-alignment provides a complementary audit of alignment robustness. We first show that minimal supervised fine-tuning reaches an LLM-judge score comparable to a multi-stage reinforcement-learning pipeline, so similar benchmark scores cannot establish robustness by themselves. We then show that recognition and refusal of compositional harm are decoupled: nine standard direction-finding methods detect compositional harm with up to AUC=0.99, yet ablating the recovered directions either leaves refusal intact or destroys model coherence. We therefore propose CMaG, a training-free un-alignment method for compositional safety. CMaG measures refusal intention with a refusal-versus-compliance log-probability margin, takes its gradient with respect to mid-layer activations, and contrasts it against partially benign pairs to isolate the cross-modal interaction term. A single backward pass over 80 examples yields a direction along which steering monotonically converts refusal into compliance. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.5-7B, CMaG reduces compositional safety scores by up to 65 points while over 98% of outputs remain coherent, outperforming gradient-based baselines; the direction also transfers to text-explicit harm and un-aligns models hardened by defensive training. Compositional safety can thus appear behaviorally strong while remaining fragile to targeted internal intervention. Warning: this paper contains unsafe model outputs, including references to self-harm.
papers.summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) can be pushed into harmful output by an image and a prompt that are each benign on their own. Strong scores from an LLM judge on compositional safety benchmarks do not show how robust that safety actually is. The authors find that recognizing compositional harm and refusing it are decoupled inside the model, and they propose `CMaG`, a training-free un-alignment method that takes the gradient of a refusal-versus-compliance margin at mid-layer activations to find a steering direction from a single backward pass over 80 examples. On `Qwen2.5-VL-7B` and `LLaVA-1.5-7B`, it **lowers compositional safety scores by up to 65 points while more than 98% of outputs stay coherent**, and the direction also un-aligns models that were hardened with defensive training.

papers.title: TileQuant: Tile as the Precision-Allocation Unit for LLM Mixed-Precision Post-Training Quantization
papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces large language model (LLM) deployment costs, but preserving quality requires accounting for uneven weight sensitivity. Uniform PTQ uses one weight bit-width, importance-aware PTQ adjusts scales or reconstructs weights within that width, and column-wise mixed precision retains selected columns at higher precision. However, sensitivity varies within columns, so whole-column retention also protects less sensitive weights, while runtime outlier detection adds decoding overhead. We therefore introduce TileQuant, a training-free framework that assigns precision to hardware-aligned 2D weight tiles. Offline calibration provides input-activation-aware scoring from forward statistics for lower calibration cost and gradient-informed scoring from loss sensitivity for stronger quality preservation. Within each projection's retention budget, the highest-scoring tiles remain at 16-bit and the rest use 8-bit. The resulting map guides reconstruction into compact weight buffers, which the kernel reuses for native integer and 16-bit computation with local accumulation to reduce memory traffic. Experiments show that TileQuant reaches 2.66x the original model's generation throughput. Across language modeling, reasoning, long-context retrieval, and question answering, it preserves quality and surpasses quantized and original models on multiple tasks. These results support selecting precision units that capture local sensitivity while enabling efficient hardware execution. The implementation is: https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TileQuant
papers.summary: Mixed-precision post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models usually keeps whole weight columns at higher precision, but sensitivity varies within columns, so protecting entire columns wastes bits. `TileQuant` instead allocates precision to hardware-aligned 2D weight tiles. It scores tiles offline using either cheap activation statistics or gradient-based loss sensitivity, keeps the top-scoring tiles at 16-bit and the rest at 8-bit, and uses a custom kernel that runs native integer and 16-bit computation over compact buffers. The authors report **2.66x the original model's generation throughput** while preserving quality across language modeling, reasoning, long-context retrieval, and question answering.

papers.title: SPILLWAY: Separating Target Admission from Sanitization to Defend Tool-Using Agents against Prompt Injection
papers.abstract: Tool-using agents act on email, files, and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or a shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but need a model to plan or route each task first. Where an action goes can instead be read from the tools' typed returns: an email's sender or a payment's account arrives in a typed field, while injected instructions arrive as free text. SPILLWAY turns this observation into a deterministic floor with no per-task plan. The check admits a call when each target value that appears in tool output but not in the user's task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions its fixed rules match before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence, and a local judge may restore a refused call, never one whose target lies in the removed text. Across three backbones, and seven task suites on one of them, no standard templated injection redirects an action to an attacker's target under SPILLWAY, at the highest observed mean utility and composite scores (NRP, ERS) of the defenses we run under that attack. A forged chat template also produces a raw zero, and mean in-scope attack success under a released reinforcement-learning attacker is .007. SPILLWAY reaches this floor with no defense-triggered backbone re-run and almost no added model call. As personal AI agents act on users' email, files, and payments, SPILLWAY gives them an auditable refusal floor on where their actions go that keeps them useful and holds across backbones.
papers.summary: Tool-using agents can be hijacked by instructions hidden in web pages or documents, and many defenses rely on a language model that may itself read the attacker's text. `SPILLWAY` adds a deterministic check: an action is allowed only if every target value (such as an email recipient or payment account) that is not in the user's task came from a typed field returned by a read-only tool, or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A rule-based sanitizer strips instruction-like text before the model sees it, and a local judge may restore a refused call but never one whose target came from the removed text. Across three backbone models and seven task suites, **no standard templated injection redirected an action to an attacker's target**, and attack success against a reinforcement-learning attacker averaged .007, with almost no extra model calls and the highest utility among the defenses tested.

papers.title: Loopback Transformer: Towards a Unified View of Residual Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: Looped Transformers reduce parameter count by repeatedly applying shared blocks, but parameter sharing alone does not determine how the results of repeated computation are reused. We take the depth-memory view of residual connections and analyze which representation is stored after each block application and how later reads weight it. A full block output contains both its input and its new update, so weighting that output also reweights the history already carried by the input. Reading individual updates instead, with the shared stack's input kept on a separate path, gives separate controls over input strength, total update weight, and allocation across updates. The Loopback Transformer implements these controls: geometric decay sets the total update weight and supplies a recency prior, and attention learns how to allocate that weight. On ClimbMix, Loopback reaches lower validation loss than standard Transformer baselines with 40-75% of their Transformer parameters (excluding token embeddings and the output head) at reference scales from 191M to 3B, with training tokens and executed depth matched. It also has higher mean accuracy over thirteen downstream tasks at 1.4B and 3B. At 191M, 374M, and 778M, it has the lowest validation loss and the highest thirteen-task mean among the standard Transformer and seven looped residual designs.
papers.summary: Looped Transformers save parameters by reusing shared blocks, but how earlier passes' results are stored and reweighted has received little systematic study. The authors argue that weighting full block outputs also reweights the history each output already carries, and propose reading individual per-pass updates instead, with the stack's input kept on a separate path. `Loopback Transformer` uses geometric decay to set the total update weight and attention to distribute it across updates. On `ClimbMix`, it reaches lower validation loss than standard Transformers **with 40-75% of their Transformer parameters** at scales from 191M to 3B, and beats seven other looped residual designs at the smaller scales.

papers.title: Recursive Sparse Attention: Million-Token Length Extrapolation at Logarithmic Cost
papers.abstract: At context lengths of about 1M tokens, dense attention is costly in prefill and decoding, and training typically relies on long documents, which become scarcer as the target length increases. Most sparse attention methods score all preceding blocks or tokens, so their selection cost per query is $O(L)$ at context length $L$; hierarchical selection reduces it to $O(\log L)$, but prior trainable hierarchical methods report accuracy only within their training length. We propose RecSA (Recursive Sparse Attention), which builds a tree over the KV cache in which each node summarizes its subtree with one key and one mean-pooled value. The keys come from one pooler per layer, shared by all levels and distilled from dense attention. Each level above the tokens selects at most $k$ candidates, so each query has $O(\log L)$ selection cost and reads $O(\log L)$ entries; the summaries of unselected candidates share one softmax with the exact tokens. Each entry's RoPE position is its index among the candidates of its level, so at any length every relative distance stays within the range seen during training. Initialized from Qwen3-4B and trained on 0.62B tokens at the original model's 32K training length, RecSA outperforms all baselines on RULER at every length from 131K to 2M; at 1M, it scores 60.5, compared with 40.0 for the best baseline, Dense + DCA. With our optimized kernels, RecSA is faster than dense attention in end-to-end prefill and decoding from 64K to 2M; at 524K on one H200 GPU, it accelerates prefill by 3.2x and decoding by 3.8x.
papers.summary: Most sparse attention methods still score every previous block, giving per-query selection cost linear in context length, and earlier hierarchical methods were only shown to work within their training length. `RecSA` (Recursive Sparse Attention) builds a tree over the key-value cache in which each node summarizes its subtree, so each query selects and reads only a logarithmic number of entries. Positions are assigned by index among candidates at each level, which keeps relative distances within the trained range at any length. Initialized from `Qwen3-4B` and trained on 0.62B tokens at 32K context, it **scores 60.5 on `RULER` at 1M tokens versus 40.0 for the best baseline** and speeds up prefill by 3.2x and decoding by 3.8x at 524K tokens on one H200 GPU.

papers.title: Neural Compression over Equivalence Classes: Exact Gauges and Functional Rate-Distortion
papers.abstract: Neural networks admit many parameterizations of the same or nearly the same function, but deployment typically stores whichever parameter vector training happens to produce. We show that this representational freedom can itself be used for compression. Rather than redesigning the codec, we search over exact function-preserving transformations and controlled functional perturbations, using the unchanged physical compressor itself to select cheaper representations. Exact gauge families provide a zero-distortion reference under the strict audit; allowing small functional changes exposes much larger rate-distortion gains. Across SmolLM2 and Qwen3, our method reduces Zstandard-compressed checkpoint size by up to 23.4\%, with similar relative reductions under gzip, Brotli, and ZipNN, establishing trained-network representational freedom as a practical storage resource.
papers.summary: Many different parameter vectors implement the same or nearly the same function, yet checkpoints store whichever one training produced. The authors search over exact function-preserving transformations and small, controlled functional perturbations, using an unchanged off-the-shelf compressor to pick the representation that compresses best. On `SmolLM2` and `Qwen3`, this **reduces `Zstandard`-compressed checkpoint size by up to 23.4%**, with similar gains under gzip, Brotli, and `ZipNN`.

papers.title: Archetypal contexts in the neurons of language models: an architecture for intelligence?
papers.abstract: We validate our previous hypothesis that a language model holds relational patterns apart from the subject domains that instantiate them (Nordfors, 2026). These archetypal contexts are patterns of relations that people recognize across many fields, such as the tipping point or winner takes all, held once and applied across domains. We show this inside the model, Qwen3.8-27B. One set of neurons carries the archetype, say the tipping point; another carries the topic, say politics, ecology or cell biology; a third carries the language, such as English, Spanish or Chinese. Silence the tipping point's neurons, and the model no longer identifies the pattern but still knows what the text is about. Silence the topic's, and it loses the topic but still names the pattern. In the neuron maps the layers organize themselves into a sandwich: the outer layers carry languages, the layers inside them topics, the layers at the heart archetypes. The sandwich emerges spontaneously during pretraining and appears in every model we mapped. Archetypes are the architecture for analogy, and we strongly suggest that this structure of archetypes and topics is the mechanism of a language model's intelligence: we see it self-organize as the model is trained. The neurons, the texts and the code are released with this paper as its reproduction package, so that anyone can repeat the test inside the model.
papers.summary: The author tests the hypothesis that language models store relational patterns, called archetypal contexts (such as a tipping point or winner-takes-all), separately from the subject domains in which they appear. In `Qwen3.8-27B`, distinct neuron sets are reported to carry archetype, topic, and language: silencing archetype neurons removes recognition of the pattern while leaving the topic intact, and the reverse also holds. Neuron maps show a layered **'sandwich' with languages in the outer layers, topics inside them, and archetypes at the core**, which the author reports emerges during pretraining in every model mapped. The paper proposes this structure as the mechanism behind language-model intelligence and releases neurons, texts, and code for reproduction.

papers.title: $D^2$-OPD: Separating Direction and Distance in Extrapolative On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model to match a teacher's next-token distributions on student-generated prefixes. Extrapolative OPD further extends the teacher's log-probability shift relative to a reference policy to construct stronger learning targets. However, existing methods couple extrapolation direction and distance, allowing the magnitude of the teacher's shift to dictate how far the target moves. We propose $D^2$-OPD, decoupling these two factors: a per-prefix hard KL constraint bounds the target's distance from the teacher, while an adaptive combination of the teacher's post-training shift and the initial student--teacher gap determines the extrapolation direction. We optimize the student toward this target using forward KL, providing learning signals even for low-probability tokens. We evaluate three settings: where standard OPD performs well, where it struggles with base-model initialization, and where no teacher reference is available. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, $D^2$-OPD attains the highest score in all three settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.45 points. Ablations validate the contributions of each component.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student to match a teacher's next-token distributions on text the student generates itself, and extrapolative variants push targets beyond the teacher. In existing methods the size of the teacher's shift also dictates how far the target moves. `D^2-OPD` separates the two: a per-prefix KL constraint caps how far the target can move from the teacher, while an adaptive mix of the teacher's post-training shift and the student-teacher gap sets the direction, and training uses forward KL. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks it scores highest in all three tested settings, **beating the strongest baseline by up to 9.45 points**.

papers.title: MAC-v2: Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels
papers.abstract: We study whether \emph{long-horizon model-based value expansion} can serve as an effective framework in pixel-based offline reinforcement learning (RL). Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels is substantially harder than state-based environments, as the agent must learn both the representation and its dynamics, and errors from either can accumulate recursively over imagined trajectories. We introduce MAC-v2, which enables long-horizon model-based expansion from pixels by training a reconstruction-free latent world model with action chunking. By learning representations from prediction and control objectives, MAC-v2 does not need to encode control-irrelevant visual details that can hinder the dynamics prediction. Action chunking further mitigates the prediction error by reducing the number of recursive model predictions required for value expansion. Across diverse visual benchmarks including visual OGBench, MMBench2, Robomimic, and LIBERO-10, MAC-v2 achieves strong performance against model-free and model-based offline RL baselines. Our analyses show that long-horizon model-based value expansion is critical for the performance of MAC-v2, and that both action chunking and latent learning objectives are essential for reliable long-horizon latent imagination.
papers.summary: Long-horizon model-based value expansion is hard in pixel-based offline reinforcement learning (RL) because errors in both the learned representation and its dynamics compound over imagined rollouts. `MAC-v2` trains a latent world model without pixel reconstruction, learning representations from prediction and control objectives, and uses action chunking to reduce the number of recursive model predictions. It performs strongly against model-free and model-based offline RL baselines on `OGBench` (visual), `MMBench2`, `Robomimic`, and `LIBERO-10`. Ablations indicate that **long-horizon expansion, action chunking, and the latent objectives are each essential**.

papers.title: KG-Neighbor: Knowledge-Guided Neighborhood Construction for Embedding Visualization
papers.abstract: In embedding visualizations, nearby instances are interpreted as semantically related, although neighborhoods derived from input embeddings may not reflect content relationships. Neighborhood-based dimensionality reduction (DR) methods can propagate this limitation by optimizing layouts from embedding-based neighborhood graphs. We propose Knowledge-Guided Neighborhood Graph Construction (KGN), which represents relational knowledge derived from each instance as a set of knowledge graph (KG) triples. It uses the degree of triple sharing as pairwise semantic evidence to adjust embedding distances and reconstruct the top-k neighborhood graph; neither KG extraction nor neighborhood construction uses class labels. We also introduce IDProfile (IDP), which interprets residual mismatches by independently assessing whether the source content supports the assigned class label and the neighborhood-majority class. Across eight text and image dataset-encoder conditions, we characterize KGN over the full guidance-strength sweep and four KG similarity measures. Across this sweep, the maximum NMI and LT_2D each exceed the corresponding kNN baseline in all eight conditions, with the largest gains reaching 0.68 and 1.35, respectively. The gains and the extent of neighborhood reconfiguration vary across conditions and are larger under encoder conditions with lower kNN baseline scores. The IDP analysis shows that the largest reductions are concentrated in Placement Issue candidates, whereas Label Issue and Unresolved Case instances account for a larger share of the remaining review set. These results indicate that KGN can narrow the evaluated gap between embedding-based neighborhoods and content-supported semantic relations, while IDP shows that a residual mismatch should not automatically be interpreted as a projection failure.
papers.summary: Neighborhoods in embedding visualizations are often read as semantic similarity, but neighbors in embedding space may not share content. `KGN` (Knowledge-Guided Neighborhood Graph Construction) extracts knowledge graph triples from each instance and uses how many triples two instances share to adjust distances before building the neighbor graph used by dimensionality reduction, without using class labels. A companion analysis, `IDProfile`, checks whether remaining mismatches reflect bad placement or questionable labels. Across eight text and image dataset-encoder conditions, the best clustering and layout scores **exceed the kNN baseline in every condition**, with the largest gains for weaker encoders.

papers.title: Goal Revelation as a Bridge Between Information-Theoretic Empowerment and Capability-Based Human Power
papers.abstract: Power matters for AI safety. Optimal agents tend to acquire power across a wide range of objectives (instrumental convergence). As we embed AI agents into socio-technical systems, humans risk gradual disempowerment. Both concerns call for a formal, quantitative measure of power. Two such measures in the context of Markov games are information-theoretic empowerment, the capacity of the channel from an agent's actions to future states, and capability-based individual power, a measure of goal attainment built from the probabilities that a human would attain each goal in a family of candidates were they pursuing it. We show where the two meet. From individual power, Fano's inequality yields a floor $B(s)$. This floor is a lower bound on what we term goal revelation, the mutual information $\mathbb{I}(G;\xi \mid s)$ between the human's latent goal and the realised trajectory. Empowerment caps revelation from above, so that $B(s) \le \mathbb{I}(G;\xi \mid s) \le \mathbb{I}(\mathbf{A}_h \to \xi \mid s) \le \mathfrak{E}_h(s)$. Each quantity can be large while the one below it stays at zero, highlighting the following failure modes. An assistant maximising empowerment can prefer an interface offering broad influence over goal-irrelevant degrees of freedom to one that lets the human attain every goal they might hold. An assistant maximising revelation cannot tell a working interface from one rewired so that every goal yields the wrong outcome, since relabelling goals leaves mutual information unchanged while zeroing every attainment probability. Positive guarantees therefore come only from the attainment end of the chain. A satisfaction floor, computable from two statistics of interaction logs, offers a way to monitor the power users retain in a deployed system, and simulations in random environments show the three quantities are correlated but far from interchangeable.
papers.summary: AI safety needs formal measures of how much power humans retain, and two candidates exist: information-theoretic empowerment and a capability-based measure of goal attainment. The authors connect them through goal revelation, the mutual information between a human's latent goal and the resulting trajectory, proving a chain in which attainment gives a lower bound and **empowerment gives an upper bound on revelation**. Each quantity can be large while the one below it is zero, so assistants maximizing empowerment or revelation can favor interfaces that leave humans unable to reach their goals. They propose a satisfaction floor computable from two statistics of interaction logs, and simulations show the three quantities are correlated but not interchangeable.

papers.title: Using Transformers for Teaching and Learning via Symbolic Distillation of Neural A-life Agents
papers.abstract: Neural networks controlling behavior of A-life agents can evolve over multiple generations.
