We introduce spectral symmetry fingerprints (SymFP), which enable discrete point-group identification through rank-template matching and continuous symmetry analysis by quantifying spectral energy beyond target rank constraints. SymFP is orientation invariant and architecture agnostic, enabling a parameter-free GNN implementation. Its spectra can be reused across multiple target groups, and the resulting leakage scores satisfy subgroup monotonicity. Across synthetic structures, molecules, coordination complexes and large biological assemblies, SymFP accurately identifies point groups, tracks controlled symmetry breaking and reveals local and degree-resolved symmetry changes that can be obscured by global geometric measures. These results establish the spectral structure of equivariant representations as a general framework for characterizing symmetry across physical systems.
papers.summary: Symmetry imposes rank constraints on the representations computed by equivariant graph neural networks (GNNs), and these constraints are normally viewed as a limit on expressive power. The authors instead use them as a signal: `SymFP` (spectral symmetry fingerprints) reads the singular-value spectrum of an equivariant representation to identify discrete point groups by matching rank templates, and quantifies continuous symmetry breaking by measuring spectral energy beyond the expected rank. The method is orientation-invariant, works with any architecture, and can run as a parameter-free GNN. Across synthetic structures, molecules, coordination complexes and large biological assemblies, it **accurately identifies point groups and tracks controlled symmetry breaking**, including local changes that global geometric measures can miss.

papers.title: Truncated backpropagation through time induces a two-sided gradient turnpike property
papers.abstract: Truncated backpropagation through time reduces the computational burden of training recurrent models by restricting gradient computations to shorter temporal contexts. This induces two distinct boundary effects: missing past information perturbs the forward state evolution, while truncating the backward recursion omits future information. This motivates decoupling the interval over which gradient contributions are averaged for the parameter update from the surrounding temporal context over which they are computed. Under exponential decay of the state-transition Jacobians and mild regularity conditions, this leads to a two-sided gradient turnpike property: the error between truncated- and full-context gradient contributions decays exponentially with the distance from both context boundaries. We derive bounds for the averaged update gradient, yielding guarantees on gradient alignment and approximate full-context stationarity; under unbiased interval sampling and a Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition, these further imply a bound on the resulting optimality gap. Numerical experiments on the Wiener-Hammerstein benchmark illustrate the role of past and future context and the trade-off between predictive performance and computational cost.
papers.summary: Truncated backpropagation through time cuts the cost of training recurrent models by computing gradients over short windows, but this loses past context in the forward pass and future context in the backward pass. The authors separate the interval over which gradients are averaged for an update from the surrounding context over which they are computed. Assuming the state-transition Jacobians decay exponentially, they prove a **two-sided gradient turnpike property**: the gap between truncated and full-context gradients shrinks exponentially with distance from both window boundaries. This gives guarantees on gradient alignment and, under a `Polyak-Lojasiewicz` condition, a bound on the optimality gap; experiments on the `Wiener-Hammerstein` benchmark show the trade-off between context length, accuracy and compute.

papers.title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions
papers.abstract:
Type theories designed for mathematics or program verification need only that a proposition holds; proof irrelevance in conversion erases, at the kernel level, how a claim was established. A persistent knowledge store, by contrast, must retain that record: who established a claim, by which derivation or external tool, and under which assumptions. This volume presents the theory of Eigenius---a store of typed knowledge over constructive institutions---and develops its metatheory from that requirement.
  The kernel theory is a dependent type theory with cumulative universes, an impredicative universe of propositions, inductive families, and an intensional identity type. Proof irrelevance is an axiom with an explicit witness rather than a conversion rule, so proofs of a proposition are provably equal yet remain distinct terms. Definitional equality is joinability under an orthogonal rewriting system---confluent, injective on type formers, and decidable by a type-free test---while a separate subsumption judgment covers universe cumulativity, codomain-covariant function types, and declared class inclusions.
  We prove consistency via a set-theoretic model; develop a justification logic over the kernel's propositions to track evidence and support; organize environments as an institution so that store extensions are signature morphisms and external verdicts enter via comorphisms; formulate a typed knowledge-graph theory with records, classes, and refinements; and prove the correctness of conversion, normalization by evaluation, and bidirectional type checking relative to termination. A Lean 4 formalization accompanies the volume.
papers.summary: Type theories built for mathematics or program verification only care that a proposition holds, but a persistent knowledge store also needs to record who established a claim, how, and under which assumptions. The authors lay out the theory of `Eigenius`, a dependent type theory in which proof irrelevance is an explicit axiom rather than a conversion rule, so different proofs of a proposition are provably equal but remain distinct terms. They **prove consistency through a set-theoretic model** and add a justification logic for tracking evidence. Environments are organized as institutions so that store extensions and external tool verdicts have a formal treatment, and they prove the correctness of conversion, normalization by evaluation and bidirectional type checking, all backed by a `Lean 4` formalization.

papers.title: IMUDINO: Self-distilled Foundation Model for Inertial Sensing
papers.abstract: We present IMUDINO, the first foundation model (FM) for inertial sensing to achieve competitive performance across diverse sensing tasks including human activity recognition (HAR), health, motion capture, and odometry. Prior inertial FMs often focus on one subfield of inertial sensing and sometimes underperform state-of-the-art supervised methods (e.g., in HAR), making their scope considerably narrower than FMs for vision and natural language. Moreover, they often require fixed input length and sampling rate, and generalize poorly to unseen sensor locations. To build a general-purpose foundation model for inertial sensing, we adapt the DINO self-supervised learning (SSL) paradigm to inertial data through a set of semantics-preserving motion transformations that simulate variations in motion pattern and sensor setup. For model architecture, we use a plain transformer encoder with frequency-aware positional encoding that natively supports varying input length and sampling rate. This simple setup proved remarkably effective for learning global and dense features generalizable across users, sensor setups, tasks, and, in the case of robot odometry, embodiments. We hope IMUDINO can serve as a backbone for inertial sensing and kickstart the development of general-purpose inertial FMs.
papers.summary: Existing foundation models (FMs) for inertial measurement unit (IMU) data tend to cover a single subfield, sometimes trail supervised methods, require fixed input lengths and sampling rates, and generalize poorly to new sensor placements. `IMUDINO` adapts the `DINO` self-supervised learning recipe to inertial data, using semantics-preserving motion transformations that simulate changes in motion patterns and sensor setups. It uses a plain transformer encoder with frequency-aware positional encoding, so it handles variable input lengths and sampling rates natively. The authors describe it as **the first inertial FM to be competitive across human activity recognition, health, motion capture and odometry**, with features that generalize across users, sensor setups and, for odometry, robot embodiments.

papers.title: Two-stage residual learning for calibrated uncertainty in solar irradiance forecasts
papers.abstract: Accurate forecasting of renewable generation requires not only point predictions but also reliable estimates of the uncertainty attached to them, particularly at extended horizons. Machine learning models are increasingly used to predict solar output, but they typically report a single value and capture the associated uncertainty poorly. The standard remedy is to train a model to predict the parameters of an assumed probability distribution directly. Here we develop an alternative two-stage method, motivated by synthetic solar signal generation, in which the forecast error is modeled separately from the expected irradiance. A first long short-term memory (LSTM) network predicts the expected global horizontal irradiance, and a second network models the distribution of the forecast error, which is added back to the mean to give both the forecast and its uncertainty. Using historical weather data from the National Solar Radiation Database and a probability integral transform evaluation, we show that explicitly modeling the error brings the predicted standard deviation markedly closer to the historical value, reducing the deviation between the two by 34.6 percent for a standalone LSTM and by 56.5 percent when the LSTM is coupled to Gaussian process regression, the most reliable of the configurations tested. Because the method models the total forecast error directly, it captures the full predictive uncertainty that matters for decisions, rather than only the model contribution that dropout-based approaches estimate.
papers.summary: Machine-learning forecasts of solar irradiance usually give a single value and capture uncertainty poorly, which matters at longer forecast horizons. Instead of predicting the parameters of an assumed distribution directly, the authors use two stages: a long short-term memory (`LSTM`) network predicts expected global horizontal irradiance, and a second network models the distribution of the forecast error, which is added back to the mean. On `National Solar Radiation Database` data, evaluated with probability integral transforms, modeling the error explicitly brings the predicted standard deviation much closer to the historical value. The gap shrinks by 34.6% for a standalone `LSTM` and by **56.5% when the `LSTM` is coupled with Gaussian process regression**.

papers.title: Latency-Aware Adaptive Best-of-$N$
papers.abstract: Test-time compute (TTC) improves language model responses by spending additional computation at inference time, and the right amount of compute depends on the prompt. Adaptive TTC methods allocate compute based on signals of response quality such as observed rewards, often by stopping once the signal exceeds a fixed threshold, and generally measure cost by the number of generations or tokens. But in online serving, latency is also a cost: it grows with server load, so a method using a fixed threshold spends too little compute when generation is fast and too much when it is slow. For Best-of-$N$ sampling, a widely used TTC method, we propose a two-stage adaptive algorithm that draws an initial batch, then uses the observed rewards and the batch's latency to decide whether to draw a second batch and at what size by comparing expected improvement against predicted cost: it draws one when the first batch's best reward is below a threshold that decreases with the first batch's latency, without explicitly measuring server load. We map each reward to its value under the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the prompt's reward distribution, so the same tradeoff parameters can be reused across tasks; a regression fitted offline on other prompts predicts a distribution for the CDF value of the first batch's best reward, giving the expected improvement in closed form. We evaluate the method by simulation on a preference-based alignment benchmark, measuring generations-equivalent cost: generations plus latency, converted to generations. The method reaches Best-of-$N$'s reward at lower generations-equivalent cost, and conditioning on the measured first-batch latency saves at least as much of that cost as fixed-threshold (latency-unaware) baselines, and more when latency is highly variable, when it grows with batch size, and when the second batch's latency is highly predictable from the first's.
papers.summary: Adaptive test-time compute (TTC) methods usually stop sampling once a quality signal crosses a fixed threshold and count cost in generations or tokens, ignoring the fact that latency in online serving rises with server load. For `Best-of-N` sampling, the authors propose a two-stage algorithm that draws a first batch and then decides whether to draw a second batch, and how large, using a reward threshold that falls as the first batch's latency rises. Rewards are mapped to their cumulative distribution function (CDF) values, so tradeoff settings carry over across tasks, and an offline regression gives the expected improvement in closed form. In simulation on a preference-based alignment benchmark, the method **matches `Best-of-N` reward at lower combined generation and latency cost**, with the largest savings over latency-unaware baselines when latency is highly variable.

papers.title: The Last Mile to the Real World: Agent-Native Primitives as Reusable Building Blocks for Solving Real-World Tasks
papers.abstract: How can an agent handle a real-world task end to end? Frontier models with their own harnesses still fall short on real-world benchmarks: on Terminal-Bench 4.0, GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex resolves 37.3% of the tasks and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code 51.8%. These tasks fail at the step from reaching a resource to applying it, which we call the last mile to the real world. Existing approaches put the resource within reach but leave the competence to apply it with the caller, so each harness rebuilds that competence. We introduce agent-native primitives, reusable units that equip a resource with a resident LLM that applies it in context and communicates with other primitives, and HEELO (Harness Engineering around Evolving Agent-Native Primitives for the Last Mile to Real-WOrld Tasks), a harness engineering framework that builds each task's harness from a library of such primitives. HEELO composes the primitives a task needs into a task-specific graph, verifies the result against evidence from the environment, revises the primitives a failure implicates, and admits new or improved primitives after validation. We instantiate HEELO with eight primitive families, each built for one kind of task, and evaluate them on more than twenty benchmarks. Dev-Primitives raise Terminal-Bench 4.0 resolution from 37.3% under Codex to 55.5% on the same backbone, Harness Primitives composed per task raise Terminal-Bench 2.0 Pass@1 from 60.0% for the seed harness to 72.2%, Tool Primitives raise ToolBench pass rate from 55.8% to 75.1%, and Navigation Primitives raise GAIA-Text-103 accuracy from 45.6% to 58.3%. On the 46 real-world tasks of our heelo.dev platform, Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex complete 9 each on their own and 39 and 35 when connected to HEELO through our MCP server, with 1.9$\times$ and 2.3$\times$ less time and 1.55$\times$ lower cost per completed task.
papers.summary: Frontier coding agents still fail many real-world tasks at what the authors call the last mile: they can reach a resource but cannot apply it correctly. They introduce agent-native primitives, reusable units that pair a resource with a resident LLM that knows how to apply it in context, and `HEELO`, a framework that assembles a task-specific graph of primitives, checks the result against evidence from the environment, revises the primitives a failure points to, and adds validated new ones. Across more than twenty benchmarks, primitives raise `Terminal-Bench 4.0` resolution from 37.3% to 55.5% on the same backbone as `Codex`, `ToolBench` pass rate from 55.8% to 75.1%, and `GAIA-Text-103` accuracy from 45.6% to 58.3%. On 46 real-world tasks, `Claude Code` and `Codex` each complete 9 tasks alone but **39 and 35 tasks when connected to `HEELO` through an MCP server**, at lower time and cost per completed task.

papers.title: FINCOSMOS: An Open-World Evaluation Paradigm for Agents in Finance
papers.abstract: Language agents increasingly work for users on the open Web, and finance is where trusting them is hardest. The data must come from the Web, the strategy lives in the user's head, and correctness depends on time, so an agent can fail silently: a strategy the user never asked for, unverified data, or a backtest that uses the future yields a report as convincing as a correct one. Existing benchmarks close the world somewhere, fixing the task, the data, or the timeline, and thereby remove these failures instead of measuring them. We introduce FINCOSMOS, an open-world evaluation paradigm for agents doing financial work. A simulated user holds a hidden strategy sampled from a compositional grammar and reveals it only when asked. The agent receives no data, so it must acquire data from the Web, build its own backtest under a data cutoff, and deliver verifiable results. Grading needs no reference answer. Programs verify point-in-time correctness and recompute every reported metric, the delivered strategy is checked against the hidden specification, and a run is accepted only when the user is satisfied and none of 15 veto checks fails. Across four coding agents and a model without tools in 150 sessions, no session is accepted: every session that the simulated user signed off fails a program check, and agents raise only 54--64\% of the details they were not told. Human experts attribute 88.33\% of failures to the agents. With FINCOSMOS feedback, an agent with persistent memory learned all ten tasks.
papers.summary: Agents doing financial work on the open web can fail silently, for example by implementing a strategy the user never asked for, using unverified data, or running a backtest that leaks future information, and still produce a convincing report. `FINCOSMOS` is an open-world evaluation in which a simulated user holds a hidden strategy and reveals details only when asked, while the agent gets no data and must gather it from the web and build its own backtest under a data cutoff. Grading needs no reference answer: programs check point-in-time correctness, recompute every reported metric, and apply 15 veto checks. Across four coding agents and one model without tools over 150 sessions, **no session was accepted**, and agents asked about only 54–64% of the unstated details; an agent given persistent memory and `FINCOSMOS` feedback eventually learned all ten tasks.

papers.title: Echoes of Error: Residual-Directional Local Rollout Consistency for Timeseries Forecasting
papers.abstract: In time-series forecasting, rollout errors are not merely one-step fitting discrepancies: once fed back into the evolving state, they can perturb future predictions. We formalize this effect through local rollout consistency, which compares the next prediction produced under teacher forcing with that produced under free running. In principle, this consistency can be enforced directly by tracking the residual-induced perturbation of the next state. In practice, however, the residual-to-state alignment operator is often difficult to design when the input state and output block have different dimensions, heterogeneous components, or architecture-dependent layouts. We therefore use a first-order local surrogate that penalizes the Jacobian-vector product of the predictor along the actual feedback perturbation, suppressing precisely the directions through which self-generated errors remain visible to future predictions. We further give the same loss a geometric interpretation near a predictive manifold: by controlling residual-induced directions that probe the normal bundle, the objective yields theoretical conditions under which free-running trajectories remain inside a stability tube around the manifold. Experiments on time series forecasting tasks support this view, showing that the proposed regularization improves predictive accuracy. More broadly, our results suggest a training principle for time-series forecasters and sequential predictors: a model should not only make small one-step errors, but also learn not to let its own errors echo into the future. Code is available at https://github.com/Wangzzzzzzzz/Echoes-Of-Error.
papers.summary: When a time-series forecaster runs on its own predictions, its errors feed back into the state and distort later predictions. The authors formalize this as local rollout consistency, comparing the next prediction under teacher forcing with the one under free running. Because aligning residuals with the state is hard to design in general, they use a first-order surrogate that **penalizes the predictor's Jacobian-vector product along the actual feedback perturbation**, suppressing the directions through which self-generated errors propagate. A geometric analysis gives conditions under which free-running trajectories stay within a stability tube around a predictive manifold, and experiments show improved forecasting accuracy.

papers.title: Adversarial Robustness of Kernel Machines: A Comprehensive Analysis
papers.abstract: Kernel machines are an important class of models in machine learning. However, the question of how robust modern kernel machines are to adversarial examples has not been studied comprehensively. In this paper, we provide a thorough empirical investigation of the adversarial robustness of kernel-based models for both binary and multiclass classification tasks, via white-box and black-box evasion attacks. We evaluate the native robustness of kernel machines, random feature classifiers, and the relatively newer Recursive Feature Machines. In addition, we provide an algorithm for approximate adversarial training of kernel machines. Our experiments on classification tasks on image and tabular datasets strongly indicate that kernel machines are natively more robust than neural networks, i.e., their performance degrades more gracefully against adversarial perturbations.
papers.summary: How robust modern kernel machines are to adversarial examples has not been studied systematically. The authors evaluate standard kernel machines, random feature classifiers and the newer `Recursive Feature Machines` against white-box and black-box evasion attacks on binary and multiclass image and tabular classification, and they propose an algorithm for approximate adversarial training of kernel machines. Their experiments indicate that **kernel machines are natively more robust than neural networks**, with performance degrading more gracefully under adversarial perturbation.

papers.title: KOSMOS: Self-scheduling Persistent Kernels for Communication-Compute Overlap
papers.abstract: Tensor and sequence parallelism (TP+SP) and expert parallelism (EP) put collectives on the critical path of transformer layers. State-of-the-art fused kernels mitigate this with fixed roles or schedules, but this rigidity leaves large idle windows. Predicting a communication-computation split does not remove them either; a predetermined split cannot follow data readiness. We present KOSMOS, a library for self-scheduling persistent kernels whose workgroups use queues ordered by consumer demand to switch between communication and computation roles as data become ready, with no scheduler, per-call cost model, or tuned split. KOSMOS fuses every TP+SP collective of a transformer layer with its GEMM, and runs an entire expert layer, from router to fold, in one launch per direction. Evaluated on AMD Instinct MI350X and AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, KOSMOS speeds up TP+SP end-to-end training in Megatron-LM by 1.10-1.28x in BF16 and 1.10-1.25x in MXFP8. KOSMOS accelerates end-to-end training of DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen3-235B proxies by 1.29-1.83x over DeepEP.
papers.summary: Tensor, sequence and expert parallelism put collective communication on the critical path of transformer layers, and existing fused kernels with fixed roles or predetermined communication-compute splits leave GPUs idle. `KOSMOS` is a library of self-scheduling persistent kernels whose workgroups switch between communication and computation as data becomes ready, using queues ordered by consumer demand, with no central scheduler, cost model or tuned split. It fuses every tensor- and sequence-parallel collective in a transformer layer with its matrix multiply, and runs a whole expert layer in one kernel launch per direction. On `AMD Instinct MI350X` and `MI355X` GPUs, it speeds up `Megatron-LM` training by 1.10–1.28x and **accelerates `DeepSeek-V3` and `Qwen3-235B` proxy training by 1.29–1.83x over `DeepEP`**.

papers.title: Localization Does Not Imply Steerability: A Mechanistic Study of Sign Errors in LLM Mathematics
papers.abstract: When large language models do multi-step mathematics, a characteristic failure recurs: the model writes one wrong sign token mid-computation -- a cofactor sign, the minus of a recursive integration-by-parts step -- then executes the rest of the arithmetic correctly, and the answer comes out wrong. We ask where inside the network that sign is written. Across six open models spanning 14B to 675B parameters, a per-layer readout shows the wrong sign is committed late -- by MLP layers in the last quarter of the network (70-100% per model and task), a pattern present, where tested (Qwen), in the base model before instruction tuning. The mechanism varies: some models carry fixed "minus-stamp" layers that push a minus regardless of the right answer, others carry amplifiers of whichever sign was already chosen, and Qwen adds a downstream rescue layer that opposes the stamp. The circuit is causal: subtracting a single sign direction from the residual stream flips 13 of 14 held-out minus-written integration-by-parts errors on Llama-3.3-70B, with flips replicating on Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral-Small (24-70% per cell), and with representation-level specificity -- the same dose breaks correctly-minus answers while sparing correct-plus answers where the direction is surgical (0/72 on Llama), and matched random-direction and control-layer interventions are null. Core claims were preregistered with pass criteria frozen in git before held-out data was seen: 23 of 29 checks passed, all misses reported. But causality is not uniform: Phi-4 implements an equally well-localized circuit at the same late depth, yet the identical intervention flips almost nothing -- the sign is written redundantly across ~15 layers with margins several times larger (median 17.8 logits). Localization, we conclude, does not imply steerability: two models can share a circuit location yet differ enormously in how overturnable it is.
papers.summary: A common failure in LLM multi-step math is writing a single wrong sign token mid-computation and then carrying out the rest correctly. Across six open models from 14B to 675B parameters, the authors find the wrong sign is committed late, by MLP layers in the last quarter of the network, with mechanisms that vary by model: fixed minus-pushing layers, amplifiers of an already chosen sign, or downstream rescue layers. Subtracting a single sign direction from the residual stream flips 13 of 14 held-out integration-by-parts errors on `Llama-3.3-70B`, and the effect partially replicates on `Qwen`, `Gemma` and `Mistral-Small`; core claims were preregistered, with 23 of 29 checks passed. However, `Phi-4` has an equally well-localized circuit that the same intervention barely moves, because the sign is written redundantly across about 15 layers, leading to the conclusion that **localization does not imply steerability**.

papers.title: SAVeR$^2$: Reasoning-based Safety Alignment for Large Reasoning Models via Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have achieved impressive performance via explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, yet this process introduces critical safety risks. We formalize LRM safety objectives as requiring non-malicious reasoning and answers, safety consistency, and explicit intent identification. We argue that existing alignment methods suffer from poor adversarial generalization, a significant ``safety tax'' on reasoning, and unfaithful coarse-grained rewards, primarily due to their neglect of the LRM's intrinsic reasoning capabilities for safety. To address these, we propose \textbf{SAVeR$^2$}, a novel \textbf{S}afety \textbf{A}lignment method via \textbf{R}ewards with \textbf{R}easoning capability. SAVeR$^2$ decomposes the safety objective into four fine-grained verifiable reward signals and utilizes a difficulty-aware data selection strategy to stabilize training. Crucially, we introduce a reasoning-preserving gradient projection mechanism that analytically resolves conflicts between safety and reasoning gradients, effectively eliminating the safety tax. Extensive experiments on models ranging from 1.5B to 671B demonstrate that SAVeR$^2$ achieves superior safety performance and significantly lower over-refusal rates across multiple benchmarks without compromising general reasoning capabilities.
papers.summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) that reason through explicit chains of thought introduce new safety risks, and existing alignment methods generalize poorly to adversarial inputs, hurt reasoning ability (a "safety tax"), and rely on coarse rewards. `SAVeR²` breaks the safety objective into four fine-grained verifiable reward signals covering non-malicious reasoning and answers, safety consistency and explicit intent identification, and it uses difficulty-aware data selection to stabilize training. A reasoning-preserving gradient projection resolves conflicts between safety and reasoning gradients analytically. On models from 1.5B to 671B parameters, the authors report **stronger safety and lower over-refusal without losing general reasoning ability**.

papers.title: Signed but Not Safe: Requirement Integrity in Multi-Agent LLM Handoffs
papers.abstract: Enterprise AI agents increasingly split a user's request across subagents and merge their results, and each handoff can summarize away, alter or ignore a requirement. We report a preregistered study with synthetic, exactly scorable tasks comparing free-text, structured JSON and signed requirement-manifest handoffs: the orchestrator extracts each requirement as a verbatim quote plus a checkable predicate, code signs the manifest with HMAC-SHA256, and deterministic code verifies the merger's decision. With Qwen3-8B (1,440 trajectories, five threats), signed manifests cut unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% (60.4 pp, 95% CI [51.4, 69.4]) with no net loss of conformant commits relative to structured handoffs. Signing is what defeats in-transit tampering: an unsigned manifest committed violations in 79% of mutated runs, the signed one in none. On identical trajectories the deterministic verifier caught 78.7% of violating decisions versus 59.0% for an LLM checker, with 7% versus 50% false alarms. An oracle manifest removed all remaining unsafe commits: the residual risk comes from extraction errors made before signing. A preregistered pre-signing injection attack confirmed this boundary: one adversarial line raised signed-manifest violations from 14.6% to 37.5% (Qwen3-8B), 11.1% to 63.9% (gpt-oss-20b) and 8.3% to 75.0% (GPT-5.6-luna), and the signature then authenticated the corrupted manifest. Signing protects requirements in transit, not at extraction; the extraction step is the trust boundary.
papers.summary: When an orchestrator splits a request across subagents and merges their results, each handoff can drop or alter a user requirement. In a preregistered study, the orchestrator extracts each requirement as a verbatim quote plus a checkable predicate, signs the manifest with `HMAC-SHA256`, and deterministic code verifies the merge; with `Qwen3-8B`, signed manifests **cut unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0%** compared with free-text handoffs, and the deterministic verifier outperformed an LLM checker with far fewer false alarms. Signing eliminated in-transit tampering, but a single injected line before signing raised violations sharply on `Qwen3-8B`, `gpt-oss-20b` and `GPT-5.6-luna`, and the signature then authenticated the corrupted manifest. The authors conclude that signing protects requirements in transit, while the extraction step remains the trust boundary.

papers.title: OPRD-Imp: a dataset of experimentally observed impurities and side products in multi-step pharmaceutical syntheses
papers.abstract: Predicting reaction impurities is a critical yet persistently data-limited challenge in pharmaceutical process chemistry. While machine learning models for reaction outcome prediction have advanced rapidly, benchmarking their ability to predict impurities remains impractical due to the absence of curated, publicly accessible datasets. We present OPRD-Imp, a dataset of 229 organic reactions drawn from 62 publications in Organic Process Research & Development, each annotated with experimentally observed impurities and their mechanistic origins. A total of 784 impurity entries is provided, classified into four origin categories. Reactions are represented as reaction SMILES and impurities as individual SMILES strings, with multi-step synthetic route connectivity preserved. All data were manually extracted from the source publications by trained chemists following a standardized extraction protocol, with expert chemical validation and manual structure drawing. OPRD-Imp is intended to serve as a benchmark resource for evaluating models that predict reaction impurities, providing experimentally reported impurity annotations and mechanistic origin labels that are not systematically represented in conventional reaction datasets.
papers.summary: Machine-learning models for predicting reaction outcomes cannot be benchmarked on impurity prediction because no curated public dataset exists. `OPRD-Imp` provides 229 organic reactions from 62 `Organic Process Research & Development` publications, annotated with **784 experimentally observed impurities** in four mechanistic-origin categories. Reactions and impurities are stored as SMILES strings with multi-step route connectivity preserved, and all entries were manually extracted and validated by trained chemists following a standard protocol.

papers.title: Statistical and Privacy Guarantees for Deep M-Regression via Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics
papers.abstract: In this article, we study deep nonparametric regression trained via stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD), a variant of stochastic gradient descent that injects carefully calibrated Gaussian noise during optimization. Using a PAC-Bayesian analysis tailored to deep ReLU networks, we establish an excess-risk bound that simultaneously accounts for network approximation error, statistical complexity, and the algorithmic cost accumulated along the SGLD trajectory. Under a Bernstein condition and within a stable SGLD regime, the excess-risk bound contains a stochastic term whose coefficient is inversely proportional to the variance of injected noise, while the estimator retains the optimal rate for nonparametric regression under the H\"older smoothness condition up to logarithmic factors. This result provides an approximation-error-aware, rate-optimal statistical perspective on the widely observed generalization benefits of moderate SGLD noise. For per-sample clipped SGLD, we further establish an exact f-DP guarantee and the corresponding asymptotic $\mu$-GDP guarantee for the proposed estimator. We establish statistical convergence rates and differential privacy guarantees for DNN estimators trained using SGLD, while explicitly accounting for both network approximation error and the effect of injected noise in the excess-risk bound. Extensive simulation studies and analyses of two real datasets examine the finite-sample predictive performance and privacy-utility behavior of the proposed procedure.
papers.summary: The authors analyze deep nonparametric regression with ReLU networks trained by stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (`SGLD`), a variant of stochastic gradient descent that injects calibrated Gaussian noise. A PAC-Bayesian analysis gives an excess-risk bound that accounts for approximation error, statistical complexity and the algorithmic cost along the training trajectory, and the estimator **retains the optimal nonparametric rate under Hölder smoothness** up to logarithmic factors. This offers a statistical explanation for why moderate injected noise helps generalization. For per-sample clipped `SGLD`, they also prove exact f-differential-privacy and asymptotic Gaussian differential privacy guarantees, supported by simulations and two real datasets.

papers.title: Learning Multi-Agent Orchestration:Higher-Order Interactions in Policy Improvement
papers.abstract: Learned orchestration has emerged as a promising paradigm for large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems, in which a central orchestrator selects agents and controls the information they receive throughout a task. Despite rapid empirical progress, existing methods train the orchestrator by crediting each decision with its own advantage, implicitly assuming that the other decisions in the episode stay fixed. This assumption fails in orchestration, where the contribution of each decision to the final outcome depends on the decisions preceding it, so the gain of a joint update is not the sum of its per-decision effects. To address this challenge, we introduce \textbf{IAPO}, an interaction-aware policy optimization framework that explicitly accounts for interactions among decisions. Specifically, IAPO exactly decomposes the performance difference between two policies into the effects of individual decisions and their interactions, which we prove can account for half of the attainable gain, and then optimizes both from sampled trajectories while certifying that every update is an improvement. On long-input versions of GSM8K, MATH, DROP, MBPP and HumanEval, against fifteen published multi-agent and workflow-search systems on the same 7B executor, IAPO's deployed plans reach the strongest system's accuracy with fewer tokens, and removing the interaction term costs 7 to 17 points of accuracy on code.
papers.summary: Learned orchestrators for LLM multi-agent systems are usually trained by crediting each decision with its own advantage, which assumes the other decisions stay fixed even though each decision's value depends on earlier ones. `IAPO` (interaction-aware policy optimization) exactly decomposes the performance difference between two policies into individual-decision effects and interaction effects, proves that interactions can account for **half of the attainable gain**, and optimizes both from sampled trajectories with certified improvement at every update. On long-input versions of `GSM8K`, `MATH`, `DROP`, `MBPP` and `HumanEval`, compared with fifteen multi-agent and workflow-search systems on the same 7B executor, it matches the strongest system's accuracy with fewer tokens. Removing the interaction term costs 7 to 17 points of accuracy on code tasks.

papers.title: ZYFA: Speed and Accuracy of FP8 FlashAttention on AMD CDNA4
papers.abstract: Attention is a core building block of frontier models and often dominates compute-bound prefill at long context. FP8 matrix instructions offer twice the peak throughput of BF16, but they accelerate only matrix multiplication, and the softmax between the two matrix multiplications of attention runs on vector units that FP8 does not accelerate. On the AMD Instinct MI355X, the vendor's AITER kernels reach 39% of peak FP8 matrix throughput at 32K tokens, compared with 49% in BF16. Attention is also more numerically sensitive to quantization than feed-forward layers, and unlike NVIDIA's Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, the MI355X does not track the completion of matrix instructions in hardware, so overlapping the softmax with the matrix multiplications depends on instruction order. We present ZYFA, prefill kernels for the MI355X built on three techniques: (1) computing each FP8 probability directly from its score with a multiply-add and an integer conversion instead of an exponential; (2) a ping-pong schedule in which one group of threads computes its softmax while another executes its matrix multiplications; and (3) scaling each block of probabilities up by a power of two before rounding, and normalizing by the sum of the rounded probabilities. On attention inputs captured from three models and timed at sustained clock speeds, ZYFA achieves 1.16-1.76x the throughput of AITER. On the Gaussian inputs of kernel benchmarks at 32K tokens, it achieves 1.26-1.37x at head dimension 128 and 1.99x for DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention. The sustained clock of the MI355X depends on operand values, so throughput on random inputs does not reliably predict throughput on real model activations. At head dimension 128, ZYFA's numerical error is within a few percent of that of Composable Kernel and Triton and 62-78% lower than that of AITER's. The source code is available at https://github.com/Zyphra/zyfa.
papers.summary: FP8 matrix instructions double peak throughput over BF16, but attention gains little from them: the softmax between its two matrix multiplications runs on vector units that FP8 does not speed up, and AMD's `MI355X` lacks hardware tracking of matrix-instruction completion, so overlapping the softmax with the matrix multiplications depends on instruction order. `ZYFA` is a set of FP8 prefill attention kernels that compute each FP8 probability with a multiply-add and an integer conversion instead of an exponential, use a ping-pong schedule in which one thread group runs its softmax while another runs its matrix multiplications, and scale probability blocks by a power of two before rounding to reduce error. On attention inputs captured from real models, it reaches **1.16-1.76x the throughput of AMD's `AITER` kernels**, and 1.99x on `DeepSeek`-style multi-head latent attention benchmarks, with 62-78% lower numerical error than `AITER` at head dimension 128. The authors also note that the GPU's sustained clock speed depends on operand values, so benchmarks on random inputs do not reliably predict throughput on real activations.

papers.title: Coverage Hides Churn: Auditing and Preserving Conformal Decisions as VLM Label Registries Grow
papers.abstract: Vision-language classifiers can learn new labels from text alone, so the label lists they serve keep growing. We show that this growth silently changes conformal decisions about old labels. Common softmax-based conformal scores compare each label with an average over all labels; adding labels changes that average, and with it the score of every old label, even when the model, the image, and the old calibration data stay the same. Recalibrating after the update keeps the coverage guarantee, yet across eleven settings it changes at least one old decision on 53-90% of new images. Coverage cannot reveal this, because it checks only the true label: in five controlled settings that keep the old calibration, so that only the normalizer changes, old-class coverage moves by at most 0.01 while 60-67% of images change. We propose a lifecycle audit that measures these changes alongside coverage and set size, and a simple fix, PrefixCP: each class keeps the label registry that existed when it was added. Its old decisions then never change, each class keeps exact class-conditional coverage under exchangeability, and one prefix scan computes all historical normalizers at once. PrefixCP recovers 40.9-58.5% of the set-size gap between never updating the reference and recalibrating, which gives smaller sets but changes old decisions.
papers.summary: Vision-language classifiers can add new labels from text alone, and adding labels silently changes conformal prediction decisions about old labels, because common softmax-based scores normalize over the whole label set. Recalibrating after an update keeps the coverage guarantee, yet across eleven settings it **changes at least one old decision on 53-90% of new images**, a shift that coverage metrics cannot detect. The authors propose a lifecycle audit that tracks these decision changes alongside coverage and set size, plus `PrefixCP`, in which each class keeps the label registry that existed when it was added. With `PrefixCP`, old decisions never change, exact class-conditional coverage is preserved, and 40.9-58.5% of the set-size gap between never updating and full recalibration is recovered.

papers.title: DelegateEval: Evaluating Platforms for Personal External Service Agents
papers.abstract: AI agents that work for an individual over time may also help that individual serve external clients. We define a personal external service agent as an agent authorized and continuously managed by a specific individual to accept client requests, deliver work, and provide ongoing support using that person's knowledge, experience, professional methods, and service boundaries. Such agents could allow individuals to serve more clients with less direct involvement and generate economic value at scale. We propose DelegateEval, a platform-level evaluation framework for agent systems that may combine large language models, reusable skills, protocols such as MCP, and executable tool environments. It covers eight dimensions: ease of creation, service discovery and matching, delivery quality, expertise inheritance, service continuity, learning and improvement, reliability and governance, and efficiency and value. These dimensions assess whether a platform enables people with different backgrounds to turn their expertise into ongoing services that deliver verifiable work, develop capabilities through experience, and remain economically feasible. We present the framework and an experimental design. Complete datasets, executable environments, a unified scoring protocol, and cross-model results remain to be developed and empirically validated.
papers.summary: The authors define personal external service agents: AI agents that an individual authorizes and manages to serve that person's clients using the person's expertise, methods, and service boundaries. They propose `DelegateEval`, a platform-level evaluation framework for agent systems built from large language models, reusable skills, protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (`MCP`), and executable tool environments. It scores platforms on eight dimensions, including ease of creation, delivery quality, expertise inheritance, service continuity, governance, and economic efficiency. Only the framework and an experimental design are presented; **datasets, environments, a scoring protocol, and empirical results have not yet been developed**.

papers.title: RLGPA: A Reinforcement Learning-Guided Granularity Planning Attack for Decision-Based Sparse Adversarial Examples
papers.abstract: Decision-based sparse attacks must reduce perturbation support using only the victim's predicted label. The best restoration strategy varies as support contracts: coarse removal works early, while tail states need finer, history-aware tests. We propose RLGPA, an online reinforcement learning method that schedules support-reduction executors and their granularity under a hard query budget. A masked Dueling Double DQN selects among seven stable policy--scale actions; each action produces support-relative restoration groups that are rebuilt after every macro decision. A feasibility-preserving executor commits only adversarial restorations and feeds support gain and query cost back to the planner. Under the matched top-1-label oracle, RLGPA reaches 61\% targeted ASR at sparsity 0.01 on CIFAR-10 (vs. 25\% SparseEvo, 0\% Pointwise), and 75.5\%/73.0\% on ResNet50/ViT at sparsity 0.005 (vs. 29.0\%/15.5\%). A fixed-probe test reduces median \(L_0\) from 165 to 23 after 40 images without any update. State-blind and state-shuffled controls degrade significantly, confirming that the learned policy uses attack state; the main gains come from state-conditioned executor scheduling and dynamic repartition. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Acui001/RLGPA.git.
papers.summary: Decision-based sparse adversarial attacks must shrink the set of perturbed pixels while seeing only the victim model's predicted label, and the best strategy for restoring pixels changes as that set contracts. `RLGPA` uses an online masked Dueling Double Deep Q-Network (`DQN`) to choose among seven support-reduction strategies and granularities under a fixed query budget, committing only restorations that keep the example adversarial. It reaches **61% targeted attack success at sparsity 0.01 on `CIFAR-10`, versus 25% for `SparseEvo`**, and 75.5%/73.0% on `ResNet50`/`ViT` at sparsity 0.005. Control experiments that hide or shuffle the attack state degrade performance significantly, showing that the learned policy relies on that state.

papers.title: Concertina: Embodying Manipulation and Cognition in One Diffusion Vision-Language Model
papers.abstract:
Most vision-language-action (VLA) policies decouple manipulation from cognition by bolting an external action mechanism onto a vision-language model (VLM)--either quantizing actions into discrete tokens whose errors bear no stable correspondence to physical displacements, or delegating continuous trajectory generation to a separate action expert whose gradients compete with or are blocked from updating the VLM backbone. We argue that manipulation and cognition should instead be embodied in the same model, shifting from a decoupled VLA to an Embodied Vision-Language Model (eVLM). We introduce Concertina, an eVLM that places continuous trajectory representation, blockwise generation, and physical-coordinate supervision directly on the computation and parameter path of a shared diffusion VLM backbone. Each control timestep is encoded as one continuous latent action token in the backbone hidden space, and the shared Transformer reconstructs temporally ordered action blocks via the same corrupt-and-reconstruct operator used for multimodal pretraining. Active action projections account for only 0.21% of parameters in the 4.46B model with zero separate action-generator layers, compared with 16.5%-35.1% dedicated action-expert capacity in representative continuous VLAs. Using our proposed Action Interface Audit, we confirm that cross-time trajectory coupling emerges in the middle and late layers of the shared backbone rather than at the action interfaces. On standard benchmarks, Concertina achieves 98.15% average success on regular LIBERO, 85.9% on the 10,030-task LIBERO-Plus benchmark, and 4.142 average completed chain length on CALVIN ABC-D.
  Code: https://github.com/lose4578/Concertina Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/collections/Traly/concertina
papers.summary: Most vision-language-action (VLA) robot policies attach a separate action mechanism to a vision-language model, either discretizing actions into tokens or adding a dedicated action-expert network. `Concertina` instead generates continuous actions inside a shared diffusion vision-language backbone: each control timestep becomes one continuous latent token, and action blocks are reconstructed with the same corrupt-and-reconstruct operator used in multimodal pretraining. Action-specific projections make up only **0.21% of the 4.46B-parameter model**, compared with 16.5-35.1% dedicated action-expert capacity in other continuous VLAs. It reports 98.15% average success on `LIBERO`, 85.9% on `LIBERO-Plus`, and an average completed chain length of 4.142 on `CALVIN` ABC-D.

papers.title: Using Transformers to Generate 3-Manifold Triangulations
papers.abstract: Using dehydration signatures as an encoding, we train GPT-2-style transformers to generate triangulations of 3-dimensional manifolds. Our main runs each use approximately 3 exaFLOPs, spanning a 200 million parameter model trained on 60 million sphere triangulations to an 11 million parameter model trained on 1.1 billion sphere triangulations. The optimal model has 10 blocks, width 640 and generates dehydration signatures of closed manifolds of various topological types at a rate of 6.9%, 82% of which are spheres. To investigate how our method scales, we use the technique of IsoFLOP curves on 15-tetrahedron triangulations of the 3-sphere, over a compute range of 6 to 3000 petaFLOPs, and observe neural scaling behaviour. We extract a parameter scaling exponent of $\alpha = 0.49$ ($[0.48, 0.50]$ stat, $\pm 0.02$ syst), and an optimal ratio of 234 tokens per parameter for training. In addition, we present a number of smaller experiments, including evidence that transformers are able to learn to count degree-one edges near-perfectly, but get progressively worse when counting edges with higher degrees.
papers.summary: The authors train `GPT-2`-style transformers to generate triangulations of 3-dimensional manifolds, encoded as dehydration signatures, using about 3 exaFLOPs per main run. The best model generates valid closed-manifold signatures 6.9% of the time, 82% of which are spheres. IsoFLOP experiments on 15-tetrahedron triangulations of the 3-sphere show neural scaling behavior, with **a parameter scaling exponent of 0.49 and an optimal 234 training tokens per parameter**. Smaller experiments show that the models count degree-one edges almost perfectly but count higher-degree edges progressively worse.

papers.title: Graph learning-assisted logic-based Benders decomposition for distributionally robust in-station train rescheduling under disruptions
papers.abstract: Uncertainty in resource reopening times complicates train holding and rerouting decisions when resource closures coincide with arrival delays and processing-time extensions. We develop a rolling-horizon distributionally robust model that updates predictions of the remaining closure duration as observations of disruption resolution become available. The model jointly optimizes train routes, sequences, and timings. It minimizes the worst-case expected total completion delay over an ambiguity set of scenario probabilities. The solution algorithm, GNN-LBBD, uses logic-based Benders decomposition to coordinate routing and resource scheduling. Conditional cuts are constructed from resource-use patterns, and a graph neural network guides the order in which resource relaxation subproblems are solved. Across 28 test instances for a five-track station, GNN-LBBD achieved a mean total completion delay of 61.13 train-min. This was 16.63\% lower than tabu search and 20.06\% lower than variable neighborhood search, with a mean total computation time close to that of tabu search. Information comparisons on six representative instances showed that using observations of disruption resolution reduced mean total completion delay by approximately 21.7\%. Scenario-based and conditional-mean predictions produced similar overall results under the same information conditions. The benefits of information were more pronounced in some instances with alternative routes. This suggests a relationship between the use of observations, the station resource structure, and the scope for schedule adjustments.
papers.summary: When a station resource is closed and trains also run late, uncertainty about when the resource will reopen makes holding and rerouting decisions difficult. The authors build a rolling-horizon distributionally robust model that jointly optimizes train routes, sequences, and timings, minimizes worst-case expected delay, and updates its closure-duration predictions as the disruption is resolved. Their solver, `GNN-LBBD`, combines logic-based Benders decomposition with a graph neural network that decides the order in which subproblems are solved. On 28 instances for a five-track station it cuts **mean total completion delay by 16.63% compared with tabu search** at similar computation time, and using observations of disruption resolution reduces delay by about 21.7%.

papers.title: Understanding Data Influence in Transportation Networks: A Physics-Constrained Influence-Function Framework
papers.abstract: Understanding how individual training observations influence model predictions is important for developing reliable and interpretable data-driven transportation systems. Existing influence-function methods, however, are primarily formulated for unconstrained learning and do not explicitly account for physical constraints that couple different components of a transportation network. Under such constraints, perturbing a training observation can affect model parameters and predictions only through physically feasible directions, potentially changing how its influence propagates across the network. This paper develops a hard physics-informed influence-function framework for constrained learning, in which training-data influence is characterized within the physically feasible space defined by network constraints. The analytical results reveal how physical constraints alter the magnitude, direction, and spatial distribution of training-sample influence relative to conventional influence measures. Using traffic prediction under flow-conservation constraints as a case study, we show that influential observations identified by the proposed framework differ systematically from those identified by classical influence functions. Through orthogonal decomposition, we quantitatively characterize how much of a perturbation in the training data is propagated through the network via the flow-conservation constraints and how much is removed by the constraint projection. The proposed influence framework provides a physically consistent approach for evaluating training-data influence in constrained transportation learning problems, with potential applications to data diagnostics, sensor evaluation, and targeted data collection.
papers.summary: Influence functions estimate how individual training observations affect a model's predictions, but standard formulations ignore the physical constraints that link parts of a transportation network. The authors develop an influence-function framework for hard-constrained learning, in which training-data influence is measured only within the physically feasible space defined by the network constraints. In a traffic-prediction case study with flow-conservation constraints, **the observations it flags as influential differ systematically from those flagged by classical influence functions**. An orthogonal decomposition separates how much of a training perturbation propagates through the network and how much the constraint projection removes.

papers.title: Goal-Branching LaCAM: Temporary Goals as Search Branches in Dense Multi-Agent Pathfinding
papers.abstract: LaCAM is a search-based solver for multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF) that runs a depth-first search over joint configurations, using PIBT to generate successors and lazily adding single-agent constraints to explore alternatives. Although LaCAM is complete, it can struggle on dense, corridor-heavy instances because extracting blocking agents from deadlocks requires coordinated moves of several agents, often away from their goals, which PIBT's greedy one-step successors rarely propose and which LaCAM can only reach by enumerating constraints one agent at a time. This paper proposes Goal-Branching, where blocking agents are given temporary goals, each tried as an additional branch of LaCAM's search. We examine random and corridor-aware rules for choosing these temporary goals and show that completeness is preserved for any such rule. On dense instances (60-90% of free cells occupied) of three maze and room maps, Goal-Branching solves 89% of instances against 44% for LaCAM*, and, on instances both solve, it finds a first solution 10-14x faster on maze-32-32-2 and room-32-32-4, and nearly 200x faster in median time at 75% density on room-32-32-4. Solution cost increases by 15-22% on instances both solve, while on open maps and the full MovingAI benchmark its solutions cost no more than those of LaCAM* and it is at most 3% slower.
papers.summary: `LaCAM` is a complete search-based solver for multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF), but it struggles on dense, corridor-heavy maps, where freeing a deadlock requires several agents to move away from their goals together. Goal-Branching assigns temporary goals to blocking agents and tries each assignment as an extra branch of the search, and the authors prove that completeness is preserved for any rule used to choose those goals. On instances where 60-90% of free cells are occupied, it **solves 89% of instances versus 44% for `LaCAM*`** and finds first solutions 10-14x faster, up to nearly 200x faster in median time in one setting. Solutions cost 15-22% more on dense instances both methods solve, but no more than `LaCAM*` on open maps and the full `MovingAI` benchmark.

papers.title: Adaptive Experimentation Can Hide Model Error:Detection Limits and Falsification Budget
papers.abstract: An experiment can be informative about the parameters of a working model and uninformative about whether that model is wrong. Adaptive design can reinforce this mismatch by repeatedly selecting settings where an incorrect model fits. We bound the power of any valid adequacy test in terms of the experimenter's own sampling distribution, then distinguish information absent from the selected data from information lost by the detector. A computable diagnostic measures unresolved error relative to a declared expansion of the working model. It motivates a training-free rule that reserves part of the design budget for falsification. The empirical record is mixed: the independently specified primary study fails detection eligibility, and a later numerator diagnostic fails its improvement criteria. After the frozen rule fails on fresh continuous-null panels, a disclosed secondary horizon-calibrated revision detects 35.8% of misspecified campaigns versus 31.7% for a class-separation control at T = 240, but has no resolved advantage at T = 480. In a corrected 289-unit measured replay it improves on random design and trails class-discrimination EIG. A conditional futility bound explains why remaining time matters without proving the gate constant or its power. These results support separating parameter learning, model checking and detector performance; they do not establish a universally superior design policy or prospective scientific discovery.
papers.summary: An experiment can be informative about a model's parameters while revealing little about whether the model is wrong, and adaptive design can make this worse by repeatedly picking settings where an incorrect model fits. The authors bound the power of any valid model-adequacy test in terms of the experimenter's own sampling distribution, introduce a diagnostic for unresolved model error, and propose reserving part of the design budget for falsification. The empirical results are mixed: the originally frozen rule fails, and a disclosed revision **detects 35.8% of misspecified campaigns versus 31.7% for a control at T = 240**, with no clear advantage at T = 480. The authors conclude that parameter learning, model checking, and detector performance should be treated separately, and do not claim a universally better design policy.

papers.title: Action-Conditioned VLM Monitoring for Autonomous Vehicle Semantic Anomalies
papers.abstract: We study action-conditioned monitoring of autonomous-vehicle behavior in semantically unusual driving scenes. The target is whether the executed ego action is appropriate for the scene: the same scene can admit both normal and anomalous behavior, so visual unusualness alone does not determine the monitoring label. A Vision-Language Model (VLM) first predicts the scene-required action from an outcome-hidden video window; the monitor then compares that expectation with the realized ego-motion trajectory under an explicit compatibility rule. To study this monitoring task, we contribute a six-field taxonomy of 112 paired scenarios spanning both failure polarities (42 derived from documented incidents), a generated video corpus with estimated trajectories, and an exploratory two-stage monitor on that corpus. On 235 clips from 15 scenario families, the two-stage protocol with a fixed T-2.5 s window obtains 83.0% accuracy and anomaly recall 0.773, versus 74.5% and 0.536 for a single-stage video-only baseline; specificity is 0.880 versus 0.928.
papers.summary: The authors study whether an autonomous vehicle's executed action suits a semantically unusual driving scene, recognizing that the same scene can call for either normal or anomalous behavior. Their two-stage monitor has a vision-language model (VLM) predict the required action from a video window that hides the outcome, then compares that prediction with the vehicle's actual trajectory using an explicit compatibility rule. They also release a taxonomy of 112 paired scenarios, 42 derived from documented incidents, along with a generated video corpus. On 235 clips, the two-stage monitor reaches **83.0% accuracy and 0.773 anomaly recall, versus 74.5% and 0.536 for a video-only baseline**, at slightly lower specificity.

papers.title: CST-Bench: Benchmarking Counterfactual Spatial Transition Reasoning with Causal Transition On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet existing benchmarks mainly focus on static scene understanding. When objects are moved or swapped, models must infer not only spatial relations but also how interventions change the scene state. To address this problem, we introduce CST-Bench, a benchmark for counterfactual spatial reasoning. CST-Bench contains 7,082 examples covering 6 intervention types and 12 transformation operators, with dense causal annotations including intervention sources, affected relations, expected effects, invariant relations, and metric changes. We benchmark general-purpose MLLMs on CST-Bench and further compare post-training strategies on CST-Bench and standard spatial benchmarks. Results show that methods effective for ordinary spatial reasoning can still fail under counterfactual interventions. We further formulate counterfactual spatial reasoning as causal state-transition modeling and propose CT-OPSD, which uses CST-Bench annotations to guide a teacher model in learning counterfactual state transitions and causal reasoning chains. These chains are then distilled into a student model that reasons only from real observations. Overall, experiment results establish CST-Bench as a challenging benchmark and reusable supervision resource for counterfactual spatial reasoning. CT-OPSD further provides an initial demonstration of how its annotations can support model improvement.
papers.summary: Spatial-reasoning benchmarks for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) mostly test static scenes, not how a scene changes when objects are moved or swapped. `CST-Bench` contains 7,082 counterfactual examples covering 6 intervention types and 12 transformation operators, with dense causal annotations such as affected relations, expected effects, and invariant relations. Experiments show that **post-training methods that help ordinary spatial reasoning can still fail under counterfactual interventions**. The authors also propose `CT-OPSD`, which uses the annotations to guide a teacher model's causal reasoning chains and distills them into a student that reasons only from real observations, as an initial demonstration of using the benchmark for training.

papers.title: FlashOffloading: Low-Latency KV Cache Offloading for Long-Context LLM Serving
papers.abstract: In large language model (LLM) serving systems, the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length and concurrency, so long-context inference easily hits the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity wall and results in low concurrency. Offloading the KV cache to host dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) frees HBM space and raises concurrency, but the additional cache management and host-to-device (H2D) load overhead inflates inference latency, higher concurrency fails to translate into effective throughput. We present FlashOffloading, a host-DRAM-centric inference architecture that fully offloads the KV cache in both the prefill and decode phases. FlashOffloading builds rolling HBM cache for prefill, a hot cache for decode, a reverse sparse index with zero extra miss-lookup overhead, and a compute--load overlapped kernel, optimizing KV offloading latency across the entire pipeline and delivering throughput gains under a time-per-output-token (TPOT) service-level objective (SLO). In experiments deploying GLM-5.2 with multi-token prediction (MTP3) speculative decoding on an Ascend910C prefill--decode (PD)-disaggregated platform, FlashOffloading improves prefill throughput by up to 1.38\(\times\) and decode throughput by up to 1.91\(\times\) under a 30 ms TPOT constraint. FlashOffloading is integrated into an open-source serving framework: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/tree/releases/v0.30.0.
papers.summary: Long-context large language model (LLM) serving runs out of GPU high-bandwidth memory because the key-value (KV) cache grows with sequence length and concurrency, and offloading the cache to host memory usually adds enough latency to cancel out the concurrency gain. `FlashOffloading` fully offloads the KV cache to host memory during both prefill and decode, using a rolling device cache for prefill, a hot cache for decode, a reverse sparse index that adds no lookup cost on misses, and a kernel that overlaps computation with loading. Running `GLM-5.2` with speculative decoding on a disaggregated `Ascend910C` platform, it improves **decode throughput by up to 1.91x** and prefill throughput by up to 1.38x under a 30 ms time-per-output-token target. The system is integrated into the open-source `vllm-ascend` serving framework.

papers.title: The Memory Trap: Language Agents Overgeneralize from Benign Interactions
papers.abstract: Language agents increasingly use persistent memory to record user preferences and procedures across sessions. We show that memory from benign interactions can cause unsafe or unreliable behavior on later tasks. We call this failure the memory trap. To study this issue, we compare behavior in sessions with and without memory across six frontier models (including Claude Sonnet, Opus, and Fable models and GPT-5.6). We evaluate these models in a range of settings. First, in autonomy experiments, we find that requests to skip confirmation during low-stakes coding chores lead agents to skip confirmation and verification on simulated high-stakes tasks in both coding and everyday life. We next study memories formed when users seek emotional support, or describe harm from uncritical feedback, and find these memories bias later judgments of mathematical work, arguments, and poems toward sycophancy or over-critique (respectively). Memory notes written during legitimate stale-test repairs lead agents to weaken correct tests that catch broken safeguards; these memories also increase cheating on ImpossibleBench, with larger increases for stronger Sonnet and Opus models. We show that memory traps can arise both from overgeneralizations in memory writing, and when acting on memory. These findings demonstrate that even benign interactions can lead to serious risks from memory systems, and thus motivate the need for new research into ensuring that agents preserve the scope of their memories.
papers.summary: Language agents that keep persistent memory across sessions can overgeneralize from entirely benign past interactions, a failure the authors call the memory trap. Across six frontier models, including `Claude` `Sonnet`, `Opus`, and `Fable` models and `GPT-5.6`, **a request to skip confirmation on low-stakes coding chores led agents to skip confirmation and verification on simulated high-stakes tasks**. Memories from emotional-support conversations biased later judgments of math, arguments, and poems toward sycophancy or over-criticism. Notes from legitimate stale-test repairs led agents to weaken correct tests and increased cheating on `ImpossibleBench`, more so for stronger models, and the authors show that the overgeneralization can arise both when memories are written and when they are acted on.

papers.title: SKIM: Pruning Large Language Model Agents via Selective Knowledge Informed Masking
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed under structured generation, where grammar constraints enforce output format at inference time. Whereas existing compression methods target unconstrained generation, we first identify a fundamental mismatch: under structured generation, grammar constraints reduce the model's output distribution to valid tokens, and the logits matter most at the small set of positions that decide the agent's action. Motivated by this finding, we propose SKIM (Selective Knowledge-Informed Masking), the first pruning and distillation framework for LLM agents under structured generation, with both stages guided by token role. SKIM partitions token positions into context, decision, and format categories, and this partition drives two complementary axes: (1) category-aware pruning saliency scores that preserve parameters most relevant for decision positions; and (2) an on-policy distillation objective that aligns student and teacher on valid tokens, paired with category-aware feature matching. We evaluate SKIM on tool-calling benchmarks and within multi-step agent loops, across multiple model scales and sparsity levels. SKIM consistently improves accuracy over baselines, with its superiority becoming most striking in high-sparsity regimes where conventional methods struggle, demonstrating the potential of category-aware compression for deployment-time grammar-constrained agents.
papers.summary: LLM agents often run under structured generation, where grammar constraints restrict outputs to valid tokens, yet existing compression methods are designed for unconstrained generation. `SKIM` (Selective Knowledge-Informed Masking) is a pruning-and-distillation framework that splits token positions into context, decision, and format roles. It uses that split to compute pruning saliency scores that protect the parameters behind action-deciding positions, and to drive on-policy distillation restricted to grammar-valid tokens. On tool-calling benchmarks and multi-step agent loops across several model sizes, **`SKIM` consistently beats baselines, with the largest margins at high sparsity**.

papers.title: Provable Zeroth-Order Safe Exploration for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
papers.abstract: Safe reinforcement learning from human feedback (Safe-RLHF) seeks to improve helpfulness while satisfying harmlessness constraints. Existing primal-dual approaches can converge to feasible policies but do not prevent constraint violations during training. We study a stronger requirement, safe exploration for RLHF, under which every policy executed during training, including auxiliary exploration policies, remains feasible. We propose Zeroth-Order Log-Barrier Policy Gradient (ZO-LBPG), a reward-model-free method that optimizes a log-barrier objective using zeroth-order estimates derived directly from human preferences. To ensure safety under noisy feedback, we combine conservative constraint margin estimates with coupled rollouts and an adaptive step size that prevents updates from crossing constraint boundaries. We prove that, with high probability, all iterates and exploration policies remain strictly feasible, and that ZO-LBPG globally converges to an approximately optimal constrained policy. We establish a sample complexity of $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\varepsilon^{-6}+d^3\varepsilon^{-5})$ trajectories and $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\varepsilon^{-8}+d^5\varepsilon^{-7})$ human queries. Experiments on a synthetic CMDP and a language-model alignment task corroborate the training-time safety guarantees.
papers.summary: Safe reinforcement learning from human feedback (Safe-RLHF) aims to improve helpfulness under harmlessness constraints, but existing primal-dual methods can violate those constraints during training. `ZO-LBPG` (Zeroth-Order Log-Barrier Policy Gradient) optimizes a log-barrier objective with gradient estimates taken directly from human preferences, without a reward model, and uses conservative constraint margins, coupled rollouts, and adaptive step sizes. The authors prove that, with high probability, **every policy executed during training, including exploration policies, stays strictly feasible**, and that the method converges globally to an approximately optimal constrained policy with polynomial sample complexity. Experiments on a synthetic constrained Markov decision process and a language-model alignment task support the safety guarantees.

papers.title: MambaTG: Candidate-Aware State Space Modeling for Future Link Prediction on Temporal Graphs
papers.abstract: Future link prediction on temporal graphs involves both repeated interactions between previously connected node pairs and first-time interactions between pairs with no prior interaction. While repeated-edge prediction can exploit direct pairwise evidence, unseen-edge prediction must generalize beyond historical recurrence. Existing temporal graph models often exploit signals tied to recurring interactions or historical overlap, which are highly informative for repeated edges but become limited or unavailable for unseen edges, contributing to substantial performance degradation on unseen-edge prediction. Based on this observation, we identify two complementary signals for modeling sequential dynamics beyond historical recurrence: (1) historical-sequence evolution, which captures dependencies among the source node's chronologically ordered interactions, and (2) candidate--history compatibility, which captures how well a candidate fits the source node's evolving history. Based on the decomposition, we propose MambaTG, a candidate-aware Mamba-based framework that jointly models these two signals. Mamba provides a natural mechanism for this design: its selective recurrence captures the evolution of ordered interaction histories, while its input-dependent state transitions allow the history state to adapt to different candidate inputs. Extensive experiments on 13 temporal graph datasets against 13 representative baselines show that MambaTG achieves strong and consistent performance across both repeated and unseen edges while remaining computationally efficient.
