papers.summary: Temporal graph models predict repeated links well but degrade on first-time links, because they rely on recurrence and historical-overlap signals that new node pairs lack. `MambaTG` models two signals that do not depend on recurrence: how a source node's ordered interaction history evolves, and how well a candidate node fits that evolving history. It uses `Mamba`'s selective recurrence for the first and its input-dependent state transitions for the second. Across 13 datasets and 13 baselines, it shows **strong, consistent performance on both repeated and unseen edges** while remaining computationally efficient.

papers.title: ACSeL: Adaptive Configuration Search for Hardware-Constrained LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Serving large language models (LLMs) under tight memory and latency service-level objectives (SLOs), including on edge devices, requires jointly selecting the model size, batch size, quantization algorithm, and mixed-precision quantization recipes. Exhaustive search over this combinatorially large space is infeasible. Unlike data-center serving, which often prioritizes throughput or generation speed, resource-constrained deployments typically set memory and latency budgets as constraints and then seek the configuration with the highest generation quality among feasible ones. To this end, we propose ACSeL, a framework that identifies configurations predicted to satisfy deployment constraints while achieving high predicted generation quality. To enable efficient quality estimation, we use Relative Model Quality Degradation (RMQD), a proxy based on the divergence between the candidate and reference models' next-token distributions over a small calibration corpus. Across the evaluated model sizes and precisions, RMQD is inexpensive to evaluate and strongly correlated with downstream benchmark performance. ACSeL combines (i) a lightweight quality surrogate that predicts RMQD directly from a configuration; (ii) Few-shot Median Calibration (FMC), which calibrates operator-profile-based latency estimates using a small number of end-to-end profiles; and (iii) a structured search algorithm BandPareto for exploring layerwise mixed-precision configurations. Experiments on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 workstation and an NVIDIA Jetson Thor edge platform show that FMC substantially improves deployment feasibility, while BandPareto + FMC achieves the highest feasibility and the lowest RMQD gaps to the best measured configurations in the evaluation set.
papers.summary: Serving LLMs under tight memory and latency budgets, including on edge devices, requires choosing model size, batch size, quantization algorithm, and per-layer mixed precision jointly, a space too large to search exhaustively. `ACSeL` searches this space using Relative Model Quality Degradation (`RMQD`), a cheap quality proxy based on next-token distribution divergence that correlates strongly with downstream benchmarks, along with a learned surrogate that predicts `RMQD` from a configuration. It also calibrates operator-level latency estimates with a few end-to-end profiles (Few-shot Median Calibration, `FMC`) and explores layerwise mixed-precision configurations with a structured search called `BandPareto`. On an `RTX A6000` workstation and a `Jetson Thor` edge board, **`BandPareto` with `FMC` achieves the highest rate of constraint-satisfying configurations and the smallest quality gap** to the best measured configurations.

papers.title: Stress Testing Chain-of-Thought Monitoring Against Covert Misalignment
papers.abstract: As LLM agents advance rapidly in autonomy, the risk of hidden objectives that bypass safety constraints becomes increasingly plausible. Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring offers a key control mechanism by reading the agent's reasoning and flagging misalignment before it materializes into action, yet its reliability depends on the realism of the red-team it is stress-tested against. Existing red-teaming efforts rely on shared templates, such as casting a side task as a prerequisite, which treat the side objective as an exogenous insertion and leave task-specific, contextually grounded evasions underexplored. We therefore ask: How robust is CoT monitoring against agents that strategically conceal misalignment? To answer this, we introduce TraceMRT, an automated Trace-level Monitor Red-Teaming framework that reframes the side task as a coherent sub-goal of the primary task and searches trace-shaping strategies whose induced trajectories complete the misaligned objective while reading as natural execution. Through black-box attacks on state-of-the-art monitors such as GPT-5.2 and Claude-4.5, we reveal substantial vulnerabilities even in top models. To counter these vulnerabilities, we propose a Bayesian Trajectory Monitoring framework, integrating global context and local segment evidence to detect covert misalignment. Empirically, our method significantly consolidates monitor robustness with 0.91 AUC and 0.74 TPR@FPR=0.05.
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring reads an agent's reasoning to catch hidden misaligned objectives, but existing red-teaming tests it with templated side tasks that are easy to spot. `TraceMRT` is an automated red-teaming framework that recasts the side task as a coherent sub-goal of the main task and searches for strategies that produce reasoning traces that look like natural execution. Black-box attacks with it **reveal substantial vulnerabilities in state-of-the-art monitors, including `GPT-5.2` and `Claude-4.5`**. As a defense, the authors propose Bayesian Trajectory Monitoring, which combines global context with local segment evidence and reaches 0.91 AUC and 0.74 true-positive rate at a 5% false-positive rate.

papers.title: Learning and Steering in Incomplete-Information Games
papers.abstract: In many modern multi-agent systems, a mediator seeks to influence strategic decision dynamics using only outcome-level feedback and without knowing agents' utilities. In this work, we study how a mediator can learn an unknown game and steer adaptive agents toward outcomes that maximize her utility using only trajectory feedback. The mediator knows the game form and her own objective, but not the agents' utilities. Moreover, she commits to nonnegative payments and provides recommendations and contexts, but receives only a single realized terminal outcome rather than full-information feedback. We develop halving-type algorithms that learn utility differences in normal-form games and conditional continuation-value differences in extensive-form games, achieving a sample complexity of $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ that matches worst-case lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. We then combine these learning procedures with a Lagrangian formulation in an online Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm that interleaves learning, equilibrium computation, and steering toward mediator-optimal extensive-form correlated equilibria (EFCE). With high probability, the Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm achieves a directness gap and an optimality gap of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/4})$, while time-average payments are of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/8})$.

papers.title: TACT-KV: Tri-Axis Cosine Transform for Compressing Volumetric KV Caches in Medical VLMs
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) applied to 3D medical scans face a structural memory wall. A single CT or MRI volume produces tens of thousands of vision tokens, and the resulting key-value (KV) cache scales linearly with both batch and context. Existing KV compression methods operate on the cache's feature or token statistics, or apply 1D and 2D transforms, leaving the three-axis spatial structure in the cache unexploited. We propose TACT-KV (Tri-Axis Cosine Transform), a calibration-free KV compression method that exploits strong spatial correlations in visual KV states along all three anatomical axes of 3D scans. This correlation concentrates the KV cache energy under a frequency-domain transform. TACT-KV applies a separable 3D discrete cosine transform to the KV cache, allocates a per-layer bit budget across frequency bins via reverse water-filling (more bits to high-energy components), and quantizes each bin with a fixed scalar codebook. We derive a close-form relation: the distortion reduction from adaptive bit allocation is dominated by the spectral concentration of the transformed cache. Across six medical VLMs and two 3D CT benchmarks, TACT-KV achieves the lowest 1-bit prediction-flip rate on eleven of twelve model and dataset pairs in our main comparison. The same advantage reproduces on four general-purpose VLMs evaluated on video tasks, indicating that the benefit of exploiting three-axis structure generalizes beyond medical imaging. At equal high-bandwidth memory (HBM), TACT-KV scales the decoding batch size on a single GPU by up to $8\times$.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) that read 3D CT or MRI scans produce tens of thousands of vision tokens, so their key-value (KV) cache quickly exhausts GPU memory. `TACT-KV` is a compression method that needs no calibration data. It applies a separable 3D discrete cosine transform to the cache along all three anatomical axes, gives more bits to high-energy frequency bins through reverse water-filling, and quantizes each bin with a fixed scalar codebook. Across six medical VLMs and two 3D CT benchmarks it has the lowest 1-bit prediction-flip rate on eleven of twelve model and dataset pairs, and the advantage carries over to four general-purpose VLMs on video tasks. With the same high-bandwidth memory, it allows **up to 8x larger decoding batches on a single GPU**.

papers.title: Evolver: Turning Agent Exploration into Evolving Capabilities
papers.abstract: Agent exploration produces valuable procedural knowledge, yet much of this experience remains confined to transient execution traces and is not systematically reused. We introduce Evolver, an experience-driven framework that transforms agent exploration into persistent, reusable capabilities without updating foundation model parameters. Built around structured Gene assets, Evolver integrates experience acquisition, retrieval, and feedback-guided evolution to support experience-conditioned execution across existing agent harnesses. We evaluate Evolver using Claude Code and Codex, two foundation model configurations, and four benchmarks: Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-rebench, and GAIA. On a selected diagnostic set of 320 paired executions, Evolver improves task success from 83.13% to 87.50% (+4.38 percentage points) while reducing recorded task-execution token consumption by 24.24%. Furthermore, among 265 pairs successful under both conditions, token consumption decreases by 17.57%, demonstrating efficiency benefits even when task success is preserved. These findings suggest that persistent procedural experience can improve both task effectiveness and execution efficiency, providing a practical foundation for transforming agent exploration into evolving capabilities.
papers.summary: Coding and tool-using agents learn useful procedures while exploring, but that knowledge usually stays in execution traces and is never reused. `Evolver` stores it as structured, reusable "Gene" assets without changing model weights, and combines experience collection, retrieval, and feedback-guided refinement on top of existing agent harnesses such as `Claude Code` and `Codex`. On a diagnostic set of 320 paired runs drawn from `Terminal-Bench 2.1`, `SWE-bench Multilingual`, `SWE-rebench`, and `GAIA`, task success rises from 83.13% to 87.50% while **token consumption falls by 24.24%**. Among tasks solved under both conditions, token use still drops by 17.57%.

papers.title: Align Before Aggregation: Basis-Consistent Federated LoRA under Heterogeneous Ranks
papers.abstract: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) under heterogeneous client capacities is increasingly important, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) with heterogeneous ranks makes it practical. Existing server-side aggregators compose local matrix updates $\Delta W_i$ from client-specific LoRA factors $(A_i,B_i)$ before aggregating them. Although these matrix updates lie in the same weight space $\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and can be averaged directly, the LoRA factors that generate them may expressed client-specific local basis. In the typical compose--aggregate--factorize--dispatch loop, this basis inconsistency can make the rank-$r_i$ reference prefix dispatched to lower-rank clients unstable after server-side refactorization. In this work, we propose \textbf{FedAbA}, a basis-consistent federated LoRA aggregation framework for heterogeneous ranks. FedAbA first extracts each client's local basis, aligns it to the corresponding prefix of the global reference basis, and constructs a basis-consistent reconstruction of each local matrix update before aggregation. It then aggregates these reconstructions with weights that combine client data size and consistency score, followed by exact coefficient-space SVD refactorization and gauge fixing before rank-prefix dispatch. Our theoretical analysis clarifies the role of basis consistency and supports the proposed consistency-aware aggregation mechanism. Extensive experiments show that FedAbA outperforms representative federated LoRA baselines, with the largest gains under the strongest rank heterogeneity.
papers.summary: When large language models are fine-tuned in a federated setting, clients with different capacities use low-rank adaptation (LoRA) at different ranks. Each client's LoRA factors are expressed in its own local basis, which can make the lower-rank slices the server sends back unstable after it re-factorizes the aggregate. `FedAbA` first aligns each client's basis to the matching part of a global reference basis, then aggregates the reconstructed updates with weights based on data size and a consistency score. It finishes with an exact SVD refactorization and gauge fixing before sending each client its rank slice. The authors support the design with theoretical analysis and report that it beats representative federated LoRA baselines, with **the largest gains when client ranks differ most**.

papers.title: Binding Paraphrased Instructions to Encountered Objects in sLLM Agents under Partial Observability
papers.abstract: Reliable deployment of LLM agents requires grounding diverse user expressions in their environments. Although RL-finetuned smaller large language model (sLLM) agents rival larger prompted LLMs on embodied tasks, their robustness to instruction paraphrases remains unclear. We introduce ALFWorld-Para to evaluate this robustness under controlled paraphrases, revealing 21-52% declines in success rates (SRs), predominantly driven by object synonyms. Despite retaining knowledge of synonym referents, agents often fail to take the corresponding objects even after observing them, exposing a gap between referential knowledge and object binding. Partial observability further complicates binding, as referents may remain unseen or have already been encountered under different labels. To address this challenge, we propose BINDIntent, a training-free framework that probabilistically binds referring expressions to observed labels using semantic proximity and estimated persistence against unseen candidates. Without additional training or LLM calls, BINDIntent improves synonym-paraphrase success of RL-finetuned sLLMs by 17.5-49.1 percentage points (pp) with only 0.4 ms of CPU overhead per step. It also raises GiGPO-7B's overall SR from 61.8% to 77.4%, surpassing a prompted 24B LLM. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/cau-hai-lab/ALFWorld-Para.
papers.summary: Small language model (sLLM) agents fine-tuned with reinforcement learning can match larger prompted models on embodied tasks, but it is unclear how well they handle reworded instructions. The new `ALFWorld-Para` benchmark shows **21-52% drops in success rate**, driven mostly by object synonyms: agents know what a synonym refers to but fail to pick up the matching object even after seeing it. `BINDIntent` is a training-free fix that probabilistically links referring expressions to observed object labels using semantic similarity and an estimate of whether an unseen candidate might still appear. It raises synonym-paraphrase success by 17.5-49.1 percentage points at 0.4 ms of CPU cost per step, and lifts `GiGPO-7B` from 61.8% to 77.4% success, ahead of a prompted 24B model.

papers.title: FisherDistill: Diffusion Distribution Distillation via Closed-Form Fisher Critics
papers.abstract: Recent advances in diffusion distillation have enabled high-quality image generation in only one or a few network function evaluations (NFEs). Despite their efficiency, aggressively distilled generators often retain a residual distribution gap from their multi-step teachers, motivating recent methods to introduce adversarial refinement with a learned discriminator. In this work, we ask whether such refinement necessarily requires a learned adversarial discriminator. We introduce \textbf{FisherDistill}, a simple alternative based on Fisher linear discriminant analysis. Using intermediate representations from the frozen teacher, we estimate the first- and second-order statistics of real and generated samples and derive a closed-form Fisher direction that maximally separates their feature distributions relative to within-class variation. This direction provides a lightweight refinement signal that complements the original distillation objective without requiring an additional adversarial discriminator or its optimization loop. Across multiple distillation frameworks, our approach consistently improves generation quality over their respective distilled baselines and substantially closes the gap to adversarially refined counterparts. Code: https://bhosalems.github.io/FisherDistill/
papers.summary: Diffusion models distilled to generate images in one or a few steps still lag behind their multi-step teachers, and current fixes add a trained adversarial discriminator to close the gap. `FisherDistill` replaces that discriminator with Fisher linear discriminant analysis. It computes the means and covariances of real and generated samples in the frozen teacher's feature space and derives a closed-form direction that best separates them, which then serves as an extra training signal. Across several distillation frameworks, this **consistently improves image quality over the distilled baselines and closes much of the gap to adversarially refined models**, without a discriminator training loop.

papers.title: Embedding-Space Fingerprinting of LoRA Fine-Tunes: Recovering the Training-Data Domain from the Model Artifact Alone
papers.abstract: When a base language model is fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), how much of the training data domain leaks into the resulting artifact? This paper studies whether a simple classifier can recover the domain of a fine-tune given only the model artifact (weight deltas, internal activations on a fixed probe set, or generated text) without ever observing the training data. Using one base model (Qwen3.5-0.8B), 36 LoRA fine-tunes are produced over 18 public datasets in five domains (medical, code, mathematics, non-English text, narrative prose), and three feature families are extracted at decreasing levels of access: white-box weights, gray-box activations, and black-box outputs. A leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) protocol, frozen before any result was seen, tests whether the domain of a fine-tune trained on a previously unseen dataset can be identified. The domain is recoverable well above chance (20%) from gray-box activations (61%) and black-box outputs (64%); white-box weight statistics reach 42%. Contrary to the pre-registered hypothesis that signal decays monotonically from weights to activations to outputs, activations and outputs were more informative than the weight-delta statistics. The black-box result holds unchanged (64%) when only generated text is used, without token probabilities. Domain accuracy is also stable when a third run per dataset is trained on an independently drawn data subsample, and black-box predictions are unaffected by the LoRA rank (8-64). All code and per-run feature vectors are released.
papers.summary: The study asks whether a LoRA (low-rank adaptation) fine-tune reveals what kind of data it was trained on, using only the released artifact. The authors trained 36 fine-tunes of `Qwen3.5-0.8B` on 18 public datasets spanning five domains, extracted features from weight deltas, activations on fixed probe inputs, and generated text, and evaluated them with a pre-registered leave-one-dataset-out protocol. The training domain can be identified well above the 20% chance level: **64% from generated text alone** and 61% from activations, but only 42% from weight statistics, which contradicts the pre-registered hypothesis that weights would carry the most signal. The results hold across independent data subsamples and LoRA ranks from 8 to 64.

papers.title: The Popular Get More Popular: Auditing Brand Bias in Generative Search
papers.abstract: The shift from traditional to generative search has fundamentally transformed online product discovery. Because conversational recommendations synthesize choices into a few direct answers, subtle systemic preferences toward specific providers can exert profound commercial impacts. In this work, we audit this phenomenon through two distinct dimensions: (i) brand popularity bias, the systematic preference for market-dominant entities over long-tail alternatives, and (ii) brand familiarity bias, the ranking advantage an entity encoded in an LLM's parametric memory holds over an unfamiliar competitor. First, evaluating commercial queries across major engines, we observe persistent brand popularity bias: dominant brands in the top quintile are cited 1.4x to 2.8x more frequently than the average brand within a sample of 1,176 top market players, already present in parametric memory that external web retrieval fails to mitigate. Second, through controlled in-context experiments holding product attributes constant, we find that substituting authentic brand signatures with unfamiliar ones significantly degrades recommendation rank. Conversely, fact-preserving content rewrites yield negligible ranking gains. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that generative search engines reinforce a ``rich-get-richer'' dynamic by favoring established market leaders and imposing a parametric barrier to entry that standard content optimization cannot overcome.
papers.summary: Generative search engines condense product recommendations into a few direct answers, so any built-in preference for particular brands has outsized commercial effects. The audit looks at two biases: favoring market-dominant brands, and favoring brands already stored in the model's parametric memory. Across major engines, top-quintile brands are **cited 1.4x to 2.8x more often than the average brand** among 1,176 market players, and web retrieval does not remove this bias. In controlled experiments with identical product attributes, replacing real brand names with unfamiliar ones lowers recommendation rank, while fact-preserving content rewrites barely help. The authors conclude that these engines create a rich-get-richer barrier that ordinary content optimization cannot overcome.

papers.title: Monotone Viability Learning for Offline Safe Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Offline safe reinforcement learning requires reliable long-horizon safety estimates from fixed data. Learning Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) viability in this setting calls for semantic preservation, convergence, and numerical stability. To address these challenges, we propose Monotone Viability Learning (MoViL), which learns viable sets from offline transitions through monotone finite-horizon set recursion. The recursion preserves finite-horizon safety semantics and converges to the infinite-horizon viability kernel. Binary supervision maintains a fixed target scale across horizons, avoiding discount-induced numerical attenuation. We further establish sufficient conditions for recovering behavior-supported viable subsets. The learned viability estimates are used to certify actions at deployment. Dubins car experiments validate the numerical accuracy of the learned viable sets. Evaluations on safe RL benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art reward-cost performance. MoViL satisfies the average cost constraint on every task and achieves the lowest average cost among the compared methods. These results highlight MoViL's potential to extend long-horizon HJ viability analysis to safety-critical systems where reliable dynamics models are unavailable and online exploration is unsafe.
papers.summary: Offline safe reinforcement learning has to estimate long-horizon safety from a fixed dataset, and learning Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) viability sets in that setting tends to be numerically unstable. `MoViL` (Monotone Viability Learning) learns viable sets through a monotone finite-horizon set recursion with binary supervision. This keeps a fixed target scale across horizons and avoids the attenuation that discounting causes, and the authors prove that it converges to the infinite-horizon viability kernel. The learned sets are used to certify actions at deployment. On safe RL benchmarks, MoViL **meets the average cost constraint on every task** while reaching state-of-the-art reward-cost trade-offs and the lowest average cost of the compared methods.

papers.title: Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution
papers.abstract: Agent harness evolution enables recursive self-improvement (RSI) without updating model weights. We examine whether higher benchmark scores yield reliable, efficient, and transferable improvement. We evaluate four methods across harnesses, general and coding tasks. Repeated evaluations, controlled agent expansion, component interventions, and admission replays reveal recurring patterns. All sixteen evolved agents gain previously uncovered tasks while losing previously covered ones. In one general-task case, reliability rises by 5.2 points despite losing ten previously covered tasks. Most reliability gains also increase deployment cost. Specific changes usually outperform generic reminders, but their benefits can change when combined. The highest-scoring agent does not yield the largest mean improvement in any of our four pools, and stricter admission can discard useful alternatives. Transfer selectively preserves gains: coverage usually falls on the general-task target across both harness types and paradigms, but rises on the coding target with the outer-layer-only harness. These findings motivate preservation-aware evaluation, tested decision rules, and explicit applicability conditions. As a constructive follow-up, EvoAudit turns these diagnostics into revisions of select, analyze, mutate, and gate, achieving the best performance.
papers.summary: Evolving an agent's harness is promoted as a way to achieve recursive self-improvement (RSI) without updating model weights. This study asks whether the higher benchmark scores it produces reflect reliable, efficient, and transferable gains. Using repeated evaluations, component interventions, and replays across four evolution methods on general and coding tasks, the authors find that **all sixteen evolved agents gain some new tasks while losing others they previously solved**. Most reliability gains also raise deployment cost, the top-scoring agent never gives the largest mean improvement, and transfer to new targets is uneven. The authors fold these diagnostics into `EvoAudit`, a revised select, analyze, mutate, and gate loop that performs best in their setting.

papers.title: Online Learning with Ordered Experts (via Two-point Feedback)
papers.abstract:
We study adversarial online learning with expert recommendations in a totally ordered action space, where the experts' recommendations may change and be reordered arbitrarily. Our focus is two-point feedback: on each round the learner plays two current recommendations, observes both, and pays their average. We study two problems. In the separated monotone problem, the loss is the sum of a hidden nondecreasing component and a hidden nonincreasing component, and a query reveals the two components separately. In the BV problem, the losses are bounded and have bounded variation (BV) along the order, and a query reveals only the loss.
  In the separated monotone problem, two paid observations achieve \[ O\bigl(\log(|\cF|T)\sqrt{T\log|\cF|}\bigr) \] regret against the best of $|\cF|$ experts, within a logarithmic factor of the classical full-information bound. For the BV problem, we obtain $\wtO(\sqrt T+|\cF|)$ regret. We give an application in dynamic pricing with expert advice, showing that two-option menus matches the full information rate up to $\log$ factors.
  The main technical ingredient is a marginal-preserving endpoint flow estimator. Two observations reveal a loss increment along the order; random paths supply telescoping identities that turn this local information into unbiased loss estimates for all current recommendations. A reversible pair sampler preserves the learner's intended marginal at both played actions. The estimator's second-moment and stability bounds support online updates for both feedback models.
papers.summary: The paper studies adversarial online learning where expert recommendations lie in a totally ordered action space and can change or be reordered every round. The learner plays two recommendations per round, sees both outcomes, and pays their average. When the loss splits into separately observed nondecreasing and nonincreasing parts, the regret is **within a logarithmic factor of the full-information bound**. For losses with bounded variation along the order, it is roughly the square root of T plus the number of experts. The key technique is an estimator that turns the observed loss difference between two points into unbiased loss estimates for all current recommendations, and the authors apply it to dynamic pricing with two-option menus.

papers.title: Redacting Personal Data: A Speed and Accuracy Comparison of Regex, Presidio and Hybrid Designs
papers.abstract: Many enterprise projects now pass free text to large language models (LLMs), and that text often contains personally identifiable information (PII) such as names, phone numbers, email addresses, home addresses and dates of birth. Once a prompt is sent, this data is copied into provider systems, application logs and observability traces. Redacting PII before the call is an obvious control, yet teams seldom have numbers on what it costs in latency or what it lets through. This paper compares four redaction designs that any LLM pipeline can adopt: a pure regular-expression (regex) redactor, Microsoft Presidio running on a spaCy model, a hybrid in which Presidio finds only person names while regex handles structured identifiers, and a fast hybrid that calls spaCy's named-entity component directly. All four share a known-entity rule, which removes the person the system already knows it is handling, and a consistent placeholder scheme, so the LLM can still tell one person from another after redaction. We evaluate the designs on a sample workflow, which we call ProfileAssist, that turns resumes into structured profiles, using 100 synthetic resumes (523 characters on average, with 900 PII values and 600 business terms that must survive). Regex ran at a 0.20 ms median but caught only 88.9% of PII, because it cannot find names that are not known in advance, such as the references listed in a resume. Presidio, hybrid and fast hybrid each caught 100% of PII and kept 100% of business terms, at median latencies of 37.59 ms, 30.23 ms and 13.48 ms. Measured against a 9,120 ms median LLM call, even the slowest option adds only 0.41% to the request. We therefore recommend the fast hybrid as a default for LLM pipelines that handle personal data, with regex kept as a safety net rather than as the only control.
papers.summary: Text sent to LLM APIs often contains personally identifiable information (PII), and teams rarely know how much latency redaction adds or how much PII slips through. The authors compare four redaction designs on 100 synthetic resumes: pure regular expressions (regex), Microsoft `Presidio` running on `spaCy`, a hybrid in which Presidio finds only names, and a fast hybrid that calls spaCy's named-entity component directly. Regex took 0.20 ms but caught only 88.9% of PII because it misses names it does not already know. The other three caught 100% of PII and kept all business terms, and **the fast hybrid did so at a 13.48 ms median**. Even the slowest option adds only 0.41% to a typical LLM call, so the authors recommend the fast hybrid, with regex as a backup layer.

papers.title: Measuring the Marginal Value of Verifier-Based RL Beyond Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) is usually evaluated as an alternative to supervised fine-tuning (SFT), or as a stage that follows it, with the implicit assumption that the RL stage contributes gains of its own. We measure that contribution directly, in a controlled setting where both stages can be run to completion and compared exactly. We built gpu-train-debug, a deterministic benchmark of 1,877 synthetic GPU and LLM training failure diagnosis tasks across 30 archetypes, graded by a programmatic verifier with partial credit, and calibrated so that a mid-tier model scores in a 0.60 to 0.75 band. A pilot produced a surprise: 1,200 gold demonstrations nearly solved the benchmark (SFT 0.785 on the hard split), while 15 steps of GRPO from the base model did not move it (0.314 vs 0.311 base). We therefore amended the study, in writing and before the full run, to ask the sharper question: what does verifier-based RL add beyond demonstrations? At the pre-registered scale (60 GRPO steps, learning rate 1e-6), the answer is: no detectable improvement in-distribution (+0.22 points, 95% CI [-0.06, +0.51]), and a modest but measurable improvement under distribution shift (+0.33 points on a held-out OOD split, CI [+0.02, +0.68]). SFT accounted for most of the available improvement, while verifier-based RL produced only modest additional gains under distribution shift. The residual errors SFT leaves are mostly systematic, identical across samples, which likely reduces the within-group learning signal available to GRPO. A full 60-step cold-start GRPO arm confirms the pilot at the full horizon. The whole study cost $8.69 of compute and is fully reproducible from archived generations, frozen configs, and tagged code.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) is usually assumed to add value on top of supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The authors measure that added value directly on `gpu-train-debug`, a deterministic benchmark of 1,877 synthetic GPU and LLM training-failure diagnosis tasks. SFT on 1,200 demonstrations nearly solved the benchmark, while pre-registered `GRPO` training on top added **no detectable in-distribution gain (+0.22 points, confidence interval spanning zero)** and only a small gain under distribution shift (+0.33 points). The errors SFT leaves behind are mostly systematic and repeat identically across samples, which likely leaves GRPO with little within-group learning signal. The full study cost $8.69 of compute and can be reproduced from archived artifacts.

papers.title: Beyond Instruction Override: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injection with Task-Tampering Attacks
papers.abstract: Indirect prompt-injection (IPI) benchmarks predominantly test planted instructions that redirect a tool-using agent toward an attacker-chosen task. Yet attacker-controlled content can instead tamper with the outcome of the task already in progress. A buyer's dispute evidence can cite a false refund policy to inflate a refund without changing the task. We define IPI by authority rather than instruction-like wording: planted content constitutes an attack when it attempts to influence a decision that its source is not authorized to determine. We introduce a benchmark that makes this boundary explicit: in each of 90 validated cases across three tool-use environments, the user request specifies the source that resolves the targeted decision. Every attack tampers with a decision required by the benign task rather than replacing that task. Each case has attacks with the same harmful outcome that target up to six parts of the agent's decision making: its objective, decision rules, available actions, expected consequences, reading of observations, or beliefs about the current state. Without a defense, attacks on three of the five other targets (decision rules, available actions, and state) have higher mean success than objective attacks across five LLMs. A detection-and-removal defense reduces objective-targeting attacks to 2.4% success but leaves observation- and state-targeting attacks at 9.5% and 12.1%; this gap persists under detection-optimized rewrites. A tool-policy defense still allows 15.4% attack success, close to 17.0% without a defense, because these attacks generally retain expected tools and manipulate values obtained during execution. Evaluations whose attacks redirect the task or target only the agent's objective can therefore overestimate the coverage of these defenses. Code and data are available at https://github.com/amazon-science/task-tampering-prompt-injection.
papers.summary: Most indirect prompt-injection (IPI) benchmarks test planted instructions that redirect a tool-using agent to a new task, but attackers can instead tamper with the outcome of the task already under way, for example by citing a false refund policy. The authors define an injection by authority: content attacks when it tries to influence a decision its source is not authorized to make. They build 90 validated cases across three tool-use environments, with attacks targeting six parts of the agent's decision making, from its objective to its beliefs about the current state. A detection-and-removal defense cuts objective-targeting attacks to 2.4% success but leaves state-targeting attacks at 12.1%. A tool-policy defense allows **15.4% success, close to the 17.0% with no defense**, which suggests that existing evaluations overestimate how much these defenses cover.

papers.title: Neural Image Compression with Internal-External Prior Fusion and Alignment
papers.abstract: Existing context models for learned image com- pression rely primarily on internal priors from the current image, overlooking common patterns and typical textures shared across natural images. To address this limitation, we propose an Internal-External Prior Fusion-Alignment (IE-PFA) context model built upon quadtree spatial-channel joint modeling, where a learnable dictionary shared by the encoder and decoder serves as an external prior. Specifically, an RWKV-based Spatial- Channel Prior Fusion (RSCPF) module efficiently fuses inter- nal and external priors along spatial and channel dimensions with linear complexity, while a training-only Self-Distilled Prior Alignment (SDPA) mechanism aligns them without inference overhead. Moreover, our model supports variable-rate coding over 64 quality levels within a single network and is accelerated by custom CUDA operators. Experiments on seven benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art rate-distortion performance, achiev- ing an average BD-Rate saving of 21.65% over VTM-22.0-Intra, with only 29.9M parameters and the fastest coding speed among advanced neural codecs (61 ms encoding and 52 ms decoding). Code is available at https://github.com/stcnjtech/DCVC-X-Intra.
papers.summary: Context models for learned image compression usually rely only on information from the current image and ignore textures and patterns that recur across natural images. `IE-PFA` adds an external prior, a learnable dictionary shared by encoder and decoder, and fuses it with internal priors using an RWKV-based module that scales linearly. A training-only self-distillation step aligns the two priors at no inference cost, and one network supports 64 quality levels. Across seven benchmarks it achieves an **average 21.65% BD-Rate saving over `VTM-22.0-Intra`** with 29.9M parameters, encoding in 61 ms and decoding in 52 ms, the fastest among advanced neural codecs.

papers.title: WaSP: Wasserstein Data Synthesis Pipeline for Solver-Free Operator Learning
papers.abstract: Neural operators offer fast surrogates for solving PDEs, but training them typically requires expensive input-solution pairs. Two solver-free alternatives include physics-informed learning and training on manufactured data. Physics-informed learning approximates solutions by minimizing PDE residuals. While the residual norm must be strong enough to control solution error, stronger norms increase mini-batch variance and hinder optimization. Manufactured data constructs input-solution pairs for learning by applying the PDE operator to artificial solutions. However, the resulting training distribution can be mutually singular with the target distribution, yielding poor accuracy on the target distribution. We introduce the Wasserstein Data Synthesis Pipeline (WaSP), which trains on manufactured input-solution pairs while gradually mitigating the distribution shift. WaSP synthesizes new pairs by applying the learned operator to a path of intermediate distributions converging to the target input distribution. Training proceeds in stages along this path. At each stage, the previous surrogate generates solutions, and the exact PDE operator derives corresponding inputs, yielding training pairs for the next surrogate. Theoretically, we prove a stepwise error-propagation bound for the distribution shift introduced during synthesis. Empirically, WaSP reduces solution error by $3.9\times$ to $9.5\times$ compared to existing solver-free methods on PDEs such as Allen-Cahn, Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, and Ginzburg-Landau, and better reproduces the two chaotic systems' statistical observables.
papers.summary: Neural operators approximate PDE solvers, but they usually need expensive solver-generated training pairs. The two solver-free alternatives each have drawbacks: physics-informed losses are hard to optimize, and manufactured data can come from a distribution far from the target. `WaSP` (Wasserstein Data Synthesis Pipeline) starts from manufactured pairs and trains in stages along a path of intermediate distributions toward the target input distribution. At each stage, the previous surrogate generates solutions and the exact PDE operator produces the matching inputs. The authors prove a stepwise error-propagation bound and report **3.9x to 9.5x lower solution error** than existing solver-free methods on Allen-Cahn, Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, and Ginzburg-Landau equations, with better statistics on the chaotic systems.

papers.title: UniGADD: Universal Generator-Agnostic Deepfake Detector
papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce Universal Generator-Agnostic Deepfake Detector (UniGADD), a novel method that employs supervised learning to achieve high accuracy on known deepfake generators, while maintaining robust performance on previously unseen ones. The proposed approach follows a two-stage optimisation process. In the first stage, a contrastive loss encourages the model to learn discriminative feature embeddings from real and known fake images, resulting in strong performance within the training domain. In the second stage, the embedding space is refined by promoting inter-cluster separation and intra-cluster compactness, applied exclusively to real samples. This refinement enhances generalisability, enabling the method to exhibit improved robustness against unseen deepfake generation techniques. UniGADD achieves accuracy on par with state-of-the-art methods for known generators, while significantly outperforming them on unseen cases, demonstrating its scalability and practical applicability for adversarial content detection.
papers.summary: Deepfake detectors trained on known generators often fail on images from new ones. `UniGADD` (Universal Generator-Agnostic Deepfake Detector) trains in two stages. First a contrastive loss learns embeddings that separate real images from known fakes, then the embedding space is refined using only real samples, making their clusters tighter and further apart. The method matches state-of-the-art accuracy on known generators while **significantly outperforming prior methods on unseen ones**.

papers.title: What the Middleman Delivers: Answer Behavior, Tool Permissions, and Billed Usage in LLM API Relays
papers.abstract: Third-party application programming interface (API) relays offer access to large language models (LLMs), often at lower prices. Users depend on these services for model quality, instruction compliance, and accurate billing. However, existing studies leave unclear whether relays meet these expectations together. We test 20 relays offering GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5. First, we compare answers to knowledge questions with batch-matched official responses. In our first-round sample, the analysis flags 7/10 low-price and 2/10 same- or higher-price relays for behavioral differences. On retesting 35 pairs, seven gain or lose a flag under the original rules, and six under matched correction families. Because answer comparisons cannot reveal every delivery problem, we examine returned content and tool permissions. No injection is confirmed in 3,332 screened responses to a fixed, non-adversarial code and setup workload, yet four relays return tool calls despite instructions disabling them in the first round. Finally, to connect reported usage to actual costs, we compare input-token counts with official references and check balances. For identical requests, five relays report 4,200 to 60,000 more input tokens than the official API. Where balances are available (six services), charges follow reported usage at listed prices, including extra reported input tokens at one service. Our study shows that advertised models and prices are insufficient to judge relay reliability. It identifies unexplained billed token quantities and tool-permission violations as risks and shows why service evaluations need repeated measurements.
papers.summary: Third-party API relays resell access to LLMs at lower prices, and users have to trust them on model quality, instruction compliance, and billing. The authors tested 20 relays offering `GPT-6 Astra` and `Claude Opus 5`. Comparing answers with official responses flagged behavioral differences at 7 of 10 low-price relays, though several flags changed on retesting. No content injection was found in 3,332 screened responses, but four relays returned tool calls even when instructions disabled them. For identical requests, **five relays reported 4,200 to 60,000 more input tokens than the official API**, and where balances could be checked, charges followed those inflated counts. The authors conclude that advertised model and price are not enough to judge a relay and that evaluations need repeated measurements.

papers.title: GraspBench: Execution-Aware Cross-Robot Evaluation of 6-DoF Grasp Generation in MuJoCo
papers.abstract: Modern 6-DoF grasp generators are often evaluated using grasp scores, dataset-level metrics, or single-robot demonstrations, yet proposal quality alone does not determine whether a grasp is executable by a particular robot. We present GraspBench, a controlled MuJoCo protocol for evaluating complete grasp-generation pipelines after robot-specific inverse-kinematics filtering, motion planning, and fixed approach-close-lift execution. GraspBench evaluates six configured pipelines across four robot embodiments, five diagnostic objects, and a structured tabletop pose grid, yielding 540 scenarios per method and 3,240 method-scenario evaluations in total. Missing outputs are conservatively counted as failures, and success follows the binary lift criterion produced by each method's execution runner. GraspGen achieves the highest overall success rate (73.1%), followed by EconomicGrasp (63.5%), while robot- and object-conditioned analyses reveal substantial variation across embodiments and object geometries. GPG produces the largest native candidate sets but achieves 44.3% success, indicating that proposal volume alone does not guarantee robot-executable grasps. Cluster-aware paired intervals support the principal method differences while not estimating repeated-execution uncertainty. The results characterize complete configured pipelines on fixed scenarios rather than intrinsic model quality or stochastic repeatability, showing that grasping performance depends jointly on the generator, robot embodiment, scene, and execution protocol.
papers.summary: Grasp generators that output 6-DoF (six degrees of freedom) grasps are usually judged by grasp scores or single-robot demos, which says little about whether a specific robot can actually execute them. `GraspBench` is a controlled `MuJoCo` protocol that runs complete pipelines through robot-specific inverse kinematics, motion planning, and a fixed approach, close, and lift sequence. It covers six pipelines, four robot embodiments, and five objects, for 3,240 evaluations in total. `GraspGen` has the **highest success rate at 73.1%**, ahead of `EconomicGrasp` at 63.5%. `GPG` produces the most candidates but succeeds only 44.3% of the time, showing that results depend jointly on generator, robot, scene, and execution protocol.

papers.title: Don't Prompt Your Agents. Equip Them: Skillware as a Modular Standard for Sovereign, Auditable, and Deterministic Capability Execution for Logical Systems
papers.abstract:
Current autonomous logical systems rely on a fragile assumption: that language models should dynamically write code, guess API payloads, and memorize operational constraints through prompt engineering. In practice, this burns massive context windows, inflates API bills, and produces brittle agents that fail unpredictably in production.
  In this work, we present Skillware, an open architectural framework and capability registry that formally separates what an agent wants to do from how that task is executed. Instead of prompting models with loose text instructions or markdown files baptized as 'skills', Skillware equips them with modular, versioned software capability bundles. Much like skill hotkeys in video games that execute deterministically under fixed world rules, each bundle combines a typed JSON input contract, deterministic Python code, task directives, bundled datasets, and automated unit tests. In-process adapters translate these capabilities into native tool declarations for any model, from frontier cloud APIs to local open-weight runtimes with zero network latency.
  Evaluating 23 frontier and open-weight models across 368 benchmark conditions, we show that small local models (3B to 8B parameters) equipped with Skillware consistently outperform unequipped frontier models on complex multi-step workflows. They cut token usage by up to 84.8%, slash inference costs by up to 97.3%, and eliminate parameter errors entirely. True agent reliability does not come from larger models or longer prompts, but from equipping logical systems with verified, deterministic software.
  Finally, we articulate the trajectory of capability bundles across an invariant continuum of information processing systems: from digital logical systems today, to IoT, drones, and embodied robotics tomorrow, establishing a foundation for auditable, real-time capability execution.
papers.summary: LLM agents that write code, guess API payloads, and memorize operational rules through prompts use a lot of context and break in production. `Skillware` is an open framework and registry that packages each capability as a versioned bundle: a typed JSON input contract, deterministic Python code, task directives, bundled datasets, and unit tests. Adapters expose these bundles as native tool declarations for both cloud and local models. Across 23 models and 368 benchmark conditions, **small local models (3B to 8B parameters) equipped with Skillware outperform unequipped frontier models** on multi-step workflows, cutting token usage by up to 84.8%, cost by up to 97.3%, and eliminating parameter errors.

papers.title: PharmAgents2: Towards Autonomous End-to-End Drug Discovery
papers.abstract: Drug discovery requires continuous scientific decision-making across a vast research space. We introduce PharmAgents2, an autonomous system for end-to-end drug discovery that combines knowledge-enhanced decision-making with organized large-scale exploration. Paper2Skill extracts transferable scientific decision knowledge from public sources and, together with expert-developed skills, supports research decisions. Self-Scaling Discovery expands exploration through parallel agents inheriting research context and decision-making capabilities across targets, scientific hypotheses, and discovery strategies. We introduce PharmAgents-Bench v0.1, comprising 121 questions across nine decision scenarios and three end-to-end tasks assessed with expert-defined process rubrics. PharmAgents2 outperforms evaluated baselines in most decision categories and achieves the highest process scores on all three end-to-end tasks. In three real-world studies, autonomous investigations generated findings subsequently supported by human-executed experiments. For LpxH, PharmAgents2 hypothesized a previously unreported allosteric site and screened compounds against it, identifying a novel inhibitor scaffold with experimentally confirmed inhibitory activity and binding. For JAK1, it prioritized a covalent inhibition strategy and nominated compounds with experimentally demonstrated activity. Starting from a known bioactive molecule, Self-Scaling Discovery explored candidate targets across the proteome and identified a new binding target, with the interaction subsequently confirmed experimentally. PharmAgents2 represents a prototype of a virtual pharmaceutical company, marking a step toward autonomous end-to-end drug discovery.
papers.summary: `PharmAgents2` is an autonomous multi-agent system for end-to-end drug discovery. It combines `Paper2Skill`, which extracts decision knowledge from the literature, with `Self-Scaling Discovery`, which runs parallel agents across targets, hypotheses, and strategies. On the new `PharmAgents-Bench v0.1`, with 121 questions and three end-to-end tasks, it outperforms baselines in most decision categories and gets the top process scores on all end-to-end tasks. In three real-world studies, human-run experiments confirmed its findings, including **a novel inhibitor scaffold for `LpxH` acting at a previously unreported allosteric site**, active covalent compounds for `JAK1`, and a new binding target for a known bioactive molecule.

papers.title: English Calibration Erodes Lithuanian in Expert-Pruned Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
papers.abstract: Expert pruning compresses Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models by removing the experts that a calibration set marks as unimportant. Studies of high-resource languages largely find that English calibration transfers well to other languages. We test this for Lithuanian: we pruned four MoE models with REAP, removing 25% or 50% of the experts with English, Lithuanian or mixed calibration, and evaluated both languages on reading comprehension, translation and language modelling. English calibration does not transfer to Lithuanian: at 25% pruning, English comprehension fell by a median of 1.7 points but Lithuanian by 21.4. The transfer is asymmetric. Lithuanian calibration removed most of the Lithuanian loss and never significantly hurt English comprehension, which was on average 2.5 points better than under English calibration; only English language modeling got slightly worse. Routing suggests why: in the last layers, Lithuanian sends 55-72% of its expert selections to just eight experts, against 19-39% for English, and English calibration removes some of these experts. Compressed models should be calibrated, and evaluated, in every language they must serve.
papers.summary: Expert pruning shrinks Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models by dropping the experts that a calibration set marks as unimportant, and earlier work on high-resource languages found that English calibration transfers well to other languages. The authors tested this for Lithuanian by pruning four MoE models with `REAP`, removing 25% or 50% of experts using English, Lithuanian or mixed calibration data, then measuring reading comprehension, translation and language modelling in both languages. English calibration did not transfer: at 25% pruning, English comprehension fell by a median of 1.7 points but **Lithuanian comprehension fell by 21.4 points**. Lithuanian calibration recovered most of that loss without significantly hurting English comprehension, and routing analysis shows that Lithuanian concentrates its last-layer expert selections on a few experts that English calibration tends to remove.

papers.title: Simple Meta-Learning for HPO and CASH Using Performance Representations
papers.abstract: Bayesian optimization for Hyperparameter Optimization (HPO) and Combined Algorithm Selection and Hyperparameter Optimization (CASH) often relies on explicit hyperparameter encodings as surrogate inputs. In high-dimensional search spaces, however, such representations can make it difficult for standard surrogates to learn useful performance models. We instead study an alternative meta-learning representation that describes each configuration directly as its historical performance across prior tasks. This representation can be paired directly with standard surrogate models. Our scope is the iterative selection component of AutoML, deciding which configuration to evaluate next from a fixed candidate set, rather than a complete framework with features such as runtime estimation, cost-aware budgeting and ensembling. We further apply this representation to maximal marginal relevance (MMR), a diversity-based re-ranking criterion from recommender systems, as a posterior-free acquisition rule. When selecting and optimising across multiple models on the TabArena benchmark, the performance-based representation paired with a linear Bayesian ridge regression model outperforms dedicated meta-learning baselines, achieving the same tuned performance in roughly half the number of trials. For single-model HPO, it remains a competitive second. Across both benchmarks this method closely matches or improves on regret at a fraction of the complexity and cost, requiring no pre-training or tuning and scaling independently of search space dimensionality. Code for reproducing our results is available at https://github.com/EWitting/simple-metalearning.
papers.summary: Bayesian optimization for Hyperparameter Optimization (HPO) and Combined Algorithm Selection and Hyperparameter Optimization (CASH) usually feeds explicit hyperparameter encodings to its surrogate model, which becomes hard to learn from in high-dimensional search spaces. The authors instead represent each candidate configuration by its historical performance on earlier tasks and pair this with standard surrogates; they also adapt maximal marginal relevance (`MMR`), a diversity-based re-ranking rule from recommender systems, as an acquisition rule that needs no posterior. On the `TabArena` benchmark, this representation combined with a linear Bayesian ridge regression beats dedicated meta-learning baselines for multi-model selection, **reaching the same tuned performance in roughly half the trials**, and ranks a competitive second for single-model HPO. The method needs no pre-training or tuning, and its cost does not grow with the dimensionality of the search space.

papers.title: Energy-Aware Open-Vocabulary Detection Scheduling for Low-Power Robotic Autonomy
papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) lets robots search for run-time object queries, but fixed-rate inference spends embedded compute on low-value frames during idle motion, map revisits, or stable viewpoints. This paper presents an energy-aware OVD scheduler for low-power mobile robots. The scheduler uses odometry, map change, and detector confidence to switch among low-, mid-, and high-power YOLO-World-S modes on a Jetson Orin Nano. We evaluate the energy-quality trade-off on an AgileX LIMO using 40 real navigation trials: two target objects, five placements per target-policy pair, and four perception policies. Across bottle and cup trials, the scheduler records 8/10 mission success compared with 7/10 for each fixed-rate baseline, while reducing mean Jetson input power (a Jetson-side power-draw metric) by 5.2% relative to an 8 Hz high-rate baseline and lowering achieved OVD call rate by 34.0%. It does not minimize mission-window Jetson input energy because longer missions can erase instantaneous power savings. A separate 60 s stationary microbenchmark isolates the perception workload: the scheduler lowers mean power from 8.045 W to 7.301 W and energy from 484.7 J to 438.1 J relative to the 8 Hz baseline. These results support robot-state-aware OVD scheduling as a promising power-management mechanism with competitive task reliability, while showing that mission-window Jetson input energy must be read together with task progress and runtime.
papers.summary: Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) lets robots search for objects named at run time, but running it at a fixed rate wastes embedded compute on low-value frames. The authors build a scheduler that uses odometry, map changes and detector confidence to switch `YOLO-World-S` between low-, mid- and high-power modes on a `Jetson Orin Nano`, and evaluate it in 40 real navigation trials on an `AgileX LIMO` robot. The scheduler completed 8 of 10 missions against 7 of 10 for each fixed-rate baseline, and **cut the detection call rate by 34.0%** while lowering mean Jetson input power by 5.2% relative to an 8 Hz baseline. Total mission energy was not always lower, because longer missions can cancel out the instantaneous power savings.

papers.title: Extracting Single-Mode Rayleigh--Taylor Instability dynamics from data via SINDy
papers.abstract: Rayleigh-Taylor instability (RTI) is of fundamental importance in fields such as inertial confinement fusion and supernova explosions, and its evolution is commonly described by potential--flow theory and buoyancy--drag models. However, both types of models struggle to accurately capture the overshoot behavior of bubble and spike velocities, as well as the subsequent reacceleration stage. To address these limitations, we develop a physics-constrained, data-driven framework based on the integral formulation of Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy), which extracts low-dimensional dynamical equations for bubble and spike evolution directly from data. By introducing the nondimensional initial amplitude $A_0 = k\eta_0$ as an explicit parameter, we identify distinct dynamical equations for the bubble and the spike based on data spanning multiple Atwood numbers and initial amplitudes. The resulting low-dimensional dynamical equations not only reproduce the overshoot behavior of the velocity with good accuracy, but also capture the reacceleration stage well, while maintaining high predictive accuracy at unseen values of the wavenumber, acceleration, and Atwood number. This work provides a physics-constrained, data-driven framework complementary to conventional potential-flow and buoyancy--drag models, accurately describing the dynamical evolution of the bubble and spike at high Atwood numbers, and provides a new perspective for directly extracting the dynamical equations of interfacial instabilities from data.
papers.summary: Rayleigh-Taylor instability (RTI) matters in inertial confinement fusion and supernova explosions, but the standard potential-flow and buoyancy-drag models fail to capture the overshoot of bubble and spike velocities and the reacceleration stage that follows. The authors use a physics-constrained, integral formulation of Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (`SINDy`) to learn low-dimensional equations for bubble and spike evolution from simulation data spanning multiple Atwood numbers and initial amplitudes, with the nondimensional initial amplitude as an explicit parameter. The learned equations **reproduce both the velocity overshoot and the reacceleration stage** and stay accurate at unseen wavenumbers, accelerations and Atwood numbers.

papers.title: Who Should Know What? Empirical Information Design for Multi-Agent LLM Economies
papers.abstract: The performance of multi-agent LLM systems depends not only on the capabilities of the underlying models but also on information-sharing policies, which govern what information each agent observes and at what level of detail. But does providing AI agents with more detailed information always improve collective outcomes, or can transparency paradoxically degrade efficiency? To investigate this, we introduce empirical information design, an experimental framework that systematically compares disclosure policies across economic markets populated by LLM agents, while holding interaction rules and models fixed. We evaluate ten frontier LLMs in multi-resource trade, bilateral bargaining, and double auctions, using ground-truth utilities to decouple identified opportunities from realized outcomes. We find that finer information disclosure yields highly model-dependent results. In trade, revealing exact valuations rather than ordinal preference rankings reduces realized gains for GPT-6 Sol (from 98% to 91% of maximum) yet increases them for Claude Sonnet 5 (from 72% to 86%). In bargaining, exact information leads Grok 4.7 to produce less balanced agreements, whereas Claude Opus 5.5 divides gains symmetrically. In double auctions, full disclosure inflates price demands, triggering market breakdown and lowering welfare for Gemini 3.1 Pro (97% to 78%), Claude Opus 5.5 (94% to 64%), and Grok 4.7 (97% to 62%). Overall, these results suggest that model selection and information design must be co-optimized, as LLMs vary in how their strategic responses to information impact system objectives.
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems depend on information-sharing policies as well as model capability, and it is not obvious that giving agents more detailed information improves collective outcomes. The authors propose empirical information design, an experimental framework that compares disclosure policies across LLM-populated markets (multi-resource trade, bilateral bargaining and double auctions) while holding interaction rules and models fixed, and they test ten frontier LLMs against ground-truth utilities. The effect of finer disclosure **depends heavily on the model**: in trade, revealing exact valuations lowers `GPT-6 Sol`'s realized gains from 98% to 91% of the maximum but raises `Claude Sonnet 5`'s from 72% to 86%. In double auctions, full disclosure inflates price demands and causes market breakdowns, cutting welfare for `Claude Opus 5.5` from 94% to 64% and for `Grok 4.7` from 97% to 62%. The authors conclude that model choice and information policy must be optimized together.

papers.title: An Information Bottleneck for Post-hoc Memorization Mitigation in LLMs
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that large language models (LLMs) can memorize and reproduce copyrighted training data, raising serious privacy and intellectual property concerns. In this work, we investigate whether memorization can be mitigated without modifying or retraining the underlying model through an information bottleneck. We propose a modular plug-and-play framework that inserts a nonparametric variational information bottleneck (NVIB) between a frozen LLM backbone and its language modeling head. By compressing the final hidden representations before token prediction, the proposed bottleneck aims to preserve general linguistic knowledge while filtering out highly specific memorized sequences. We evaluate our approach on memorization extraction tasks involving book passages and on standard language modeling benchmarks to measure the trade-off between memorization reduction and downstream utility. Our experiments show that the NVIB layer substantially reduces extractability while maintaining competitive performance on benchmark tasks. These results suggest that adding an information bottleneck offers a practical and architecture agnostic direction for post-hoc memorization mitigation in pretrained LLMs.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can memorize and reproduce copyrighted training text, and the authors ask whether this can be reduced without retraining the model. They insert a nonparametric variational information bottleneck (`NVIB`) between a frozen LLM backbone and its language-modeling head, compressing the final hidden representations so that general linguistic knowledge passes through while highly specific memorized sequences are filtered out. In experiments on extracting book passages and on standard language-modeling benchmarks, the plug-in layer **substantially reduces extractability while keeping benchmark performance competitive**, and the approach does not depend on the underlying architecture.

papers.title: Calibrated Target Noise Recovers Curvature from the Gradients
papers.abstract: Estimating curvature information from gradients alone is a fundamental problem in machine learning. The challenge becomes particularly acute in settings where only aggregate mini-batch gradients are available, yet curvature information is still required for applications such as preconditioning in optimisation, sampling, and early stopping. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that a simple target-perturbation scheme suffices to recover such curvature information from gradients alone. Our method injects zero-mean noise into the targets, with variance calibrated to the local output curvature. The covariance of the resulting noisy batch gradients then recovers practical curvature matrices, without requiring per-sample gradients, second-order derivatives, or other internal network quantities. For a broad class of non-linear models, our scheme recovers the Generalised Gauss--Newton (GGN) matrix; for feed-forward ReLU networks, it additionally recovers the diagonal blocks of the population Hessian. We demonstrate that the resulting estimator is simple, lightweight, provably optimal, and easy to integrate into existing training pipelines. Experiments demonstrate accurate curvature recovery, faster optimisation when the estimator is used for preconditioning, and the utility of the estimated GGN for early stopping.
papers.summary: Optimisation preconditioning, sampling and early stopping all need curvature information, which is hard to get when only aggregate mini-batch gradients are available. The authors show that injecting zero-mean noise into the training targets, with variance calibrated to the local output curvature, makes the covariance of the resulting noisy batch gradients recover practical curvature matrices without per-sample gradients or second derivatives. For a broad class of non-linear models the scheme **recovers the Generalised Gauss-Newton (GGN) matrix**, and for feed-forward ReLU networks it also recovers the diagonal blocks of the population Hessian. The authors prove the estimator is optimal, and experiments show accurate curvature recovery, faster optimisation when it is used for preconditioning, and useful early-stopping signals.

papers.title: Instrumental Variables in Continuous-Time Stochastic Processes
papers.abstract: Causal questions often arise in systems that evolve in continuous time. While instrumental variable (IV) methods provide a principled approach to identify causal effects in static or discrete-time settings, even in the presence of unobserved confounding, they do not yet extend to continuous-time dynamics. In this work, we develop an IV framework for stationary continuous-time stochastic processes parameterized by stochastic differential equations (SDE), where the instrument itself takes the form of a stochastic process. We encode the structural sparsity and causal effects directly at the infinitesimal level of the drift, and contrast these assumptions with the IV assumptions on the discretized version of the same process. Based on these structural assumptions, we derive moment restrictions using path-valued instruments. We show how these restrictions simplify for Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes and present an identification condition together with a corresponding consistent estimation method. Finally, we extend our estimation framework to nonlinear causal effects by expressing the path-based moment restrictions leveraging the signature kernel. Empirically, our method recovers causal effects in confounded continuous-time systems where maximum-likelihood-based estimation and discrete-time IV methods are systematically biased.
papers.summary: Instrumental variable (IV) methods can identify causal effects despite unobserved confounding in static or discrete-time settings, but they have not been extended to systems that evolve in continuous time. The authors build an IV framework for stationary continuous-time processes described by stochastic differential equations (SDEs), in which the instrument is itself a stochastic process and causal structure is encoded in the drift. They derive moment restrictions from path-valued instruments, give an identification condition and consistent estimator for Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, and extend the approach to nonlinear effects using the signature kernel. In experiments, the method **recovers causal effects in confounded systems where maximum-likelihood and discrete-time IV estimators are systematically biased**.

papers.title: Randomized Parallel Complexity of Weakly Convex Optimization
papers.abstract: We study the minimum number of query rounds needed to find approximate stationary points of nonsmooth weakly convex functions, measured by the gradient of the Moreau envelope. Each round permits multiple simultaneous queries. In the stated parameter regime, the standard subgradient rate is optimal in sufficiently high dimensions, even for randomized algorithms making polynomially many parallel queries per round. We then show how the order structure of the real line enables faster search: a deterministic algorithm using only function values achieves logarithmic round complexity, with a further reduction through parallel queries. Matching lower bounds hold even when each query returns the entire subdifferential. Together, these results clarify the role of dimension in determining the benefits of parallel queries for weakly convex optimization.
papers.summary: The authors study how many rounds of queries, with many simultaneous queries allowed per round, are needed to find approximate stationary points of nonsmooth weakly convex functions, with stationarity measured by the gradient of the Moreau envelope. In sufficiently high dimensions, **the standard subgradient rate is optimal even for randomized algorithms making polynomially many parallel queries per round**. In one dimension, a deterministic algorithm that uses only function values exploits the ordering of the real line to reach logarithmic round complexity, which parallel queries reduce further, and matching lower bounds hold even when each query returns the full subdifferential.

papers.title: $O(1/n)$ Convergence Rate for RVI $Q$-Learning
papers.abstract: We establish finite-time convergence guarantee for synchronous relative value iteration (RVI) $Q$-learning for finite weakly communicating Markov decision processes (MDPs). For stochastic Krasnosel'ski\u{\i}--Mann iterations driven by a non-expansive, linearly regular map on a finite-dimensional normed space, we establish last-iterate mean-squared residual bounds under martingale-difference noise whose conditional second moment grows at most linearly with the squared residual. Suitable polynomial stepsizes of order $n^{-a}$ yield an $O(n^{-a})$ rate for $0<a\leq1$. We verify linear regularity and the noise condition for the centered Bellman operator for finite weakly communicating MDPs. Applying the general result gives an $O(n^{-1})$ bound on the mean-squared Bellman span residual of RVI $Q$-learning iterates when a suitable stepsize sequence is used. The positive gap between optimal and suboptimal stationary deterministic policies then yields an $O(n^{-1})$ bound on the expected suboptimality of the greedy policy. Consequently, $O(\epsilon^{-1})$ synchronous iterations suffice for an $\epsilon$-optimal policy in expectation. These guarantees are instance-dependent, with constants that depend on the hitting-time parameters and the suboptimality gap of the second-best policy.
papers.summary: The authors give finite-time convergence guarantees for synchronous relative value iteration (`RVI`) `Q-learning` on finite, weakly communicating Markov decision processes (MDPs) under the average-reward criterion. They first prove last-iterate mean-squared residual bounds for stochastic Krasnosel'skii-Mann iterations driven by non-expansive, linearly regular maps, then verify that the centered Bellman operator meets these conditions. With suitable stepsizes this yields an O(1/n) bound on the Bellman span residual and on the expected suboptimality of the greedy policy, so **O(1/ε) iterations suffice for an ε-optimal policy in expectation**. The constants depend on the MDP's hitting times and on the suboptimality gap of the second-best policy.

papers.title: ReferClaw: Disambiguating User Intent for Egocentric Assistance
papers.abstract: Users of egocentric AI assistants often ask short, ambiguous questions whose intended referents cannot be uniquely resolved from video and dialogue history. For example, "Where did I leave it?" may refer to several previously handled objects. Existing VideoQA systems typically commit to a single interpretation, risking plausible but intention-misaligned answers. We introduce ReferClaw, an agentic framework that formulates egocentric streaming QA as an interactive process: the assistant asks clarifying questions to resolve user intent before answering. Three cooperating agents identify candidate interpretations, request clarification, and generate answers grounded in the resolved intent and visual evidence. A bounded, cost-aware policy balances expected information gain against user effort while limiting clarification turns and question complexity. Referclaw learns from interaction through intent-specific skill updates and process-reward-guided policy optimization with agent-level credit assignment. Evaluations on augmented egocentric QA benchmarks demonstrate improved answer accuracy and joint answer-and-grounding performance over existing baselines, alongside zero-shot transfer across datasets. These findings support interactive clarification as a practical approach to resolving online user intent in egocentric streaming assistance.
