papers.summary: Users of egocentric (first-person video) AI assistants often ask short, ambiguous questions such as "Where did I leave it?", and existing video question-answering systems commit to one interpretation that may not be the one the user meant. `ReferClaw` treats streaming egocentric QA as an interactive process in which three cooperating agents propose candidate interpretations, ask clarifying questions, and answer from the resolved intent and the visual evidence. A cost-aware policy weighs the expected information gain of a question against the effort it asks of the user, and the system improves from interaction through intent-specific skill updates and process-reward-guided policy optimization with agent-level credit assignment. On augmented egocentric QA benchmarks it **improves answer accuracy and joint answer-and-grounding performance** over baselines and transfers zero-shot across datasets.

papers.title: MCPHallu: Benchmarking Reasoning, Execution, and Memory Hallucinations in MCP Agents
papers.abstract:
Large language model agents are increasingly deployed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows them to discover and invoke tools across multiple servers at runtime. Existing MCP benchmarks primarily measure task completion; where they diagnose failures, they do so after execution rather than building specific reasoning, execution, and memory failure risks into task construction.
  We introduce MCPHallu, a benchmark for diagnosing hallucination-prone agent failures in MCP environments along three axes: reasoning, execution, and memory. MCPHallu contains 358 tasks across five capability domains and runs on 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers. Each task is designed with a structural trigger that makes one of four subtypes the dominant failure risk: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, or Context Forgetting. This design enables subtype-level analysis rather than aggregate task success alone.
  We evaluate fourteen frontier LLM agents from eight vendors on 5{,}012 trajectories. Current MCP agents remain vulnerable to hallucination-inducing tool environments, achieving an average score of 0.642 on a $[0,1]$ scale (higher is better). Failures concentrate on Unreachable Goal tasks, where the average score drops to 0.458 and 23.2\% of runs pass, indicating that agents often continue issuing tool calls or claim successful completion rather than recognizing infeasible goals. Subtype rankings diverge sharply: a model's rank shifts by 6.9 of 13 positions on average across subtypes, and Branch Collapse is uncorrelated with Unreachable Goal across models ($r = -0.12$). MCPHallu is released at https://github.com/J1zz/mcp_hallu.
papers.summary: Existing benchmarks for agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) mostly measure task completion and diagnose failures only after execution. `MCPHallu` instead builds hallucination risks into task design: 358 tasks run on 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers, and each task contains a structural trigger for one of four failure types (Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse or Context Forgetting) across reasoning, execution and memory. Across 5,012 trajectories from fourteen frontier LLM agents, the average score was 0.642 out of 1. Failures cluster on infeasible tasks, where **only 23.2% of Unreachable Goal runs pass** because agents keep calling tools or falsely claim success. Model rankings shift by 6.9 of 13 positions on average across failure types, so a single aggregate score hides large differences between models.

papers.title: Randomized and Oracle-Based Feasible Directions Methods for Nonsmooth Nonconvex Constrained Optimization
papers.abstract: Minimizing nonsmooth nonconvex objectives over general convex sets using no derivatives of the objective, together with structural access to the constraint set, poses a fundamental geometric difficulty: at boundary points, the feasible direction cone may fail to be closed, preventing the construction of finite sets of search directions that capture all feasible descent directions. We develop a feasible-directions framework for problems structured as the difference between a continuously differentiable function and a convex function over a closed convex set, and access the objective without knowledge of its decomposition, through exact line searches along feasible segments. To address the geometric obstruction, we introduce $\eta$-feasible directions, which remain uniformly separated from the boundary of the feasible direction cone, enabling finite-direction search even in the presence of nonlinear constraints. We present two algorithmic realizations of this framework. The first assumes access to an $\eta$-direction oracle and extends feasible-directions methods from linear to general convex constraints. The second replaces the oracle by a noise-augmented randomization scheme that constructs spanning directions from the affine-hull inner normal and almost surely avoids nonsmooth boundary points when initialized outside that set. Under curvature bounds and Lipschitz continuity of the smooth component's gradient, we jointly control the spanning coefficients and feasible step lengths of the oracle construction. This yields finite-time approximate $d$-stationarity along every unit feasible direction admitting a prescribed positive step length. For both methods, we also establish a rate in the proximal directional minimization (PDM) measure, assuming uniformly bounded direction-set sizes. Randomized exploration ensures that, almost surely, every accumulation point is $d$-stationary.
papers.summary: The authors address derivative-free minimization of nonsmooth nonconvex objectives (a smooth function minus a convex one) over general convex sets, where at boundary points no finite set of search directions may capture all feasible descent directions. They introduce η-feasible directions, which stay uniformly separated from the boundary of the feasible direction cone, and build two methods on exact line searches: one that assumes an oracle supplying such directions, and one that replaces the oracle with a noise-augmented randomization scheme. Both methods come with rates in a proximal directional minimization measure, and the randomized method guarantees that **almost surely every accumulation point is d-stationary**.

papers.title: Non-Parametric Mutual Information Estimation with Vine Copulas
papers.abstract: We introduce VINE: a non-parametric mutual information (MI) estimator based on simplified D-vine copulas. Approximating the joint density with a simplified D-vine allows the density ratio to simplify to a product of pair copulas, which we can estimate non-parametrically. This structural simplification yields VINE, a flexible and computationally efficient MI estimator. We compare VINE against SotA neural MI estimators on a range of datasets, both under settings where the simplified D-vine assumption holds and where it is violated, demonstrating competitive accuracy at a lower computational cost for low- to medium-dimensional datasets.
papers.summary: `VINE` is a non-parametric mutual information (MI) estimator that approximates the joint density with a simplified D-vine copula, so the density ratio becomes a product of pair copulas that can each be estimated non-parametrically. The authors compare it with state-of-the-art neural MI estimators on datasets where the simplified D-vine assumption both holds and is violated. `VINE` reaches **competitive accuracy at lower computational cost** on low- to medium-dimensional data.

papers.title: Equivariant Deep Learning in Direct-Product Space for Electronic-Structure Hamiltonian Prediction
papers.abstract: Most existing equivariant architectures for Hamiltonian prediction propagate features in direct-sum spaces of irreducible spherical tensors, whereas the target Hamiltonian is naturally an operator block in a direct-product representation over local orbital and spin bases. This representation mismatch fragments contiguous Hamiltonian blocks, obscures direct manipulation of orbital couplings, and organizes features into irregular angular-momentum components that require numerous transformations and are poorly aligned with efficient hardware execution and memory management. To address both the representation mismatch and computational bottleneck, we propose DP-Learner, an equivariant learning framework that performs message passing directly on Hamiltonian-like operator blocks in the direct-product space. Theoretically, we propose Lie-generator-based directional embedding and invariantly weighted left--right products and contractions that preserve equivariance to SO(3), SU(2), and spatial inversions, without explicit Clebsch--Gordan decomposition or inverse reconstruction. Methodologically, we instantiate this principle as a Transformer architecture, in which Hamiltonian-like feature matrices or tensors evolve through equivariant operators in the direct-product space, while non-linear invariant scalar routing controls structured gating over matrix units, directional propagation, attention, and environment-embedded context interactions. We further construct MP-HAM-110K, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset comprising more than 110,000 material structures covering 68 elements with both Hamiltonian and wavefunction data. Experiments on MP-HAM-110K and Materials-HAM-SOC demonstrate that DP-Learner dramatically improves Hamiltonian prediction accuracy and inference efficiency over the state-of-the-art method.
papers.summary: Most equivariant networks for predicting electronic-structure Hamiltonians work with direct sums of irreducible spherical tensors, but the target Hamiltonian is naturally an operator block in a direct-product space over orbital and spin bases. This mismatch fragments Hamiltonian blocks and maps poorly to efficient hardware execution. `DP-Learner` is a Transformer that passes messages directly on operator blocks in the direct-product space, using Lie-generator-based directional embeddings and invariantly weighted products that preserve SO(3), SU(2) and inversion equivariance without Clebsch-Gordan decompositions. The authors also release `MP-HAM-110K`, a dataset of more than 110,000 material structures covering 68 elements, and report that `DP-Learner` **substantially improves both Hamiltonian prediction accuracy and inference efficiency** over the previous state of the art on it and on `Materials-HAM-SOC`.

papers.title: InfMasking: A Unified Variational Framework for Synergistic Multimodal Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal models are expected to exploit synergistic information, that is, information available only when multiple modalities are observed together. In practice, however, a fusion module can fit the training objective by relying on a dominant modality or on information that modalities share, and the synergy between modalities is often left unused. We propose InfMasking, a unified multimodal learning framework based on Infinite Masking. Before fusion, InfMasking randomly masks the features of each modality; each sampled mask produces a different partial combination of cross-modal evidence and a fused representation of the corresponding modality interactions. All masked fused representations are required to remain consistent with a reference target: the unmasked fused view when training is unsupervised, and the class proxy of the task label when labels are available. Maintaining this consistency across diverse partial combinations discourages reliance on a dominant modality or on shared information alone, and drives the fusion module to learn cross-modal interaction patterns that remain meaningful under partial observations. Since the objective is an expectation over infinitely many masks, we model the masked fused representations as Gaussian and optimize closed-form variational bounds, whose population-moment gaps are controlled by the masking-induced covariance under this model. On the evaluated benchmarks, InfMasking improves predictive performance and yields higher mean PID estimates of task-label synergy in learned modality-specific representations, alongside higher InterSHAP interaction attribution in the trained predictors. Code is available at https://github.com/brightest66/InfMasking.
papers.summary: Multimodal fusion models often fit their training objective by leaning on a dominant modality or on information the modalities share, leaving synergistic information (available only when modalities are seen together) unused. `InfMasking` randomly masks each modality's features before fusion and requires every masked fused representation to stay consistent with a reference target: the unmasked fused view in unsupervised training, or a class proxy when labels are available. Because the objective is an expectation over infinitely many masks, the authors model masked representations as Gaussian and optimize closed-form variational bounds. On the evaluated benchmarks the method improves predictive performance and **yields higher measured task-label synergy**, using partial information decomposition (`PID`) estimates and `InterSHAP` interaction attribution.

papers.title: Towards Generalist Graph-Level Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Graph-level anomaly detection (GLAD) aims to identify graphs that deviate significantly from the majority. While recent advances have achieved competitive performance, existing approaches mainly follow a dataset-specific paradigm, requiring substantial in-domain data and training cost when applied to new application scenarios. This limits their scalability and practicality in real-world applications where labeled data is scarce and diverse domains are continuously emerging. In this paper, we investigate the problem of generalist GLAD, which seeks to learn a single unified model capable of detecting anomalous graphs across multiple domains with minimal supervision on the target data. This problem introduces key challenges, including learning transferable patterns from heterogeneous graph datasets and effective adaptation under limited supervision. To address these challenges, we propose GenGLAD, a generalist GLAD approach that leverages discriminative subgraph extraction as the core mechanism to learn transferable anomaly knowledge and enable efficient adaptation to new domains. Specifically, GenGLAD employs a graph neural network-based discriminative subgraph extraction model to learn the anomaly-discriminative substructures that distinguish anomalous and normal graphs across diverse domains. During the test-time adaptation phase, multi-dimensional discrepancies between the extracted subgraph and multi-level contextual information are calculated to characterize anomalies from multiple perspectives. For efficient adaptation, a lightweight scoring module is introduced to automatically decide the most informative signals, improving robustness against misleading patterns. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves strong performance, superior generalization ability, and improved data efficiency compared to existing methods.
papers.summary: Graph-level anomaly detection (GLAD) identifies whole graphs that deviate from the majority, but current methods are trained per dataset and need substantial in-domain data. `GenGLAD` targets a generalist setting: a single model that detects anomalous graphs across domains with minimal supervision on the target data. It uses a graph neural network to extract anomaly-discriminative subgraphs that transfer across domains, and at test time it compares those subgraphs against multi-level context, with a lightweight scoring module that picks the most informative signals. Experiments across diverse benchmarks show **strong cross-domain generalization and better data efficiency** than existing methods.

papers.title: CAMP: Context-Aware Mapping and Placement for LLMs on 3D-IMC Arrays
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) incur severe memory-access overheads due to the cost of loading large weight matrices and key-value (KV) caches. Analog In-Memory Computing (AIMC) is an emerging solution that enables computation directly on static weights stored in memory, substantially reducing energy and latency. 3D-IMC further stacks memory arrays into vertical tiers, increasing capacity but revealing a new challenge: how weights are placed in memory determines which matrix-vector multiplications (MVMs) can execute concurrently, affecting latency and throughput. The concurrency aspect of 3D-IMC weight-mapping remains underexplored in the literature, leading to sub-optimal utilization of compute resources on 3D-IMC chips. In this context we propose CAMP (Context-Aware Mapping and Placement), an inference-context-aware weight mapping algorithm for 3D-IMC-based LLM accelerators. CAMP captures the potential resource contention resulting from the architecture, targeted network, and runtime context in a conflict matrix, enabling throughput-optimized weight mapping. This mapping is refined through a profiling-driven feedback loop that efficiently prunes the search space and returns optimized mappings within practical runtimes. CAMP is an offline, software-based solution requiring no hardware changes and improving 3D-IMC compute utilization from 42.4% to 60.3%, delivering up to 2.0x higher 3D-IMC throughput and 1.74x higher end-to-end throughput over state-of-the-art mapping algorithms.
papers.summary: Analog in-memory computing (AIMC) performs matrix-vector multiplications directly on weights stored in memory, and 3D in-memory computing (3D-IMC) stacks memory arrays into vertical tiers. In such stacks, where weights are placed determines which multiplications can run concurrently, which affects LLM inference throughput. `CAMP` is an offline weight-mapping algorithm that records resource contention between the architecture, the model and the runtime context in a conflict matrix, then refines the mapping through a profiling-driven feedback loop. Without hardware changes, it raises compute utilization from 42.4% to 60.3% and delivers **up to 2.0x higher 3D-IMC throughput** and 1.74x higher end-to-end throughput than state-of-the-art mapping algorithms.

papers.title: Pediatric ECG foundation model via adult-to-pediatric fine-tuning: downstream tasks and clinical evaluation
papers.abstract: Pediatric electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation is complicated by age-dependent electrophysiological changes that limit direct transfer of adult AI models. We asked whether an adult ECG foundation model could be adapted to pediatric ECGs. Using 339,563 12-lead ECGs from 238,189 children, we compared direct application, pediatric fine-tuning, and training from scratch under an identical architecture. Direct transfer was poor (mean AUC 0.8256). Fine-tuning reached 0.9695, above de novo training (0.9661), and attained 0.9079 using only 1% of training data. On 10,999 external ECGs, fine-tuning achieved a mean AUC of 0.9385 across 30 labels. It generalized to age regression (MAE 1.12 years) and congenital heart disease classification (AUC 0.9562). Across 17 clinicians and 100 cases, diagnostic accuracy rose from 56.8% to 65.4% (p < 0.001) and did not decline when AI erred. Adult ECG foundation models require pediatric adaptation; fine-tuning offers a data-efficient route to scalable pediatric ECG AI.
papers.summary: Children's electrocardiograms (ECGs) change with age, which limits how well adult AI models transfer to them. Using 339,563 12-lead ECGs from 238,189 children, the authors compare direct application of an adult ECG foundation model, pediatric fine-tuning, and training from scratch. Direct transfer performs poorly (mean AUC 0.8256), while fine-tuning reaches 0.9695, edges out training from scratch, and **reaches an AUC of 0.9079 with only 1% of the training data**. The fine-tuned model generalizes to external data, age regression and congenital heart disease classification, and in a study of 17 clinicians it raised diagnostic accuracy from 56.8% to 65.4%.

papers.title: Multimodal Information Interactions Bottleneck for Multimodal Self-Supervised Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal self-supervised learning is challenged by heterogeneity, unequal informativeness, and complex information interactions across multimodal data sources such as images, text, audio, and tabular data. While contrastive methods effectively align shared semantics, they typically rely on strong multi-view redundancy assumptions, overlooking modality-specific and synergistic information, thus leading to suboptimal representations. We propose the Multimodal Information Interactions Bottleneck (MIIB), a principled framework grounded in Partial Information Decomposition that explicitly encodes redundant, unique, and synergistic information within multimodal interactions. MIIB employs a dual-path model architecture for modality-specific encoding and multimodal fusion, optimized using surrogate tractable entropy-based objectives that enforce minimal sufficient representations without requiring explicit mutual information estimation. By leveraging variational bounds and score-based entropy estimation, MIIB efficiently captures complex cross-modal interactions while suppressing superfluous information. Experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art multimodal self-supervised methods. Code is available at https://github.com/wanglingzaishi/MIIB.
papers.summary: Contrastive multimodal self-supervised learning assumes strong redundancy across views and so tends to miss modality-specific and synergistic information. The Multimodal Information Interactions Bottleneck (`MIIB`) uses Partial Information Decomposition to explicitly encode redundant, unique and synergistic information. It pairs a dual-path architecture for modality-specific encoding and fusion with tractable entropy-based objectives, built on variational bounds and score-based entropy estimation, that need no explicit mutual information estimation. Across diverse benchmarks it shows **consistent improvements over state-of-the-art multimodal self-supervised methods**.

papers.title: Evaluating Language Model Features for Zero-Shot Time-Series Anomaly Detection Under Isolation Assumption
papers.abstract: Time-Series Anomaly Detection (TSAD) is a fundamentally challenging task: it is unsupervised, requires high local precision capabilities, and suffers from limited labelled data. Recent work has explored adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to time-series via cross-modal transfer. However, existing approaches are poorly suited to Multivariate TSAD (MTSAD), as tokenisation often obscures fine-grained temporal and variables structures, and most methods optimise auxiliary objectives such as forecasting or reconstruction. We posit that these surrogate objectives become unreliable as model capacity increases. Highly expressive models risk reconstructing or forecasting anomalies, undermining the foundations of both strategies. Instead, we propose to use LLMs purely as feature extractors and directly analyse their induced feature spaces. In this work, investigate the ability of LLMs to provide useful representations for MTSADs in a zero-shot setting through classification. To this end, we study the separability of the extracted features, under the assumption that anomalous features should be isolated from normal ones. We analyse their temporal and contextual discriminative ability using simple step-wise tokenisation schemes, with one time-step per token, which preserve fine-grained local information. Their usability for MTSAD is assessed using an unsupervised Isolation Forest, enabling a direct evaluation of the resulting representation quality. We further investigate whether the observed performance can be attributed to the language-related pre-training of the LLMs or arises independently of it. Our results provide empirical insight into the ability of LLMs to represent multivariate time-series for anomaly detection and highlight broader applications of cross-modal foundation models.
papers.summary: Time-Series Anomaly Detection (TSAD), especially the multivariate case (MTSAD), is hard because it is unsupervised and needs fine-grained local precision. Most attempts to adapt Large Language Models (LLMs) to it rely on forecasting or reconstruction objectives, which the authors argue break down because highly expressive models can also forecast or reconstruct the anomalies themselves. Instead, the work uses LLMs **purely as frozen feature extractors in a zero-shot setting**, with one time-step per token, and tests whether anomalous features are isolated from normal ones using an unsupervised `Isolation Forest`. It also examines whether the useful representations come from language pre-training or arise independently of it.

papers.title: Continued Training of Continuous Language Flows with Token Identity Squared Supervision
papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow models have recently been extended to language modeling, generating text through continuous denoising in token embedding spaces. Pretrained models provide token representations and contextual prediction capabilities, but improving generation with limited additional training requires an appropriate connection between supervision and continuous generation. Continuous MSE evaluates a predicted vector obtained by weighting token embeddings with predicted probabilities; different probability distributions can yield the same vector and are therefore indistinguishable under this objective. We propose Token Identity Brier Flow (TIBF), which applies squared supervision directly to token identities when continuing pretrained language flows. TIBF combines network scores with token-matching scores under a Gaussian observation model, supervises token probabilities using the Brier loss, and uses probability-weighted embeddings for continuous generation. With fixed token embeddings, we show that the squared error between predicted token probabilities and the true posterior bounds the squared errors of continuous denoising predictions and flow velocities. A risk decomposition separates uncertainty inherent in the observation from posterior fitting error, motivating continued training that preserves pretrained embeddings and focuses on probability prediction. We also establish convergence to token embeddings under ideal predictions and sufficient conditions for local convergence with prediction error. From common pretrained initializations and under matched continuation budgets, frozen-embedding TIBF achieves Gen.PPL values of 33.96 on OWT and 81.17 on LM1B, outperforming continuous-MSE and CE continuation controls. It attains the lowest Gen.PPL at every tested sampling budget on both datasets, together with the lowest repetition rate on LM1B.
papers.summary: Continuous flow models for language generate text by denoising in token-embedding space, but the usual continuous mean-squared-error (MSE) objective cannot tell apart different token distributions that average to the same embedding vector. `Token Identity Brier Flow` (`TIBF`) applies squared (Brier) supervision directly to token probabilities when continuing training of pretrained language flows, keeping the embeddings frozen. The authors prove that this probability error bounds the errors in denoising predictions and flow velocities. Under matched continuation budgets, `TIBF` reaches **generative perplexity of 33.96 on `OWT` and 81.17 on `LM1B`**, beating continuous-MSE and cross-entropy continuation at every tested sampling budget.

papers.title: Reinforcing What the Student Has Learned: Teacher-Guided On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model reasoning through dense teacher feedback on student-generated responses.We first observe an amplitude disparity in this feedback: on math reasoning responses, style-related positions exhibit 3.5 times the mean absolute teacher--student log-probability difference of mathematical positions.Scaling OPD updates by these discrepancies thus directs much of the update strength toward matching the teacher's expression. We instead take the student's own pretrained base as a reference: the student--base difference records the token preferences acquired during post-training and provides supervision that does not depend on the student's distance from the teacher. Building on this reference, we propose Student-Delta On-Policy Distillation (SD-OPD), which uses centered student--base differences as update coefficients, keeps each coefficient only when its sign agrees with centered teacher--student feedback, and recomputes the student signal every training round. Across 5 teacher--student configurations with Qwen3 students of 1.7B to 8B parameters, SD-OPD improves six-task mathematics average pass@1 (avg@16) over OPD by 7.76 to 10.37 percentage points. Code is available at https://github.com/aim-uofa/sd-opd.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model on its own outputs using dense token-level feedback from a teacher. The authors find this feedback is dominated by style: on math responses, style tokens show 3.5 times the teacher–student log-probability gap of mathematical tokens, so updates mostly teach the student to copy the teacher's phrasing. `Student-Delta On-Policy Distillation` (`SD-OPD`) instead weights updates by how the student differs from its own pretrained base model, keeping a coefficient only when its sign agrees with the teacher's feedback. Across five teacher–student pairs with `Qwen3` students from 1.7B to 8B parameters, `SD-OPD` **improves average math pass@1 over standard OPD by 7.76 to 10.37 percentage points**.

papers.title: Static Recovery Is Not Dynamic Stability: Dynamics-Aware Benchmarking of Protein Motif Scaffolding
papers.abstract: Protein motif scaffolding benchmarks assess whether generative models can build scaffolds around functionally important residues. Their conclusions depend on which motifs are tested and which criteria define success. Existing benchmarks typically use small hand-curated motif sets and static refolding criteria, but protein function often depends on conformational ensembles and transitions. Here, we address both benchmark scope and success criteria. We introduce BILBY-PRO, a systematically derived benchmark of structurally conserved functional motifs from PROSITE-linked experimental structures, comprising 220 cases from 174 PROSITE motif-pattern entries. Evaluating six recent scaffold-generation models reveals distinct patterns in target coverage and unique-solution yield: RFDiffusion and Proteina solve more targets, whereas ESM3 produces more unique successful scaffolds on the targets it solves. We further introduce BILBY-MD, a reference-based all-atom molecular dynamics evaluation framework. Applied to statically solved designs from the original MotifBench benchmark, it compares motif drift, scaffold drift, motif-contact preservation, and motif-dihedral free-energy landscapes against reference simulations. Of 55 statically solved model-problem pairs, 31 satisfy our MD-supported criterion and only 8 pass all checks. Compact, self-contained motifs are often MD-supported, whereas interface-like or context-dependent motifs fail more frequently. Static refolding success therefore provides useful evidence of local motif recovery but does not establish dynamical fidelity of the full scaffold. BILBY highlights three complementary axes of motif-scaffolding evaluation: target coverage, unique-solution yield, and MD-supported dynamical fidelity.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for protein motif scaffolding, where generative models build a protein structure around key functional residues, usually rely on small hand-picked motif sets and judge success only by whether the static structure refolds correctly. The authors introduce `BILBY-PRO`, 220 motif cases systematically drawn from `PROSITE`-linked structures, and `BILBY-MD`, an all-atom molecular dynamics evaluation that checks whether designs remain stable over time. Among six models, `RFDiffusion` and `Proteina` solve more targets, while `ESM3` produces more unique successful scaffolds. Of 55 designs that passed the static `MotifBench` criteria, **only 8 pass all dynamics checks**, with interface-like and context-dependent motifs failing most often.

papers.title: Seeing Beyond the Next Step: World-Model-Guided Human-Like Navigation in Multi-Agent Scenes
papers.abstract: Selecting a next motion in a populated scene is not just a matter of avoiding what is currently in the way: an action can be locally feasible yet drift onto the road instead of the crosswalk, cut into a stream of crossing pedestrians, or bottleneck a narrow passage. These failure modes are invisible from the current state alone, and acting on them requires reasoning about what each candidate action will cause. World models offer exactly this, namely action-conditioned predictions of the future, but rolling them out at every decision step is a cost deployable navigation systems cannot pay, and the field has largely traded foresight for speed. We argue this is a false dichotomy. The natural place for a world model in human-aware navigation is at training time, as a preference oracle that distills foresight into a fast policy, rather than at inference time, as an online planner. We pair a discrete visual action prior with two task-aligned world models, one for nearby social dynamics and one for future scene semantics, that score candidate actions by their predicted consequences and refine the policy through group-relative preference distillation. At deployment, both world models are removed and the policy acts in a single forward pass. Across five held-out evaluation scenarios, this yields navigation that is simultaneously safer, more socially and group-coherent, and more goal-directed than strong reactive and learned baselines, with naive observers rating the resulting motion as more human-like. Taken together, our findings point to a different approach for bringing world-model foresight into deployable agents: not accelerating rollouts, but amortizing them into the policy so that the cost of looking ahead is confined to training. Project page: https://seoneun.github.io/-NeurIPS-2026-Seeing-Beyond-the-Next-Step/
papers.summary: Navigating among crowds requires anticipating the consequences of an action, such as drifting onto a road or cutting through a group, but running a world model at every decision step is too slow for deployed systems. The authors use world models only at training time, as preference oracles: one predicts nearby social dynamics and one predicts future scene semantics, and together they score candidate actions to refine a discrete visual policy through group-relative preference distillation. At deployment both world models are removed and the policy acts in a single forward pass. Across five held-out scenarios, the resulting navigation is **safer, more socially coherent, and more goal-directed than reactive and learned baselines**, and observers rated it as more human-like.

papers.title: O$^2$PD: Overlap-Gated On-Policy Distillation on Reliable Prefix
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) supplies dense token-level supervision by aligning a student to the teacher's next-token distribution on its own generated rollouts. Existing works mostly implement top-$k$ OPD, applying reverse Kullback-Leibler ($\RKL$) divergence between the teacher's and the student's renormalized distributions over teacher top-$k$ support. However, the teacher scores student-generated rollouts that are inherently off-policy for itself, leaving the reliability of its next-token guidance unclear. Restricting the divergence to the teacher top-$k$ support also discards the remaining mass outside that support. These gaps leave two questions implicit: 1) which tokens to align, and 2) how to align those tokens. To answer these questions, we propose Overlap-gated On-Policy Distillation (O$^{2}$PD). As for 1), we quantitatively analyze the reliability of teacher supervision and find that alignment on the student's trajectory prefix is more reliable than alignment on the full context. Therefore, our O$^{2}$PD is applied only to the 20\% prefix tokens of each student rollout. As for 2), we theoretically characterize two problems of top-$k$ OPD: the \emph{Teacher-support Uncovering} and the \emph{Dominant-Mode Mismatch}. Based on these analyses, we propose two support strategies: the \emph{Reset Support} strategy attaches a reset atom to every token, pooling mass outside the teacher top-$k$, and the \emph{Support Convergence} strategy converges the support to the already aligned intersection. Our O$^{2}$PD employs the designed overlap-gated $\alpha$-divergence to interpolate between mode-covering and mode-seeking for per-token alignment, where the overlap is used as a gate to switch the support and adaptively modulate $\alpha$.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) usually aligns a student to a teacher using reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence restricted to the teacher's top-k tokens, which raises two questions: whether the teacher's guidance is reliable on student-generated text, and what to do with probability mass outside the top-k. The authors' analysis finds that teacher supervision is more reliable early in a rollout, so `O²PD` **aligns only the first 20% of tokens in each student rollout**. To handle the support problem, it adds a reset atom that pools mass outside the teacher's top-k and gradually narrows alignment to tokens where the two models already overlap. An overlap-gated α-divergence then interpolates between mode-covering and mode-seeking behavior for each token. The abstract reports no experimental results.

papers.title: Evaluating Token Probabilities as Confidence Estimators in Human Behavior Simulations: A Case Study in Luxembourgish Next Like Prediction
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, their operational validity is typically assessed through accuracy alone, implicitly treating human behavior as deterministic. We argue that on noisy digital trace data, a model's performance depends not only on predicting the correct outcome but on its calibration. We present a case study testing whether the token probabilities of open-weight LLMs can serve as confidence estimates in a Next Like Prediction task: predicting how a user of the Luxembourgish news platform RTL.lu rates a comment, conditioned on their prior interactions. Evaluating Ministral 3 (3B, 8B), we find that, with in-context learning only, the tested models are overconfident and are outperformed on accuracy and calibration by a simple statistical baseline. Accuracy and calibration do not move together: scaling from 3B to 8B improves accuracy while degrading calibration, and longer behavioral histories raise accuracy while confidence declines. Task-specific supervised fine-tuning acts as an effective calibration intervention, reducing Expected Calibration Error from 0.2 to 0.006 while improving accuracy from 0.536 to 0.758. We conclude that confidence estimation should be evaluated alongside accuracy to improve validity when using LLM-based agents.
papers.summary: When large language models (LLMs) are used to simulate human behavior, they are usually judged on accuracy alone, which ignores how noisy real human behavior is. In a case study predicting how users of the Luxembourgish news site `RTL.lu` rate comments, the authors test whether token probabilities from `Ministral 3` (3B and 8B) work as calibrated confidence estimates. With in-context learning alone, the models are overconfident and lose to a simple statistical baseline, and accuracy and calibration move apart: the larger model is more accurate but worse calibrated. Task-specific supervised fine-tuning **reduces Expected Calibration Error from 0.2 to 0.006 while raising accuracy from 0.536 to 0.758**.

papers.title: Extending Reasoning in Typed Decision Models via Looping
papers.abstract: Typed decision models choose among a fixed set of answer options in a single forward pass, so unlike generative language models they cannot spend more test-time compute on hard inputs by generating more tokens. Looping a block of layers offers this compute in latent space without adding parameters, but prior work found no gain from loops retrofitted into conventionally pretrained models. We show that such loops help when trained together with the decision model. Our method, RELOAD (retrofitted loops for adaptive decisions), fine-tunes a pretrained encoder or decoder with a damped loop over its middle block and a lightweight controller picks the number of passes adaptively for each input. Across six models from 0.4B to 4B parameters, looping improves both accuracy and calibration, mostly on problems that need longer chains of reasoning than any seen in training, where encoders gain up to 23 points. Neither matched training compute nor more data closes this gap, and separate layers for each pass come close only with nearly twice the parameters. The controller keeps most of the gain at about three quarters of the compute.
papers.summary: Models that choose among a fixed set of answers in one forward pass cannot spend extra test-time compute on hard inputs the way generative models do by producing more tokens. `RELOAD` fine-tunes a pretrained encoder or decoder with a damped loop over its middle layers, adding compute without adding parameters, and a lightweight controller picks how many passes to run for each input. Across six models from 0.4B to 4B parameters, looping improves both accuracy and calibration, mostly on problems that need longer reasoning chains than any seen in training, where **encoders gain up to 23 points**. Matched training compute or extra data does not close the gap, and the controller keeps most of the gain at about three quarters of the compute.

papers.title: Comparing Classification and Feature Learning by Analyzing Their Loss Functions in Normalized Spaces with Different Scale Factors
papers.abstract: Classification and feature learning are two closely interrelated fundamental tasks. Feature learning in supervised settings is typically achieved by training classification models, under the common assumption that higher classification accuracy implies better feature quality. In this paper, we first point out that classification accuracy reflects the sample-wise local properties of a model on a dataset, whereas feature learning aims to learn features with good dataset-level global properties, such as intra-class compactness and inter-class separability. From the first principle of feature learning, we redesign the binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, a counterpart of the cross-entropy (CE) loss used in classification. Then, in normalized feature space, we analyze the minima of the BCE and CE losses and show that both can lead to neural collapse, where sample features from different classes become maximally compact and maximally separated. More importantly, by investigating the convergence behaviors of the two losses as the scale factor $\gamma$ varies in the normalized space, we reveal how classification accuracy and feature quality change differently across spaces of different sizes. Under a fixed training strategy, a very large $\gamma$ achieves perfect classification accuracy but slows convergence toward the ideal feature geometry, whereas a very small $\gamma$ makes classification highly sensitive to small perturbations. A moderate $\gamma$ is therefore necessary for simultaneously achieving reliable classification and well-structured features. Extensive experiments validate these findings and demonstrate that BCE loss exhibits advantages in long-tail and open-set recognitions, as it better aligns with the global requirements of feature learning.
papers.summary: Supervised feature learning usually assumes that higher classification accuracy means better features, but the authors argue that accuracy reflects per-sample behavior while good features need dataset-level properties such as compact classes that are well separated from each other. They redesign the binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss from feature-learning principles and show that both BCE and cross-entropy (CE) can reach neural collapse in normalized feature space. Analyzing how the scale factor γ affects convergence, they find that **a very large γ gives perfect accuracy but slows convergence toward the ideal feature geometry, while a very small γ makes classification fragile**, so a moderate value is needed. Experiments show BCE has advantages in long-tail and open-set recognition.

papers.title: Ordering Multivariate Time Series by Volatility Memory: A Temporal Convolutional Approach to Volatility Heredity
papers.abstract: Volatility dynamics can carry information about temporal relationships that is not apparent in the conditional mean. Extracting this information is difficult because the persistence of each variable can obscure its dependence on other variables. This paper presents QS-TCN, a method for ordering multivariate time series that combines statistical estimates of volatility memory with temporal convolutional learning. Persistence estimates obtained by quasi-maximum likelihood and temporal modes extracted by the Matrix Pencil method define structured filters within the network. Together with learned filters, they represent the history of the target and support comparisons of directional evidence between variables. These comparisons are combined into a global order of precedence, which does not identify a causal graph. The method is evaluated on synthetic systems with linear and nonlinear volatility interactions and on the Finance and fMRI benchmarks, whose reference relations are known. Across the four synthetic volatility regimes studied, QS-TCN reaches a higher mean ordering quality than an external lead--lag ordering and its squared-input adaptation, although the gain over the adaptation is uncertain in two regimes. Applications to currency, gold and cryptocurrency markets are reported descriptively.
papers.summary: `QS-TCN` orders multivariate time series by how volatility in one variable precedes volatility in another, information that may not show up in the mean of the series. It builds structured filters inside a temporal convolutional network from persistence estimates (via quasi-maximum likelihood) and temporal modes (via the Matrix Pencil method), then combines pairwise directional evidence into a global precedence order rather than a causal graph. On synthetic volatility systems, it **reaches higher mean ordering quality than an external lead–lag method** and its squared-input adaptation, though the gain over the adaptation is uncertain in two of four regimes. It is also evaluated on the `Finance` and `fMRI` benchmarks and applied descriptively to currency, gold, and cryptocurrency markets.

papers.title: ConvPE: Convolutional Position Embedding Improves Transformers
papers.abstract: ConvPE (Convolutional Position Embedding) improves both the performance and efficiency of Transformer models in language modeling, long-context extension, and vision. It injects a windowed, content-dependent bias into attention scores through a lightweight causal convolution over a low-dimensional projection of the hidden states. As a lightweight plug-in, ConvPE is compatible with RoPE, attention masks, and KV concatenation. It also supports high-dimensional position embeddings via high-dimensional convolutions. In a reproduction, ConvPE outperforms five 1D baselines and eight 2D baselines. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/wzhagi/convpe.
papers.summary: `ConvPE` (Convolutional Position Embedding) adds a windowed, content-dependent bias to attention scores by running a lightweight causal convolution over a low-dimensional projection of the hidden states. It works as a plug-in alongside `RoPE`, attention masks, and KV concatenation, and extends to 2D and higher-dimensional positions through higher-dimensional convolutions. The authors report gains in performance and efficiency for language modeling, long-context extension, and vision, with **`ConvPE` outperforming five 1D and eight 2D position-embedding baselines** in their reproduction.

papers.title: Foresee to Trade: Forecast-Augmented Policy Optimization for Portfolio Management
papers.abstract: Online investment services must translate asset opportunities into investment outcomes for users' accounts, yet the same market opportunity can warrant different account actions. We study how supervision from future asset opportunities can strengthen account-level trading decisions and propose Forecast-Augmented Relative Policy Optimization (FRPO). FRPO separately supervises asset opportunities and account decisions through a jointly learned representation: a Financial State Head (FSH) learns future relative-return targets to provide asset-level opportunity supervision, while Same-Path Group-Relative Optimization compares trading trajectories under the same market path and initial account to provide account-level relative-outcome supervision. An Adaptive Gate coordinates auxiliary supervision using predictive variance and gradient alignment. FSH is used only during training; inference uses the encoder and policy for trading. Across DJIA30, TOPIX Core30, and three investment-style portfolios, ten-seed evaluations show that FRPO achieves the highest mean cumulative and annualized returns among the compared methods in all five settings. These results support strengthening investment agents' trading decisions through joint supervision from asset opportunities and trading outcomes.
papers.summary: Online investment services must turn market opportunities into trades for individual accounts, and the same opportunity may call for different actions in different accounts. `Forecast-Augmented Relative Policy Optimization` (`FRPO`) trains a trading policy with two sources of supervision: a Financial State Head that predicts future relative returns of assets during training only, and a group-relative objective that compares trading trajectories under the same market path and starting account. An adaptive gate balances the auxiliary signal using predictive variance and gradient alignment. Across `DJIA30`, `TOPIX Core30`, and three style portfolios over ten seeds, **`FRPO` achieves the highest mean cumulative and annualized returns in all five settings**.

papers.title: Neural Collapse on Imbalanced Datasets and Open-Set Scenario
papers.abstract: Neural collapse (NC) describes the elegant geometric structure that sample features and classifier vectors exhibit when a classification model's loss reaches its minimum. Class imbalance, however, generally distorts standard NC. In this paper, we theoretically reformulate NC on imbalanced datasets and in open-set settings. Our analysis is based on an optimization problem over class-wise averaged losses, rather than the global averaged losses used in prior NC studies. We prove that when class-wise averaged losses attain their minima, standard NC is achieved on balanced or imbalanced datasets, for both cross-entropy (CE) and binary cross-entropy (BCE) losses. We further extend the analysis to an open-set-inspired scenario, where some classes contain no training samples yet are still assigned classifier vectors in the losses. We find that in this scenario, when class-wise averaged losses reach their minima, standard NC still emerges on the known classes with training samples, while the classifier vectors of unknown classes without training samples overlap with each other and become orthogonal to those of the known classes. Finally, we analyze Softmax- and Sigmoid-based contrastive losses re-balanced by inverse sample frequency, proving that at their minima on balanced or imbalanced datasets, sample features of different classes likewise form standard NC.
papers.summary: Neural collapse (NC) is the symmetric geometry that features and classifier vectors settle into when a classifier's loss is minimized, but class imbalance normally distorts it. By analyzing losses averaged per class rather than over the whole dataset, the authors prove that **standard NC is reached on both balanced and imbalanced data** for cross-entropy and binary cross-entropy losses. In an open-set-style setting where some classes have classifier vectors but no training samples, the known classes still collapse normally, while the unknown classes' vectors overlap with each other and become orthogonal to the known ones. The same result holds for Softmax- and Sigmoid-based contrastive losses re-balanced by inverse sample frequency.

papers.title: Scaling Laws for SAE Training Data
papers.abstract: Activation storage is often a bottleneck in sparse autoencoder (SAE) training. We study how many unique activations an SAE needs when its total training budget is fixed. Quality improves rapidly as the buffer grows, then reaches a plateau where replaying the buffer is nearly as effective as using fresh activations throughout training. Beyond this point, additional unique activations bring little benefit to reconstruction or interpretability, so the buffer need not grow with the training budget. We describe this tradeoff between diversity and repetition with a scaling law for limited data. We validate it across dictionary sizes and token budgets, early, middle, and late layers of Llama-3.1, Qwen3 model sizes, and BatchTopK, TopK, and JumpReLU SAEs. Sweeps using mathematical text and Python code test the effect of changing the activation source. Evaluation covers explained variance (EV), reconstruction MSE, feature absorption, automated interpretability, and sparse probing. These results give a practical training rule: choose the smallest buffer that reaches the quality plateau and replay it for the remaining budget. In our experiments, this reduces activation storage by $8\text{--}64\times$ with negligible quality loss.
papers.summary: Storing model activations is often the bottleneck when training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for interpretability, so the authors study how many unique activations are needed under a fixed training budget. Quality improves quickly as the activation buffer grows, then plateaus, and beyond that point replaying the buffer works nearly as well as fresh data. They fit a scaling law for this tradeoff between diversity and repetition and validate it across `Llama-3.1` layers, `Qwen3` sizes, `BatchTopK`, `TopK`, and `JumpReLU` SAEs, and math and Python code data. The resulting rule, pick the smallest buffer that reaches the plateau and replay it, **cuts activation storage by 8–64× with negligible quality loss**.

papers.title: RIVER: Evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval for enzyme--reaction discovery
papers.abstract: Enzyme function annotation and the identification of candidate enzymes for a given reaction are essential steps in connecting genomic information to biochemical reaction networks. However, existing methods rely on sequence or structural similarity or on training with known enzyme--reaction pairs, making it difficult to integrate biochemical evidence across large candidate spaces; they also struggle with retrieval tasks involving enzyme families whose members are highly similar. Here, we introduce RIVER (Reaction--enzyme Inference via Evidence-guided Retrieval), a multi-agent framework for bidirectional enzyme--reaction retrieval that identifies potentially catalyzed reactions for a given enzyme and ranks candidate enzymes for a given reaction. RIVER coordinates large language models, specialized biochemical computational tools, and external knowledge resources to assemble evidence at multiple levels, including reaction chemistry, protein sequences and domains, catalytic mechanisms, and database annotations. Dedicated validation modules further examine evidence gaps and potential conflicts and rerank candidates using traceable evidence records. On public benchmarks, RIVER achieves the highest success rates in both enzyme retrieval and enzyme annotation. In family-specific enzyme retrieval, RIVER outperforms the evaluated baselines on the selected datasets and metrics. In Escherichia coli enzyme retrieval tasks constructed from recent literature, RIVER achieves the best retrieval results with closed-source and open-source model configurations, substantially outperforming closed-source general-purpose and biology-specialized multi-agent systems, including Claude Code, Codex, and Phylo Max. These results suggest that evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval can prioritize biochemically supported enzyme--reaction relationships, providing a basis for subsequent experimental validation.
papers.summary: Matching enzymes to the reactions they catalyze is hard for methods based on sequence or structure similarity, especially within families of near-identical enzymes. `RIVER` is a multi-agent framework that coordinates large language models, biochemical computation tools, and external databases to gather evidence on reaction chemistry, protein domains, catalytic mechanisms, and annotations, with validation modules that flag gaps and conflicts and rerank candidates using traceable evidence records. It works in both directions, finding likely reactions for an enzyme and ranking candidate enzymes for a reaction. `RIVER` achieves the highest success rates on public benchmarks and **substantially outperforms general-purpose and biology-specialized agent systems, including `Claude Code`, `Codex`, and `Phylo Max`**, on E. coli retrieval tasks built from recent literature.

papers.title: Optimal Learning in Games with Arbitrary Delays: Best-of-Both-Worlds for Self-Play and Adversarial Opponents
papers.abstract: We study learning in zero-sum games with delayed feedback. We introduce Multi-Anchor Optimistic Online Mirror Descent (MAO-OMD), a single algorithm which obtains optimal fast rates in self-play on smooth games, while simultaneously maintaining minimax optimal guarantees against arbitrary opponents. In particular, in smooth zero-sum games with arbitrary and unknown feedback delays, MAO-OMD obtains $O(\sigma_{\max}+1)$ social and individual regrets when used by both players, where $\sigma_{\max}$ denotes the maximum number of outstanding gradients, while also guaranteeing minimax optimal $O(\sqrt{T+d_{\mathrm{tot}}})$ individual regret against arbitrary opponents, where $d_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total delay. Moreover, we show that these optimal rates cannot be obtained simultaneously using the standard black-box reduction to the undelayed setting. We also extend our results to multi-player games, and to games with player-dependent delay sequences.
papers.summary: In zero-sum games where feedback arrives after arbitrary, unknown delays, learning algorithms usually have to choose between fast convergence in self-play and robustness against adversarial opponents. `Multi-Anchor Optimistic Online Mirror Descent` (`MAO-OMD`) is a single algorithm that achieves both: regret bounded by the maximum number of outstanding gradients when both players use it in smooth games, and **minimax-optimal regret against arbitrary opponents**. The authors also prove that the standard black-box reduction to the undelayed setting cannot achieve both rates at once, and extend the results to multi-player games and player-specific delays.

papers.title: Adapters as Data: The Latent Space of LoRAs
papers.abstract: LoRA adapters are usually treated as finished artifacts rather than as a data modality. Prior work has shown that LoRA adapters populate a low-dimensional manifold that a linear PCA basis already organizes well enough to support different operations such as sampling, editing, and inversion. We ask what a learned, nonlinear latent adds beyond this. We train a transformer autoencoder on the same population of LoRA identity adapters, mapping each into a latent space and compare every operation against the identical operation applied directly to the raw adapter weights. The latent preserves the capabilities already available in weight space, sampling diverse identities and editing individual attributes. Beyond preservation, we show that the latent is far more robust to displacement than weight space, degrading into distorted but still valid faces rather than texture. Fixed-dimensional weight-space representations cannot natively host adapters of more than one rank, so we extend our sequential autoencoder to hold mixed-rank adapters within one shared latent. This gives a path toward treating adapter weights of varying architecture as a single, general modality rather than one tied to a fixed rank, and points to a learned, nonlinear latent as the mechanism that could carry this generalization further, toward heterogeneous populations of adapters.
papers.summary: LoRA adapters are usually treated as finished artifacts, but earlier work showed that populations of them lie on a low-dimensional manifold that a linear PCA basis already organizes. The authors train a transformer autoencoder on a population of LoRA identity adapters for face generation and compare sampling, editing, and inversion in its learned latent space against the same operations on raw adapter weights. The latent keeps the existing capabilities and is **far more robust to displacement, degrading into distorted but still valid faces rather than texture noise**. The sequential autoencoder also holds adapters of different ranks in one shared latent, which fixed-size weight-space representations cannot do.

papers.title: The Intrusion Pathway: How Non-Evidential Context Degrades Language Model Performance
papers.abstract: Language models lose accuracy when a prompt contains non-evidential context: irrelevant statements from unrelated domains, or random off-distribution tokens, with no competing answer and no semantic overlap with the query. Such noise pervades retrieval-augmented, tool-using, and long-context deployments, yet the failure has lacked a mechanistic account. We trace the corruption to the Intrusion Pathway, which starts with MLPs enriching both query-subject and irrelevant-token representations, parroting heads carry prefix-token content to the prediction position, and relational readers largely avoid unrelated sources. Nevertheless, preserved subject enrichment and selective reading do not prevent intrusion in the broader computation. We then localize part of this interference to a sparse set of attention heads, which we call intrusion heads. Their prefix-derived writes promote distractor-related content, while their reduced support for the correct answer arises primarily from weaker non-prefix contributions rather than direct suppression by the prefix. The same heads transfer across tasks and distractor types and are largely weight-disjoint from the heads that integrate relevant contextual evidence, enabling a class-conditional intervention. Replacing the corrupted last-token residual with its clean counterpart, an oracle probe that requires a matched clean forward pass, recovers 97.6% on average of the distractor-induced drop across four downstream tasks. A deployable mask level knockout of about ten heads, roughly 1% of the model's attention heads, recovers 57% at bounded cost to helpful context.
papers.summary: Language models lose accuracy when prompts contain irrelevant context, such as unrelated statements or random tokens, a common situation in retrieval-augmented, tool-using, and long-context deployments. The authors trace this failure mechanistically to an "Intrusion Pathway" and localize much of it to a sparse set of "intrusion heads" that promote distractor content, transfer across tasks and distractor types, and are largely separate from the heads that use relevant context. Replacing the corrupted final-token state with a clean one recovers 97.6% of the accuracy drop, but this requires a matched clean forward pass. A practical intervention that **knocks out about ten heads, roughly 1% of the model's attention heads, recovers 57% of the drop** at limited cost to helpful context.

papers.title: Bridging Structure and Semantics: Knowledge Graph Verification via Triple-to-Text Alignment
papers.abstract: Semantic accuracy is an important dimension of knowledge graph quality. Graph-based scoring methods exploit relational structure, while textual representations allow classifiers to draw on knowledge encoded by pre-trained language models (PLMs). We present GenVer, a generative verifier that scores triples using both their serialized form and generated natural language representations (NLRs). A triple-text alignment procedure selects training pairs for a sequence-to-sequence generator; a BERT-based classifier then combines features from each triple and its generated NLR. On four FactFB variants, constructed from FB15k using perturbed negative triples, GenVer obtains the highest classification accuracy among the evaluated baselines, ranging from 88.56% to 91.52%. The experiments suggest that generated representations can help triple classification, while the case analysis also exposes semantic drift and high-confidence errors.
papers.summary: Checking whether knowledge-graph triples are factually correct can rely either on the graph's structure or on text processed by pre-trained language models. `GenVer` combines both: a sequence-to-sequence generator, trained on pairs chosen by a triple-to-text alignment procedure, turns each triple into a natural-language sentence, and a `BERT`-based classifier scores the triple using both its serialized form and the generated text. On four `FactFB` variants built from `FB15k` with perturbed negative triples, **`GenVer` reaches 88.56% to 91.52% accuracy**, the best among the evaluated baselines. Case analysis also shows semantic drift in the generated text and high-confidence errors.

papers.title: PBPO: Prefix-Block Policy Optimization for Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) commonly decode responses by proceeding autoregressively across blocks while iteratively denoising multiple tokens within each block. This structure makes block-level policy optimization a natural adaptation of autoregressive policy optimization. However, the exact likelihood of a completed block is intractable because it marginalizes over the intermediate states and reveal orders of the denoising process. To realize the block-level formulation, we construct a prefix-block state and use a single model evaluation to define a factorized one-step surrogate for the block likelihood. The resulting block surrogate ratio is a product of its token surrogate ratios, allowing variation at individual positions to propagate across the entire block before clipping. We therefore introduce Prefix-Block Policy Optimization (PBPO), which preserves block-level conditioning but applies surrogate importance weighting and clipping separately to each token. PBPO further diversifies repeated updates by resampling corrupted views of the prompt and revealed prefix, a design motivated by masked-dLLM pre-training. Under our analysis assumptions, block-product weighting amplifies the variance of gradient contributions relative to token-local weighting. Across two LLaDA-family initializations, six benchmarks, and three generation lengths, PBPO achieves competitive performance against existing dLLM RL methods.
papers.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) often decode block by block, denoising several tokens within each block, which makes block-level reinforcement learning a natural fit, except that the exact likelihood of a completed block is intractable. `Prefix-Block Policy Optimization` (`PBPO`) estimates block likelihood with a factorized one-step surrogate from a single model evaluation, but applies importance weighting and clipping to each token separately, since the authors show that weighting by the full block product amplifies gradient variance. It also resamples corrupted views of the prompt and prefix to diversify repeated updates. Across two `LLaDA`-family models, six benchmarks, and three generation lengths, `PBPO` is **competitive with existing dLLM reinforcement-learning methods**.

papers.title: EnergyBench: a live, gate-aligned benchmark of day-ahead forecasts for European power markets
papers.abstract: Energy forecasting models are usually compared on backtests and fixed public datasets. Backtests can use data that did not yet exist when the forecast would have been made, and a fixed test set, reused across studies and possibly contained in the pretraining data of foundation models, invites overfitting to the benchmark. EnergyBench evaluates every entry live instead. Each day at 11:30 CET/CEST, thirty minutes before the day-ahead (SDAC) gate closes, every model forecasts the next day's price, wind and solar generation and load on the 15-minute grid for six bidding zones (BE, NL, FR, DE-LU, DK1, DK2). Unlike existing live benchmarks, EnergyBench runs the models itself, on one information set that it freezes at the cut-off and publishes, including three numerical weather prediction models, so that foundation models can be compared with and without the same weather covariates under the actual market deadline. Errors are pooled per series against a seasonal-naive baseline, and models are ranked by a Bradley-Terry rating on the Elo scale with a day-bootstrap interval. The field spans baselines, linear and gradient-boosted models on the frozen weather, eighteen time-series foundation models from eleven families, ensembles, and the grid operators' own forecasts. Over the first thirty-two live days, the covariates reduced the error of each of the ten foundation models run with and without them by 37-51% on matched races (64-73% on wind, 48-61% on solar). Used zero-shot, these models match or outperform a LightGBM model trained on the same covariates. Model size, from 3M to 331M parameters, has a much smaller effect, and median ensembles of the covariate models rank highest. The grid operators' pre-gate forecasts remain ahead on wind and solar, where the best single foundation models have 16-22% more error; on load the gap is 4-6%, within the intervals.
papers.summary: Energy forecasting models are usually compared on backtests and fixed datasets, which can leak future information or end up in foundation-model pretraining data. `EnergyBench` instead runs every model live each day at 11:30 CET, thirty minutes before the European day-ahead market gate closes. Each model forecasts the next day's price, wind, solar and load on a 15-minute grid for six bidding zones, using one frozen information set that includes three numerical weather prediction models. Models are ranked with a Bradley-Terry rating on the Elo scale. Over the first 32 days, adding weather covariates cut the error of time-series foundation models by **37-51%**, and these models used zero-shot matched or beat a trained `LightGBM`. Model size mattered far less, median ensembles ranked highest, and grid operators' own forecasts stayed ahead on wind and solar.

papers.title: Decodability Is Not Validity: Evaluating Nuisance Sensitivity in Language Model Concept Probes
papers.abstract: Two concept probes can be equally accurate at predicting a concept from a language model's hidden states while their scores contain different mixtures of the target concept and a correlated nuisance attribute. In four target--nuisance settings (two aspect sentiments in CEBaB; occupation and gender in BiasBios; Amazon review sentiment with negation, and with first-person framing), two LLMs, and a population of concept extractors, we compare decodability with discriminant evidence: the score's dependence on the nuisance at fixed target, and its response to input edits intended to change only the nuisance, filtered by two LLM judges and compared against placebo edits. Under correlated training data, extractors that are statistically equivalent in held-out AUROC differ up to several-fold in nuisance sensitivity in three of the four settings, and decodability is not a reliable proxy for it: their rank correlation changes sign across settings. The effect follows the probe's training data, not the nuisance's natural association with the target: first-person framing, unrelated to sentiment in natural reviews, is absorbed at least as much as negation, which co-occurs with negative sentiment, and decorrelated training removes the systematic effect. Selecting extractors with nuisance-aware development diagnostics, which need nuisance labels but no counterfactuals, lowers counterfactual nuisance sensitivity wherever the default choice is sensitive, at a small accuracy cost. Concept measurements should be validated, not just decoded.
papers.summary: Concept probes read a concept such as sentiment from a language model's hidden states, but equally accurate probes can also pick up a correlated nuisance attribute to very different degrees. The authors test this in four target-nuisance settings drawn from `CEBaB`, `BiasBios` and Amazon reviews, using two LLMs. They measure nuisance sensitivity both statistically and with counterfactual input edits that are checked by LLM judges and compared against placebo edits. Probes with statistically equivalent held-out AUROC (area under the ROC curve) differed **up to several-fold in nuisance sensitivity**, and decodability was not a reliable guide to it. The effect comes from correlations in the probe's training data, and choosing probes with nuisance-aware diagnostics reduces it at a small cost in accuracy.

papers.title: Axis-LoRA: Probing and Adapting Embedding Models for Personal-Memory Retrieval
papers.abstract: As LLMs are increasingly asked questions about a user's personal experiences, retrieval must distinguish memories by time, place, person, and event. Current personal-memory pipelines rely on frozen dense embedding models to embed memories for retrieval, but we find that these models do not capture the four axes well. Swapping a memory's date or place barely shifts its embedding, and a trained projection on top of the frozen embedding does not recover the missing signal. The problem lives inside the model, where each axis is encoded by a distinct attention-head pattern. Guided by these findings, we propose Axis-LoRA, a per-axis adapter that places four LoRA branches inside the embedding model and combines them via a per-query gate. Across three standard embedding models evaluated on LongMemEval, ATM-Bench, and LoCoMo, Axis-LoRA improves 4-benchmark mean R@10 by $+1.28$ to $+1.56$~pp while training only a small fraction of the base parameters on a small axis-counterfactual training set. Code is available at https://github.com/dohoonkim-ai/axis-lora.
papers.summary: Retrieving a user's personal memories requires telling them apart by time, place, person and event, but frozen dense embedding models barely change their embedding when a memory's date or place is swapped. The authors trace each of these axes to a distinct attention-head pattern inside the model and propose `Axis-LoRA`: four LoRA (low-rank adaptation) branches placed inside the embedding model and combined by a per-query gate. Trained on a small axis-counterfactual dataset, it raises mean R@10 by **+1.28 to +1.56 percentage points** across three embedding models on `LongMemEval`, `ATM-Bench` and `LoCoMo`.

papers.title: Generate-then-Rank: Learning Symbolic Goal Interpretation for Embodied Agents
papers.abstract: Goal interpretation is to translate a natural language instruction into a formal symbolic goal that a planner can execute. It is critical for embodied agents because any error here propagates to every downstream planning and action step. Doing it well requires both generating suitable candidates and reliably selecting among them. We present a two-stage generate-then-rank approach to Goal Interpretation in the Embodied Agent Interface (EAI). First, supervised fine-tuning adapts a Large Language Model (LLM) to EAI's output convention. Second, Candidate-Output Ranking from Errors (CORE) learns preferences over complete outputs from the model's own generated alternatives. We conducted experiments on the household scenes of the Embodied Agent Interface Benchmark. Multiple open source LLMs including DeepSeek-V3 chat, DeepSeek-Reasoner, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-72B were evaluated. The proposed method outperformed the baseline models including LLMs with simple prompting, chain-of-thought, and knowledge graph based approaches.
papers.summary: Embodied agents need natural-language instructions translated into formal symbolic goals that a planner can execute, and any error at this step carries through to every later action. The proposed two-stage method first fine-tunes an LLM on the output format of the `Embodied Agent Interface` (EAI). It then applies `CORE` (Candidate-Output Ranking from Errors), which learns preferences over the model's own complete generated alternatives. On the EAI household scenes, with models including `DeepSeek-V3`, `DeepSeek-Reasoner` and `Qwen2.5`, the approach **outperformed simple prompting, chain-of-thought and knowledge-graph baselines**.

papers.title: Estimating Spectrum-Free Information Bounds for Generative Surrogates Beyond Conditional Collapse
papers.abstract: Conditional generative surrogates in high-energy physics, such as models that predict reconstructed jets from partons, are often evaluated on $1\text{D}$ marginal divergences among other metrics. Taken alone these metrics can reward conditional collapse. On a CMS simulation benchmark, a sampler that ignores the conditioner beats a trained Mixture Density Network (MDN) on all four target marginals under both KL and Wasserstein-1, and cannot be stably separated from a Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) model on two of the four. We instead score the models with the Continuous Ranked Probability Skill Score (CRPSS) from forecast verification, taking the exact marginal as the reference. We show how global skill depends on the evaluation spectrum, and we also report it within bins of a conditioning variable, where that dependence largely goes away. We then introduce a data-driven $k$-Nearest-Neighbor ($k$-NN) extrapolation that estimates the best CRPS the conditioning information allows. Both models agree with this estimate on all four targets, which suggests that current architectures have reached the information available in the conditioner, at least as far as these per-target scores can tell.
papers.summary: Conditional generative surrogates in high-energy physics are often scored on one-dimensional marginal divergences, which can reward models that ignore their conditioning input. On a CMS simulation benchmark, a sampler that ignores the conditioner **beats a trained Mixture Density Network on all four target marginals** under both KL divergence and Wasserstein-1. The authors instead use the Continuous Ranked Probability Skill Score (CRPSS) from forecast verification, report it within bins of a conditioning variable, and add a k-nearest-neighbor extrapolation that estimates the best score the conditioning information allows. Both a Mixture Density Network and a `Conditional Flow Matching` model reach this estimate, which suggests current architectures already extract the information available in the conditioner.

papers.title: Instantiating the Knowledge Plane
