papers.abstract: In 2003, Clark et al. proposed the "Knowledge Plane", a layer of intelligent agents that share rich information about network state in order to collaboratively manage the Internet across administrative boundaries. The technology of the day lacked the two capabilities it demanded most: reasoning and unstructured communication. Thus, automated network management has remained largely confined to single domains, while interdomain problems are still resolved by human operators on the phone. We argue that agentic large language models can finally unlock the potential of the Knowledge Plane, but that doing so will require solving new research problems that arise particularly in this decentralized, multi-agent, coopetitive setting that have received limited attention in the literature thus far.
papers.summary: In 2003, Clark et al. proposed the Knowledge Plane: intelligent agents that share information about network state to manage the Internet jointly across administrative boundaries. That technology lacked reasoning and unstructured communication, so problems spanning multiple networks are still mostly resolved by human operators on the phone. This position paper argues that **agentic LLMs can finally make the Knowledge Plane workable**. It also lays out new research problems that arise because the setting is decentralized, multi-agent and coopetitive, meaning the networks both cooperate and compete.

papers.title: STAG-Net: Structure-Aware Attention over Landmark Groups for Lightweight Head Pose Estimation
papers.abstract: Head pose estimation is important for human computer interaction and driver monitoring, but many image based methods remain too costly for resource constrained deployment. We propose STAG-Net, a structure-aware attention over landmark groups for lightweight head Pose estimation that estimates head pose from facial landmarks using movement aware selection, spatial clustering, compact DeepSet encoders, self attention, and a global geometry descriptor. We develop variants using FaceMesh and Face Alignment Network landmarks and evaluate them under cross dataset and subject independent protocols on 300W-LP, AFLW2000, and BIWI. STAG-Net achieves the lowest mean absolute error among all compared landmark based methods in every evaluated setting. On BIWI frames with valid detections, the FAN variant also records the lowest overall error among all compared methods, reaching $3.51^\circ$ under cross dataset evaluation and $2.39^\circ$ under subject independent evaluation. The regressors use only 0.012 to 0.043 million parameters and 24.1 to 83.6 thousand FLOPs, about three orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs than FSA-Net. Despite including landmark extraction and regression, the FaceMesh pipeline reaches 322.9 frames per second on a Tesla T4 GPU, nearly twice the 164.5 frames per second of the fastest measured image based baseline, and 111.0 frames per second on CPU. After normalization by dataset size, STAG-Net processes training samples seven to eight times faster than FSA-Net and more than one hundred times faster than HopeNet and TokenHPE, while complete training finishes within 28 minutes. These results show that STAG-Net combines leading landmark based accuracy with substantially lower training and inference cost.
papers.summary: `STAG-Net` estimates head pose from facial landmarks rather than raw images, aiming at resource-constrained uses such as driver monitoring. It groups landmarks by movement and spatial clustering, encodes the groups with compact DeepSet encoders and self-attention, and adds a global geometry descriptor. It achieves the lowest error among landmark-based methods on `300W-LP`, `AFLW2000` and `BIWI`, with regressors of only 12K to 43K parameters. **The full `FaceMesh` pipeline runs at 322.9 frames per second on a T4 GPU and 111 frames per second on CPU**, and training finishes within 28 minutes.

papers.title: THG-Omni: Traceable Human-Centric Graph Supervision for Video Reasoning
papers.abstract: Omni-modal models can answer questions about video, but their predictions rarely show which participant, event, or interval supports an answer. Moreover, answer-level supervision alone does not teach a model to interpret structured video evidence. To systematically mitigate this issue, we present THG-Omni, a human-centric graph-supervision framework that links Segment Anything Model~3 participant tracks with temporally grounded Qwen3-VL annotations. Candidate semantic claims are checked against the source video and available audio before they are used to construct training questions, while track geometry provides explicit spatial and temporal supervision. The resulting questions teach an omni-modal reasoning model to interpret participant attributes, actions, affect, interactions, and their timing from a structured graph. At inference, THG-Omni uses a predicted graph constructed from the evaluation video. Experiments on IntentBench show consistent improvements over the unadapted backbone across social reasoning, emotion understanding, and deception perception. On NExT-QA, THG-Omni achieves 89.54\% accuracy with the matched graph, compared with 85.10\% without graph input. Further validation experiments show that compact graph input achieves 78.22\% accuracy, compared with 78.02\% using the full graph and 77.58\% without graph input. A complementary diagnostic demonstrates that the predicted graph preserves evidence useful for answering questions even without the source video and audio. Together, these findings show that THG-Omni improves human-centric video reasoning while grounding its evidence in identifiable participants and events. Our codes are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/review-n94hhfcwp5666/
papers.summary: Omni-modal models can answer questions about video but rarely show which participant, event or time interval supports the answer. `THG-Omni` builds human-centric graphs by linking `Segment Anything Model 3` participant tracks with time-grounded `Qwen3-VL` annotations, checks candidate claims against the source video and audio, and turns the graphs into training questions. These questions teach a reasoning model to interpret participant attributes, actions, emotions and interactions from structured evidence. It improves on the unadapted backbone across social, emotion and deception tasks in `IntentBench`, and **reaches 89.54% on `NExT-QA` with graph input versus 85.10% without**.

papers.title: Enhanced MRI brain tumor detection using deep learning in conjunction with explainable AI SHAP based diverse and multi feature analysis
papers.abstract: Recent innovations in medical imaging have markedly improved brain tumor identification, surpassing conventional diagnostic approaches that suffer from low resolution, radiation exposure, and limited contrast. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is pivotal in precise and accurate tumor characterization owing to its high-resolution, non-invasive nature. This study investigates the synergy among multiple feature representation schemes such as local Binary Patterns (LBP), Gabor filters, Discrete Wavelet Transform, Fast Fourier Transform, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and Gray-Level Run Length Matrix alongside five learning algorithms namely: k-nearest Neighbor, Random Forest, Support Vector Classifier (SVC), and probabilistic neural network (PNN), and CNN. Empirical findings indicate that LBP in conjunction with SVC and CNN obtained high specificity and accuracy, rendering it a promising method for MRI-based tumor diagnosis. Further to investigate the contribution of LBP, Statistical analysis chi-square and p-value tests are used to confirm the significant impact of LBP feature space for identification of brain Tumor. In addition, The SHAP analysis was used to identify the most important features in classification. In a small dataset, CNN obtained 97.8% accuracy while SVC yielded 98.06% accuracy. In subsequent analysis, a large benchmark dataset is also utilized to evaluate the performance of learning algorithms in order to investigate the generalization power of the proposed model. CNN achieves the highest accuracy of 98.9%, followed by SVC at 96.7%. These results highlight CNN's effectiveness in automated, high-precision tumor diagnosis. Code: https://github.com/asifrahman557/BrainTumorDetection
papers.summary: This study compares hand-crafted and learned feature representations for brain tumor detection in MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scans. The features include Local Binary Patterns (LBP), Gabor filters, wavelet and Fourier transforms, and CNN features, each paired with classifiers such as k-nearest neighbors, random forests, support vector classifiers and CNNs. LBP combined with a support vector classifier or a CNN gave the best specificity and accuracy, and chi-square tests and `SHAP` analysis were used to confirm which features mattered. On a larger benchmark dataset, **the CNN reached 98.9% accuracy**.

papers.title: Masked diffusion as random sequential adsorption: an exactly solvable model for parallel decoding
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models generate text by reversing a stochastic masking process. Unlike autoregressive LLMs, which generate text one token at a time, they can reveal many tokens in parallel, at the price of an error, since tokens revealed together are drawn independently. We show that this trade-off maps onto the statistical physics of driven many-particle systems. (i) For any data, the error of parallel generation is the entropy production of the generation process relative to the reversed masking process. (ii) For Markov data, generation is a random sequential adsorption process with labelled gaps, which we solve exactly for any number of steps. (iii) For many steps, the error becomes the dissipation of a slowly driven system: the unmasking schedule plays the role of the driving protocol, the number of steps that of its duration, and the error is set by a thermodynamic metric that we obtain in closed form from the mutual information between tokens. Optimal schedules are geodesics of this metric. The exact solution shows how correlations in the text shape both the error and the quality of the output. The longer the correlations, the more the error concentrates at the start of generation. Schedules that start with small steps then gain more, both in path error and in perplexity, and need fewer steps to reach their asymptotic behaviour.
papers.summary: Masked diffusion language models can reveal many tokens at once, but tokens revealed together are sampled independently, which introduces error. The authors map this trade-off onto the statistical physics of driven many-particle systems and show that **the error of parallel generation equals the entropy production of the generation process**. For Markov data they solve generation exactly as random sequential adsorption. For many steps, the error becomes the dissipation of a slowly driven system, and optimal unmasking schedules are geodesics of a closed-form metric derived from the mutual information between tokens. The exact solution shows that longer-range correlations concentrate error at the start of generation, so schedules that begin with small steps give lower error and perplexity.

papers.title: Computation, not weight access: large language models as auditors of clinical prediction networks
papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have been reported to read, edit and write the weights of small neural networks, raising the prospect of auditing clinical prediction models from their files alone. Public demonstrations, however, mixed reading raw weights with running code. We separated these conditions in internally pre-specified simulation experiments. Tanh networks of 105 to 38,401 weights were trained on simulated cohorts of patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage, each with a planted relationship or none, and one network was trained on labels that under-recorded deaths in a subgroup. GPT-6 Astra and four other GPT models answered single prompts under a default or an explicit system instruction, either with the weights in the prompt and no tools, or with a calculation-only tool that exposed the weights (white box) or only the network's predictions (black box). Without tools, Astra recovered planted relationships in 353-weight networks but became unreliable at 3,457 weights, and under the default instruction it declined 11 of 12 audit and repair tasks as unidentifiable; the explicit instruction removed these refusals. With the tool, it recovered the planted relationship in all 29 runs on networks of up to 38,401 weights, raised no false alarm in 15 runs on null networks, and found the biased subgroup in 6 of 6 runs. Black-box access performed as well as white-box access, and other GPT-6 models read as accurately. A well-designed script matched the comparator models on the audit and the best LLM repair. For auditing these networks, what mattered was computation and elicitation, not access to the weights.
papers.summary: Frontier LLMs have been reported to read and edit the weights of small neural networks, which raises the prospect of auditing clinical prediction models from their files alone. In pre-specified simulation experiments on networks trained on simulated patient cohorts, the authors separated reading raw weights from running computation. Without tools, `GPT-6 Astra` became unreliable at about 3,457 weights and refused most audit tasks under its default instruction. With a calculation-only tool, it **recovered planted relationships in all 29 runs on networks up to 38,401 weights**, raised no false alarms, and found a biased subgroup in every attempt. Black-box access to predictions alone performed as well as access to the weights, and a well-designed script matched the other models on the audit.

papers.title: CORE: Coarse-to-Fine Search with Context Management for Deep Research
papers.abstract: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent's context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE, a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus-CM), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.
papers.summary: Deep research agents face a trade-off: search works best over long passages, but every returned observation stays in the agent's context for the rest of the task. `CORE` is a training-free harness that retrieves passages with a dense retriever and then reuses token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Its context management also lets the agent expand the text around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled comparisons against the `Tongyi DeepResearch` and `OpenResearcher` harnesses, it **achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall** across three agent models and three `BrowseComp` variants, on corpora of up to 553M documents.

papers.title: PlayGen2: Learning Real-Time Playable Worlds with Explicit 3D State
papers.abstract: Building a playable world requires more than generating plausible video: it demands responsive control, persistent spatial structure, and coherent interactions with dynamic entities. Using generated frames as the sole recurrent world representation ties these requirements to view-dependent appearance synthesis, making it difficult to maintain long-term spatial and temporal consistency in generation and interaction. We present PlayGen2, a real-time interactive world model that separates learned 3D state evolution from neural rendering. PlayGen2 maintains a persistent world memory comprising static geometry represented by a volumetric occupancy grid and identity-indexed 3D states for the player and other entities. Within a fixed-size local region, its world-state model jointly learns action-conditioned entity dynamics, geometry completion, and entity discovery, committing updates to a persistent world memory. A separate neural renderer synthesizes first-person observations from depth and semantic projections of the world state, without feeding generated images back into state prediction. Using Doom as a testbed, we demonstrate that the model successfully learns world dynamics including geometry-aware player motion and player--NPC interactions. The framework is computationally efficient, enabling the complete simulation and rendering pipeline to achieve approximately 160ms backend latency on a MacBook Pro with an M4 Pro chip. Beyond single-player interaction, we demonstrate zero-shot deployment on unseen Doom maps, multiplayer interaction through the composition of single-player models, and programmable gameplay through rule-based state interventions. These capabilities demonstrate the transferability and extensibility of the learned game-world model. Code and pretrained model weights are publicly available.
papers.summary: World models that feed their own generated frames back as state struggle to keep space and time consistent during long interactive play. `PlayGen2` separates learned 3D state from rendering. It keeps a persistent world memory of a volumetric occupancy grid plus 3D states indexed by entity identity, learns action-conditioned dynamics within a local region, and uses a separate neural renderer to draw first-person frames from depth and semantic projections. Using Doom as a testbed, it learns geometry-aware player motion and interactions with non-player characters, and it **runs at about 160ms backend latency on a MacBook Pro with an M4 Pro chip**. It also works zero-shot on unseen maps, supports multiplayer by composing single-player models, and allows programmable gameplay through rule-based edits to the state.

papers.title: FARR: Forecast-Aware Residual Refinement with Matched Endpoint Evidence for Long-Horizon Time-Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Large language models use auxiliary conditioning to incorporate additional information into time-series forecasts. However, auxiliary conditioning does not consistently improve accuracy and can increase forecasting error when its influence is poorly matched to the observed temporal context. We propose Forecast-Aware Residual Refinement (FARR), which learns to correct forecasts using endpoint evidence. FARR obtains a valid forecast under the standard condition and a null forecast under a predefined null condition. Their difference reveals how conditioning changes the prediction. A shared residual refiner combines this endpoint evidence with historical features to estimate the remaining error of the valid forecast. Horizon-wise gating then controls the contribution of the predicted residual to the final output. Experiments on four long-horizon forecasting benchmarks show that FARR achieves the best dataset-average MSE and MAE among the compared methods. Code will be released at https://github.com/blossomrichzyy-star/farr-forecast-aware-residual-refinement.
papers.summary: LLM-based time-series forecasters use extra conditioning information, but this information can raise error when it does not fit the observed temporal context. `FARR` (Forecast-Aware Residual Refinement) produces one forecast with the conditioning and one under a predefined null condition, and treats their difference as evidence of how the conditioning changes the prediction. A shared refiner combines this evidence with historical features to estimate the remaining error, and gating per forecast horizon controls how much of the correction is applied. FARR **achieves the best dataset-average MSE and MAE** among the compared methods on four long-horizon benchmarks.

papers.title: Responsible GenAI Use During Active Armed Conflict: Evidence from Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms
papers.abstract: Armed conflict can increase the value of Generative AI (GenAI) while undermining the conditions required for its responsible use. Yet the perspectives of community-based humanitarian responders working under these conditions remain underrepresented in responsible AI research. We examine GenAI use in Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs), a community-led humanitarian network, through an exploratory survey of 89 respondents and 15 semi-structured interviews with GenAI users and non-users. War reconfigures GenAI's role, making it most useful where its outputs are hardest to verify. ERR responders turned to GenAI when conflict made human expertise difficult or dangerous to reach. However, participants cautioned that GenAI could not independently establish rapidly changing local conditions, and that relying on its outputs could lead to harmful decisions when human verification was difficult. Risks arose before GenAI was used. For some volunteers, carrying a phone or accessing the internet could expose them to danger. Others were concerned that sharing sensitive beneficiary or operational information with GenAI could put people at risk. Participants feared that AI-assisted reports could undermine their credibility with donors, whose funding sustains the food and medical aid ERRs provide. Access to GenAI was uneven, and volunteers using it sometimes relied on colleagues with relevant expertise or local knowledge to verify its results. Our findings show that responsible use of GenAI during conflict depends not only on model performance or individual adoption, but also on whether responders can safely access these tools, verify their outputs against local conditions, and recognize when limiting or avoiding GenAI is the more responsible choice.
papers.summary: Responsible-AI research rarely hears from community humanitarian responders working in active armed conflict. Through a survey of 89 respondents and 15 interviews with members of Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms, a community-led aid network, the authors find that **war makes generative AI most useful exactly where its outputs are hardest to verify**. Volunteers turned to it when human experts were dangerous or impossible to reach. Their concerns included the danger of carrying phones, exposing sensitive beneficiary data, uneven access, and losing credibility with donors. The authors conclude that responsible use depends on whether responders can safely access the tools, verify outputs against local conditions, and recognize when avoiding them is the better choice.

papers.title: Which Signals of Code Correctness Survive Distribution Shift? Hidden-State and Causal Predictors of Program and Verdict Correctness
papers.abstract:
Large language models increasingly judge code, yet without external feedback such judgments are unreliable, and verifying them by executing tests or by extended reasoning is costly. Instead, execution-free correctness predictors use signals from the model's output probabilities, sampled solutions, or hidden states to identify judgments that warrant further verification. However, these predictors may degrade under distribution shifts when generalizing across projects and languages.
  We compare six execution-free predictors from four families on Qwen3-Coder-30B and gpt-oss-20b under benchmark shift between LiveCodeBench and BigCodeBench and language shift across Python, C++ and Java. We evaluate two targets: whether the model's own verdict on a program can be trusted, and whether the program itself is correct. Besides established approaches, we adapt two novel causal localization methods to code, which have been shown to be more robust out-of-distribution on natural language tasks. For verdict correctness, causal localization improves robustness to language shift. For Qwen3-Coder a probe on the causally localized subspace stays 0.09 AUROC ahead of output confidence under language shift (0.11 in distribution), significantly outperforming the best non-causal predictor by 0.04 AUROC on average. This advantage, however, does not generalize consistently to gpt-oss or to benchmark shift. For program correctness, predictors transfer more successfully between benchmarks, largely by identifying problems on which the model tends to fail. However, their ability to rank candidates within the same problem is limited.
papers.summary: LLM judgments of code correctness are unreliable without execution, so cheap predictors based on output probabilities, sampled solutions or hidden states are used to flag which judgments need checking. The authors compare six such predictors on `Qwen3-Coder-30B` and `gpt-oss-20b`, under shifts between `LiveCodeBench` and `BigCodeBench` and across Python, C++ and Java. These include two causal localization methods newly adapted to code. For Qwen3-Coder, **a probe on the causally localized subspace stays 0.09 AUROC ahead of output confidence under language shift**, but this advantage does not carry over to gpt-oss or to benchmark shift. Predictors of program correctness transfer better between benchmarks, but mostly by spotting problems the model tends to fail, and they rank candidate solutions to the same problem poorly.

papers.title: Network Effect Decomposition for Causal Effect Estimation under Network Interference
papers.abstract: Estimating causal effects from observational network data requires accounting for both individual treatment and neighborhood exposure. Existing outcome models commonly incorporate these intervention variables into a joint predictor and estimate causal effects through prediction contrasts, leaving the corresponding response components implicit. We propose the $\underline{N}$etwork $\underline{E}$ffect $\underline{D}$ecomposition $\underline{Net}$work (NEDNet), which parameterizes the conditional outcome response as a query-invariant pre-treatment baseline plus separate treatment- and exposure-response pathways. Path-specific neighborhood contextualization supplies local pre-treatment information to the two pathways. We characterize the fitted response through a unique reference-normalized decomposition, which is equivalent to a zero mixed treatment--exposure contrast. Experiments on semi-synthetic benchmarks derived from BlogCatalog and Flickr show that NEDNet achieves the lowest PEHE among the compared methods for individual, peer, and total effects across homogeneous and covariate-heterogeneous response settings.
papers.summary: Estimating causal effects on networks requires accounting for both a unit's own treatment and its neighbors' exposure, and existing models usually leave these response components implicit inside one joint predictor. `NEDNet` (Network Effect Decomposition Network) models the outcome as a pre-treatment baseline plus separate pathways for treatment response and exposure response, each given its own neighborhood context. The authors show that the fitted response has a unique reference-normalized decomposition. On semi-synthetic benchmarks built from `BlogCatalog` and `Flickr`, **NEDNet achieves the lowest PEHE** (precision in estimating heterogeneous effects) for individual, peer and total effects.

papers.title: InnerLogic-Surg: An Open Surgical Foundation Model via Continual Pretraining
papers.abstract: Vision foundation models are the backbone of modern surgical image analysis, yet most surgical systems still rely on encoders pretrained on natural images or on specialist models trained from scratch on comparatively small datasets. Pretraining encoders on large amounts of surgery-specific data has the potential to generally enhance the performance of surgical image analysis methods simply by providing stronger backbones. Here we present InnerLogic-Surg, an open family of surgical vision encoders (21M--300M parameters) obtained by continually pretraining a transformer-based image encoder on millions of surgical images curated from 11,965 internet-sourced surgical videos spanning ~2,900 hours and more than fifteen procedure types. Our training recipe inherits DINOv3's pretraining stage to preserve representation ability after surgical adaptation, and additionally applies a learned feature-upsampling module for high-resolution dense prediction at low token cost. Across a benchmark covering workflow, instrument and anatomy recognition, segmentation, detection, and monocular depth, under the same architecture, the largest InnerLogic-Surg model achieves the best linear-probe performance in all 20 surgical tasks. We demonstrate that surgical continual pretraining yields transferable representations that generalize across procedures, anatomical regions, and task types, showing our surgical image encoders as a promising and scalable alternative to the procedure-specific representation learning approaches that have traditionally dominated surgical computer vision.
papers.summary: Surgical image analysis mostly relies on encoders pretrained on natural images or on small specialist models. `InnerLogic-Surg` is an open family of vision encoders from 21M to 300M parameters, continually pretrained from `DINOv3` on millions of frames from 11,965 internet surgical videos covering about 2,900 hours. A learned feature-upsampling module supports high-resolution dense prediction at low token cost. **The largest model achieves the best linear-probe performance on all 20 surgical tasks** tested, which span workflow, instrument and anatomy recognition, segmentation, detection and depth estimation.

papers.title: When, Where, How: Active In-Context Learning for Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) adapt to a new task only through the labeled rows in their context. However, labels are expensive to acquire in real-world scenarios due to the need for highly specific domain knowledge to ensure high-quality data. Active in-context learning transfers classical acquisition rules to this setting, in which the model that guides acquisition changes with every label added. We ask how the value of diversity, predictive uncertainty and target-aware information gain changes as a frozen TFM acquires more context. For that, we study Target-Aware Nearest Neighbor (TANN) acquisition and the Expected Predictive Information Gain in Context (EPIC) and evaluate them against classical rules. Our study across twenty benchmarks with two well-established TFMs and classical GBDTs highlights three findings: (i) When: diversity-based acquisition is best during the first acquisition iterations; (ii) Where: labeling pool rows that serve the target inputs via a simple target-aware nearest-neighbor rule matters substantially; (iii) How: EPIC yields the best models at the label budget, retains on average 80--87% of the chance-corrected full-data performance with only 5-10% of the pool labeled on the eight benchmarks with the largest pools, and selects labels that also improve the predictive performance of gradient-boosted decision trees.
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models adapt to a new task only through the labeled rows in their context, so choosing which rows to label matters when labels are expensive. The authors study how the value of diversity, uncertainty and target-aware selection changes as a frozen model acquires more context. They introduce a target-aware nearest-neighbor rule (`TANN`) and Expected Predictive Information Gain in Context (`EPIC`). Across twenty benchmarks, diversity works best early on and target-aware selection matters substantially. **`EPIC` retains on average 80-87% of chance-corrected full-data performance with only 5-10% of the pool labeled**, and its chosen labels also improve gradient-boosted trees.

papers.title: When Bigger Becomes Brittle: Why Compression Hurts More as Language Models Scale
papers.abstract: Quantization and pruning reduce the cost of deploying language models, but their effects are usually reported as benchmark scores. Such scores record only the loss that remains at the output. Inside the model, compression damages some components more than others, and the rest of the network can partly compensate. The observed loss therefore reflects both the damage and this compensation, which benchmark scores cannot separate. How the two combine, and whether their balance changes with model size, remains unclear. We study this compensation for in-context retrieval, a capability carried by a small, identifiable set of attention heads. To separate the two, the expected loss from ablating these heads is decomposed exactly into the part restored by the rest of the network, attributed to the components responsible, and the part that reaches the output. This decomposition is then compared across model sizes. For damage of comparable size, smaller models restore most of the loss, whereas larger models retain most of it, because the compensating responses offset less of it as models grow. Compressing the heads produces the same pattern. Compression that is nearly harmless in small models can therefore be costly in large ones.
papers.summary: Benchmark scores after quantization or pruning show only the loss that reaches the output, not how much damage the rest of the network quietly compensated for. Focusing on in-context retrieval, which relies on a small set of identifiable attention heads, the authors exactly decompose the loss from ablating those heads into a part restored by other components and a part that reaches the output. **For damage of comparable size, smaller models restore most of the loss while larger models retain most of it**, and compressing these heads produces the same pattern. As a result, compression that is nearly harmless in small models can be costly in large ones.
papers.highlight_summary:
Compression is usually judged by benchmark scores, but those scores mix two things: the damage done inside the network and the partial compensation ("self-repair") the rest of the model provides. The authors separate them for in-context retrieval on indirect-object identification (`IOI`) prompts. They use an exact accounting identity that splits the loss from damaged retrieval heads into what other components restore and what reaches the output, and find that larger models restore much less.

- The identity is **H = D − R − B − N**, where D is the logit contribution lost from the targeted retrieval heads, H is the harm that reaches the output, R is copy-suppression release, B is the net backup response from all other heads and MLPs, and N is a final-normalization term. It is applied to zero-ablation, 4-bit per-channel weight quantization, and structural head pruning across `GPT-2 XL`, `Llama 3.1 8B`, six `Pythia` models (410M to 12B), and `OPT`.
- At a matched deficit of 0.5 logits, `Pythia-410M` repairs about **0.55 logits** and ends slightly above its clean margin, while `Pythia-12B` keeps about **0.38 logits as output harm**. Under 4-bit quantization of the retrieval heads, the share of the deficit that reaches the output rises from **0.55 at 410M to 0.91 at 12B**.
- Both repair channels weaken with scale: standing copy suppression falls from about **25% of the clean logit difference at 410M to about 5% at 12B**, leaving less to release, and the net attention backup offsets about **80% of the remaining deficit at 410M versus about 9% at 12B**.
- Backup heads still protect the larger models: holding the selected backup heads at their clean outputs adds about **0.30 logits** of harm at 12B, even though their net attention response is only 0.07 logits. The authors suggest, but do not test, that opposing changes spread across many heads cancel out in the net sum.
- The study covers only templated `IOI` retrieval and uses simulated quantization with dequantized fp32 weights rather than deployment kernels. Copy-suppression heads are excluded from compression, pruning results are non-monotonic for random masks, and the link between intermediate-layer "overshoot" and suppression is correlational only.

papers.title: DISCERN: Distributional Synthetic Replay for Retain-Free Incremental Machine Unlearning
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific training data from a trained model without retraining from scratch. In real deployments, however, deletion requests arrive over time, calling for incremental class unlearning (ICU): classes are removed sequentially, previously forgotten knowledge must remain forgotten, and the remaining classes must be preserved. We present DIstributional SynthetiC rEplay for Retain-free iNcremental unlearning (DISCERN), an intervention-based class unlearning method that replaces access to the retain set with synthetic embeddings sampled from per-class parametric distributions. Unlike prototype-based replay, which assumes an isotropic Gaussian around each class centroid, DISCERN fits Euclidean (Gaussian, Laplace, Student's $t$) and directional (von Mises--Fisher, Fisher--Bingham) families to each class and selects among them through statistical tests and, when none of them accepts, cross-validated log-likelihood. This design is motivated by the architecture-dependent latent geometry: transformer embeddings lie approximately on a hypersphere and concentrate around class directions, unlike those of convolutional networks. We evaluate DISCERN against seven retain-free baselines on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 with two convolutional and two transformer backbones, under single-class, multi-class, and incremental unlearning. DISCERN is competitive when classes are removed at once and is the most stable method in ICU on transformers: on ViT-B/16, after 20 sequential deletions it retains a harmonic mean of $0.797$, whereas the strongest method in the simultaneous setting drops from $0.918$ to $0.048$. A paired ablation shows that per-class distribution selection substantially reduces the resurfacing of previously forgotten classes, acting as a stabilizer of accumulated forgetting rather than a uniform improvement.
papers.summary: Real deployments receive data-deletion requests over time, so models need incremental class unlearning (ICU): removing classes one after another, keeping forgotten classes forgotten, and preserving the rest, all without access to the original retain set. `DISCERN` (Distributional Synthetic Replay for Retain-free Incremental unlearning) replaces the retain set with synthetic embeddings drawn from per-class distributions, choosing for each class among Euclidean families (Gaussian, Laplace, Student's t) and directional families (von Mises–Fisher, Fisher–Bingham) using statistical tests or cross-validated likelihood. The motivation is that transformer embeddings sit roughly on a hypersphere, unlike convolutional ones. Tested against seven retain-free baselines on `MNIST`, `CIFAR-10`, and `CIFAR-100`, it is competitive for one-shot deletion and the most stable method under sequential deletion: on `ViT-B/16` after 20 deletions it keeps **a harmonic mean of 0.797, while the best simultaneous-setting method collapses from 0.918 to 0.048**.

papers.title: Persistent Retrieval for Conversational Agents: A Study of Retrieval Efficiency
papers.abstract:
Conversational agents can retrieve information directly or delegate retrieval to a subagent. This design choice affects how retrieval history is maintained, what context each model call receives, and what information must be re-retrieved in follow-up questions. We compare three designs: skill-based retrieval in the main agent, a non-persistent retrieval subagent that generates a findings response, and our persistent retrieval subagent, which maintains retrieval history across turns and returns retrieved evidence directly to the main agent. Our approach also allows the main agent to request corrections from the same subagent.
  We evaluate the three designs on enterprise questions posed independently, within shared conversations, and as dependent follow-ups. Across five multi-turn settings, our approach uses 43.3% fewer recorded agent-model tokens and incurs 45.0% lower estimated API cost than skill-based retrieval, while reducing average response time by 9.1%. Compared with non-persistent retrieval, it reduces response time by 15.6 seconds per question, while using 65.1% more tokens and incurring 29.1% higher estimated API cost.
  Our approach shifts the retrieval subagent from producing synthesized responses to maintaining retrieval state and supplying evidence that the main agent can directly evaluate and use for answer generation.
papers.summary: A conversational agent can run retrieval itself or hand it to a subagent, and that choice affects context size, latency, and how much must be re-retrieved for follow-up questions. The authors compare skill-based retrieval in the main agent, a non-persistent subagent that returns a synthesized findings response, and a persistent subagent that keeps retrieval history across turns, returns raw evidence to the main agent, and can be asked for corrections. On enterprise questions across five multi-turn settings, the persistent design uses **43.3% fewer agent-model tokens and 45.0% lower estimated API cost than skill-based retrieval**, with 9.1% faster responses. Against the non-persistent subagent it answers 15.6 seconds faster per question but uses 65.1% more tokens and costs 29.1% more.

papers.title: Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning
papers.abstract: Knowledge of the hidden interior structure of an object, including the presence and location of cavities, is essential for predictive simulation, robotic manipulation, and nondestructive inspection. However, such cavities leave no direct signature on the static visible surface, making collision-induced deformation one of the few cues used to infer their presence. Structure from Collision (SfC) addresses this problem by recovering the hidden interior structure of an object from multiview observations of a collision event. SfC is challenging for two reasons: hidden cavities are only indirectly observable through surface motion, and voids correspond to the absence of material, making direct optimization using standard density representations difficult. The density-based SfC baseline inherits both difficulties. Surface-matching gradients do not directly indicate the cavity location, while density gradients can be weak or uninformative inside or near void regions. Therefore, we reformulate SfC as hypothesis-space reasoning, representing hidden cavities as explicit structural hypotheses whose variables encode available structural assumptions rather than relying on implicit density updates. A global stage performs gradient-free optimization over this hypothesis space using forward-only material point method (MPM) simulation. A local stage then refines the selected hypothesis as a Lagrangian particle system through gradient-based optimization using differentiable MPM simulation. On the SfC benchmark, our method improves hidden-structure reconstruction and future prediction over the density-based SfC baseline. Interior-topology stress tests and robustness analyses characterize its scope and limitations. The project page is available at https://www.kecl.ntt.co.jp/people/kaneko.takuhiro/projects/sfc-hypothesis/.
papers.summary: Structure from Collision (SfC) tries to recover hidden interior cavities of an object from multiview video of a collision, a hard problem because voids leave no surface signature and density-based optimization gets weak gradients near empty regions. The authors reformulate SfC as reasoning over explicit structural hypotheses about the cavities. A global stage searches this hypothesis space without gradients using forward-only material point method (`MPM`) simulation, and a local stage refines the chosen hypothesis as a particle system with differentiable `MPM`. On the SfC benchmark the method **improves hidden-structure reconstruction and future-motion prediction over the density-based baseline**, and stress tests on interior topology map out where it works and where it does not.

papers.title: EDGAR: Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement via Synthetic Failure
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Gaussian splatting have enabled efficient and photorealistic head avatar reconstruction, yet monocular video-based or image-based methods still suffer from under-constrained geometry and texture, leading to artifacts such as blurring, stretching, and temporal instability. We present EDGAR (Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement), a conditional diffusion framework designed to enhance the quality of Gaussian avatars by correcting artifacts while preserving identity fidelity. To train EDGAR, we construct EDGAR-SET, a hybrid triplet dataset composed of real-captured and synthetic-rendered samples, which simulates realistic Gaussian avatar failure cases by pairing degraded renderings with ground-truth and reference images. EDGAR refines degraded frames through a fusion block that injects identity features extracted by the self-supervised Sapiens model into a one-step diffusion backbone, enabling effective artifact removal without sacrificing efficiency. Our EDGAR model incorporates a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture to address diverse degradation types and severity levels. The refined multi-view renderings are subsequently used as pseudo-targets to optimize a single underlying Gaussian avatar, so that the final avatar can be rendered without applying EDGAR to every output frame. Experiments on three different Gaussian avatar reconstruction methods, each evaluated under three different settings, show improvements in both perceptual and reconstruction measures over the raw outputs and an SDEdit-style refinement baseline. In addition, cross-view evaluation demonstrates improved calibrated consistency, while tests under large yaw and open-mouth expressions verify robustness under extreme settings. These results collectively indicate a useful operating regime for recoverable appearance artifacts. The code is available at https://kwanyun.github.io/edgar/
papers.summary: Gaussian-splatting head avatars built from monocular video or images often show blurring, stretching, and temporal flicker because geometry and texture are under-constrained. `EDGAR` is a one-step conditional diffusion refiner that removes these artifacts while preserving identity. It injects identity features from the self-supervised `Sapiens` model and uses a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) design to handle different kinds and severities of degradation, and it is trained on `EDGAR-SET`, a hybrid dataset of real and synthetic renderings that imitate typical avatar failures. The refined multi-view frames then serve as pseudo-targets to re-optimize the avatar itself, so the refiner is not needed at render time. Across three avatar reconstruction methods, this **improves perceptual and reconstruction metrics over both the raw outputs and an `SDEdit`-style baseline**, including at large head turns and with open-mouth expressions.
papers.highlight_summary:
Gaussian head avatars built from a single video or a few images tend to show blur, stretched textures and floating artifacts in views and expressions the capture didn't cover. `EDGAR` trains a reference-conditioned, one-step diffusion refiner on synthetic examples of these failures, then uses its refined multi-view renderings as targets to re-optimize the avatar, so rendering needs no diffusion pass per frame.

- The training set, `EDGAR-SET`, holds about **400K triplets** of degraded render, ground truth and reference image across about 1,600 identities, built from `NeRSemble`/`RGBAvatar` avatars trained with 1–4 views and synthetic `CAFCA`/`3DGS` avatars trained with 5 or more views; roughly half the pairs are dropped by an LPIPS filter so that only recoverable artifacts remain.
- The refiner is built on `SD-Turbo`: features of the reference image from the self-supervised `Sapiens` model enter through zero-initialized cross-attention fusion blocks, a six-expert `MoE` router handles different kinds and severities of degradation, and a `POSTER V2` expression loss helps preserve facial motion.
- On `RGBAvatar` and `GaussianAvatars`, EDGAR leads on all four metrics (CLIP, L1, LPIPS, PSNR) at every input count, for example lifting `RGBAvatar` with 8 videos from **20.51 to 22.99 dB PSNR**; on `CAP4D` results are mixed, with EDGAR best on CLIP and L1 while the unrefined baseline keeps the best LPIPS and an `SDEdit`-style baseline the best PSNR.
- Identity is mostly preserved in cross-identity reenactment (CSIM **0.517 vs. 0.551** for the base avatar, against 0.318 for `SDEdit`), refinement takes a one-time **5–17 minutes per avatar** with rendering speed within 2% of the original, and users preferred EDGAR over raw `CAP4D` **96.67%** of the time overall.
- Limitations: severe structural errors and artifacts in unobserved regions are left in place, temporal flicker gets worse for `GaussianAvatars` (warping error 4.93 to 5.94 ×10⁻³), cross-view consistency for single-video `RGBAvatar` drops, and the `MoE` contributes only marginal gains in the ablations.

papers.title: GuidedWAM: Training-Free Energy Guidance for World Action Models in Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) for autonomous driving couple the driving policy and the visual world model in a single generative network whose objectives are fixed post-training. Conditioning on a new driving objective requires retraining. We study energy guidance as a general mechanism and present GuidedWAM, a model-agnostic framework for injecting driving objectives into frozen WAMs at sampling time. Our framework constructs each objective as differentiable energies on the sampler's intermediate clean-action estimate, which needs only forward access to the frozen model, and is stabilized by sampling-time guidance scheduling, per-energy normalization, and velocity-bounded correction. On the NAVSIM v2 hard-split, guidance improves all three frozen, publicly released WAMs by 1.8 to 3.6 EPDMS, averaged over three sampler seeds, and adds less than 10% to the sampling time per step. These results position energy guidance as a practical post-training control channel for WAMs.
papers.summary: World action models (WAMs) for autonomous driving combine the driving policy and a visual world model in one generative network, so adding a new driving objective normally requires retraining. `GuidedWAM` adds objectives to frozen WAMs at sampling time by expressing each one as a differentiable energy on the sampler's intermediate clean-action estimate, which needs only forward access to the model. Guidance scheduling, per-energy normalization, and velocity-bounded corrections keep sampling stable. On the `NAVSIM v2` hard split, guidance **improves three publicly released frozen WAMs by 1.8 to 3.6 EPDMS** while adding less than 10% to per-step sampling time.

papers.title: Same Answer, Different Future: Matched Predictions Do Not Imply Matched Belief Updating in Language Models
papers.abstract: Language models can produce similar probabilistic predictions after observing outcomes, reading summaries, receiving instructions, or undergoing activation interventions. Whether these routes induce equivalent belief states remains unclear: agreement in current predictions does not establish how a model will respond to subsequent evidence. We investigate this distinction in a Bernoulli inference task with an analytic Bayesian reference. Across three open-weight language models, we prepare states through four textual routes and two activation-level interventions, measure both next-outcome continuations and explicit probabilistic estimates, and append identical new evidence from each prepared state. We quantify the persistence of the initial belief through its effective evidence weight, the number of new observations it is worth. We find that the format of evidence decides which readouts express its content: outcome sequences primarily affect continuations, whereas summaries and stated rates primarily affect explicit estimates. Moreover, effective weights differ substantially across routes, with summaries receiving weights that scale weakly with their stated observation counts and elicitation questions changing inferred weights by orders of magnitude. In a one-shot steering setting, an intervention that reproduces a natural record's immediate prediction loses most of its effect under subsequent evidence. These results show that agreement in current readouts is insufficient to establish equivalence in belief updating: how a belief is acquired and how it is read jointly determine its subsequent dynamics.
papers.summary: Language models can arrive at the same probabilistic prediction through different routes, such as seeing outcomes, reading a summary, following an instruction, or receiving an activation intervention, but that does not mean they will update the same way on new evidence. The authors test this on a Bernoulli inference task with an exact Bayesian reference, using three open-weight models, four textual routes, and two activation-level interventions, and they measure how much each prepared belief is worth in equivalent new observations. The format of the evidence determines where it shows up: outcome sequences mostly shift next-token continuations, while summaries and stated rates mostly shift explicit estimates, and summaries get weights that scale only weakly with the number of observations they report. A steering intervention that matches a natural record's immediate prediction **loses most of its effect once new evidence arrives**, which shows that matching current outputs does not establish equivalent belief updating.

papers.title: Adaptive Semantic Branching: Disagreement-Localized Cross-Trajectory Regeneration for Reasoning Candidate Expansion
papers.abstract: Reasoning trajectories generated for the same problem often arrive at conflicting answers. These disagreements reveal alternative intermediate decisions that can be reused to explore new solutions. We introduce Adaptive Semantic Branching (ASB), a training-free inference procedure that turns cross-trajectory disagreement into targeted candidate generation. ASB first groups independently sampled trajectories by extracted final answer, selects a representative from each group, and aligns their reasoning steps with a monotonic dynamic program. A persistent-divergence objective identifies the point at which initially similar reasoning paths develop different continuations. For each selected directed pair, ASB retains the source trajectory's textual prefix, extracts a short reasoning window from a competing donor trajectory, and generates a fresh solution conditioned on both. A diversity-aware policy allocates up to three additional generations according to the answer-cluster structure. In a 500-problem MATH evaluation with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, ASB increases oracle candidate coverage from 445/500 (89.0%) with seven initial samples to 455/500 (91.0%), recovering correct candidates for 10 of the 55 initially uncovered problems. The method uses 576 additional generation calls across the evaluation set, averaging 8.152 calls per problem. We provide a precise specification of the branching operator, alignment objective, generation policy, and experimental configuration.
papers.summary: When several sampled reasoning traces for the same problem reach different answers, the points where they diverge can be reused to explore new solutions. `Adaptive Semantic Branching` (`ASB`) is a training-free procedure that clusters traces by final answer, aligns representative traces step by step with dynamic programming, and finds where initially similar paths split. It then generates new solutions that keep one trace's prefix and borrow a short reasoning window from a competing trace, adding up to three extra generations per problem. On 500 `MATH` problems with `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct`, oracle coverage rises from **89.0% with seven samples to 91.0%**, recovering correct candidates for 10 of the 55 problems no initial sample solved, at an average of 8.152 generation calls per problem.

papers.title: How Finite Brains Generalize Without Bound: Spatial Memory as a Universal Computer
papers.abstract: A child who learns to add small numbers adds numbers of any length. LSTMs and Transformers trained on short sequences fail on longer ones. We trace the difference to what a learner reads when it decides. A position, a count or a time keeps taking new values as the input grows: it is a coordinate, and a learner that reads one meets in every long input values its experience never covered. Whether two things are the same has the same two answers at every size: it is a coincidence, and a learner that reads only coincidences finds in a long input nothing that short inputs lacked, so finite experience fixes its rule for every size. The memory carries the size of the input and the rule stays finite, and this determines the memory a generalizing brain can have: a memory that grows while what the learner reads of it stays finite has to look the same from every place, so it is made of cycles, and the past is reached by asking what happened when the cycles last stood where they stand now. The cycles are the grid modules, the cells that detect their return the place cells, the records the hippocampal index; a prefrontal controller moves the cycles and never sees them. Reading only coincidences costs no power: what finite experience fixes in such a learner is what Turing machines compute in step with their input, which is why a circuit that evolved to find the way home can learn arithmetic and grammar. In a network of neurons this machine of cycles is the dynamics seen through its symmetry, and symbols are its invariants. Trained on strings up to 40 symbols, the machine is at least 99% correct, on average over lengths 41 to 500, on nine of fifteen benchmark tasks, five of them tasks that no LSTM or Transformer solves; given new cycles after training it reverses strings of 15,015 symbols without error and fails beyond that on the curve the theory predicts; and its controllers run unchanged on neurons.
papers.summary: LSTMs and Transformers trained on short sequences fail on longer ones, while children who learn small-number addition can add numbers of any length. The author argues the difference lies in what the learner reads: values such as positions or counts keep taking unseen values as inputs grow, whereas same-or-different coincidences do not, so a learner that reads only coincidences has its rule fixed by finite experience. The theory says such a memory must be built from cycles and maps them onto grid cells, place cells, and the hippocampal index, with a prefrontal controller. It also claims this setup can compute what Turing machines compute in step with their input. Trained on strings of up to 40 symbols, the resulting machine is at least 99% correct on lengths 41 to 500 on nine of fifteen benchmark tasks, five of which no LSTM or Transformer solves, and given new cycles after training it **reverses strings of 15,015 symbols without error**.

papers.title: ZeroRAG: Adaptive Semantic Peer Routing for Decentralized Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a standard approach to enhance the reliability of large language model (LLM) outputs by retrieving documents relevant to a query and supplying them in the LLM prompt. Today's RAG systems collect, index, and serve these documents from centralized stores. In practice, however, documents are owned by organizations, devices, and individuals who cannot or will not surrender custody of them to a central party, e.g., because of privacy, copyright or regulatory compliance. Existing modern decentralized retrieval techniques either reintroduce a coordinating authority, or rely on a global data structure that requires continuous network-wide coordination (e.g., DHTs). We present ZeroRAG, a decentralized routing layer for document retrieval in RAG that performs semantic query routing across an overlay of peers with- out global data structures or centralized orchestration. Documents remain with the peers that own them, and each peer keeps only lightweight local state: a bounded set of neighbor advertisements and a cache of recently routed queries. Using these, ZeroRAG steers each query through a best-first walk that progressively rewires the overlay toward semantically relevant neighbors, so recall improves over time as the network self-organizes. We evaluate ZeroRAG using three real-world workloads and two decentralized baselines. We find that ZeroRAG outperforms baselines in terms of recall and required network messages, approaches the recall and LLM answer accuracy of a centralized document store, self-heals after catastrophic peer failures, and scales to 100 000 peers.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) usually depends on a central document store, but many document owners cannot hand over custody for privacy, copyright, or regulatory reasons, and existing decentralized options either reintroduce a coordinator or need network-wide structures such as distributed hash tables (DHTs). `ZeroRAG` routes queries semantically across a peer overlay in which each peer keeps only a bounded set of neighbor advertisements and a cache of recent queries. A best-first walk forwards each query and gradually rewires the overlay toward semantically relevant neighbors, so recall improves as the network self-organizes. On three real-world workloads it beats two decentralized baselines on recall and message count, **approaches the recall and answer accuracy of a centralized store**, recovers after catastrophic peer failures, and scales to 100,000 peers.

papers.title: Flux as a Codec: Zero-Shot Lossy Compression with Flux
papers.abstract: We propose FluxC, a zero-shot codec that uses Flux as a compression prior. Although DiffC has shown that pretrained diffusion models can serve as zero-shot codecs, we ask how the choice of coding path and reconstruction method affects rate--distortion--perception behavior. We analyze FluxC along three axes: coding cost and bit allocation, reconstruction method, and low rate distortion. At matched signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), we show that the path choice does not affect the ideal information rate, but changes how bits are allocated across time steps. For reconstruction, we compare ancestral sampling, one-step ODE reconstruction, and many-step ODE reconstruction. Our analysis shows that ODE-based reconstruction can achieve lower distortion than ancestral sampling, especially in the low rate regime. Experiments on Gaussian sources and natural images support this prediction. Moreover, FluxC performs competitively with, and in some cases outperforms, recent neural image compression methods, suggesting that Flux can serve as a principled zero-shot codec.
papers.summary: Earlier work (`DiffC`) showed that pretrained diffusion models can work as zero-shot lossy codecs. `FluxC` uses the `Flux` model as the compression prior and studies how the choice of coding path and reconstruction method affects the trade-off between rate, distortion, and perceptual quality. At matched signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), the coding path leaves the ideal information rate unchanged but shifts how bits are spread across timesteps. Comparing reconstruction methods, ODE-based decoding (solving an ordinary differential equation) gives **lower distortion than ancestral sampling, especially at low bitrates**, which experiments on Gaussian sources and natural images confirm. `FluxC` is competitive with, and sometimes beats, recent neural image compression methods.

papers.title: AttnSR: Attention Step Reward for Long-Horizon Agentic RL
papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents make multi-step decisions, yet outcome-reward-only reinforcement learning provides little direct supervision for individual steps. We introduce AttnSR, a step-level reward augmentation method that derives reward allocations from policy attention extracted during training replay, without a separately trained reward model or additional rollouts. AttnSR traces backward through the policy model attention graph to estimate the relevance of earlier steps to the final response. The terminal step, measured relative to a running baseline, determines whether these rewards reinforce or penalize the selected steps. In a controlled Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct study, AttnSR consistently outperforms the PPO baseline across all evaluated checkpoints on ALFWorld, raising final held-out success from 91.2% to 97.1%. The ablation experiment shows that the benefit depends on how intermediate rewards are assigned, rather than simple accumulation of step rewards over time. AttnSR also improves ScienceWorld at every checkpoint while cutting environment interactions by 29.9%. These results support policy attention as a practical prior for step-level reward allocation in long-horizon agentic RL. Code is available at https://github.com/fairyshine/AttnSR .
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning for long-horizon LLM agents usually rewards only the final outcome, which gives little signal about which intermediate steps mattered. `AttnSR` assigns step-level rewards by tracing backward through the policy model's own attention during training replay to estimate how relevant each earlier step was to the final response, so it needs no separate reward model and no extra rollouts. The terminal outcome, compared against a running baseline, decides whether those steps are reinforced or penalized. With `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct`, it beats the `PPO` baseline at every checkpoint on `ALFWorld`, **raising held-out success from 91.2% to 97.1%**, and on `ScienceWorld` it improves every checkpoint while using 29.9% fewer environment interactions.

papers.title: The Blindfolded Controller: Decision Model-Guided Training for Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a framework for continuous improvement through interaction with an environment. However, RL agents struggle against tasks that offer exploration challenges and sparse rewards, because learning efficient policies from scratch is slow and sample-inefficient. In contrast, decision models (DMs), given a description of the environment and task, can perform well in sparse-reward tasks, but, as they do not learn from reward, they are not able to improve towards the optimal solution. In this paper, we present Decision Model-Guided Training (DMGT), a technique that uses a DM with a description of the environment and task to initialise an RL policy, combining the DM's ability to act without training with RL's ability to improve from reward. Instead of exploring from scratch, the agent reaches the goal and receives reward from its first episodes, and RL then improves its policy beyond what the DM achieves. We demonstrate through experiments on seven tasks that our approach outperforms RL in all seven and DM in five. In addition, we provide comprehensive guidelines, derived from ablation studies, for describing an environment and task to a DM.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) agents learn slowly in tasks with sparse rewards and hard exploration, while decision models (DMs) given a text description of the environment and task can act well immediately but cannot improve from reward. `Decision Model-Guided Training` (`DMGT`) uses a DM to initialize the RL policy, so the agent reaches the goal and collects reward from its first episodes and RL then improves past the DM's level. Across seven tasks, **`DMGT` outperforms plain RL on all seven and the DM alone on five**. Ablations produce practical guidelines for how to describe an environment and task to a DM.

papers.title: Towards Scalable Diagnostic-Driven Whole-Slide Image Retrieval for Pathology Archives
papers.abstract: The growing adoption of digital pathology has rapidly expanded collections of hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide images, yet efficient navigation through these archives remains challenging, as metadata is often inconsistent or unavailable. Content-based image retrieval addresses this challenge by identifying similar cases directly from visual representations instead of manual annotations or metadata. Existing retrieval systems have demonstrated promising performance but largely rely on handcrafted indexing pipelines and predefined sampling strategies, constraining scalability and generalization. Here, we present CLEAR-WSI (Constant-Length Embedding for Automatic Retrieval of Whole-Slide Images) as a scalable, diagnostic-driven slide-retrieval framework, validated on both public and clinical data. Using a fixed-length slide embedding, CLEAR-WSI refines retrieved candidates with either a predicted diagnostic label or the ground-truth label, depending on the retrieval setting. Newly processed cases are subsequently added to the expanding memory bank, allowing the retrieval archive to grow over time. On a comprehensive benchmark consisting of two public and one private clinical datasets representing four retrieval tasks, CLEAR-WSI improves Precision@5 over the strongest evaluated baseline, with gains on CAMELYON16 (3.10), BRACS-1 (2.75), BRACS-2 (1.95), and X-HER2 (3.75). Additional ablation and latency studies further examine the contribution of each component and highlight its potential for scalable deployment.
papers.summary: Digital pathology archives of hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide images are growing quickly, but inconsistent metadata makes them hard to search, and existing content-based retrieval systems depend on handcrafted indexing and fixed sampling strategies. `CLEAR-WSI` (Constant-Length Embedding for Automatic Retrieval of Whole-Slide Images) represents each slide with a fixed-length embedding, refines retrieved candidates using a predicted or ground-truth diagnostic label, and adds new cases to a growing memory bank. On two public datasets and one private clinical dataset covering four retrieval tasks, it **improves Precision@5 over the strongest baseline by 1.95 to 3.75 points**, on `CAMELYON16`, `BRACS`, and `X-HER2`. Ablation and latency studies assess each component and the method's suitability for deployment.

papers.title: Joint Modeling of Conditional Mean and Variability in Multilevel Functional Data: Application to Postprandial Glucose Trajectories in the AEGIS Study
papers.abstract: Functional data analysis provides a framework for studying time-varying associations between covariates and high-frequency biological signals. In digital health, participants often contribute repeated functional trajectories, yet existing multilevel regression methods largely focus on the conditional mean, overlooking variability and its role in biological heterogeneity. We propose a heteroskedastic functional mixed-effects regression framework that jointly models the conditional mean and variance of repeated trajectories, with participant-specific random effects in both components. We also develop a participant-level bootstrap to quantify uncertainty in estimated functional parameters. We apply the method to postprandial glucose trajectories from the AEGIS study. Premeal glucose, carbohydrate intake, and meal type show distinct time-dependent associations with glucose variability, whereas HbA1c is more strongly associated with the conditional mean than with variability. Substantial between-participant differences in residual variability remain even after accounting for observed covariates. These findings show that modeling conditional variability alongside the mean provides insights into glucose regulation and individual heterogeneity that mean-focused analyses may miss. More broadly, the proposed framework enables joint characterization of average responses, variability, and participant-specific heterogeneity in repeated biological signals.
papers.summary: Multilevel functional regression methods for repeated biological signals usually model only the conditional mean and ignore variability. The authors propose a heteroskedastic functional mixed-effects model that jointly estimates the mean and variance of repeated trajectories, with participant-specific random effects in both, plus a participant-level bootstrap for uncertainty. Applied to post-meal glucose curves from the `AEGIS` study, premeal glucose, carbohydrate intake, and meal type show distinct time-varying links to glucose variability, while HbA1c is tied more to the mean. **Large between-participant differences in variability remain after accounting for covariates**, which mean-only analyses would miss.

papers.title: CardioLM: A multilingual suite of small language models for the cardiology domain
papers.abstract:
Background: Cardiovascular care generates large volumes of clinical free-text documentation in local languages. However, clinical natural language processing (NLP) resources remain concentrated in English, and no existing benchmark is cardiology-specific, multilingual, and broad in entity coverage.
  Methods: We present two contributions. The first is CardioCCC, a corpus of 508 cardiology case reports originally published in Spanish and extended to Czech, Dutch, English, Italian, Romanian, and Swedish through machine translation, annotation projection, and clinician review, with annotations covering diseases, symptoms, procedures, and medications. The second is CardioLM, comprising CardioBERTa, a set of language-specific encoders obtained by continued pretraining on cardiology and biomedical corpora, and CardioNER, a set of named entity recognition (NER) models fine-tuned on CardioCCC.
  Results: Cardiology-specific pretraining reduced pseudo-perplexity by up to a factor of eight, yet changed strict span-level F1 by at most 0.04, with benefits concentrated in languages whose backbones lacked biomedical coverage. The jointly trained multilingual XLM-RoBERTa-large models achieved the best strict F1 in nearly every language and entity type, exceeding the strongest monolingual system by up to 0.13 F1. A large share of residual errors concerned boundary detection: relaxed matching recovered 0.10-0.23 F1 for disease, procedure, and symptom, but only 0.01-0.07 for medication. Clinicians rated CardioNER well above a rule- and dictionary-based baseline, with the mean rating across entity types rising from 26% to 73%.
  Conclusions: Specialty-specific pretraining is not the decisive factor for downstream entity recognition, whereas multilingual joint training yields the strongest results in nearly all settings and a simpler deployment path for multi-country clinical information extraction.
papers.summary: Clinical natural language processing (NLP) resources are concentrated in English, and no existing benchmark is cardiology-specific, multilingual, and broad in entity coverage. The authors release `CardioCCC`, 508 Spanish cardiology case reports extended to six more languages through machine translation, annotation projection, and clinician review, together with `CardioLM`, a set of cardiology-pretrained encoders (`CardioBERTa`) and named entity recognition (NER) models (`CardioNER`). Domain pretraining cut pseudo-perplexity by up to eightfold but changed strict F1 by at most 0.04, while **jointly trained multilingual `XLM-RoBERTa-large` models scored best in nearly every language and entity type**, by up to 0.13 F1 over the best monolingual system. Clinicians rated `CardioNER` far above a rule- and dictionary-based baseline (73% versus 26%).

papers.title: tok: a textual concrete syntax of BPMN and DMN for humans and AI agents
papers.abstract: tok is a plain-text notation for Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) 2.0.2 process models and Decision Model and Notation (DMN) 1.5 decisions. One engine checks a tok document against both standards, compiles the document to XML with an automatic diagram, and serves language-model applications through the Model Context Protocol. The paper classifies the notation as an alternative concrete syntax of the BPMN and DMN metamodels and reports one study. A tok model takes 2.2 times fewer tokens than the smallest BPMN XML of 893 files exported by 37 tools and 7.7 times fewer than the files as exported. The checker signals 98.2% of 1,411 injected faults, against 85.8% for the XML Schema with bpmnlint. Four language models new to tok write valid tok from a one-page reference for 85.7 to 100% of 87 process descriptions from two datasets and valid BPMN XML for every description, and the strongest model writes tok with 25% and 19% fewer tokens than BPMN XML. As agents with a lean skill and one checker tool, the models write valid tok for 97.6 to 100% of the descriptions, the strongest model spends 21% and 14% fewer tokens on tok than on BPMN XML, and a skill which sends the model to read the reference through a tool costs 1.7 to 2.8 times the tokens of the lean skill. Of 47 event logs simulated from public models, 44 fit their source models, and tok imports every model discovered from the logs.
papers.summary: `tok` is a plain-text notation for `BPMN` (Business Process Model and Notation) process models and `DMN` (Decision Model and Notation) decisions, with a single engine that validates documents against both standards, compiles them to XML with an automatic diagram, and serves LLM applications through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). A `tok` model uses 2.2 times fewer tokens than the smallest `BPMN` XML across 893 files from 37 tools, and the checker catches 98.2% of 1,411 injected faults, compared with 85.8% for XML Schema plus `bpmnlint`. Four LLMs that had never seen `tok` wrote valid `tok` from a one-page reference for 85.7% to 100% of 87 process descriptions, and **as agents with a lean skill and one checker tool they reached 97.6% to 100% validity**. A skill that makes the model read the reference through a tool cost 1.7 to 2.8 times as many tokens as the lean skill.

papers.title: ChemE-as-Code: An Open-Source Platform for Agentic AI in Chemical Engineering
papers.abstract: ChemE-as-Code provides an open-source environment in which AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) can carry out chemical engineering work and engineers can check it. Its calculation tools range from catalysis through process simulation to plant layout, HAZOP and life cycle assessment, and skills tell a general-purpose agent how to use them. Engineering files are linked, machine-readable and versioned in Git; calculations run outside the LLM, each value records its origin, and automated checks report inconsistencies and out-of-date results by file and line. In an illustrative ammonia case, agents developed a written task into a preliminary basic-engineering package (simulation files, P&IDs, layout, HAZOP, datasheets, relief) for USD 224 of API cost in the design sessions. Planted faults and engineering changes show that the checks find what their rules cover and miss the rest, so they guide human review rather than replace it. No independent engineer has reviewed the design.
