papers.summary: `ChemE-as-Code` is an open-source environment in which LLM agents carry out chemical engineering work and engineers can check it. It provides calculation tools from catalysis and process simulation to plant layout, hazard and operability studies (HAZOP), and life cycle assessment, plus skills that tell a general-purpose agent how to use them. Engineering files are machine-readable and versioned in Git, calculations run outside the LLM with each value's origin recorded, and automated checks flag inconsistent or outdated results by file and line. In an ammonia plant case study, agents turned a written task into a **preliminary basic-engineering package for USD 224 in API cost**. Planted faults showed that the checks catch only what their rules cover, so they support human review rather than replace it, and no independent engineer has reviewed the design.

papers.title: Circe: Training-Free LLM Self-Evaluation via Component Interaction Consistency
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, evaluating the correctness of their responses is crucial for reliable use. However, such evaluation is challenging because reference answers are rarely available in practice. Existing reference-free methods mainly rely on output signals, which may assign high scores to incorrect responses and thus do not necessarily reflect correctness. This motivates exploring the model's internal computation for complementary correctness signals. Recent studies exploit internal states, but they mainly analyze hidden-state trajectories across layers, which record only the combined updates of attention and feed-forward networks (FFNs) and overlook how these components interact. We therefore propose Circe, a training-free self-evaluation method that assesses a response using both internal and external signals, without reference answers or repeated sampling. For internal signals, we first introduce component interaction consistency (CIC), which measures the directional alignment between attention updates in earlier layers and attention-induced FFN output changes in later layers. We further incorporate representation geometry (RG) to characterize normalized displacement and angular changes along layerwise hidden-state trajectories. For the external signal, we convert the mean negative log-likelihood of generated tokens into a bounded likelihood confidence (LC) score. Finally, we fuse CIC, RG, and LC into a unified correctness score. Experiments on five LLMs and six benchmarks across four domains show that our method distinguishes correct from incorrect responses more effectively than existing baselines, and generalizes to multilingual, multimodal, and open-world settings.
papers.summary: Judging whether an LLM's answer is correct without a reference answer is hard, and output-only signals often score wrong answers highly. `Circe` is a training-free self-evaluation method that needs neither references nor repeated sampling and combines three signals into one correctness score. Component interaction consistency (CIC) measures how well attention updates in earlier layers align with the attention-driven feed-forward network (FFN) output changes in later layers, representation geometry (RG) tracks displacement and angle changes across the layer-by-layer hidden-state trajectory, and likelihood confidence (LC) turns the mean token negative log-likelihood into a bounded score. Across five LLMs and six benchmarks in four domains, **`Circe` separates correct from incorrect responses better than existing baselines**, and it generalizes to multilingual, multimodal, and open-world settings.

papers.title: Leakage- and Label-Aware Benchmarking of Class-Imbalance Strategies for Multimodal Chest X-Ray and EHR Classification
papers.abstract: Benchmarks of class-imbalance strategies for multimodal chest X-ray (CXR) and electronic health record (EHR) prediction are often evaluated on record-level splits of cohorts in which one patient contributes several radiographs. We audit such a benchmark on 29,083 MIMIC-CXR radiographs of 10,479 patients with eight diagnosis targets. First, the record-split benchmark was misleading: a lookup table that copies the label of a development-set radiograph with the same EHR vector nearly matched the best model, and on unseen patients every model fell to the level of predicting every case positive. Second, tracing the labels back to MIMIC-IV explained why: each patient's labels are keyword matches on the diagnosis codes of a single admission, copied, with one EHR vector per patient, to all of the patient's radiographs, so about a third of the radiographs carry labels that differ from the codes of their own admission. Third, under patient-separated evaluation with admission-aligned and rule-refined labels, the initial conclusions do not hold: in the evaluated configurations no imbalance strategy raised the observed mean macro F2 over no augmentation by more than 0.01, tuned tree ensembles showed no consistent advantage over tuned logistic regression, and the released EHR variables stayed at the level of the all-positive baseline, whereas the diagnostic history available at imaging time and image embeddings exceeded it, including, with rule-refined labels, a CheXpert-trained encoder that never saw these radiographs; RAD-DINO had seen 96.6% of them during self-supervised pretraining. Adding either encoder to the diagnostic history gave no statistically significant F2 gain; exploratory AUROC gains were significant with RAD-DINO but not with DenseNet. We provide reusable diagnostics, a leakage-aware protocol and a checklist.
papers.summary: The authors audit a benchmark of class-imbalance strategies for multimodal chest X-ray (CXR) and electronic health record (EHR) diagnosis built on 29,083 `MIMIC-CXR` radiographs from 10,479 patients. Under the benchmark's record-level splits, a lookup table that copies the label of a development-set radiograph with the same EHR vector nearly matched the best model, and **on unseen patients every model fell to the level of predicting every case positive**. The labels turn out to be keyword matches on a single admission's diagnosis codes copied to all of a patient's radiographs, so about a third of images carry labels from the wrong admission. With patient-separated splits and corrected labels, no imbalance strategy improved macro F2 by more than 0.01 and tuned tree ensembles showed no consistent edge over logistic regression. Only diagnostic history and image embeddings beat the all-positive baseline, and the authors provide a leakage-aware protocol and checklist.

papers.title: Invariance before structure: two modes of emergent compression in representation learning
papers.abstract: Learned representations show striking invariance across biological and artificial neural networks, with different substrates and variations driven by drift, heterogeneity and initialisation. To understand this invariance, we propose Emergent Adaptive Representation Learning (EARL), a framework that distinguishes two modes of emergence in learned representations: state-space compression, where a learned representation gains predictive power over its own future beyond what the network's units can predict individually, and parameter-space compression, where networks with different micro-level parameters converge to the same representation. We formalise both as Fisher sensitivities and introduce ensemble-level information-theoretic measures for each. In a recurrent reservoir with a trained bottleneck, parameter-space compression rises within the first few epochs of training and partly independently of the task, whereas state-space compression rises about 30 epochs later and only when the network begins to learn the temporal structure of the task. These results suggest that invariance to the substrate and task-specific emergent structure are acquired in distinct phases of learning.
papers.summary: Learned representations look strikingly similar across biological and artificial networks despite different substrates, drift, and initialization. `EARL` (Emergent Adaptive Representation Learning) separates two kinds of emergence: state-space compression, where a representation predicts its own future better than its units do individually, and parameter-space compression, where networks with different parameters converge to the same representation. Both are formalized as Fisher sensitivities and measured with ensemble-level information-theoretic quantities. In a recurrent reservoir with a trained bottleneck, **parameter-space compression rises within the first few epochs and partly independently of the task, while state-space compression appears about 30 epochs later**, once the network starts learning the task's temporal structure.

papers.title: A Behavioural Framework for Predicting and Understanding Loss of Control in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Systems
papers.abstract: Frontier artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly operating over longer horizons with diminishing human oversight, raising the risk of loss of control: systems acting beyond effective human control with potentially irreversible consequences. Because such failures may become observable only after containment is difficult, they must be assessed prospectively. We introduce a behavioural framework that decomposes loss-of-control risk into three factors: misaligned motive, harm-enabling capability, and monitoring evasion. We operationalise these factors through 13 measurable aspects and 29 evaluation tasks, whose scores are combined into a single loss-of-control (LoC) score. Across 13 frontier models, the LoC score shows strong prospective validity, correlating with failure rates in contained long-horizon risk scenarios (Pearson r = 0.84). Risk varies systematically across models and cannot be explained by capability alone. We further show that the framework can guide targeted mitigations: fine-tuning and monitoring directed at diagnosed vulnerabilities reduce failure rates while largely preserving general performance. These results provide a practical basis for predicting, understanding, and mitigating loss-of-control risk before it materialises.
papers.summary: Frontier AI systems now run over longer horizons with less human oversight, so failures that put them beyond human control may only become visible once they are hard to contain. The authors split loss-of-control risk into three factors: misaligned motive, harm-enabling capability, and monitoring evasion. They measure these through 13 aspects and 29 evaluation tasks, which combine into a single loss-of-control (LoC) score. Across 13 frontier models, the score predicts failure rates in contained long-horizon risk scenarios with **Pearson r = 0.84**, and capability alone does not explain the risk. Fine-tuning and monitoring aimed at each model's diagnosed weak points lowered failure rates while largely preserving general performance.

papers.title: CoRD: Coupled Rollouts Fill the Blind Spot of On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation trains a student on its own rollouts, so states the teacher would reach but the student does not are seldom supervised. We introduce CoRD (coupled-rollout distillation), which keeps the on-policy loss and moves only the distribution of training states toward the teacher, drawing rollouts from a geometric interpolation of student and teacher through the maximal coupling of speculative decoding. The coupling keeps the student's token wherever the two distributions agree and otherwise substitutes a token from the part of the target the student underweights, so interventions are as rare as any exact sampler allows and recede as the student learns. Across six base students from two model families (Qwen3 and Qwen3.5, 0.6B to 4B), CoRD raises average pass@1 over on-policy distillation by 0.9 to 2.0 points and pass@8 by 1.2 to 3.4 points on five public math benchmarks at equal steps and data. On frozen teacher-reached states, a 4B student trained with CoRD reaches in 16 steps a gap closure that on-policy distillation does not reach in 80, and substitution rules intervening at least as often in other directions fall short of CoRD.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation trains a student model on its own rollouts, so states the teacher would reach but the student does not are rarely supervised. `CoRD` (coupled-rollout distillation) keeps the on-policy loss but draws rollouts from a geometric interpolation of student and teacher, using the maximal coupling from speculative decoding. The coupling keeps the student's token wherever the two distributions agree and substitutes a teacher-leaning token only where the student underweights it, so interventions fade as the student learns. Across six `Qwen3` and `Qwen3.5` students from 0.6B to 4B parameters, `CoRD` raises pass@1 by 0.9–2.0 points and pass@8 by 1.2–3.4 points on five math benchmarks at equal steps and data. On states the teacher reaches, a 4B student **closes as much of the gap in 16 steps as standard on-policy distillation does not reach in 80**.

papers.title: TCSExam: Evaluating Frontier LLMs on the Full Range of TCS Research
papers.abstract: Can large language models (LLMs) advance theoretical computer science and resolve its long-standing open conjectures? To study progress toward this goal, we introduce TCSExam, a unified framework and benchmark covering the full range of TCS research. It evaluates theorem proving, solver engineering, and constructions alongside direct attempts to resolve open conjectures, capturing both concrete research accomplishments and progress toward long-standing research goals. TCSExam-Full contains 100 expert-reviewed tasks, with submissions checked by the Lean kernel or an executable task checker. TCSExam-Lite selects 20 tasks, five per track, reducing the number of task attempts by 80% at the same per-attempt budget. We evaluate eight agents on Full and nine on Lite. The TCSExam Index combines all four tracks: GPT-6 Astra leads Full (71.9), and Opus 5.5 leads Lite (72.3). Full and Lite rankings are strongly aligned across eight shared agents (Spearman's $\rho=0.93$), supporting Lite as a compact, discriminative benchmark. The evaluations yield improved solver outputs and mathematical constructions, together with independently verified special cases and bounds from open-conjecture attempts. TCSExam provides an extensible framework with task sources, Docker build recipes, and evaluation tools for reproducible use.
papers.summary: `TCSExam` is a benchmark that tests whether LLM agents can do research across theoretical computer science (TCS). Its four tracks are theorem proving, solver engineering, mathematical constructions, and direct attempts at open conjectures. The full version has 100 expert-reviewed tasks, each checked by the Lean kernel or an executable checker, and a 20-task `TCSExam-Lite` cuts evaluation cost by 80%. `GPT-6 Astra` leads the full benchmark (71.9) and `Opus 5.5` leads Lite (72.3), and **the two versions rank models almost identically (Spearman ρ = 0.93)**. The runs also produced improved solver outputs and constructions, plus independently verified special cases and bounds on open conjectures.

papers.title: Tight Asymptotic Bounds on the Maximum Number of Linear Regions of Piecewise-Linear Kolmogorov--Arnold networks
papers.abstract: Schoots et al.~\citep{schoots2025relating} (AISTATS 2025) established a generally loose upper bound on the number of linear regions of continuous piecewise-linear (CPWL) Kolmogorov--Arnold networks (KANs), without providing a lower bound. We consider a $T$-layer network with width vector $\mathbf n=(n_0,\ldots,n_T)$, input dimension $n_0=d$, output width $n_T=1$, and at most $k\geq2$ affine segments per edge. Our matching upper and lower bounds determine the tight growth order $\Theta_{\mathbf n}(k^{\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}\rho_{\ell-1}})$ in $k$, where $\rho_{\ell-1}:=\min_{0\leq s\leq\ell-1}n_s$. When every hidden width is at least $d$, the tight order simplifies to $\Theta_{\mathbf n}(k^{dT})$. The upper bound of \citep{schoots2025relating} is $k^{\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}n_{\ell-1}n_\ell}$. Our upper bound improves it by a factor of $\Theta_{\mathbf n}\!\left(k^{\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}n_{\ell-1}n_\ell-\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}\rho_{\ell-1}} \right)$, with strict asymptotic improvement whenever a hidden layer has width greater than one. We further compare CPWL KANs with rectified linear unit (ReLU) networks using dense parameterizations with at most $\Lambda$ parameters per model and the same fixed nonlinear depth $T$. Counting trainable knot locations and optimizing the widths and $k$, we prove that the maximum region count of CPWL KANs divided by that of ReLU networks is $\Theta_{d,T}(\Lambda^{d\lfloor T/2\rfloor})$ as $\Lambda\to\infty$, yielding a polynomial advantage for KANs when $T\geq2$. These tight bounds characterize the attainable geometric complexity of CPWL KANs, providing a foundation for understanding their expressive power and guiding architectural design.
papers.summary: The work studies how many linear regions a continuous piecewise-linear Kolmogorov–Arnold network (KAN) can carve its input space into. Earlier work gave only a loose upper bound. The authors prove matching upper and lower bounds, giving a tight growth order in the number of affine segments per edge; when every hidden layer is at least as wide as the input, this simplifies to k^(dT). Comparing against rectified linear unit (ReLU) networks with the same parameter budget and depth, they show that **piecewise-linear KANs have a polynomial advantage in maximum region count once depth is at least two**.

papers.title: QRAE: Query-Relevant Attention Entropy for Context Compression in DeepSearch Agents
papers.abstract: DeepSearch LLM agents repeatedly search and carry retrieved sources into subsequent reasoning steps. This expanding context increases token consumption and latency, although many results do not contribute to later reasoning. We propose Query-Relevant Attention Entropy (QRAE), an online context compression method that uses sparse evidence-assessment heads to decide which intact retrieved chunks should persist across reasoning steps. It scores bounded candidate batches through paired prefills: a query-free control suppresses shared attention responses, while normalized entropy measures the breadth of the positive response within each chunk. High-scoring chunks enter a persistent evidence whitelist and are included in the reasoning context. Uncertain chunks remain outside the reasoning context but are retained in a candidate cache, where they can be retrieved for later reevaluation. QRAE requires neither an additional generative compression pass nor modification of the attention operator. Across multiple DeepSearch benchmarks and reasoning models, QRAE improves task success by an average of 2.35 percentage points and reduces end-to-end latency and reported token usage by an average of 30% and 45%, respectively. These benefits generalize to a model with nearly 100B parameters.
papers.summary: DeepSearch LLM agents carry every retrieved source into later reasoning steps, which raises token use and latency even though many results are never used. `QRAE` (Query-Relevant Attention Entropy) compresses the context online by deciding which intact retrieved chunks should persist. It uses a small set of attention heads that assess evidence, compares runs with and without the query, and measures how broadly each chunk responds. High-scoring chunks enter the reasoning context, while uncertain ones are cached for later re-evaluation, with no extra generation pass or change to the attention operator. Across several DeepSearch benchmarks and reasoning models, `QRAE` raises task success by 2.35 points on average while **cutting latency by about 30% and token usage by about 45%**, and the gains hold for a model of nearly 100B parameters.

papers.title: Technohybridism: Recursive Semantic Normalization in AI-Mediated Societies
papers.abstract: Language-generating AI systems are no longer only objects of linguistic interaction: their outputs increasingly re-enter the communicative and institutional practices from which their training material was drawn. Drawing on social theory, social epistemology, and the philosophy of language, this article develops a sociotechnical account of that re-entry. We introduce recursive semantic normalization: the process through which machine-generated formulations, once recurrently taken up, evaluated, reused, and institutionally retained, participate in the reproduction and transformation of semantic regularities. Under the heading of technohybridism, we argue that the relevant unit of analysis is the hybrid semantic system, a recursively coupled configuration of human practices, computational generation, and institutional uptake. First, we distinguish the concept from neighbouring accounts, including model collapse, looping effects, machine habitus, machine culture, and the epistemology of AI testimony. Second, we develop an analytical model that separates generation, selection, uptake, and persistence and distinguishes machine-attributable change from change that would have occurred anyway. Third, we analyse uptake as routinized, institutionally diffused, and socially stratified practice and state conditions under which machine-derived regularities become norms. Fourth, we identify social-epistemic consequences: the laundering of provenance that weakens epistemic vigilance, the erosion of the cognitive diversity on which collective inquiry depends, and the narrowing of shared hermeneutical resources. An evidential ladder for empirical research follows. The account attributes no normative authority to machine outputs; what changes is the field within which human and institutional uptake operates.
papers.summary: This theoretical essay examines what happens when text produced by language-generating AI flows back into the human and institutional practices its training data came from. Drawing on social theory and philosophy of language, it introduces **recursive semantic normalization**: machine-generated phrasings that are repeatedly adopted, reused, and retained by institutions come to shape shared meanings. The essay separates the stages of generation, selection, uptake, and persistence, and distinguishes its idea from related ones such as model collapse and machine culture. It identifies risks including hidden provenance that weakens scrutiny, reduced cognitive diversity, and narrower shared interpretive resources, and it proposes a ladder of evidence for empirical study.

papers.title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction
papers.abstract: It is well established that molecular substructures can contribute unequally to chemical and physical properties, with specific motifs or side chains often playing dominant roles. Fragment-based representations have therefore emerged as an effective strategy for incorporating chemically meaningful inductive biases, as exemplified by molecular fingerprints and fragment-based attention mechanisms. However, many existing fragmentation-based machine learning methods rely on predefined chemical rules, which may yield suboptimal fragmentation for previously unseen or chemically unfamiliar structures and often overlook the importance of multiscale molecular representations. To address these limitations, we formulate molecular fragmentation as a radius-constrained optimization problem inspired by the k-center formulation, where the number of clusters is not fixed a priori but emerges from the specified radius, and propose a geometry-based fragmentation method that partitions arbitrary molecular or material structures using largely geometric information, without relying on predefined chemical fragmentation rules. The method provides flexible control over fragment size, enabling the construction of multiscale fragment representations for scale-adaptive modeling. Building on this framework, we develop a geometric fragment-based attention mechanism that integrates multiscale structural information and incorporate it into a multimodal machine learning model combining p-SMILES representations with three-dimensional (3D) conformational information. Experiments on a benchmark polymer dataset show that incorporating 3D conformational information improves prediction accuracy for several properties over models based exclusively on p-SMILES representations. Explainable artificial intelligence analyses further provide insights into the physical relevance of the learned representations.
papers.summary: Machine learning models for molecules often split structures into fragments using fixed chemical rules, which can fit unfamiliar structures poorly and ignore that structure matters at several scales. The authors instead fragment molecules by geometry, posing it as a radius-constrained clustering problem similar to k-center, where the number of fragments follows from the chosen radius. The resulting multiscale fragments drive an attention mechanism inside a multimodal model that combines `p-SMILES` strings with 3D conformations. On a benchmark polymer dataset, **adding 3D conformational information improves prediction accuracy for several properties** over models that use `p-SMILES` alone, and explainability analyses link the learned representations to physical properties.

papers.title: Learning Dynamics of On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is emerging as an important paradigm for language-model post-training, combining dense teacher supervision with training on student-generated trajectories. This creates a feedback loop where each update changes the student and thereby the training distribution that generates subsequent updates. Yet, how this feedback shapes learning and generalization remains poorly understood. We conduct a mechanistic analysis of OPD's learning dynamics, distinguishing the two feedback loop stages: conversion of the distillation signal into parameter updates, and broadcast through which these updates change predictions across prefixes and reshape the rollout distribution. This framework helps us understand both limited student responsiveness despite substantial teacher-student disagreement, and degeneration when updates that improve local teacher agreement also increase the probability of unsuccessful continuations, exposing the student to unreliable supervision in subsequent rollouts. Finally, we show that offline distillation can prepare a student for OPD without significantly improving immediate held-out accuracy. While OPD alone may degrade generation, it can yield substantial accuracy gains after sufficient offline preparation. Together, our results connect teacher supervision, student geometry, and the evolving rollout distribution in determining the learning dynamics of OPD and its effects on downstream performance.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own outputs with dense supervision from a teacher, so each update changes the data that produces the next update. The authors analyze this feedback loop in two stages: how the teacher's signal becomes parameter updates, and how those updates change predictions across prefixes and reshape later rollouts. The analysis explains why students can respond weakly despite large disagreement with the teacher, and why training can degenerate when updates that improve local agreement also make unsuccessful continuations more likely. They also find that **offline distillation first can prepare a student so that OPD yields large accuracy gains**, even though the offline phase barely improves held-out accuracy on its own.
papers.highlight_summary:
On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts against a teacher's next-token distributions, so every update also changes which prefixes the student will be trained on next. The authors use a tangent-kernel framework to split this feedback loop into two stages: **conversion**, where teacher–student disagreement becomes parameter updates, and **broadcast**, where those updates shift predictions and the rollout distribution at other prefixes.

- The teacher's per-prefix disagreement signal (the "request field") converts into policy motion with a gain that factors into **accessibility × coherence**. Accessibility is how responsive the student's tangent map is to the request, and coherence is how well per-prefix gradients add up rather than cancel. Broadcast is split into **routing** (changes in which prefixes get visited) and **drift** (changes in predictions at a fixed prefix).
- Larger same-family teachers (`DeepSeek-7B/14B`) stall even though they score higher on benchmarks, while RL-trained siblings (`JustRL-1.5B`, `AceReason-Nemotron-7B`) transfer well. At 7B, the healthy teacher's requests have **2.75–3.24× higher coherence** and **2.27–2.62× higher collective gain**. At 1.5B, the healthy run's kernel reorients toward the teacher's requests and its leading eigenvalue strength grows to **2.31×** by step 200, while the stalled run's shrinks to **0.67×**.
- Degeneration has a clear mechanism. When `JustRL-1.5B` teaches `Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct`, the student is routed into long, high-entropy rollouts where the teacher itself is unconfident: loss rises **0.58 → 0.85** over steps 1–20, driven mainly by routing. The student then spends later training fitting that unreliable supervision, and its MATH accuracy drops within 100 steps. By step 100 its probability of committing to an answer falls from **0.74 to 0.07**, and the "continue" branch reaches a correct answer only **8%** of the time.
- Offline distillation on teacher solutions before OPD barely moves immediate accuracy but changes what OPD can achieve. At 1.5B, one to four preparation passes leave strict `MATH-500` pass@1 at 45.7–47.1%, yet raise the 100-step OPD endpoint from **45.9% to 56.2%**. Across `Qwen-2.5` and `Llama-3.1` students, the prepared OPD runs beat compute-matched offline training on pooled `AIME 2024/2025` pass@k up to k=32 and on per-problem solve rates.
- The experiments cover only mathematical reasoning and a small set of model families. Routing and drift are estimated over 20-step windows rather than per step, and the continuation-advantage term is only approximated with probe rollouts.

papers.title: GTAFL: Addressing Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning in Medical Image
papers.abstract: In healthcare, protecting patient privacy is crucial due to the sensitivity of medical data and its extensive accessibility. Federated Learning (FL) offers a decentralized and privacy-preserving training paradigm, making it an ideal solution for healthcare applications. A critical challenge in healthcare is that real-world medical data often exhibits long-tailed distributions in local and global views. Existing methods addressing long-tailed FL problem typically assume that the model will be evaluated on uniform test data distribution. However, practical test data in healthcare systems is often agnostic and unpredictable, leading to potential model failures in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we introduce a novel task termed Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning and propose GTAFL, a comprehensive framework to address this challenge. During the training stage, GTAFL employs adaptive re-sampling, expert classifier retraining, and self-supervised learning to correct biased classifiers and distorted feature spaces caused by long-tailed training distributions. During the inference stage, an ensemble mechanism combines retrained expert classifiers to handle test data with unknown distributions. Extensive experiments on CIFAR10 and two medical datasets manifest that our framework outperforms other state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/cgy-lavine/GTAFL
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) lets hospitals train a shared model without pooling patient data, but medical data is often long-tailed, with a few common classes and many rare ones. Existing long-tailed FL methods assume the test set has a uniform class distribution, which real clinical data often does not. `GTAFL` targets this test-agnostic setting by using adaptive re-sampling, retrained expert classifiers, and self-supervised learning during training, then ensembling the experts at inference to handle unknown test distributions. On `CIFAR10` and two medical datasets, the framework **outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods**.

papers.title: Reproducing Kernel (Quasi-)Banach Spaces with the $\ell^p$ Coefficient Norms
papers.abstract:
This paper advances the theory of reproducing kernel Banach spaces (RKBSs) by investigating the general $\ell^p$ regularization framework, with a particular focus on the non-convex regime $0<p<1$.
  While our preceding work established the foundation for RKBSs with the $\ell^1$ norm, the pursuit of stronger sparsity---closer to the $\ell^0$ pseudo-norm---naturally motivates this exploration into $\ell^p$ quasi-norms.
  For $0<p<1$, we construct reproducing kernel quasi-Banach spaces (RKQBSs) with $\ell^p$ quasi-norms and establish existence and sparsity results for interpolation and regularized learning under appropriate assumptions.
  We characterize the linear and relaxed representer theorems in terms of a generalized Lebesgue constant and derive bounds under kernel decay, sample spacing, and stability assumptions.
  For $p>1$, we construct RKBSs using a fixed countable dictionary, establish minimizer existence, and identify the optimal relaxed representer factor through an off-sample coefficient operator.
  These results reveal fundamental differences between the regimes $0<p<1$, $p=1$, and $p>1$.
  Numerical experiments compare the accuracy and sparsity of solutions for these three cases.
papers.summary: Building on earlier work with ℓ¹ norms, this work extends reproducing kernel Banach spaces (RKBSs) to general ℓ^p coefficient norms, aiming at sparser solutions that come closer to the ℓ⁰ pseudo-norm. For 0 < p < 1, the authors build reproducing kernel quasi-Banach spaces and prove that interpolation and regularized learning problems have sparse solutions under suitable assumptions. They characterize representer theorems through a generalized Lebesgue constant and derive bounds based on kernel decay and sample spacing. For p > 1, they build spaces from a fixed countable dictionary. The results and numerical experiments show **fundamentally different behavior in the three regimes 0 < p < 1, p = 1, and p > 1**.

papers.title: Should We Pay This Much for Robustness? Efficient Proxy Certificates with Marginal Guarantees
papers.abstract: Modern classifiers remain sensitive to small input perturbations, while strong model-agnostic robustness certificates such as randomized smoothing are often too expensive for deployment, requiring an extensive number (e.g. 2000) of model forward passes per input. We propose a framework that delegates certification to a cheap proxy function while statistically controlling its deviation from the original sound certificate. Given an exchangeable unlabeled calibration set, we tune the proxy via robust conformal risk control to guarantee a bounded marginal (rather than pointwise) false-approval rate: the probability, over future inputs, that the proxy accepts an input whose prediction is flipped due to perturbation. The resulting proxy certificate can be used either as a standalone marginal certificate or as a fallback mechanism that invokes the expensive certificate only when the proxy rejects. We provide both single-sample and sample-heavy calibration recipes. Empirically, as a standalone certificate our method reduces the test-time certification cost to a single model forward while retaining much of the certified performance of randomized smoothing at small radii, and as a fallback it recovers the certified ratio of randomized smoothing at a more modest speedup. This enables cheap yet effective robustness guarantees for larger architectures such as vision transformers and language models.
papers.summary: Robustness certificates such as randomized smoothing prove a classifier's prediction will not flip under small input changes, but they can need around 2000 forward passes per input. The authors hand certification to a cheap proxy function and tune it with robust conformal risk control on unlabeled calibration data. This bounds the marginal false-approval rate, meaning the chance across future inputs that the proxy approves an input whose prediction actually flips. The proxy can serve as a standalone certificate, or as a fallback that calls the expensive certificate only when the proxy rejects. As a standalone certificate, it **cuts test-time cost to a single forward pass** while keeping much of randomized smoothing's certified performance at small radii, which makes certificates practical for vision transformers and language models.

papers.title: Secure Formal Raising: Protecting the Development of AI through Executable Properties
papers.abstract: Model raising revisits Turing's developmental view of machine intelligence. Formal Raising (FR) has recently been proposed to complement this view with explicit behavioral properties. This paper extends that proposal to the security of the raising environment. Secure Formal Raising (SFR) models policy integrity, authorization, and confidential data flow using four-valued evidence that preserves unknown and inconsistent assessments. We prove six security invariants and show that they force admission to accept only confirmed evidence. A plain-C reference implementation satisfies the invariants in a bounded exhaustive exploration, which also exposes a confused-deputy gap for tool calls that a provenance requirement closes.
papers.summary: Formal Raising treats building an AI system as a developmental process governed by explicit behavioral properties. `Secure Formal Raising` extends it to the security of that development environment, modeling policy integrity, authorization, and confidential data flow with four-valued evidence that can represent unknown and contradictory assessments. The authors prove six security invariants that **force the system to admit only confirmed evidence**. A reference implementation in plain C satisfies the invariants under bounded exhaustive exploration. That exploration also exposed a confused-deputy gap in tool calls, which a provenance requirement closes.

papers.title: KeHoSu: Keyed Homoglyph Substitution for Authenticated Text Provenance over Copy-Paste Channels
papers.abstract: Nowadays, large language models produce text at scale, and much of it is redistributed across platforms. A moderator who finds a suspicious comment, post or article may want to know which platform generated it and for which account. In this paper we study attribution over the channel through which such text actually travels, copy-paste, which discards document metadata but keeps Unicode code points. We present KeHoSu, which turns the confusable characters of homoglyph attacks into a keyed attribution channel: the variant chosen for each carrier letter encodes one bit of an identifier made of a platform field, a user field and a truncated authentication tag. Moreover, given that reshared text is often quoted in fragments, and the placement therefore keeps no positional state, we show that KeHoSu is invariant to sentence reordering up to a constant boundary layer and depends on a partial quotation only through the retained length. We characterize the code-point channel by its capacity, removability and detectability, and provide an achievable region that relates the three. We evaluate KeHoSu over a wide range of use cases and show that the mark survived copy-paste across 18 common platforms, attributing the majority of all excerpts to the correct account at 178 letters (about two sentences) on LLM-generated stories and 167 letters (about one sentence) on standard English prose.
papers.summary: When LLM-generated text spreads by copy-paste, document metadata is lost but Unicode code points survive. `KeHoSu` (keyed homoglyph substitution) uses look-alike characters to embed a keyed identifier in the text, with each carrier letter encoding one bit of a platform field, a user field, and a truncated authentication tag. Because the mark carries no positional state, it survives sentence reordering and partial quotation, and the authors characterize the channel's capacity, how easily it can be removed, and how easily it can be detected. The mark survived copy-paste across 18 common platforms and **attributed most excerpts to the correct account from about 170 letters**, roughly one or two sentences.

papers.title: Performance metrics in machine learning: a scenario-based guide from the confusion matrix to calibration, regression and uncertainty
papers.abstract: Performance metrics can yield different conclusions from the same predictions. This methodological tutorial explains the effects of class prevalence, decision thresholds, aggregation rules and software conventions through controlled scenarios. Twenty-two confusion-matrix metrics are organized in a prevalence-coded map. Fifteen scenarios cover binary and multi-class classification, score discrimination, probability calibration, regression, uncertainty and consistency checks. Inputs are fixed in released files, and one factor is varied in each scenario. All 205 verification checks passed; 202 were independent and 3 were internal. An always-negative rule achieved an accuracy of 0.990 at a prevalence of 0.010, with balanced accuracy of 0.500. At fixed sensitivity and specificity, precision fell from 0.889 to 0.008 as prevalence fell from 0.5 to 0.001. Three probability variants shared a ROC-AUC of 0.825 but had calibration slopes of 2.08, 1.04 and 0.52. With 10 participants, participant-majority accuracy of 0.700 had a 95% interval of 0.348-0.933. Fold-averaged scores were falsely flagged as inconsistent under an inappropriate pooled-test-set model. A goal-based metric table and a reporting checklist are provided. The scenarios illustrate mechanisms and do not estimate their frequency in published studies. A literature audit and a real-data demonstration are specified as future protocols and were not executed.
papers.summary: This tutorial shows through controlled scenarios how the same predictions can lead to different conclusions depending on class prevalence, decision thresholds, how results are aggregated, and software conventions. It maps 22 confusion-matrix metrics by their dependence on prevalence and works through 15 scenarios covering classification, calibration, regression, and uncertainty, varying one factor at a time from fixed released inputs. Examples include a rule that always predicts negative reaching 0.990 accuracy but only 0.500 balanced accuracy, and **precision falling from 0.889 to 0.008 as prevalence drops, with sensitivity and specificity held fixed**. A goal-based metric table and a reporting checklist are included.

papers.title: When Imperfect Automated Fact-Checking Backfires: Social Learning in the Presence of Misinformation
papers.abstract: Automated fact-checking tools, cheap and fast but imperfect, are increasingly available on social platforms. We study when such tools can backfire in a sequential social learning model of misinformation. Agents observe an article's reliability and their predecessors' actions, which indicate whether they liked or disliked the article. They may also pay to fact-check it. We examine how welfare, defined as the probability of a correct cascade, changes when a free, error-prone automated tool supplements costly but perfectly accurate manual fact-checking. Two opposing effects arise. Broader use of fact-checking helps agents escape wrong cascades. At the same time, errors from the automated tool can mislead agents who would otherwise have verified the article perfectly, reducing the likelihood of correct cascades. We prove that adding the tool strictly lowers welfare for articles of intermediate reliability when truthful articles are not too informative and manual checking is sufficiently costly. Simulations show that the tool can help on either side of the intermediate range, and that it improves on manual-only checking on average only above a threshold accuracy.
papers.summary: The authors model social learning about misinformation as a sequence of agents. Each agent sees an article's reliability and earlier agents' reactions, and can pay for perfect manual fact-checking. They then ask what happens when a free but error-prone automated fact-checker is added. Wider checking helps agents escape wrong cascades, but the tool's errors can mislead agents who would otherwise have verified the article correctly. They prove that **the tool strictly lowers the probability of a correct cascade for articles of intermediate reliability** when manual checking is costly enough, and simulations show it helps on average only above a threshold accuracy.

papers.title: NutriVisRAG: Multimodal Exemplar Grounding for Nutrient Estimation with Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Diet is a major determinant of health, yet accurate dietary assessment from free-living meal images remains challenging. Existing retrieval-based Vision-Language Model (VLM) approaches to nutrient estimation typically rely on textual food representations, while, to our knowledge, direct grounding on visually similar annotated meals has not been investigated. We present NutriVisRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation framework that uses a vision encoder to retrieve similar meals with known nutritional annotations and provide them as multimodal in-context exemplars for VLM nutrient estimation at inference time, without task-specific fine-tuning. We evaluate NutriVisRAG across four datasets, four VLMs, three retrieval encoders, and two prompting strategies, including free-living meals from adults with insulin-treated diabetes, where carbohydrate estimates are compared against two dietitians' annotations. Across all 96 configurations (4 datasets x 4 VLMs x 3 retrieval encoders x 2 prompting strategies), NutriVisRAG reduced the primary estimation error in 56, with improvements more frequent under whole-meal (35/48) than per-item prompting (21/48). Across the evaluated configurations, the lowest NutriVisRAG error was below the best Vanilla error in 13 of 16 VLM--dataset pairs. For GPT-5.4-mini, under whole-meal prompting, the best-performing retrieval encoder for each dataset reduced the primary error on all four datasets relative to Vanilla, with reductions of 1.7--35.7%. Overall, our results show that grounding in multimodal exemplars comprising images and respective annotations can improve nutrient estimation at inference time without task-specific fine-tuning, although the benefits remain configuration-dependent.
papers.summary: `NutriVisRAG` estimates nutrients from meal photos with vision-language models (VLMs). A vision encoder retrieves visually similar meals with known nutrition labels and supplies them as image-and-annotation examples in the prompt, with no task-specific fine-tuning. The evaluation spans 96 configurations of four datasets, four VLMs, three retrieval encoders, and two prompting strategies, including meals from adults with insulin-treated diabetes compared against dietitians' carbohydrate annotations. Retrieval reduced error in 56 of the 96 configurations, and **its best configuration beat the best non-retrieval baseline in 13 of 16 model–dataset pairs**, although the benefit depends on the setup.

papers.title: Can an LLM Actually Reason and Program about Neural Network's Weights or is it just memorization on steroids? Exploring "Weight-Space Programming"
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been reported to read and write the raw weights of neural networks directly, a capability termed weight-space programming. We ask whether the reading side of this capability reflects reasoning about weight flows or a combination of local arithmetic at the network's edges and memorized priors over public datasets. We test Claude Opus 5.5 on small convolutional networks of about 125,000 parameters trained on five image datasets, providing every weight as plain text with no tools, no forward passes, and no dataset or class names. The model performs accurate local calculations: batch-normalization statistics lead it to infer about three optimizer steps on networks stopped after three updates, and output-layer sign patterns recover the vehicle/animal split of CIFAR-10. The sessions report reading the first and last layers closely and sampling the middle, and several claims built on partial tracing fail verification, although we did not run a direct forward-pass test. Semantic judgments lean on familiar datasets: the model names CIFAR-10 for CIFAR-10 networks but also for all three fast-food networks, relabels KMNIST as MNIST, reads a 99.57%-accurate SAT-6 network as CIFAR-10 animal photos, and calls "frog" the output favored by a feature that fires most on trees. Permuting CIFAR-10's labels preserves the output split at the new indices, but every class pair the model interprets is then wrong, indicating reliance on remembered label order. These are exploratory results from mostly single runs. We conclude that zero-shot weight reading by this model is better described as local arithmetic plus dataset priors than as weight-flow tracing, and we provide a protocol for auditing future weight-space claims.
papers.summary: LLMs have been reported to read and write raw neural network weights directly, and this exploratory study tests whether the reading side reflects genuine reasoning. `Claude Opus 5.5` received every weight of small convolutional networks (about 125,000 parameters) as plain text, with no tools and no dataset or class names. It calculated well at the network's input and output layers, for example inferring roughly how many optimizer steps a network had taken and recovering `CIFAR-10`'s vehicle/animal split. Its semantic judgments, however, leaned on familiar datasets: it labeled fast-food and satellite networks as `CIFAR-10`, and **after `CIFAR-10`'s labels were permuted, every class pair it interpreted was wrong**, showing it relied on a remembered label order. The authors conclude that zero-shot weight reading is best described as local arithmetic plus dataset priors, and they propose a protocol for auditing such claims.

papers.title: Optimal Competitive Ratios for Chasing Convex Functions with Quadratic Growth
papers.abstract:
Chasing convex function has attracted much attention in recent years, which can be formulated as a game between a learner and an adversary. In each round, the adversary reveals a convex function, and the learner selects a decision and incurs a hitting cost and a movement cost for changing its decision. The performance of the learner is measured by the \emph{competitive ratio}, which compares its cumulative cost with that of an optimal offline decision sequence. For Euclidean movement, existing upper and lower bounds for $\kappa$-well-conditioned functions exhibit a polynomial gap. For squared Euclidean movement, dimension-free competitive guarantees have been established under quadratic growth, but the optimal competitive ratio remains unclear.
  In this paper, we establish optimal dimension-free competitive ratios for convex function chasing under two types of movement costs. For Euclidean movement, we propose Clipped Proximal Descent (CPD), which combines a balanced proximal step with a clipped correction toward the current minimizer. CPD achieves an $O(\kappa^{1/3})$ competitive ratio for smooth convex functions satisfying quadratic growth, improving the previous $O(\sqrt{\kappa})$ upper bound and matching the existing $\Omega(\kappa^{1/3})$ lower bound. For squared Euclidean movement, we establish the exact optimal dimension-free competitive ratio for convex functions satisfying quadratic growth. Our result is based on a new tight competitive analysis of Regularized Online Balanced Descent (R-OBD) and a matching lower bound against randomized algorithms.
papers.summary: In convex function chasing, a learner faces a new convex cost each round and pays both that cost and a cost for moving its decision, and is judged by its competitive ratio against the best offline sequence. For Euclidean movement costs, the authors propose `Clipped Proximal Descent`, which achieves **an O(κ^(1/3)) competitive ratio for smooth functions with quadratic growth, matching the known lower bound** and improving on the previous O(√κ). Here κ is the functions' condition number. For squared Euclidean movement, a new tight analysis of `Regularized Online Balanced Descent` plus a matching lower bound against randomized algorithms gives the exact optimal dimension-free ratio.

papers.title: DictLLM: Post-training Compression of Large Language Model with Dictionary Kernels
papers.abstract: Efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices requires balancing performance with compute and memory constraints. Post-training compression is an effective approach to managing this trade-off, while requiring much less computation than in-training counterparts. We propose DictLLM, a dictionary-based compression scheme in which weight matrices within grouped layers are decomposed into a shared dictionary and layer-specific sparse coefficients, directly obtained from a pre-trained model without further training. Specifically, we cast DictLLM as a four-step post-training optimization. First, we obtain shared dictionaries via singular value decomposition (SVD) of input-scaled weight matrices, amortizing rank across grouped layers; second, we sparsify the layer-specific coefficients to the target compression ratio using a dictionary-aware Hessian; and third, we refine the dictionaries given the resulting sparse coefficients. Finally, we aggressively quantize both components using factor-specific Hessian information: input covariance for the dictionaries and the dictionary-aware Hessian for the coefficients. The resulting representation reduces memory footprint by storing a single shared dictionary per layer group, along with sparse layer-specific coefficients. On language modeling and zero-shot reasoning benchmarks, DictLLM consistently outperforms existing post-training low-rank compression methods and pushes the Pareto frontier between model size and performance. DictLLM compresses the original LLaMA-7B model by 5.1x with only a 2.9-point increase in WikiText-2 perplexity, achieving a 3.6x higher compression ratio than the state-of-the-art low-rank method.
papers.summary: `DictLLM` compresses a pre-trained LLM for mobile deployment without retraining. Weight matrices within groups of layers are decomposed into one shared dictionary plus sparse coefficients for each layer. The method builds the dictionaries with singular value decomposition (SVD) of input-scaled weights, sparsifies the coefficients using Hessian information, refines the dictionaries, and then quantizes both parts aggressively. It outperforms existing post-training low-rank compression methods on language modeling and zero-shot reasoning, and **compresses `LLaMA-7B` 5.1× with only a 2.9-point increase in `WikiText-2` perplexity**, a 3.6× higher compression ratio than the best prior low-rank method.

papers.title: MUSS: A Multi-scale and Sequence-based Model for Single-cell Gene Regulation
papers.abstract: Modeling gene regulation in single cells requires jointly representing DNA sequence, chromatin accessibility, and gene expression across regulatory scales. Sequence-based models capture DNA-level regulatory grammar but often lack cell-level resolution, whereas many single-cell omics models represent genes and peaks as fixed-vocabulary tokens without their underlying sequence. Here, we present MUSS, a sequence-based multi-scale model for single-cell gene regulation that preserves both DNA-level and cell-level resolution. MUSS derives peak- and gene-level representations from DNA using a frozen pre-trained sequence encoder and integrates them through peak-peak self-attention and distance-biased peak-gene interactions. Peak masked language modeling followed by training on paired scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq aligns these representations with cell-specific regulatory states. Across gene expression prediction, enhancer-gene linking, motif-guided regulatory prioritization, and zero-shot cell clustering, MUSS achieves strong performance against sequence-based and single-cell omics baselines. It further predicts expression for genes and peaks unseen during task training. These results support sequence-grounded, multi-scale representations for decoding cell-type-specific regulatory programs. Code, datasets, and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Lotfollahi-lab/MUSS_neurips26.
papers.summary: Models of gene regulation in single cells usually capture either DNA sequence grammar or cell-level resolution, but rarely both. `MUSS` derives representations of chromatin-accessibility peaks and genes from DNA using a frozen pre-trained sequence encoder. It combines them with peak-to-peak self-attention and distance-biased peak-to-gene interactions, then trains on paired single-cell chromatin accessibility (`scATAC-seq`) and gene expression (`scRNA-seq`) data. It performs strongly on expression prediction, linking enhancers to genes, and zero-shot cell clustering, and **it can predict expression for genes and peaks not seen during task training**.

papers.title: Value or Attention: Investigating Layer-wise Relevance Propagation for Graph Attention Networks
papers.abstract: Graph Attention Networks (GATs) are increasingly used in domains where scientists need to read a model's reasoning, from medicine to materials science, yet the routing they learn remains opaque to most explainers. Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) follows the model's computation, but in an attention layer the relevance reaching a node is the sum of two mechanically different quantities: its content relevance through the value path and its routing relevance through the attention path. Existing rules either drop one or add them into a single number. We write a single product rule with free weights on the two factors that recovers current approaches as special cases. The value path measures what content a node supplied against a zero baseline; the attention path measures how the node shaped what was passed relative to its neighborhood, and its sign records whether the node's features moved the gating the way the prediction demanded. On a ground-truth classification task, we show that the same node receives negative, positive and near-zero relevance under three settings of the rule. The separated relevance maps yield a hypothesis about the model: it gains by not reading that node. We give reading rules for both paths and argue that they should be interpreted separately.
papers.summary: Graph Attention Networks (`GAT`s) are used in fields like medicine and materials science, but the way they route information between nodes is hard to explain. In an attention layer, a node's Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (`LRP`) relevance mixes two separate quantities: content relevance through the value path and routing relevance through the attention path. Existing rules either drop one of these or add them into a single number. The authors propose a single product rule with free weights on the two factors, which recovers existing approaches as special cases. On a ground-truth classification task, **the same node receives negative, positive, or near-zero relevance depending on the rule setting**, and the authors argue that the two paths should be read separately.

papers.title: SAE Interprets MoE: Sparse AutoEncoders Reveal That MoE Experts Exhibit Human-Interpretable Fine-Grained Specialization
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models route each token to a few of many experts, yet what an individual expert is responsible for remains unsettled. Existing analyses count how often an expert is selected on domain-labeled corpora, an instrument that fixes the taxonomy in advance, stays coarse, and records selection rather than contribution. We instead study specialization in feature space by training a sparse autoencoder (SAE) on the output of an MoE layer. Since this output is a router-weighted sum of expert outputs and the SAE encoder is affine, the pre-activation of every latent decomposes exactly over the experts. Aggregated over a corpus, this gives each expert a dominant set of latents whose activation it principally drives. On layers 4, 30 and 46 of Qwen3-30B-A3B, contribution is far more concentrated than gating, most latents have only one or two dominators, and the overlap between dominant sets concentrates on a few expert pairs. Auto-interpreting these sets reveals a division of labor below coarse domains, with distinct experts for Java and front-end web code, or for geometry and for arithmetic and polynomials, while the coarse domains themselves take very unequal numbers of experts. Our SAEs and code are available at https://github.com/Bytedance-Seed/SAE-Interprets-MoE.
papers.summary: It is still unclear what each expert in a Mixture-of-Experts (`MoE`) model is responsible for, and analyses that count how often experts are selected on domain-labeled data give only a coarse picture. The authors train a sparse autoencoder (`SAE`) on an MoE layer's output. Because that output is a router-weighted sum of expert outputs, each latent's pre-activation splits exactly across the experts, so each expert can be assigned the set of latents it mainly drives. On three layers of `Qwen3-30B-A3B`, **contribution is far more concentrated than gating, and most latents are dominated by only one or two experts**. Auto-interpretation shows specialization finer than coarse domains, such as separate experts for Java and for front-end web code, or for geometry and for arithmetic and polynomials.

papers.title: Gabor Gabor: E-Gaborformer, a Strictly Causal Speech Recognizer with Gabor-Dictionary Convolutions and Delta-Rule Memory
papers.abstract: Real-time voice agents need a speech recognizer that never waits for future audio and whose memory per call does not grow with the length of the call. We present E-Gaborformer, a strictly causal encoder that combines Gated DeltaNet-2 recurrent layers with sliding-window attention in a 3:1 ratio, and builds every temporal convolution from a fixed dictionary of causal Gabor atoms. Its streaming state is constant, about 19 MB per call at production scale including the prediction network, where a causal-attention encoder of the same size accumulates over 1 GB after ten minutes. In a controlled causal study on LibriSpeech, E-Gaborformer leaves the initial plateau earlier, reaches a given accuracy up to 18% sooner, and matches or beats an E-Branchformer trained with the identical front end and recipe. At production scale, a 0.6B-parameter Hebrew and English streaming transducer built on E-Gaborformer has 28 to 31% lower word error rate (WER) than NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 ASR Streaming, a model of the same size, on English voice-agent traffic, and up to 20% lower Hebrew WER than our previous production system. The same weights serve strictly causal and 480 ms-lookahead decoding with no loss in accuracy, and a two-class formulation of the RNN-T lattice trains the transducer 2.6x faster with exact loss and gradients.
papers.summary: Real-time voice agents need a speech recognizer that never waits for future audio and whose memory does not grow with call length. `E-Gaborformer` is a strictly causal encoder that combines `Gated DeltaNet-2` recurrent layers with sliding-window attention in a 3:1 ratio, and it builds every temporal convolution from a fixed dictionary of causal Gabor atoms. This keeps streaming state at about 19 MB per call, while a causal-attention encoder of the same size passes 1 GB after ten minutes. A 0.6B-parameter Hebrew and English streaming transducer built on it achieves **28 to 31% lower word error rate than NVIDIA's `Nemotron 3.5 ASR Streaming`** on English voice-agent traffic, and a two-class formulation of the RNN-T loss trains the transducer 2.6x faster with exact loss and gradients.

papers.title: Gradient Boosting for Efficient Rank Discovery in Tensor Network Kernel Machines
papers.abstract: Tensor network kernel machines (TNKMs) combine nonlinear features with low-rank tensor representations to model complex relationships efficiently. However, selecting an appropriate tensor rank remains challenging, as conventional rank-search methods require training multiple candidate models, increasing computational costs. In this work, we focus on a canonical polyadic (CP) tensor network parameterization and propose GB-CPKM, a gradient boosting framework that builds a higher-capacity predictor by sequentially adding fixed-rank learners. This approach provides a new perspective on rank selection by incrementally increasing model capacity, with ensemble size selected based on validation performance rather than through explicit rank search. Experiments on real-world regression benchmarks show that GB-CPKM trains up to 6x faster and uses up to 2x less peak memory than a conventional rank-selection method based on cross-validation, while achieving comparable predictive performance. These results highlight the potential of gradient boosting to improve the computational efficiency and scalability of tensor-network learning.
papers.summary: Tensor network kernel machines combine nonlinear features with low-rank tensor representations, but choosing the tensor rank usually means training many candidate models. `GB-CPKM` uses a canonical polyadic (CP) parameterization and replaces rank search with gradient boosting: it adds fixed-rank learners one at a time and picks the ensemble size on validation data. On real-world regression benchmarks it **trains up to 6x faster and uses up to 2x less peak memory** than cross-validated rank selection, with comparable accuracy.

papers.title: PersonaAgent: Retrieval-Augmented Transaction Anomaly Scoring with Refreshable Multi-Entity Persona Memory
papers.abstract: In large-scale payment networks, entities (card, merchant, etc.) and their interactions play a key role in transaction anomaly detection. However, transaction patterns between different entities usually change more frequently than the production model refresh schedule. Meanwhile, entity embedding tables suffer from high-cardinality and sparse interaction issues. To resolve the above challenges, we present PersonaAgent, an agentic transaction anomaly detection framework which represents the latest entity behavior signals as personas and saves them in a refreshable memory. Offline, a weekly scheduled batch job is used to extract the latest behavior signals and update them in the memory. At inference time, a lightweight adapter retrieves the corresponding entity behavior signals of each transaction from memory and uses them to augment the base anomaly classifier's scoring. Through comprehensive benchmarking with different anomaly detection models at Visa, PersonaAgent is able to score transactions efficiently (a 1,000-transaction CPU batch in 1-2 ms), lifting the PR-AUC by 0.65-6.58% and the production business metric by 8.93-14.24% relatively in deployment.
papers.summary: In payment networks, transaction patterns between cards and merchants change faster than production fraud models are retrained, and entity embedding tables suffer from very high cardinality and sparse interactions. `PersonaAgent` stores each entity's latest behavior signals as a persona in a memory that a batch job refreshes weekly. At inference time, a lightweight adapter retrieves these personas to adjust the base anomaly classifier's score. Benchmarked at Visa, it scores 1,000 transactions on CPU in 1-2 ms and **lifts the production business metric by 8.93-14.24% relative** in deployment, with PR-AUC gains of 0.65-6.58%.

papers.title: Identifying Neural Dynamics Using Nonlinear Interventional State Space Models
papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs) recover low-dimensional latent dynamics from high-dimensional observations, but latents are generally not identifiable from observational data alone. Interventional state-space models (iSSMs) use perturbations to break observational symmetries and identify parameters up to permutation, scaling, and shift. However, prior work restricts identifiability to linear latent dynamics and piecewise-linear emissions, excluding many behaviors characteristic of neural circuits. We extend iSSMs to a substantially broader model class: we prove that (i) affine identifiability holds under general injective emission functions and Gaussian latent transitions, and (ii) with interventions, identifiability up to permutation, scaling, and shift is preserved under general nonlinear latent dynamics. We validate our theory on simulated FitzHugh-Nagumo dynamics, and then demonstrate two applications: adjudicating between competing models of decision-making; and predicting responses to unseen micro-stimulation in macaque and human neural recordings, with proof-of-concept generalization to a held-out stimulation site in the latter. Finally, simulations yield practical guidance for designing stimulation protocols that improve identifiability.
papers.summary: State-space models recover low-dimensional latent dynamics from high-dimensional neural recordings, but those latents generally cannot be identified from observational data alone. Earlier interventional state-space models (`iSSM`s) used perturbations to fix this, but only for linear dynamics and piecewise-linear emissions. The authors prove that, with interventions, **identifiability up to permutation, scaling, and shift holds under general nonlinear latent dynamics** and injective emission functions. They validate the theory on simulated `FitzHugh-Nagumo` dynamics, use it to compare competing models of decision-making, and predict responses to unseen micro-stimulation in macaque and human recordings.

papers.title: Create Your Own Work Stack: Deploying Self-hosted AI and Tooling in a Tech Startup
papers.abstract:
Self-hosting AI is often presented as a way to reduce inference costs and increase control, but deployment introduces its own costs. We report our experience deploying a hybrid AI stack at Grayhat Developers, a small software company with an AI-intensive development workflow. Our initial motivation was to counter the growing cost of commercial AI usage: Claude/Codex incurred approximately \$325 per month, with more than 25.93 billion recorded tokens. We experimented with local open-source models as replacements for commercial coding agents, but after learning that their performance and inference speed were insufficient, we adopted a hybrid approach in which commercial agents remained responsible for complex tasks while local models handled lower-complexity tasks, organizational information retrieval, and synchronization with self-hosted tools including Outline, Plane, and ERPNext.
  We estimated that approximately 30--40\% of our commercial AI workload was associated with context transfer, documentation synchronization, task management, and related operational coordination. By moving this work to local models, we estimate that approximately 90\% of this coordination workload could be handled without commercial inference, corresponding to an estimated 27--36\% reduction in overall commercial-AI workload or cost-equivalent usage. Our first internal deployment nevertheless failed to achieve adoption because it introduced UX friction. Replacing it with a centrally configured deployment substantially improved feedback and adoption. We conclude that local inference is most useful not as a wholesale replacement for commercial AI, but as part of a hybrid architecture that assigns tasks according to their capability requirements, cost, context demands, and operational sensitivity.
papers.summary: A small software company reports on replacing part of its commercial coding-agent spending (`Claude` and `Codex`, about $325 per month across more than 25.93 billion tokens) with self-hosted open-source models. Local models were too slow and too weak to replace commercial agents outright, so the team moved to a hybrid setup. Commercial agents kept complex tasks, while local models handled coordination work such as context transfer, documentation sync, retrieval of internal information, and integration with self-hosted tools like `Outline`, `Plane`, and `ERPNext`. The authors estimate this shifts **27-36% of commercial AI workload to local inference**, and they note that their first deployment failed to get adopted because of user-experience friction until they switched to a centrally configured setup.

papers.title: Who Can Evaluate AI Independently? A Framework for Analysing Evaluation Infrastructure
papers.abstract: AI evaluation is increasingly central to AI safety and governance, yet taking part in an evaluation does not by itself confer authority over its design, its execution or the resources it depends on. This paper examines how infrastructure arrangements distribute that authority, and so shape who can evaluate AI systems independently. Drawing on Science and Technology Studies, political economy and applied evaluation standards, we introduce PAAI (Power, Access, Adequacy, Independence), a framework for examining who controls evaluation infrastructure, the terms on which it is available, whether it is adequate to the evaluation's purpose and what autonomy it supports. We apply PAAI to twelve African AI evaluation projects (2022-2025) and to the documented roles of all ten member institutes in the three published joint testing exercises of the international network of AI Safety Institutes. We identify three recurring configurations: extractive collaboration, dependent innovation and constrained independence. African actors often contribute data, language expertise and task design while external institutions retain authority over infrastructure and evaluation frameworks; design authority without infrastructure authority never yielded more than partial independence. The joint testing exercises show a similar division among mostly high-income members: the institutes that led each exercise also ran the models, while Kenya, the network's only African member, moved from annotation to task design with no documented model execution. Participation in evaluation does not by itself produce evaluative authority. For evaluation to serve as a credible governance mechanism, access must come with control over priorities, methods, publication and continuity.
papers.summary: The authors argue that taking part in an AI evaluation does not by itself give a participant authority over the evaluation's design, execution, or resources. They introduce `PAAI` (Power, Access, Adequacy, Independence), a framework for analyzing who controls evaluation infrastructure. They apply it to twelve African AI evaluation projects and to the three joint testing exercises of the international network of AI Safety Institutes. African actors often contributed data, language expertise, and task design while outside institutions kept control of infrastructure, and **design authority without infrastructure authority never produced more than partial independence**. In the joint exercises, the institutes that led each one also ran the models, while Kenya moved from annotation to task design with no documented model execution.

papers.title: How Far Can Untrained Neural Networks Go in Anomaly Detection? From Tables to Pixels
papers.abstract: Anomaly detection (AD) is often framed as a representation-learning problem, where strong performance is expected to require learned features or AD-specific optimization. However, this view can overlook the intrinsic separability of anomalies from normal references, even in the absence of learned representations. We therefore investigate how far untrained neural networks can go in anomaly detection. To this end, we propose PRISM, a framework combining fixed random nonlinear features with normal-reference Mahalanobis scoring for tabular detection and dense visual localization. Across 47 tabular datasets in ADBench, PRISM-T achieves the highest mean AUROC (86.4%) and the second-highest mean AUPRC (65.9%) among the compared methods. On MVTec AD and VisA, covering 27 visual categories, PRISM-V achieves mean image-level and pixel-level AUROCs of 90.4% and 96.4%, respectively. Notably, both models achieve these results without neural weight optimization or pretrained representations. A theoretical analysis further characterizes how nonlinear transformations affect the mean and covariance contributions to the Mahalanobis score gap, while empirical analyses examine the resulting score separability. These findings establish PRISM as both a competitive anomaly detector and a prior-to-learning baseline for assessing the added value of learned representations in anomaly detection.
papers.summary: Anomaly detection is usually treated as a representation-learning problem, but the authors test how far untrained neural networks can go. `PRISM` combines fixed random nonlinear features with Mahalanobis-distance scoring against normal reference data, in variants for tabular data and for pixel-level visual localization. With no weight optimization and no pretrained features, `PRISM-T` reaches **the highest mean AUROC (86.4%) across 47 `ADBench` tabular datasets**, and `PRISM-V` reaches 90.4% image-level and 96.4% pixel-level AUROC on `MVTec AD` and `VisA`. The authors propose it as a pre-learning baseline for measuring what learned representations actually add.

papers.title: Detecting Silent Faults at the Environment-Trainer Boundary in Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract:
Robot reinforcement learning increasingly runs environments outside the trainer: in another process, on another machine, in another language. Many faults at this boundary raise no error. We make the boundary a wire protocol and ask what notices a fault in it.
  On Pendulum, HalfCheetah, Hopper and a 7-joint arm (Pusher), we injected up to 23 faults into what crosses the wire and 2 into the trainer's log, from one value to every value. Unless every value was wrong, a learning-curve threshold caught at most one run in ten, and a comparison with ten fault-free seeds at most 21%. A clean evaluation of all 1,060 final policies agreed with the curves: of the 728 boundary-fault runs both curve checks passed, 723 scored no more than three standard deviations below fault-free seeds, though nearly all ended on other weights and, for reward faults, logged other returns.
  Checks of the run itself, not of its outcome, saw every fault. A step ledger kept on both sides and compared step by step caught and located every fault that crossed, on Pendulum, Hopper and Pusher on one machine and on Pendulum across two, with no fault-free run and, on Pendulum, a median 3% more training time. An episode record kept at the environment caught the faults in the trainer's log. We list such faults found in practice, in Gymnasium 1.3 and our own code and, reported by others, in five multi-agent libraries, and recommend a step ledger and episode counts kept at the environment.
