papers.title: Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Self-improving embodied agents are increasingly being developed and compared on robot simulation benchmarks. Several recent works expose the benchmark's success criteria to the learning agent, a practice we call Criteria Exposure (CE). These criteria, originally written to verify policies trained by imitation learning, often demand more than the corresponding language instructions, so a score from such a verifier may not faithfully reflect whether the instructed task was completed, especially for robot-control programs written by an agent. As embodied coding agents report ever higher benchmark scores, a natural question arises: when a coding agent is exposed to the benchmark's criteria, does it generate code that better performs the instructed task, or code that simply overfits to the verification criteria? We conduct controlled experiments with a self-improving agent with and without CE, and find that with CE the agent quickly produces code with a higher success rate under the given criteria, but this advantage disappears when the criteria are changed slightly without departing from the original instructions. More importantly, the skills the agent develops under CE transfer poorly across tasks. We further propose instruction-faithful criteria and show that they better reflect the performance of agent-generated programs.
papers.summary: Several self-improving embodied agents are shown the benchmark's success criteria while learning, a practice the authors call Criteria Exposure. Those criteria often demand more than the language instruction itself. In controlled experiments with a self-improving coding agent that writes robot-control programs, exposure quickly raised success rates under the given criteria, but **the advantage disappeared when the criteria were changed slightly** while staying faithful to the instructions. Skills learned under exposure also transferred poorly across tasks. The authors propose instruction-faithful criteria that better reflect how well agent-generated programs actually perform.

papers.title: Discovering Learning Rules that Shape Others
papers.abstract: In general-sum games, self-interested learners can reach outcomes that are poor for everyone, which has motivated methods that shape the opponent's learning. Methods like Learning with Opponent-Learning Awareness (LOLA), which differentiates through the opponent's learning process, and Model-Free Opponent Shaping (M-FOS), which uses model-free optimisation methods for long-horizon opponent shaping, have enabled mutual cooperation and exploitation of learners. However, these methods require access to the opponent's parameters, policy, rewards or learning rule during deployment. In single-agent reinforcement learning, update rules discovered by meta-learning have achieved state-of-the-art results (e.g. DiscoRL). These rules are separate from the policy they train and read only the agent's own experience. We hereby extend this framework to general-sum settings by introducing Discovered Update Rule for Opponent Shaping (DUOS). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first method to discover an update rule for an agent in general-sum games. DUOS meta-trains the rule to maximise the agent's expected return over its lifetime, and updates an inner network using the agent's own experience. We show that our discovered rule exhibits behaviour consistent with opponent shaping without reading opponent policies or parameters, and ranks 1st in normalised mean score and 1st in self-play among tournament entrants.
papers.summary: Opponent-shaping methods such as Learning with Opponent-Learning Awareness (`LOLA`) and Model-Free Opponent Shaping (`M-FOS`) can steer self-interested learners toward cooperation in general-sum games, but at deployment they need access to the opponent's parameters, policy, rewards, or learning rule. `DUOS` extends meta-learned update rules in the style of `DiscoRL` to multi-agent settings. It meta-trains a rule that maximizes lifetime return using only the agent's own experience. The discovered rule **shapes opponents without reading their policies or parameters**, and it ranks first in normalised mean score and in self-play among tournament entrants.

papers.title: Enhancing Local and Global Structure in Compressed AI Agent Memory
papers.abstract: AI agents store text as embedding vectors and compress them at scale. A compression is accepted when each item's nearest neighbors survive, but agents also consolidate, delete, and compare memories, tasks that depend on which items lie far apart. We evaluate both ends with two label-free fidelities from our prior work: the local fidelity $L$ at 10 neighbors and the global fidelity $G$ at 30 to 50 percent of the memory. At 96 bytes per passage, rescored binary codes reach an $L$ of 0.97 yet move 10.1 percent of passages to another theme; PCA with 8-bit codes, at an $L$ of 0.77, moves 1.7 percent. Rescoring leaves the stored codes, and thus $G$, unchanged. We prove that across the $G$ band, $1-\nu_k$ is at most 2 to 2.18 times the square root of the near-far rank-violation rate, and that this rate follows the distance noise of the compression (correlation 0.979). Our locality-aware quantization (LAQ) turns the bound into a hinge objective on the codebooks of an OPQ index, keeping its bytes, rotation, and search. To our knowledge, LAQ is the first quantizer whose objective comes from a proven bound on the far end. Reconstruction alone raises $G$ in 0 of 52 held-out runs; the far hinge raises it in all 52. LAQ raises $G$ in all 52 ($p=8.5\times 10^{-4}$ over 13 memory-encoder groups), including the external FinDER memory, has the highest $G$ of seven equal-size quantizers in all 12 Multi-Doc-2025 runs, scales to a million passages, and keeps evidence recall.
papers.summary: AI agents compress their stored embedding memories, and compression is usually judged by whether each item's nearest neighbours survive. However, consolidating, deleting, and comparing memories also depends on which items lie far apart. Using a local fidelity metric and a global one, the authors show that rescored binary codes keep local fidelity at 0.97 yet move 10.1% of passages to another theme. They prove a bound that links global fidelity to near-far rank violations, and they turn it into locality-aware quantization (`LAQ`), a hinge objective on the codebooks of an `OPQ` index that keeps the same storage cost. `LAQ` **raised global fidelity in all 52 held-out runs**, scales to a million passages, and preserves evidence recall.

papers.title: 4D Point Splatting for mmWave Radar Micro-Doppler Differentiable Rendering
papers.abstract: Millimeter-wave radar resolves the micrometer displacements of a moving body as micro-Doppler, enabling gait, gesture, activity, pose and vital-sign sensing. Each task relies on a downstream model trained on real data, yet radar datasets lag orders of magnitude behind vision and language. Brute-force collection will not close that gap, and existing synthesis methods (forward-only simulators, learned generators and static-scene inverse renderers) cannot fit a real capture of a moving body, leaving a sim2real gap. We present 4D Point Splatting (4DPS), a physics-based differentiable renderer that fits an explicit moving scene to a real capture. Using the synchronized camera to initialize the room and body, we represent the scene as oriented points carrying material, normal and velocity, and splat each point into range and Doppler bins. Our output is the raw complex return a real radar records, so we apply the same signal processing on the rendered data to obtain any representation for training any SOTA downstream model. We fit 235 sequences on HuPR and 100 on RT-Pose, two datasets with different radars. Our reconstructions set the state of the art, with median correlations of 0.940 and 0.830 on range-azimuth, 0.829 and 0.695 on range-Doppler, and 0.988 and 0.966 on micro-Doppler. Our renders also set the state of the art in downstream sim2real gap. On RT-Pose, a pose model trained on them reaches 21.9 cm MPJPE on real data, against 16.7 cm for real training and 127.6 cm for the RF-Genesis baseline, where both the rendered- and real-trained models learn nearly the same features. Our custom CUDA kernels fit a sequence in 5.7 minutes on HuPR and 12.9 on RT-Pose on one H100, making dataset-scale inverse rendering of mmWave radar possible for the first time. This work can enable synthetic data generation for any human-centered downstream task and model, and scene editing for data augmentation.
papers.summary: Millimeter-wave radar datasets for sensing gait, pose, and vital signs are far smaller than vision datasets, and existing simulators cannot fit real captures of moving bodies. 4D Point Splatting (`4DPS`) is a physics-based differentiable renderer that represents a scene as oriented points carrying material, normal, and velocity. It splats each point into range and Doppler bins to reproduce the raw complex radar return. It sets the state of the art for reconstruction on `HuPR` and `RT-Pose`. A pose model trained on its renders reaches **21.9 cm error on real data, versus 16.7 cm for real training and 127.6 cm for the `RF-Genesis` baseline**. Custom CUDA kernels fit a sequence in minutes on a single H100.

papers.title: USB Gym: A Gymnasium Testbed for Closed-Loop Ultrasound View Matching
papers.abstract:
Background and Objective: Our main goal is ultrasound guidance: moving a probe until its image matches a target view. Published methods for each part of a guide are evaluated in separate simulators. We asked whether these methods, combined into one guide, are good enough.
  Methods: We built USB Gym, a testbed whose standard engine simulates ultrasound from public patient CT, with a network drawing organ textures from CT labels. Its guide has three replaceable parts (slots), an organ segmenter, a controller and a reward, which received 20 published methods, each run on the same 60 episodes of six held-out patients. In each slot, a published method replaced ours only if detectably better on these patients. The better of this combination and our original guide on 20 new CTs is the benchmark baseline. A pose oracle, reading the exact probe pose available only in simulation, set the reference. The results below are exploratory.
  Results: On these CTs, the probe started on average 16.0 mm from the target view; the pose oracle brought it to 1.5 mm. Of the results known when the combination was fixed, only an image-similarity reward (SSIM) was slightly but detectably better, so the combination was our guide with that reward. This combination was the benchmark baseline, ending at 13.7 mm (16% of the oracle's progress).
  Conclusions: Combining untuned published methods with ours did not guide the probe near the target view; the task remains under-explored. The testbed accepts new methods; no guide was tested on hardware.
papers.summary: `USB Gym` is a Gymnasium testbed for ultrasound guidance: moving a probe until its image matches a target view. It simulates ultrasound from public patient CT scans. The guide has three swappable parts, an organ segmenter, a controller, and a reward, and the authors tried 20 published methods in those slots under identical episodes. Only an image-similarity reward based on `SSIM` helped detectably. The resulting baseline moved the probe from 16.0 mm to **13.7 mm from the target, only 16% of the progress made by a pose oracle**, which suggests the task remains largely unsolved.

papers.title: Unifying Central Flow, Rod Flow, and the Edge Coupling
papers.abstract: At the edge of stability, the iterates of gradient descent oscillate along the sharp directions of the Hessian. This poses a significant challenge for continuous-time models as the usual continuous-time approximation -- the gradient flow -- admits no oscillations. Several continuous-time models have been proposed to capture the behavior at the edge of stability, among them central flow and rod flow. Although both models can be interpreted as performing a coarse-graining in time, the connection between them remains poorly understood. Here we show that both flows can be derived from a third object, the edge coupling: a functional on consecutive iterates whose critical points are the fixed points and period-two orbits of gradient descent. It is revealed that the two flows correspond to coarse-grainings at different time scales. Rod flow coarse-grains over only the fastest time scale, while central flow coarse-grains over both the fast and intermediate time scales. Furthermore, using the edge coupling, we derive rod flows and central flows for momentum methods such as heavy ball and Adam. We verify the derived flows experimentally on representative neural network architectures, where they track the discrete iterates throughout all phases of training -- including the transition from the stable regime to the edge of stability.
papers.summary: At the edge of stability, gradient descent oscillates along sharp directions of the loss surface, which ordinary gradient flow cannot capture. Two continuous-time models, central flow and rod flow, were proposed to describe this regime. This work derives **both from a single object, the edge coupling**, a functional whose critical points are the fixed points and period-two orbits of gradient descent. In this view, rod flow averages over only the fastest time scale, while central flow also averages over an intermediate one. The framework also yields rod and central flows for heavy-ball momentum and `Adam`, and experiments show these flows track real training through the transition into the edge of stability.

papers.title: StrataFlux: Memory-Hierarchy-Native Low-Bit LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Quantization reduces the memory and bandwidth demands of large language model (LLM) inference but can degrade accuracy; offloading higher-precision data can instead stall generation. We introduce StrataFlux, a framework that challenges this tradeoff by recovering accuracy lost to low-bit weight and key-value (KV) cache quantization while retaining quantization's memory and speed advantages. StrataFlux co-designs refinement representation, selection, and delivery to make host RAM and solid-state drives useful sources of additional precision. Its selective precision streaming reduces transfer volume, overlaps delivery with computation, and reuses fetched precision across decoding steps so generation need not wait for every transfer. We evaluate 2-4-bit weights and 2-3-bit KV-cache on dedicated GPUs and unified-memory platforms. For 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, StrataFlux reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while maintaining 95.4% of the quantized base's throughput on RTX 5090. With 2-bit weights and KV, StrataFlux raises Qwen3-8B's AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use. At 128K context, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 3-bit weights and 2-bit KV achieves comparable perplexity and speed to vLLM's 4-bit AWQ weights and 8-bit KV on RTX 5090, using approximately half the GPU memory. These results show that GPU-resident precision need not set the accuracy ceiling, nor offloading-tier latency dictate decoding speed.
papers.summary: Low-bit quantization of weights and the key-value (KV) cache shrinks LLM memory needs but costs accuracy, while offloading higher-precision data tends to stall generation. `StrataFlux` stores precision refinements in host RAM and on solid-state drives and streams only the selected refinements, overlapping transfers with computation and reusing them across decoding steps. With 2-bit weights and KV cache, it **raises `Qwen3-8B` accuracy on `AIME` 2024/2025 from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory**. At 128K context on an RTX 5090, a 3-bit-weight, 2-bit-KV `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` matches the perplexity and speed of vLLM's 4-bit `AWQ` setup with 8-bit KV cache while using about half the GPU memory.

papers.title: SHORE: Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Online Bin Packing
papers.abstract: Online 3D bin packing with a processing buffer requires choosing which box to pack, its orientation, and its placement while keeping the stack stable under unknown future arrivals. A collapse ends the episode and forfeits the remaining volume. Existing methods use geometric rules or hard stability masks, limiting how risk can influence the joint choice of box, orientation, and placement. We propose Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning (SHORE), which combines a learned stability probability of a placement with an on-policy estimate of its return conditional on stability. A 3D U-Net learns stability from executed outcomes and simulated alternatives, revealing outcomes of actions underrepresented in early rollouts. A discrete on-policy actor--critic uses stability predictions in both its action values and policy prior, with gates that limit the effect of an untrained or changing model. In deployment, SHORE does not require additional search or simulation overhead. In Isaac Gym, SHORE reaches 73\% space utilization by 0.4M environment steps, while the same learner without stability modeling reaches that level at about 1M. On the expanded 60-box set, SHORE achieves 0.734 space utilization versus 0.588 for the GOPT state-of-the-art baseline, with a higher placement-failure frequency (1.03\% vs. 0.63\%), trading more risk for greater packed volume. The results show faster learning and higher utilization on the more demanding realistic box arrival set. Ablations suggest that simulated alternatives provide useful early supervision, while executed outcomes alone sustain later performance. We also demonstrate the method on a real robot to verify the simplicity of integrating the method to real bin packing pipelines.
papers.summary: In online 3D bin packing with a buffer, an agent must choose which box to pack, its orientation, and its placement without letting the stack collapse. `SHORE` combines a stability probability learned by a 3D U-Net with an on-policy actor-critic. The actor-critic estimates return conditional on stability, with gates that limit the influence of an immature stability model. In Isaac Gym, `SHORE` reaches 73% space utilization by 0.4M environment steps, versus about 1M without stability modeling. On a 60-box set it achieves **0.734 utilization versus 0.588 for the `GOPT` baseline**, at a slightly higher placement-failure rate. The method was also demonstrated on a real robot.

papers.title: VisionSIM: Beyond Idealized Sensors - A Multi-Modal Simulator for Robot Perception
papers.abstract: Robotic perception increasingly relies on heterogeneous sensor suites combining cameras with emerging modalities (event, SPAD, iToF/dToF, and thermal). Yet existing simulators idealize these sensors, hiding critical modality-specific failure modes that limit real-world deployment. We present VisionSIM, a unified, physically grounded simulation platform that elevates sensor realism to a first-class concern by modeling the raw physical measurement process for diverse conventional and emerging modalities. We expose fine-grained control over physical sensor parameters, reproducing failure modes overlooked by general-purpose simulators: pileup and glare for LiDAR; phase wrapping, saturation, and motion artifacts for iToF; refractory drops for event cameras; and history-dependent emission for thermal cameras. This enables principled cross-modality comparison on identical scenes and trajectories. We release the platform and a large indoor dataset with synchronized raw measurements and rich ground-truth annotations.
papers.summary: Robot perception increasingly combines cameras with event, SPAD, time-of-flight, and thermal sensors, yet simulators model these sensors in idealized form. `VisionSIM` simulates the raw physical measurement process of each modality. It **reproduces failure modes such as LiDAR pileup and glare, time-of-flight phase wrapping and motion artifacts, event-camera refractory drops, and history-dependent thermal emission**. Identical scenes and trajectories allow principled comparison across modalities. The platform is released together with a large indoor dataset of synchronized raw measurements and ground-truth annotations.

papers.title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
papers.abstract: Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal less about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient's condition throughout a course of care. To close this gap, we introduce NPCBench, a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). NPCBench mirrors specialist training, from guideline and foundational knowledge to case planning, longitudinal review, CarePath integration, and open-ended consultation. It contains 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. The episode-level evaluation tests whether diagnostic and care answers are jointly correct within a care pathway. By linking stepwise tasks to patient-level care trajectories, NPCBench evaluates whether models ground decisions in visual evidence, interpret changes in patient state, and meet clinical requirements in consultation. Across 30 evaluated models, we observe a composition gap: strong performance on individual tasks does not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, strict CarePath success reaches at most 23%. Paired controls and physician calibration further examine evidence grounding, longitudinal revision, and consultation judging. Overall, NPCBench broadens the evaluation of medical artificial intelligence beyond static question-answering paradigms to an apprenticeship-oriented assessment of clinical workflows, thereby offering a testbed for evidence-based and temporally coherent reasoning in oncology care.
papers.summary: `NPCBench` evaluates medical AI on nasopharyngeal carcinoma the way specialists are trained, moving from guideline knowledge through case planning, longitudinal review, and consultation. It has 4,777 items and a 100-patient care-pathway cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. Across 30 models, the authors find a composition gap: strong scores on individual tasks do not mean a model gets the diagnostic and care answers jointly right for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, **strict care-pathway success reaches at most 23%**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Medical AI benchmarks usually score isolated exam questions or single images, so they can't tell whether a model gets the diagnosis and every care decision right for the same patient across a course of treatment. `NPCBench` tests this for nasopharyngeal carcinoma with a ladder modeled on specialist training. It runs from guideline recall through pathology and MRI evidence grounding to longitudinal revision and linked `CarePath` patient episodes, plus rubric-scored open-ended consultations.

- The benchmark contains **4,777 component and consultation items** and a 100-patient `CarePath` cohort with **417 scored tasks** (100 pathology, 100 MRI T-stage, 217 care decisions); its `Strict` metric counts a patient as correct only if pathology, T-stage, and every care answer are all correct.
- Across 30 models (21 multimodal), knowledge doesn't carry over cleanly to planning: guideline recall exceeds **92%**, but the best case-planning accuracy is **71.9%**, and removing multiple-choice options lowers guideline accuracy by 7.0–15.5 points.
- Imaging is the weakest link: the best T- and N-stage accuracies (**43.5%** and **42.8%**) barely beat majority-class baselines (37.5% and 40.0%), and on the 18-structure anatomical panel, full tumor-invasion correctness and evidence-grounded T-staging both stay **below 5%**.
- The headline composition gap appears in `CarePath`, where `Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview` reaches **89.9% Care accuracy but only 11.0% Strict success** and the best Strict score is **23.0%** (`Claude-Sonnet-4.6`); in consultations, top scorer `GPT-5.1` (58.4) still triggers major-error criteria in **14.6%** of responses.
- Limitations include mostly single-center retrospective data, assigned rather than patient-matched pathology in 75 of 100 `CarePath` episodes, scores that are sensitive to class imbalance, and a consultation judge (`GPT-OSS-120B`) that agrees with physicians only **70.5%** of the time (51.8% sensitivity) on the expanded audit.

papers.title: MOMASPLAT: Dynamic Novel-View Demonstration Augmentation for Mobile Manipulation
papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies trained through imitation learning are highly sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint. This is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa), where robots rarely execute manipulation from the exact same base pose used during demonstration collection due to navigation uncertainty, localization drift, and environmental constraints. Recent approaches use novel-view synthesis (NVS) to augment demonstrations with unseen viewpoints, but they assume static scenes and therefore fail to re-render the manipulated object during the post-contact interaction phase, leaving the most critical parts of the demonstration unaugmented. We present MOMASPLAT, a novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes full manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions. Our key insight is that standard MoMa data collection naturally provides the multiview observations needed to reconstruct both the static scene and the manipulated object in 3D. MOMASPLAT combines 3D Gaussian Splatting, feed-forward 3D foundation models, and kinematics-based action retargeting to separately reconstruct the scene and manipulated object, render them from novel viewpoints, and generate geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations paired with transformed actions. We evaluate MOMASPLAT on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving both rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, and validate the fidelity of its synthesized demonstrations against ground truth in simulation. MOMASPLAT substantially improves robustness to unseen base poses, more than doubling the average success rate of the strongest baseline and maintaining non-trivial success at large base displacements where all baselines fail, while reducing the need for largescale real-world data collection.
papers.summary: Imitation-learned visuomotor policies break when the camera viewpoint changes, which is common in mobile manipulation because the robot's base rarely ends up in the same pose as during demonstrations. Earlier view-augmentation methods assume static scenes and cannot re-render the object once it has been grasped. `MOMASPLAT` uses 3D Gaussian Splatting, feed-forward 3D foundation models, and kinematic action retargeting to reconstruct the scene and the manipulated object separately, then synthesizes full demonstrations from new base poses. On five real-world tasks it **more than doubles the average success rate of the strongest baseline** and keeps working at large base displacements where baselines fail.

papers.title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout
papers.abstract: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.
papers.summary: Linear attention models such as Gated DeltaNet-2 (`GDN-2`) compress context into a fixed-size state. The authors show that state updates are much less sensitive to erasure than to writes, and that slow-decaying state rows dominate readout. `Muir` fuses all gates into a low-rank projection sized to each gate's sensitivity, adds a matched-filter readout gate, spends the saved parameters on a wider feed-forward network, and uses a parallel update that stays numerically stable at large chunk sizes. From 166M to 1.34B parameters, it lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over `GDN-2` and 2.5-3.6% over Transformers. At 1.34B it **extrapolates from 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift**, while matching `GDN-2` throughput.

papers.title: Module-Aware Optimization for Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Different optimizers impose different geometries on parameter updates. Adaptive methods such as Adam and AdamW use coordinate-wise updates, while matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon utilize weight-matrix structure through orthogonalized updates. For Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), however, the effective geometry of its weight matrices is shaped not only by its learned channel-mixing weights, but also by the graph-propagated representations it acts on. Thus, even if an update is well normalized as a matrix, its effect on the layer output can be amplified when applied to graph-propagated features. To address this gap, we introduce GraphMuon, a graph-aware optimizer that adapts Muon's matrix updates to the covariance structure of graph-propagated layer inputs. GraphMuon performs orthogonalization in a metric defined by these propagated representations and normalizes step sizes according to the update's induced effect on the layer representation. We show that theoretically, vanilla Muon can suffer from graph-induced update amplification, while our GraphMuon can mitigate this effect. As such, our GraphMuon yields a graph-metric analogue of Muon's polar update step. Empirically, GraphMuon achieves $1.32\times$-$2.42\times$ validation-loss time-to-target speedups over AdamW on three large-scale OGB benchmarks. Across 15 dataset-architecture configurations spanning node classification, inductive graph classification, and graph regression, it achieves lower time-to-target in 13 cases, while maintaining competitive or superior predictive performance. Code is available at https://github.com/guy-hadad/GraphMuon.
papers.summary: Matrix-aware optimizers such as `Muon` ignore the fact that a graph neural network (GNN) layer's weights act on graph-propagated features, which can amplify the effect of an update. `GraphMuon` performs Muon's orthogonalization in a metric defined by the covariance of those propagated inputs and normalizes step sizes by the update's effect on the layer output. The authors show theoretically that vanilla `Muon` can suffer this amplification and that `GraphMuon` mitigates it. It achieves **1.32x-2.42x faster time-to-target than `AdamW`** on three large `OGB` benchmarks and is faster in 13 of 15 configurations, with competitive or better accuracy.

papers.title: FedReason: Large Language Models as Weight-Space Meta-Aggregators for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning servers combine client models with a fixed aggregation rule, and each rule in common use is designed for one kind of heterogeneity. We study whether a large language model (LLM) that inspects the client models can choose the rule itself, without any training on the server. In FedReason, the LLM is called every ten rounds. It analyses the weights by running code in a restricted server-side sandbox, sees only the printed results, may score a few candidates on a 500-image proxy set, and submits a short Python aggregation program. The server applies the program until the next call and falls back to FedAvg whenever its output is invalid. Full weight tensors never leave the server. We evaluated FedReason with Claude Opus 5.5 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18 under Dirichlet label skew, width-heterogeneous sub-models and Byzantine clients, in 168 runs against 14 baselines. Across 12 paired label-skew runs it beat FedAvg by 1.26 percentage points on average (10 wins), and a control that spends the same per-round proxy budget on choosing among standard rules by 1.08 points. It was the strongest server-side rule on CIFAR-100 but did not beat SCAFFOLD, which changes client training. With three of ten clients malicious, it excluded all sign-flipping clients from the first round and stayed about one point below FLTrust without training a root model. Without proxy feedback, accuracy fell from 73.8% to 38.8% in one seed. A 60-round run cost 0.79 USD in API fees on average.
papers.summary: Federated learning servers usually merge client models with one fixed aggregation rule, and each common rule is built for only one kind of client heterogeneity. In `FedReason`, a large language model (LLM) is called every ten rounds to inspect client weights by running code in a restricted server-side sandbox. It may score candidate rules on a small proxy set and then writes a short Python aggregation program, with `FedAvg` as the fallback if the program's output is invalid. With `Claude Opus 5.5` on `CIFAR-10` and `CIFAR-100` using `ResNet-18`, it beat `FedAvg` by **1.26 percentage points on average across label-skew runs** and excluded sign-flipping Byzantine clients from the first round. It did not beat `SCAFFOLD`, which changes client training, and a 60-round run cost about 0.79 USD in API fees.

papers.title: Hybrid Machine Learning for Imbalanced Landing-Phase Safety Event Prediction from Flight Data
papers.abstract: Landing-phase safety-event prediction requires the detection of rare abnormal approaches within strongly imbalanced multivariate flight data. Capturing coupled temporal behavior while distinguishing event-specific signatures across airport operating contexts remains a central modeling challenge. This study proposes an interpretable hybrid feature-fusion framework for multiclass landing-phase safety-event prediction. A long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder trained on nominal flight windows characterizes deviations from routine approach behavior. Its continuous reconstruction-error descriptor is fused with parameter-specific statistical flight-history features and supplied to a class-weighted XGBoost classifier to distinguish Normal, Speed High, Path High, and Flaps Late windows. The framework is evaluated using 53,750 NASA DASHlink approach windows from three arrival airports. Pooled and airport-specific learning strategies are compared alongside component-level benchmarks, repeated pipeline retraining, and feature-attribution analysis. The results demonstrate strong class-balanced detection, with mean macro recall above 0.90 across all airports under repeated partitioning and retraining. Component comparisons establish the importance of class weighting and show that continuous feature fusion outperforms reconstruction-error-only and hard-gate alternatives. Airport-level comparisons reveal benefits from local specialization at the two airports with larger datasets and from pooled training at the airport with the smallest dataset. Feature attributions associate predictions with operationally relevant vertical-path, configuration, speed, and approach-context variables. The framework provides an interpretable approach to rare-event detection and practical guidance for adapting flight-data monitoring models to airport-level data availability.
papers.summary: Rare abnormal aircraft approaches are hard to predict from flight data because nearly all approaches are normal. The proposed framework trains a long short-term memory (`LSTM`) autoencoder on normal flight windows and feeds its reconstruction error, together with statistical flight-history features, into a class-weighted `XGBoost` classifier. The classifier separates normal windows from three event types: speed high, path high, and late flaps. On 53,750 `NASA DASHlink` approach windows from three airports it reaches **mean macro recall above 0.90**. Airport-specific models helped at the two airports with more data, while pooled training worked better at the airport with the least data.

papers.title: Learning a patient world model for health system simulation in intensive care
papers.abstract: Designing healthcare strategies requires anticipating their clinical and operational consequences before implementation, a task that often relies on health system simulation. Such a simulation necessitates modeling how patient states evolve and generate care demands. However, conventional approaches typically tailor compact state transitions to a single policy question and omit history-dependent dynamics, thus requiring the redefinition of states and transitions when there is a new question that entails different clinical information. We propose to learn a patient world model from longitudinal EHRs using a neural network to provide a shared clinical representation of patient trajectories that can serve simulation questions across scenarios. Taking ICU operations as an example, we train the model on MIMIC-IV, freeze it, and couple its time-queryable predictions to shared ICU calendars, resources, and queues via scenario-specific mappings, so that one model renders admission demand, care tasks, and discharge proposals across simulations evaluating ICU bed capacity, care dispatch, and post-ICU transfer capacity. Experiments show that our model matches Markov and semi-Markov comparators in aggregate occupancy and directional responses to capacity and dispatch policies. It also reproduces policy gains from replayed observed trajectories. For patients entering the same support state from different prior trajectories, the learned representation captures a 24-h recovery difference (-6.4 predicted versus -6.7 observed percentage points), a contrast missed by compact state models, which propagates into distinct simulated care demand, queue burden, and bed use. These results indicate that a learned world model of patient dynamics has the potential to replace question-specific state models, allowing new care policies to be evaluated by reconfiguring the scenario without model rebuilding.
papers.summary: Health system simulations usually rely on compact patient-state models built for a single policy question, so each new question means rebuilding the model. Instead, the authors train a neural patient world model on longitudinal electronic health records from `MIMIC-IV`, freeze it, and connect its predictions to intensive care unit (ICU) calendars, resources, and queues through scenario-specific mappings. One model then drives simulations of bed capacity, care dispatch, and post-ICU transfer capacity. It matches Markov and semi-Markov baselines on aggregate occupancy, and it also captures a history-dependent **24-hour recovery difference (-6.4 predicted versus -6.7 observed percentage points)** that the compact state models miss.

papers.title: Synthesis of Ovarian Cancer Multi-Omics Datasets: A Biology-Informed Evaluation Framework
papers.abstract: Paired multi-omic cancer cohorts are costly to assemble and difficult to share, motivating synthetic cohorts as a complementary resource. As generative model development accelerates, we shift the focus from proposing yet another architecture to defining evaluation criteria that determine whether synthetic data preserve biologically relevant structure. We introduce a biology-informed and patient-disjoint framework for evaluating the generation of paired RNA expression and copy-number variation (CNV) profiles, and apply it to the longitudinal DECIDER high-grade serous ovarian cancer cohort. The framework assesses modality-specific fidelity and coherence between RNA and CNV pairs using agreement between real training and held-out data as a reference, alongside complementary training-data proximity diagnostics. We adapt three multi-omic integration architectures based on variational autoencoders to generate paired profiles. The model leading several fidelity and coherence measures also shows the strongest training-data proximity. The protocol and case study offer the community a reference for comparing future multi-omic generators.
papers.summary: Rather than proposing a new generator for synthetic cancer cohorts, the authors define how to judge whether synthetic paired multi-omic data keeps biologically relevant structure. Their patient-disjoint framework evaluates generated RNA expression and copy-number variation (CNV) profiles for fidelity within each modality and for coherence between the two. It uses agreement between real training and held-out data as the reference point and adds diagnostics for how close samples sit to the training data. Applied to three variational-autoencoder models on the `DECIDER` ovarian cancer cohort, it shows that **the model leading several fidelity and coherence measures also sits closest to its training data**.

papers.title: StepBack: Step-Level Error-Localized Resampling for Efficient Test-Time Reasoning
papers.abstract: Self-consistency (SC) is a widely used decoding strategy for improving chain-of-thought reasoning, but it requires sampling many complete reasoning trajectories with a preset budget. Its efficient variants reduce the cost mainly by stopping full-trajectory sampling early or distributing the number of samples across questions. In this paper, we propose StepBack, a step-level error-localized resampling method for efficient test-time reasoning. Given a small set of draft trajectories, StepBack localizes likely first error positions using lightweight signals and then resamples the detected error step and its suffix, followed by majority answer voting. Empirically, StepBack matches the accuracy of SC on average across seven mathematical reasoning and multi-hop QA benchmarks, while reducing token usage by up to 41.26%. In addition, by nature, StepBack can be combined with adaptive inference methods such as Adaptive Consistency, further improving their inference-time efficiency.
papers.summary: Self-consistency (SC) improves chain-of-thought reasoning by sampling many complete reasoning paths and taking a majority vote, which uses a lot of tokens. `StepBack` starts from a few draft solutions, uses lightweight signals to find the step where each one most likely first goes wrong, and resamples only from that step onward before voting. Across seven math and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks it matches SC accuracy on average while **cutting token usage by up to 41.26%**. It can also be combined with adaptive methods such as `Adaptive Consistency` for further savings.

papers.title: Social Humanoid: Socially Responsive Human-Humanoid Interaction
papers.abstract: Humanoid robots are typically trained as solitary agents, leaving them unable to coordinate physically with human partners who naturally anticipate and adjust to one another. To bridge this gap, we present Social Humanoid, a hierarchical system that generates and executes socially responsive whole-body motion on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 conditioned on a human partner's motion. Its high-level policy performs flexible sequence modeling of human and humanoid motion through a shared tokenized representation, generating reactive humanoid motion and anticipating the partner's motion when they are occluded, while a low-level whole-body tracking controller executes the generated motion on the robot. To train the system, we introduce a two-phase adaptive retargeting procedure that retargets one interaction partner to the robot while morphing the other partner to preserve contact dynamics, reachability, and relative body scale. We apply this procedure across five motion-capture datasets to produce a new Human-Humanoid Interaction (HHI) benchmark of 260 hours of human-humanoid interactions. Our results demonstrate that Social Humanoid produces coordinated, human-aligned behavior across diverse interaction types in simulation and the real world. Project page: https://von31.github.io/social-humanoid/
papers.summary: Humanoid robots are usually trained to act alone and cannot physically coordinate with a human partner. `Social Humanoid` uses a high-level policy that models human and robot motion as one shared token sequence, generating reactive whole-body motion and predicting the partner's motion when the partner is occluded; a low-level tracking controller then executes that motion on a 29-joint `Unitree G1`. For training, a two-phase retargeting procedure maps one person in recorded interactions onto the robot while preserving contact and relative body scale. Applied to five motion-capture datasets, it yields the **260-hour `Human-Humanoid Interaction (HHI)` benchmark**, and the system produces coordinated behavior in simulation and on real hardware.

papers.title: Conformal Prediction for Time-Dependent PDEs
papers.abstract: Uncertainty quantification is crucial in scientific machine learning, where models inform safety-critical tasks such as flood forecasting, financial risk management, and thermal control in machines. Conformal prediction provides distribution-free coverage guarantees, but in time-dependent settings common to physics and engineering, these guarantees can break down, leading to systematic undercoverage. We study this problem in the context of surrogate models for time-dependent physical systems described by partial differential equations. We prove that in a function space setting, distributions at arbitrarily close times can be mutually singular, making exact coverage guarantees impossible. We further show that in discretized settings, the total variation distance between distributions often saturates exponentially fast with the grid resolution, mandating restrictions on the spatial discretization to ensure coverage. Finally, for certain settings, we show how to use principled weighted conformal prediction to obtain finite-sample coverage guarantees over growing time horizons.
papers.summary: Conformal prediction gives distribution-free uncertainty guarantees, but these guarantees can fail for surrogate models of physical systems that evolve over time under partial differential equations (PDEs). In function space, the authors prove that distributions at arbitrarily close times can be mutually singular, which makes **exact coverage guarantees impossible**. In discretized settings, they show that the total variation distance between distributions often saturates exponentially fast as grid resolution increases, so spatial discretization has to be restricted to keep coverage. For certain settings they derive weighted conformal methods with finite-sample coverage guarantees over growing time horizons.

papers.title: The Gold Rush in AI4Math, II: What are signatures of AI-assisted Proofs?
papers.abstract:
The growing use of AI in mathematics raises a question: can we detect AI involvement in proofs, separately from AI assistance with writing? Historical arXiv papers, recent papers disclosing substantive AI use, and manuscripts released by OpenAI provide a rich empirical basis for studying this question. However, several challenges remain: lack of matched case-control pairs; potential incompleteness of disclosure; and lack of ready-to-use features designed to capture signals of AI involvement in proofs.
  To address these challenges, we construct five cohorts comprising 8,281 papers by combining existing manuscripts with those we produced using generative AI. These cohorts span different levels of AI involvement and include matched pairs of papers addressing the same research problems. We then introduce ProofTrace, a framework that represents each paper as a graph of immediate proof support (GIPS) and extracts interpretable features of mathematical organization.
  Our study yields three discoveries. First, principal-component projections of our features reveal a qualitative gradient of AI involvement, where AI-reworded papers remain close to human papers, the two AI-generated cohorts depart in broadly shared directions, and papers disclosing substantive AI use occupy intermediate positions which shifts toward AI-generated cohorts over time. Second, we identify recurring signatures of AI-generated proofs, such as fewer externally cited results, greater reliance on intermediate conclusions, and altered graph connectivity; many of these signatures persist under controls for research field, manuscript length, or graph size. Finally, in a separate detection experiment, ProofTrace distinguishes human-written papers from those disclosing substantive AI use. Its performance remains stable under AI rewording, whereas the performance of state-of-the-art text-based detectors declines sharply.
papers.summary: The study asks whether AI involvement in mathematical proofs can be detected, as opposed to AI help with wording. The authors assemble five cohorts of 8,281 papers, including matched human and AI-generated pairs that address the same problems. Their `ProofTrace` framework represents each paper as a graph of which results support which, called a graph of immediate proof support (`GIPS`), and extracts interpretable features from it. AI-generated proofs cite fewer external results, rely more on intermediate conclusions, and have different graph connectivity, and **`ProofTrace` stays accurate under AI rewording while text-based detectors drop sharply**.

papers.title: Spectral and Subspace Dynamics of LoRA in Supervised Fine-Tuning and Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is commonly used in both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), often under similar optimizer settings. Yet, how the different dynamics of the two stages manifest in the low-rank increment that LoRA optimizes remains unclear. Tracking the singular spectrum and subspaces of LoRA updates on mathematical reasoning tasks, we find that RL concentrates the spectrum at every learning rate, while SFT expands it at moderate learning rates; moreover, RL rotates the singular subspaces much faster than SFT at small learning rates. Interpolating between SFT and RL one ingredient at a time, we pinpoint group-mean baseline subtraction as the source of both contrasts. A quadratic multi-index model updated via LoRA unveils the underlying mechanism: group-mean baseline subtraction tilts the balance between two competing forces, coherent fitting and gradient noise, toward spectral concentration and faster subspace rotation, while forcing the risk-favorable learning rate to be low. Guided by these dynamics, we tailor LoRA updates to each stage: in SFT, we flatten the spectrum of the full update to spread adaptation across singular directions, whereas in RL, we flatten the part of the update outside the current LoRA increment span to promote subspace rotation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks across multiple models show that the respective configurations for SFT and RL yield the best performance among the compared methods in most evaluated settings.
papers.summary: Low-rank adaptation (`LoRA`) is used for both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), but how the low-rank update behaves differently in the two stages has not been clear. Tracking the singular values and subspaces of `LoRA` updates on math reasoning tasks, the authors find that RL concentrates the spectrum and rotates subspaces faster, while SFT spreads the spectrum. They trace **both contrasts to group-mean baseline subtraction** and explain the mechanism with a quadratic multi-index model. They then tailor the update for each stage, flattening the full update spectrum in SFT and flattening the out-of-span part in RL, which gives the best results in most tested settings.

papers.title: Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks
papers.abstract:
Coding agents are among the most economically consequential deployments of LLMs to date, making reliable evaluation increasingly important. Yet even benchmarks that are carefully validated at release can become stale. As models improve, they can discover valid solutions that existing verifiers reject, while changes to evaluation infrastructure can invalidate assumptions embedded in tasks and tests. We call the resulting accumulation of defects benchmark maintenance debt: a growing gap between benchmark scores and the capabilities they are intended to measure. We introduce a continuous-validation workflow for agentic benchmarks that combines community reports, task artifacts, agent traces, automated oracle checks, and human-gated repairs. We apply this workflow to Terminal-Bench 2.0, a benchmark that underwent extensive human and LM-assisted review and red-teaming before release. Our audit identifies issues in roughly 30% of the benchmark, and we release the resulting repairs as Terminal-Bench 2.1. These repairs change evaluation results: accuracy increased by over 10 percentage points and leaderboard positions move by up to three ranks, even as the overall ranking remains highly correlated (Spearman rho = 0.958).
  We evaluate how resource allocation shapes benchmark conclusions. We show that fixed wall-clock can materially change agent performance: For example, extending the time limit closes a 20pp harness gap on GPT 5.4 and shrinks a 30 pp gap on GPT 5.4 mini to 5 pp. Benchmark maintenance is therefore not only about repairing task artifacts: resource budgets are part of the measurement specification and must be validated alongside the tasks themselves.
  More broadly, benchmark maintenance debt is not just accumulated implementation bugs: our results show that as models improve, both evaluation assumptions and resource settings may need to be revalidated.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for coding agents can go stale after release, as stronger models find valid solutions that verifiers reject and infrastructure changes break the assumptions built into tasks. The authors call this benchmark maintenance debt and propose a continuous-validation workflow that combines community reports, agent traces, automated oracle checks, and human-gated repairs. Applied to `Terminal-Bench 2.0`, it found **issues in roughly 30% of tasks**, and the fixes, released as `Terminal-Bench 2.1`, raised accuracy by over 10 points and moved leaderboard positions by up to three ranks. Wall-clock limits also matter: extending them closed a 20-point harness gap on `GPT 5.4`, so the authors argue resource budgets should be validated as part of the benchmark.

papers.title: On the limitations of molecular representations
papers.abstract: Molecular representations such as fingerprints and learned embeddings play a central role in cheminformatics and small-molecule machine learning. They serve as the primary input for a diverse array of tasks, including clustering, dataset splitting, and virtual screening, yet their evaluation is often limited to downstream model performance on narrow benchmark tasks. We carried out a systematic investigation of the quality of molecular representations, finding that none of the state-of-the-art molecular embedding models capture graph structure, 3D shape, or ADMET endpoint similarity better than fingerprints or physicochemical descriptors. However, classical fingerprints also revealed their own material limitations. For example, we show that depending on the representation, between 225M and $\sim$4B molecules have non-unique representations in the 10.8B Enamine REAL database, with implications for virtual screening. Our findings provide an insight into the current limitations of molecular representations, outlining future research directions for the development of more robust encodings of small molecules.
papers.summary: Molecular representations such as fingerprints and learned embeddings drive clustering, dataset splitting, and virtual screening, yet they are mostly judged by performance on narrow downstream benchmarks. A systematic evaluation finds that **no state-of-the-art molecular embedding model captures graph structure, 3D shape, or ADMET similarity better than classical fingerprints or physicochemical descriptors**. Classical fingerprints have their own flaws: depending on the representation, between 225 million and about 4 billion molecules in the 10.8-billion-molecule `Enamine REAL` database do not get a unique representation, which affects virtual screening.

papers.title: Data-driven discovery of intrinsic Lie point symmetries of differential equation systems
papers.abstract: Discovering continuous symmetries directly from differential-equation data can reveal geometric structure for model reduction and scientific machine learning without symbolic determining equations or a closed-form representation of the governing system. We formulate intrinsic Lie point-symmetry discovery as an operator-theoretic problem on sampled jet-space data. Admissible generators are identified from a sampled determining operator and separated from redundant, solution-dependent, and geometrically trivial directions. The framework combines prolongation, sequential subspace restrictions, and a fixed nonlinear dictionary linear in trainable coefficients. A rank-stabilization preflight test diagnoses systems whose represented intrinsic symmetry algebra does not stabilize under dictionary refinement. On a controlled differential-equation benchmark with an analytically known 11-dimensional represented intrinsic symmetry algebra, the method recovers the complete represented generator set, reproduces its Lie-bracket structure to numerical precision, and approximates a known generator beyond the training domain. Here we show that explicit intrinsic continuous-symmetry generators can be recovered from data obtained from exact or approximate differential systems.
papers.summary: The authors recover continuous Lie point symmetries of differential equation systems directly from data, without symbolic determining equations or a closed-form model. They pose the task as an operator problem on sampled jet-space data, combining prolongation, sequential subspace restrictions, and a fixed nonlinear dictionary with trainable linear coefficients. A preflight test flags systems whose symmetry algebra does not stabilize as the dictionary is refined. On a benchmark with a known 11-dimensional symmetry algebra, the method **recovers the complete generator set and its Lie-bracket structure to numerical precision**.

papers.title: Failure Prediction and Classification in Vision-Language-Action Models Via Calibrated Latent Probing
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable general-purpose embodied intelligence, but their performance is brittle under distribution shift, where unanticipated failures can damage equipment or endanger people. Deploying VLAs in real-world systems therefore requires a runtime monitor that is timely, calibrated, and informative while being efficient enough to run on the edge. Existing methods fail to fulfill these requirements. We present VLA-Tug, a lightweight probe over the latent layers of a VLA backbone that improves early failure detection and bounds the missed-detection and false-alarm rates, with minimal inference overhead. We show that supervising on the pre-failure segment of a trajectory increases early failure detection at matched false-positive rates by up to 30% over the strongest learned baseline. Under shift to unseen tasks, the bounds on missed-detection and false-alarm rates remain valid in up to 86% of runs, versus at most 21% for baselines. Unlike existing methods, VLA-Tug predicts the failure mode to enable corrective actions, raising top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks by up to 44% over a majority baseline. VLA-Tug enables real-time monitoring where the well-timed and informative probe supports lightweight steering that improves task success. We release a dataset of 3,180 annotated manipulation episodes to support future work on latent failure detection in VLAs at https://vla-tug.github.io.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) fail unpredictably under distribution shift, so deployed robots need a fast and calibrated runtime monitor. `VLA-Tug` is a lightweight probe on a VLA backbone's latent layers that detects failures early, bounds missed-detection and false-alarm rates, and predicts the failure mode. Training on the segment of a trajectory just before failure improves early detection by up to 30% at matched false-positive rates, and **the error-rate bounds hold in up to 86% of runs on unseen tasks versus at most 21% for baselines**. The authors release 3,180 annotated manipulation episodes.

papers.title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI
papers.abstract: Chat remains the default surface for many large language model (LLM) tasks, even as agentic tools such as OpenCode excel at coding and automation. Yet the model sees the current dialogue but not the workspace around it. We explore meta access---giving the assistant a structured, permissioned view of the interface itself and propose a ladder of levels: feature tutoring; metadata, settings, and preference access; retrieval over summaries and messages, confirmed mutation, and full orchestration. Meta access can turn a chat client from many screens into one entry point for finding, navigating, organising, and operating it, while raising risks around grounding, privacy, prompt injection, and trust. General-purpose agentic harnesses are runtimes; because they can change their own settings, meta access becomes reflexive and needs a separate control-plane boundary. We ground this in the Meta Chat prototype of the Chat AI client. It builds bounded context from, e.g., summaries, settings, and relevant messages; links references to conversations, topics, and personas; supports confirmed, reversible changes; offers a browsable tutorial library; and recommends personas as user-started conversations. By exposing application state in structured form, meta access can extend screen readers from widget descriptions to semantic workspace operations. Meta access thus turns chat from a window onto one conversation into a control layer for the whole workspace, extending chat toward agentic capability without surrendering user control. As assistants become embedded in IDEs, dashboards, office suites, and operating systems, AI-era interfaces should expose a structured, permissioned model of their state and capabilities, ideally by opening their existing metamodels through a debugger-like interface.
papers.summary: Chat assistants see the current conversation but not the application around it. The authors propose meta access, a structured and permissioned view of the interface itself, organized as a ladder of levels from feature tutoring up to confirmed changes and full orchestration. They argue that agentic harnesses able to change their own settings need a separate control-plane boundary, and they discuss risks around grounding, privacy, prompt injection, and trust. The `Meta Chat` prototype builds bounded context from summaries and settings and supports confirmed, reversible changes, and the authors argue that **AI-era interfaces should expose a structured, permissioned model of their state and capabilities**.

papers.title: MedGraph: Maintaining Patient State with Graph Memory for Long-Term Medical Dialogue
papers.abstract: LLM-based medical assistants that follow a patient across visits need a memory that keeps the patient's clinical state correct as it changes. We examine the errors of five memory systems on longitudinal medical dialogue and find three recurring causes: the retrieved evidence gives an outdated state, includes another person's health facts, or lacks a safety fact the answer depends on. We present MedGraph, a graph memory built for these three cases. Construction extracts dated facts from each session, attributes each fact to the person it describes, and links medication, diagnosis, and measurement records into chains that keep earlier states. Retrieval ranks the patient's chains as units, reads each chain at the time the question asks about, and adds the original dialogue text; a patient profile lists every recorded safety fact with every question. On MedMemoryBench, MedGraph has the highest overall accuracy with both a GPT and a Qwen backbone, 10.5 and 10.4 points above the strongest of five baselines, with efficient memory construction and answering in the GPT setting.
papers.summary: Medical assistants built on large language models (LLMs) that follow a patient across visits need memory that keeps the patient's clinical state current. An error analysis of five memory systems traces failures to outdated states, facts about other people, and missing safety facts. `MedGraph` builds a graph memory of dated facts tied to the person they describe, links medication, diagnosis, and measurement records into chains that keep earlier states, reads each chain at the time the question asks about, and includes every recorded safety fact with each question. On `MedMemoryBench` it scores **10.5 and 10.4 points above the strongest baseline** with GPT and `Qwen` backbones.

papers.title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety
papers.abstract: Neural networks are likely to be among the most consequential artefacts in human history. As these systems become more capable and autonomous, their potential to cause societal harm also grows, making AI safety one of the defining challenges of our time. Yet we continue to build increasingly powerful systems without fully understanding how they work, how they will behave in unfamiliar situations, or how to reliably control them. Mechanistic interpretability offers a path towards understanding these systems by studying their internal representations and computations, with the aim of evaluating, predicting, and controlling behaviour. We survey mechanistic interpretability for AI safety in order to answer the question: Does understanding how models work actually make them safer? We place mechanistic interpretability in the broader context of interpretability research and compare its mechanistic evidence with behavioural evaluation. We introduce the foundations of mechanistic interpretability, including features, polysemanticity, transformer computation, and circuits, and survey methods for feature extraction and analysis, circuit discovery and causal verification, explaining intermediate representations in natural language, learning dynamics, and training-data attribution. Beyond surveying existing methods, we propose a unified framework for evaluating mechanistic interpretability claims and characterise six research orientations by their goals, assumptions, and trade-offs. Finally, we examine how mechanistic understanding can support AI safety, including knowledge editing, steering, and monitoring, and assess its limitations, failure modes, open problems, and relationship to behavioural safety measures. We also release a repository of code notebooks with worked examples that reproduce key findings from surveyed methods, allowing readers to build intuition through hands-on experimentation.
papers.summary: The survey asks whether understanding how neural networks work internally actually makes them safer. It covers the foundations of mechanistic interpretability, including features, polysemanticity, and circuits, and reviews methods for feature extraction, circuit discovery and causal verification, natural-language explanations of internal representations, learning dynamics, and training-data attribution. The authors propose a unified framework for evaluating interpretability claims, describe six research orientations, and assess how interpretability supports editing, steering, and monitoring, along with its limitations. They also **release code notebooks that reproduce key findings** from the surveyed methods.

papers.title: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes
papers.abstract: Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies, produced by three separate processes and checked for overlap with the training data, with five candidates per question and, for eight of them, also with eighteen. On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (English-derived jargon, office slang, department names), the augmented release is more accurate in every setting, by up to 0.24. Eleven of these fourteen gains survive a Holm correction (slang with eighteen candidates and descriptive sentences with five do not), and for jargon on all labels the label-level interval excludes zero in both settings. On abbreviations and opaque codes it gives no usable gain: on abbreviations it is not better, and worse on the clean slice, and on opaque codes both releases stay at or below chance once labels related to training options are removed. In most cells where accuracy rises, the risk-coverage area falls, but with eighteen candidates confident errors rise on jargon and slang. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.
papers.summary: Typed-decision models score answer options that callers supply at request time, so their accuracy depends on how labels are worded. Two releases of `Ru-Jev`, a 307-million-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, are compared, where the later release was trained with labels shown in several surface forms. With the questions held fixed and only the wording of the routing labels varied, the augmented release is **up to 0.24 more accurate on unfamiliar ordinary or borrowed words** such as jargon and slang. It gives no usable gain on abbreviations or opaque codes, where both releases stay at or below chance once labels related to training options are removed.

papers.title: A Hidden Markov Preference Model for Online Prediction of Adversary Actions
papers.abstract: A defender anticipating an attacker needs a probability distribution over the attacker's next action from information available before that action occurs. Two structures complicate this: the attacker's behavioral regime persists and can switch within an episode, and each action combines an operation with state-dependent arguments whose feasible values change over time. We capture both with a hidden Markov model whose latent state is the active regime and whose regime-conditioned action law is defined on a feasibility-masked tree of executable actions. The same likelihood forms the next-action distribution and updates the regime belief once the action is seen, and a partially observed prefix contributes its resolved local factors. Estimation separates into convex logistic fits that Baum-Welch reuses when regimes are unlabeled. We derive a reach-weighted nodewise KL expression for regime information, a sequence-wise log-loss bound for switching regime paths, and a uniform fallback guarantee. On the CAGE 2 cyber defense benchmark the filtered latent state is worth 0.8 nats per step, and after a controller switch the loss begins to fall in three steps against ten for a recurrent baseline.
papers.summary: A cyber defender anticipating an attacker needs a probability distribution over the attacker's next action, even though the attacker's behavior regime can switch partway through an episode. The authors model the regime as the hidden state of a hidden Markov model and define actions over a tree of currently executable operations and arguments. Estimation reduces to convex logistic fits that Baum-Welch reuses when regimes are unlabeled, and the paper derives log-loss bounds and a fallback guarantee. On the `CAGE 2` cyber defense benchmark the filtered regime belief is worth 0.8 nats per step, and after the attacker switches controllers **prediction loss starts falling within three steps versus ten for a recurrent baseline**.

papers.title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts
papers.abstract: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.
papers.summary: Coding agents that reproduce machine learning experiments often have to reconstruct details missing from papers and released code. `ReproBridge` is an agent workflow that packages recovered knowledge into refined artifacts: a cleaned codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide. On `ReproBridge-Bench`, with 1,029 tasks from 36 papers and a separate auditor agent checking execution evidence, refined artifacts **raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6%** and cut API spending by 19.7% across four models. The success-rate spread between models narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 points, and code and environment setup matter most in ablations.

papers.title: Unpacking the Compute Efficiency of Strong-to-Weak OPD against GRPO
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher's per-token supervision. Does this dense signal reduce the training FLOPs needed to reach a target accuracy compared with reinforcement learning? We systematically compare vanilla reverse-KL OPD with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) across task difficulty, student and teacher size, domain, and optimization choices, measuring held-out accuracy against training FLOPs. With an external post-trained teacher, OPD generally loses to GRPO in accuracy per training FLOP at matched settings, even when the teacher is further trained with GRPO, and often suffers response-length inflation. Yet a different teacher changes the picture: when the teacher is the student's own GRPO checkpoint, OPD recovers that checkpoint's accuracy on math with $50\times$ fewer distillation FLOPs than GRPO needs to reach the same accuracy. Following the same teacher setting, we consistently observe this high efficiency with a larger student, on code, and in a second model family. On a single domain, however, the GRPO checkpoint is already the desired model, so distilling it adds to total compute. Across domains, separate GRPO checkpoints hold different capabilities, and no single checkpoint serves every domain. Multi-teacher OPD (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) consolidates per-domain GRPO experts into a single student that matches each expert's accuracy, with the distillation stage costing only 5.2% (on 2 domains) and 8.0% (on 4 domains) of the specialist training FLOPs. Counting specialist training and distillation together, this pipeline reaches joint GRPO's performance on the 2-domain mix with 42.0% fewer total FLOPs.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own outputs with token-level supervision from a frozen teacher. The authors test whether this denser signal saves training compute compared with `GRPO` (Group Relative Policy Optimization), a reinforcement learning method. With an external post-trained teacher, OPD generally loses to `GRPO` in accuracy per training FLOP and often inflates response length. When the teacher is the student's own `GRPO` checkpoint, however, **OPD recovers that checkpoint's accuracy with 50 times fewer FLOPs**, and multi-teacher OPD that merges per-domain `GRPO` experts matches joint `GRPO` on a two-domain mix with 42.0% less total compute.

papers.title: Adversarial Training with Large Step Sizes: Implicit Bias, Optimization, and Sharpness
papers.abstract: Adversarial Training (AT) is an important method for improving model robustness. We study the dynamics of deterministic Gradient Descent (GD) in AT. Most existing works in this direction focus on the small or vanishing step sizes regime, where GD resembles a continuous-time flow. However, such step sizes can make training inefficient and are rarely used in practice. In this paper, we study the AT dynamics of GD with large constant step sizes. We first study GD in adversarial linear logistic regression, focusing on two aspects: where the model parameters converge (implicit bias) and how quickly the losses decrease (optimization). We then turn to neural networks training and study how the sharpness of losses evolve during AT.
