Our results advance the understanding of the behaviors of GD with large step sizes in AT and highlight three key differences from its behavior in Standard Training (ST): (i) the implicit bias gap between AT and ST, previously established only for small step sizes, persists for arbitrarily large constant step sizes, (ii) different from ST, there is no uniform rate of convergence for the optimization error in AT, and (iii) sharpness can exhibit two-stage dynamics that differ from the Edge-of-Stability behavior observed in ST.
papers.summary: Most theoretical analyses of adversarial training (AT), a standard way to make models more robust, assume small or vanishing step sizes that are rarely used in practice. The authors study deterministic gradient descent (GD) with large constant step sizes, first in adversarial linear logistic regression, where they analyze where parameters converge (implicit bias) and how quickly losses fall, and then in neural network training, where they track how loss sharpness evolves. They identify three differences from standard training (ST): **the implicit bias gap between AT and ST persists for arbitrarily large constant step sizes**, AT has no uniform convergence rate for the optimization error, and sharpness can follow two-stage dynamics that differ from the Edge-of-Stability behavior seen in ST.

papers.title: Towards interpreting any residual stream direction by scaling activation inversion
papers.abstract: To interpret a direction in a language model's residual stream, we can look for text that strongly activates it. But when such text is found by scanning a corpus, it is limited to what that corpus contains. We develop Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels (MAEMs), language models which map residual stream directions from a subject model to text exemplars that strongly activate those directions. Our objective is to maximise the cosine similarity of a supplied residual stream direction with the activations of the text generated by the MAEM. This label-free RL objective helps to scale MAEMs on diverse sources of residual stream directions. Empirically, we find the resultant metamodel produces informative exemplars: a Qwen3.6-27B MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus search or a natural-language autoencoder (NLA), beats corpus search (at 10M tokens) on a majority of held-out languages/domains, and activates 89% of held-out SAE features. It also identifies concepts behind steering vectors about as well as NLAs, recovers the payloads of LoRA backdoors more often than corpus search, and can even verbalise some model workspace inner monologue. Unlike explanations produced by other metamodels (e.g. NLAs), MAEM exemplars can be verified with a forward pass on the subject model, making the MAEM objective a grounded alternative for scaling the training of metamodels.
papers.summary: Interpreting a direction in a language model's residual stream usually means finding text that strongly activates it, but scanning a corpus can only find what that corpus contains. The authors train Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels (`MAEM`s), language models that take a residual stream direction and generate text exemplars that activate it. Training uses a label-free reinforcement learning objective that maximizes the cosine similarity between the target direction and the activations of the generated text. A `Qwen3.6-27B` MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus search or a natural-language autoencoder (`NLA`) and **activates 89% of held-out sparse autoencoder (SAE) features**; it also recovers LoRA backdoor payloads more often than corpus search, and every exemplar can be checked with a single forward pass on the subject model.

papers.title: Same Behavior, Different Mechanism: What Finite Experiments Can Certify About Integrated Information
papers.abstract: Interpretability, AI auditing and assessments of machine consciousness increasingly rest on mechanism-level quantities: functionals of a system's causal transition law that describe how it computes, not what it outputs. Experiments see that law only through finite, partial and noisy interventions. We ask when such a quantity is identifiable from an experiment's access, continuous in the mechanism and certifiable from finite data, and answer exactly for a deliberately demanding case - the integrated information $\varphi$ of integrated information theory - in stochastic networks of four and five units with known ground truth. Behavior can be silent: a recurrent and a feed-forward network with identical input-output laws at their response delay carry 0.28 and 0 bits, yet internal recordings separate them within 4-53 trials. Partial access can be just as blind: in our examples, units left out of a one-step recording impose precision floors of 0.30-1.02 bits that no sample size lowers, and in all-but-self parity networks, recordings of any length see several hidden units only through the product of their fidelities - a symmetry that one intervention broke in exact checks. The measure has sharp edges: because $\varphi$ selects a partition, and the cause and effect it specifies, by one criterion and reports another, infinitesimal changes of mechanism that cross an edge change it by 25-100% at 99% of the edges we found in random networks, and about 1% of surrogate models that fit interventional data almost perfectly misreport it by more than 20%. One-sided claims survive: the same data certify a lower bound on both sides of an edge, and we prove $\varphi>1.004$ bits throughout a 64-dimensional region of mechanisms and certify it from about $10^7$ controlled transitions with false-certificate probability at most $\alpha$. Measurability is thus a design question with computable answers.
papers.summary: Interpretability, AI auditing, and machine-consciousness assessments increasingly depend on mechanism-level quantities, yet experiments observe a system's causal mechanism only through finite, partial, and noisy interventions. Using the integrated information `φ` from integrated information theory as a demanding test case, the authors work out exactly when such a quantity can be identified and certified in small stochastic networks with known ground truth. A recurrent network and a feed-forward network with identical input-output behavior carry 0.28 and 0 bits respectively, and leaving units out of the recording imposes precision floors that no sample size removes. Because `φ` is discontinuous, tiny changes in mechanism can shift it by 25-100%, but **one-sided lower bounds remain certifiable**: the authors prove `φ` > 1.004 bits across a 64-dimensional region of mechanisms and certify it from about 10^7 controlled transitions.

papers.title: XStack: A Benchmark for ML Repo Migration
papers.abstract: ML code should run where researchers choose, not where it was first written. Today, machine learning code mainly lives in two ecosystems, PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs and JAX on Google TPUs. Migrating repositories between them means building and testing across frameworks and hardware. This migration is (1) a practical need, since it unlocks different hardware for researchers, and (2) a natural benchmark: it involves different frameworks and hardware, covers whole repositories, and is long-horizon and challenging. We introduce XStack, a benchmark that evaluates agents on migrating ML repositories between these two ecosystems. Each agent receives a PyTorch repository and a clean TPU machine and must deliver a JAX repository. Its output passes if it meets our grading criteria, based on the source repository's published result, authenticated and calibrated by us. Migration by agents remains unreliable: Claude Opus 5 passes 75%, GPT-5.6-sol 45%, and every other agent at most 40%. XStack is a step toward freeing ML code from its ecosystem. We release XStack to make progress toward reliable migration across frameworks and hardware measurable.
papers.summary: Machine learning code mostly lives in two ecosystems, PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs and JAX on Google TPUs, and moving a repository between them requires building and testing across both frameworks and hardware. `XStack` is a benchmark in which an agent receives a PyTorch repository and a clean TPU machine and must deliver a working JAX repository, graded against the source repository's published results after the authors authenticate and calibrate them. Repository-scale migration remains unreliable: **`Claude Opus 5` passes 75% of tasks**, `GPT-5.6-sol` passes 45%, and every other agent tested passes at most 40%.

papers.title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists
papers.abstract: AI-Scientists arrived, but a world for them to grow in did not. Human scientists take theirs for granted $-$ centuries of open problems and shared ideas, waiting in the scientific literature. To AI-Scientists, that world is readable but not runnable, so we build Scientist World for them: every research paper becomes an executable environment. Our autonomous pipeline extracts each paper's open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved. We release the first 1,000 verified environments. With the world as an evaluation, we found that frontier AI-Scientists can already surpass the human researchers 74% of the time. As a record of how AI does science, it contains 6,400 hours of research traces, with every idea, experiment, failure, and success. As a training ground, we are able to raise (+158%) a small model to match frontier models in research ideation. At last, AI-Scientists' own world has arrived, grown from and growing with science itself.
papers.summary: `Scientist World` turns research papers into executable environments for AI scientist agents: an autonomous pipeline extracts each paper's open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as a baseline, so an agent can be scored against what the human authors achieved. The first release contains 1,000 verified environments and 6,400 hours of research traces recording ideas, experiments, failures, and successes. The authors report that **frontier AI scientist agents beat the human researchers' results 74% of the time**, and that training on the environments improves a small model's research ideation by 158%, bringing it level with frontier models.

papers.title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
papers.abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.
papers.summary: LLM-guided evolutionary search improves programs for mathematical and computational problems, but it is slow because each round generates long textual chains of thought, many times over, to keep the population diverse. `SwarmEvolve` instead runs hundreds of low-cost agents per round in swarms that reason in latent space without decoding to text and share information by passing KV caches. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct ideas by measuring distances between agents' hidden states, and a summarizer agent combines ideas by reading the merged KV caches of a swarm. Across 21 mathematical discovery and scientific computing problems it achieves the highest average score and **reaches in a median of 3-8 minutes the best scores other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes**; on several problems, `SwarmEvolve` running `Qwen3 8B` improves on solutions first found by `AlphaEvolve` with frontier LLMs.

papers.title: User Embeddings are Superpositions of Interpretable Behavioral Modes
papers.abstract: User embeddings are central components of modern recommendation, personalization, and behavioral modeling systems. Though these embeddings can compactly encode rich behavioral information, they are inherently dense and opaque, limiting interpretability. To address this gap, we argue that user embeddings can be understood as sparse superpositions of interpretable behavioral modes. This structure is directly predicted by generative models of user behavior for linear embeddings and extends approximately to deep-learning representations by the superposition hypothesis. Superimposed modes can naturally be recovered by sparse dictionary learning methods, such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and recovered modes can be automatically named and queried in natural language. We validate mode recovery against known ground truth on synthetic data, where SAEs recover modes better than classical sparse baselines, including on transformer-encoded embeddings. We then apply the method to classical and transformer-based user embeddings from two real-world datasets. We also show how the corresponding natural-language labels enable zero-shot audience retrieval and characterization over embeddings never trained on text. The framework is post-hoc and model-agnostic, requiring no modification to the upstream embedding system.
papers.summary: User embeddings in recommendation and personalization systems are dense and hard to interpret. The authors argue that these embeddings are sparse superpositions of interpretable behavioral modes, a structure that generative models of user behavior predict for linear embeddings and that the superposition hypothesis extends approximately to deep representations. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) recover these modes, which can then be named and queried automatically in natural language. On synthetic data with known ground truth, **SAEs recover modes better than classical sparse baselines**, including for transformer-encoded embeddings; on two real-world datasets the resulting labels enable zero-shot audience retrieval over embeddings never trained on text, without modifying the upstream embedding system.
